pdf_filename: 3D environments with games characteristics for teaching history The VRLerna case study.pdf

bibliographic.title: 3D Environments with Games Characteristics for Teaching History: The VRLerna Case Study
bibliographic.venue: Proceedings of the 29th ACM International Conference on Design of Communication (SIGDOC '11)

study_characteristics.sample_description: 17 students aged 14-15 years old (8 girls, 9 boys) from a 3rd high school grade class (Key Stage 5, 16-18 years old designation) in a small town in central Greece. The class was chosen because students had been previously involved in activities related to the Early Helladic Period.
study_characteristics.study_design: quasi_experimental
study_characteristics.aim: To present a theoretical educational framework for the use of interactive 3D virtual environments with game characteristics that aims at initiating motivation and enhancement of learning for history education, and to evaluate this framework through the VRLerna prototype application.

eligibility.concerns: Very small sample size (N=17) from a single class. The study uses a pre-post test design without a control group.

rq1.conceptualization: The study conceptualizes gamification as the integration of video game characteristics into 3D virtual environments for educational purposes. The authors identify specific game elements (fantasy, curiosity/mystery, rules/goals, control, interaction, realism, and game environment) that should be embedded within a constructivist educational framework to initiate motivation and enhance learning. They frame this as creating '3D VEs that reflect the main characteristics of video games' rather than using the term 'gamification' explicitly. The approach combines VR technology with game design elements within a pedagogical framework grounded in constructivist learning theory and experiential/discovery learning methods.
theoretical_frameworks: Malone and Lepper's taxonomy of intrinsic motivations for learning

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Pre-test and post-test comparison using multiple choice knowledge questions (7 questions on educational content). Mean correct answers measured before and after interaction with VRLerna. Post-test also included 19 questions (16 closed, 3 open) assessing motivation, imagination, mystery/curiosity, interest, entertainment, and understanding of educational content.
rq2.statistical_results: Mean correct answers rose from 7.57 (pre-test) to 13.43 (post-test). Wilcoxon signed-rank test showed the improvement was statistically significant (Z=-2.226, p=0.026). Motivation results: 64% found the experience very or extremely interesting; 53% found it very or extremely entertaining; 35% reported the environment contributed much or very much to triggering imagination; 47% reported the game created a mysterious atmosphere generating curiosity; 59% considered VRLerna contributed much or very much to understanding the educational content; 64% considered the 3D object rotation feature contributed much or very much to careful observation of archaeological finds.
rq2.comparative_methodology: Within-subjects pre-post test design without a control group. Students completed a pre-test after a 25-minute lecture, then interacted with VRLerna for 45 minutes, followed by a post-test. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test was used due to the small sample size and concerns about normality.
rq2.key_outcomes: Statistically significant improvement in learning performance after using VRLerna. The application succeeded in attracting student interest (64% found it very/extremely interesting) and providing entertainment (53% found it very/extremely entertaining). The majority of students (59%) felt VRLerna contributed to understanding the prehistoric period in Greece.
rq2.engagement_results: 64% of students found the experience very or extremely interesting; 53% found it very or extremely entertaining; 35% reported the environment triggered their imagination much or very much (though 48% said 'a little' and 18% said 'not at all'); 47% reported the game created a mysterious atmosphere generating curiosity.

game_design_elements: Fantasy/imagination (reconstruction of ancient archaeological site)
Curiosity/mystery (exploration of unfamiliar spaces, quest for archaeological finds)
Rules and goals (clear game objectives presented at start, level-based progression)
Control (user-driven navigation and object interaction)
Interaction (navigation, choosing and manipulating 3D objects, rotating artifacts)
Realism (3D geometrical models, textures, lighting)
Levels (8 levels: 1 house yard, 6 basement rooms, 1 floor)
Quiz/knowledge assessment (quiz at end of each level with increasing difficulty)
Feedback (performance feedback after quiz answers, instructions during exploration)
Challenge (increasing difficulty of quiz questions across levels)
technological_platforms: VRML (Virtual Reality Modelling Language) for VE interactions
Adobe Flash for informative material presentation
HTML, PHP, MySQL for unified interactive environment
Web browser-based (Mozilla Firefox 2.0+, Internet Explorer 5.5+, Netscape Navigator 6.0+)
instructional_strategies: Constructivist learning theory (learner-centered, active knowledge construction)
Experiential learning (learning through exploration and interaction with the VE)
Discovery learning (learners discover archaeological finds and construct knowledge)
Pre-instruction lecture followed by interactive application use
Multimedia pre-briefing on historical period before VE exploration
Progressive knowledge assessment quizzes between levels
Scaffolded instructions provided by the system during exploration
rq3.content_integration: History content is integrated through a 3D reconstruction of the 'House of Tiles' at Lerna, an archaeological site from the Early Helladic Period (3000-2000 BC). Learners explore rooms of the reconstructed building, discovering 3D reconstructions of actual archaeological finds from the Lerna excavations. Each artifact can be selected, viewed in a separate window, rotated and examined closely. The game levels correspond to different physical areas of the building (yard, basement rooms, floor). Historical information is provided through multimedia presentations at the start, and knowledge about the period is gained through exploration and interaction with artifacts rather than through narrative descriptions. The content covers aspects of ancient Greek history not typically covered in the ordinary curriculum, specifically the Early Helladic Period social and economic developments.

implementation_barriers: Technical problems during student interaction requiring researcher intervention
Hardware requirements (minimum 2GHz processor, 1GB RAM, 1024x768 screen)
Software dependencies (VRML viewer plugin, Flash plugin, specific browser versions)
Students shared PCs in pairs due to limited computer availability
Time-consuming 3D reconstruction process requiring thorough archaeological bibliography study
methodology_limitations: Very small sample size (N=17) from a single class
No control group for comparison
Pre-post test design without random assignment
Sample determined by class size, not statistical power analysis
Imagination and mystery are subjective and difficult to measure objectively, as acknowledged by the authors
Students worked in pairs sharing PCs, which may confound individual learning measurement
Single school in a small town limits generalizability
negative_effects: 48% of students reported the environment triggered their imagination only 'a little' and 18% 'not at all'
Graphics realism was insufficient compared to popular commercial video games, as noted in conclusions
mitigation_strategies: Authors recommend improving realism (graphics, textures, sound and lighting) to approach commercial video game quality
Authors recommend including further activities that trigger learners' imagination
Authors recommend isolating and studying secondary motivation factors (mystery, imagination) separately
An experimental 3D VE was provided for familiarization before using VRLerna
Students received a 25-minute lecture and multimedia application before the VE interaction

domain1.q1_evidence: The class was selected based on convenience: 'The particular class has been chosen based on the fact that in the past they have been involved in activities related to Early Helladic Period.' The sample of 17 students was 'determined by the number of the students in the 3rd grade class' rather than by any systematic selection criteria or power analysis.
domain1.q2_evidence: The sample consists of only 17 students from a single 3rd grade class in 'a small town in central Greece.' This is a convenience sample from one school, with no discussion of how representative it is of the broader secondary education population. Prior involvement with Early Helladic Period activities may make this group atypical.

domain2.q3_evidence: The pre-test comprised 'ten closed statistical questions' (7 on educational content, 3 on computer attitudes/experience). The post-test had two parts: 7 multiple choice questions on learning outcomes and 19 questions (16 closed, 3 open) on motivation. However, no information is provided about the validation of these instruments, their reliability, or whether they were piloted before use.
domain2.q4_evidence: The authors used the Wilcoxon signed-rank test for pre-post comparison, which they justify as 'suitable when the sample is small and there are serious doubts about the regularity of the population.' This is an appropriate non-parametric test for their paired, small-sample design. Results are reported with Z-statistic and p-value (Z=-2.226, p=0.026).

domain3.q5_evidence: The authors interpret the statistically significant pre-post improvement as evidence that 'the pilot application contributed in a significant degree in improving the learning efficiency of the students.' However, without a control group, this improvement cannot be attributed solely to VRLerna, as the preceding 25-minute lecture and multimedia application could also have contributed. The authors do not discuss this confound.
domain3.q6_evidence: The conclusions acknowledge that 'failings and weaknesses have been noted' regarding realism and imagination triggering, and recommend improvements. However, the paper does not discuss key methodological limitations such as the absence of a control group, the small sample size limiting generalizability, the confound of the pre-instruction lecture, or the potential bias from students working in pairs.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study has high overall risk of bias due to: (1) a very small convenience sample (N=17) from a single class in one school with no systematic selection criteria; (2) no control group, making it impossible to attribute learning gains specifically to VRLerna versus the preceding lecture and multimedia application; (3) no validation information for the measurement instruments; (4) students working in pairs potentially confounding individual assessment; and (5) limited discussion of methodological limitations. While the statistical analysis method is appropriate for the design, the fundamental design weaknesses (no control, convenience sampling, confounded intervention) significantly limit the strength of causal claims.

pdf_filename: Application of Virtual Reality and Gamification in the Teaching of Art History.pdf

bibliographic.title: Application of Virtual Reality and Gamification in the Teaching of Art History
bibliographic.venue: HCI International 2019 (HCII 2019), Learning and Collaboration Technologies (LNCS 11591)

study_characteristics.sample_description: 15 higher education students (ages 17-22, 60% male, 40% female) studying Painting at the top-level, at Universidad Nacional de San Agustin de Arequipa; all had prior gaming experience with virtual reality and other types
study_characteristics.study_design: Single-group post-test only (user elicitation study with questionnaire-based evaluation)
study_characteristics.game_type: Virtual reality educational game (virtual museum with gamification elements)
study_characteristics.game_name: Virtual museum VLE (unnamed prototype built in Unity3D)
study_characteristics.aim: To implement a virtual reality game using gamification elements to improve the teaching of Art History by simulating a virtual museum with predefined stages exposing works from different artistic currents

eligibility.concerns: The study focuses on Art History rather than general history education; the gamification elements are not deeply specified beyond scoring and stage progression; the study uses a very small sample (n=15) with no control group and only post-test measures

rq1.conceptualization: Gamification is implicitly conceptualized as the use of video game elements (scores, stages, interactive challenges) applied to a virtual learning environment to enhance educational engagement and motivation. The paper mentions 'gamification by elements of video games' and references 'principles of gamification' from prior literature but does not provide a formal definition.
theoretical_frameworks: No explicit theoretical framework cited; references prior work on gamification principles for collaborative learning in engineering education (Gasca-Hurtado et al. 2015)

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Two questionnaires evaluated: (1) Usability of Virtual Reality (11 criteria, Likert-type scale, means ranging from 3.47 to 4.20 on a 5-point scale), (2) Virtual Learning Environment (11 criteria, means ranging from 1.67 to 2.27 on what appears to be a lower scale). Cronbach's Alpha = 0.753 for the instrument. Coefficient of Variation computed for all criteria. Correlation matrices computed for both instruments.
rq2.statistical_results: Cronbach's Alpha = 0.753 (acceptable internal consistency). VR Usability: highest mean scores for Application ease of use (4.20) and Realism (4.13); lowest for Organization (3.47). CV for VR usability ranged from 0.099 to 0.192 (good, under 20%). VLE evaluation: highest mean for Easy manipulation (2.27) and Learning (2.13); lowest for Utility (1.67). CV for VLE ranged from 0.12 to 0.43. Strongest correlations in VR usability: Task-Navigation (0.715), Navigation-Movement (0.717). No significant correlations found in VLE evaluation.
rq2.key_outcomes: Students achieved good interaction with the application; the VR usability was rated positively with means mostly above 3.5 on a 5-point scale; the application improved learning in Art History and motivated students; strong correlations found between task completion, navigation, and movement in VR usability; no single dominant variable in VLE evaluation
rq2.engagement_results: Students reported positive interaction with the virtual museum; motivation in learning scored a mean of 1.87 (on VLE scale); satisfaction scored 2.07; sense of belonging in the virtual environment scored 1.93; intention to use the application scored 1.93. The authors concluded the application achieved 'more active learning'.

game_design_elements: Scores/points (displayed at end of tour through chambers)
Predefined stages/levels (5 rooms representing different artistic currents)
Exploration and navigation through virtual museum chambers
Interactive objects (paintings, sculptures, characters, animations, sounds)
Progress tracking through room completion
technological_platforms: Desktop PC (computer-based VR, not head-mounted display)
instructional_strategies: Virtual museum simulation with thematic rooms (Surrealism, Impressionism, Symbolism, Abstract art, Sculptures)
Self-paced exploration of artistic currents and their representative works
Interactive simulation allowing students to interact with objects, characters, animations, and sounds
Brief pre-experiment training on application characteristics and interaction possibilities
rq3.content_integration: Art History content was integrated through 5 themed museum rooms: 4 rooms for painting movements (Surrealism, Impressionism, Symbolism, Abstract art) each containing 4 paintings with their main representations, and a 5th room exposing representative sculptures from different authors. Each room provided contextual information about the artistic current and its works.

implementation_barriers: Small sample size (only 15 students) limiting generalizability
Students presented certain difficulties during interaction, though these were overcome
Application limited to desktop PC VR (no head-mounted display integration)
methodology_limitations: No control group or pre-test/post-test design
Very small sample (n=15) with no power analysis
No standardized learning assessment; only usability and perception questionnaires
VLE evaluation scale appears to use a different (smaller) scale than VR usability, but this is not clearly documented
No significant correlations found in the VLE evaluation, suggesting weak relationships between measured variables
Coefficient of variation for some VLE criteria exceeded 40% (Utility: 0.43, Ease: 0.41), indicating high variability in responses
negative_effects: Some disadvantages noted in the application (not specified in detail by authors)
Students presented certain difficulties during initial interaction with the application
mitigation_strategies: Brief pre-experiment training provided to students on application characteristics and interaction possibilities
Future work proposed to add new rooms with current artists and integrate augmented reality technology to improve interaction

domain1.q1_evidence: No clear inclusion/exclusion criteria for participant selection. The study states 15 students from a Painting program participated but does not explain how they were selected or recruited. Convenience sampling is implied.
domain1.q2_evidence: Sample of only 15 art students from a single university in Peru (Universidad Nacional de San Agustin de Arequipa). Very limited demographic diversity (ages 17-22, single institution, single discipline). Not representative of broader higher education populations.

domain2.q3_evidence: Two questionnaires were used but their validation is not clearly established. The authors cite prior works for the questionnaire design but do not report on the questionnaires' psychometric properties beyond Cronbach's Alpha (0.753). The VLE evaluation appears to use a different scale than VR usability, but this is not documented. No standardized learning outcome measures were used.
domain2.q4_evidence: Only descriptive statistics (means, standard deviations, coefficient of variation) and correlation matrices were computed. No inferential statistics, no hypothesis testing, no effect sizes reported. No pre-test/post-test comparison. The claim of 'improved learning' is not supported by comparative data. The coefficient of variation analysis is basic and the interpretation is simplistic.

domain3.q5_evidence: The conclusions claim the application 'improved the learning' and achieved 'more active learning' but these claims are not supported by the data presented (no learning assessment, no comparison group, no pre/post measures). The paper overstates findings from descriptive usability data.
domain3.q6_evidence: No explicit limitations section is provided. The conclusions briefly mention 'certain difficulties' and 'some disadvantages' but do not discuss methodological limitations such as the lack of a control group, small sample size, or absence of learning outcome measures.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study has high risk of bias across all domains. It uses a very small convenience sample (n=15) with no control group and no pre-test/post-test design. There are no standardized learning assessments, only perception questionnaires. The statistical analysis is limited to descriptive statistics and correlations with no inferential testing. The conclusions overstate the findings by claiming learning improvement without supporting comparative evidence. Methodological limitations are not discussed.

pdf_filename: Are Pairs More Attentive Towards Feedback Than Individuals A Glance Into Feedback Neglect for Middle-School Students Using an Educational Game in History.pdf

bibliographic.title: Are Pairs More Attentive Towards Feedback Than Individuals? A Glance Into Feedback Neglect for Middle-School Students Using an Educational Game in History
bibliographic.venue: CSCL 2023 Proceedings (International Society of the Learning Sciences)

study_characteristics.sample_description: 106 middle-school students (44 boys, 62 girls) from 6 classes in 5th and 6th grade (10-12-year-olds) in southern Sweden who met the inclusion criterion of receiving at least one CCF in both sessions. Originally 209 students were recruited. Teachers rated students' achievement levels (higher, medium, lower) based on reading comprehension.
study_characteristics.study_design: Quasi-experimental within-subjects repeated measures design with two conditions (individual play vs. pair play on a shared tablet)
study_characteristics.game_type: Educational history game (drill-and-practice with narrative elements, concept maps, timelines, multiple-choice questions)
study_characteristics.game_name: Not explicitly named; described as an educational game in history used in prior research (Silvervarg et al., 2020; Ternblad & Tärning, 2020; Tärning et al., 2020)
study_characteristics.aim: To investigate whether middle-school students playing an educational history game in pairs attend to critical constructive feedback (CCF) more frequently than when playing individually, whether this behavior is affected by severe and/or repeated failing, and whether feedback behavior differs between higher- and lower-achieving students.

eligibility.concerns: The study focuses on feedback neglect behavior in a history educational game context rather than on history learning outcomes directly. Gamification elements (feedback systems, game-based tasks, progression mechanics) are present but the primary focus is on collaborative learning and feedback engagement rather than gamification per se.

rq1.conceptualization: The study does not explicitly define gamification. It uses an educational game in history as the learning environment, featuring game elements such as time travel narrative, task-based progression, feedback systems (task assessment and critical constructive feedback), concept maps, timelines, and multiple-choice questions. The focus is on critical constructive feedback (CCF) within the game context rather than on defining gamification itself.
theoretical_frameworks: Productive agency in collaborative learning (Schwartz & Lin, 2000)

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Binary measure of feedback attendance (CCFatt): whether students kept CCF messages displayed on screen for more than 4.25 seconds (attended) or dismissed them earlier (ignored). Logistic mixed-effects regression model with repeated measures was used. Model fit: C-value = 0.79, Somers Dxy = 0.58. Likelihood ratio test: chi-squared(10) = 77.11, p < .001.
rq2.statistical_results: PlayCnd[Pair]: coefficient = -1.20, OR = 0.30, p < .05. AchLev[MediumLower]: coefficient = -0.79, OR = 0.45, p = 0.07. Nr (trial number): coefficient = -0.38, OR = 0.68, p < .01. TaC[QuiteWrong]: coefficient = -0.89, OR = 0.41, p < .001. TaC[VeryWrong]: coefficient = -1.47, OR = 0.23, p < .001. Interaction AchLev[MediumLower]:PlayCnd[Pair]: coefficient = 1.64, OR = 5.16, p < .01. Nr:PlayCnd[Pair]: coefficient = 0.37, OR = 1.45, p < .05. Three-way interaction Nr:AchLev[MediumLower]:PlayCnd[Pair]: coefficient = -0.45, OR = 0.64, p < .05.
rq2.comparative_methodology: Within-subjects design comparing individual play vs. pair play on the same tablet. Students played in both conditions across two sessions (35-40 min each). Order was counterbalanced (single-to-pair vs. pair-to-single) randomly assigned to each class. Students were matched into homogeneous pairs by achievement level.
rq2.key_outcomes: Medium/lower-achieving students were more attentive towards feedback when working in pairs compared to working individually. Higher-achieving students were more inclined to attend to feedback when playing individually than in pairs. However, higher-achieving students playing in pairs were more resilient to repeated failing, maintaining consistent attention to CCF across multiple trials. The probability of attending to CCF decreased with more errors on a task (Quite Wrong and Very Wrong categories) and with repeated failures on the same task.
rq2.engagement_results: Students tended to dismiss CCF to a larger extent after several attempts on the same task. Higher-achieving students playing in pairs were less sensitive to this decline from repeated failing, suggesting collaborative settings may buffer higher-achievers against frustration-driven feedback neglect. A teachable agent was noted to have a stronger impact on feedback acceptance than pair play in comparison to earlier studies.

game_design_elements: Critical constructive feedback (CCF) messages with error-specific hints
Two-part feedback system (general task assessment + specific CCF)
Graded assessment categories (Passed, Almost Correct, Quite Correct, Quite Wrong, Very Wrong)
Time travel narrative through history of science
Task-based progression (concept maps, timelines, multiple-choice questions)
Information gathering from historical scientists
Sequential task completion requirement
technological_platforms: Tablet-based educational game (shared tablet for pair condition)
instructional_strategies: Collaborative learning via pair play on shared tablet
Homogeneous pairing by achievement level
Within-subjects crossover design (individual and pair sessions)
Critical constructive feedback with actionable hints
Graduated difficulty levels across tasks
Teacher-supported but non-interventionist classroom implementation
rq3.content_integration: The game integrates history of science content featuring historical scientists including Copernicus, Galilei, Newton, Châtelet, and Gutenberg. Students travel through time, visit historical scientists, search for information in books and conversations with characters, and solve tasks related to each scientist's inventions and contributions. Tasks involve concept maps, timelines, and multiple-choice questions about historical content.

implementation_barriers: COVID-19 pandemic required remote coordination with teachers, preventing classroom visits for data collection
Game not specifically designed for collaborative use, limiting pair interaction design
Large number of students excluded from analysis due to incomplete participation or lack of CCF messages (209 recruited, 106 analyzed)
Some pairs were reorganized on site making them difficult to track
Remote implementation made it impossible to record student conversations or human-to-human interactions
methodology_limitations: Feedback display time on screen used as proxy for 'attending to feedback' may not accurately reflect genuine engagement with feedback content
Assumption that pair behavior derived from both students democratically may not hold true in all cases
Cannot distinguish whether data logs from pairs originated from one or both students
No qualitative data (observations, interviews, recordings) to complement quantitative log analysis
Interpreting attention towards feedback in pairs as collaborative behavior supporting learning is not clear-cut
Working in pairs may automatically slow all interaction down due to negotiations and practicalities (e.g., competing over the screen), not necessarily indicating deeper engagement
Unequal group sizes between conditions (37 single-first vs. 69 pair-first)
negative_effects: Higher-achieving students were less inclined to attend to feedback when playing in pairs compared to individually
Repeated failing on tasks led to increased feedback neglect across conditions
More severe errors (Quite Wrong, Very Wrong categories) led to lower probability of attending to feedback
mitigation_strategies: Introduced threshold of maximum 6 trials per task per student to exclude excessive repeated failing data
Merged medium and lower achievement categories to address small sample sizes
Used within-subjects design to control for individual differences
Counterbalanced session order to avoid order effects
Homogeneous pairing to ensure equal contribution from both pair members
Authors suggest future studies should complement log data with observations/recordings of pair interactions
Authors suggest students could actively request feedback rather than having it automatically displayed

domain1.q1_evidence: Clear inclusion criteria specified: students had to have received at least one CCF in both sessions. 209 recruited, 106 included in final analysis with transparent reporting of exclusion reasons (non-attendance at both sessions, reorganized pairs, no CCF messages received).
domain1.q2_evidence: Convenience sample from 6 classes in southern Sweden. Large attrition from 209 to 106 participants. Unequal distribution between conditions (37 single-first vs. 69 pair-first). Teachers rated achievement levels subjectively based on reading comprehension. Sample limited to one geographic region.

domain2.q3_evidence: Feedback attention measured via time-stamped data logs with a 4.25-second threshold (validated in a prior study by Silvervarg et al., 2020). However, the authors acknowledge that keeping a message displayed on screen does not necessarily equal attending to or understanding it. No direct measure of learning outcomes or feedback comprehension.
domain2.q4_evidence: Appropriate use of logistic mixed-effects regression model with repeated measures. Step-wise forward procedure for model selection. Model fit reported (C-value = 0.79, Somers Dxy = 0.58). Random effects accounted for individual subject variation. All variables and interaction effects clearly specified and reported with coefficients, odds ratios, standard errors, z-values, and p-values.

domain3.q5_evidence: Findings are interpreted cautiously and consistently with the statistical results. Authors acknowledge that effects of pair play are small. Interaction effects between achievement level and condition are discussed with reference to prior literature. Comparison with teachable agent studies provides context.
domain3.q6_evidence: Extensive limitations section covering: proxy nature of feedback display time, assumption about equal pair contribution, ambiguity of interpreting pair attention as collaborative behavior, lack of qualitative data, game not designed for collaboration, and study conducted during COVID-19 pandemic affecting data collection.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study has a clear within-subjects design and uses appropriate statistical methods with transparent reporting. Main concerns relate to the large attrition rate (209 to 106), the indirect measure of feedback attention (screen display time rather than direct engagement), the inability to distinguish individual contributions within pairs from log data alone, the unequal group sizes between conditions, and the absence of qualitative data to validate quantitative findings. The study was also conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic with remote implementation, limiting researcher control over the experimental conditions.

pdf_filename: Assassin’s Creed reminds us that history is human experience Students’ senses of empathy while playing a narrative video game.pdf

bibliographic.title: "Assassin's Creed reminds us that history is human experience": Students' senses of empathy while playing a narrative video game
bibliographic.venue: Theory & Research in Social Education
bibliographic.publisher: College and University Faculty Assembly of National Council for the Social Studies

study_characteristics.sample_description: 14 male high school students (grades 9-12) enrolled at a private Catholic boys' preparatory school in a mid-size Midwestern U.S. city; all had completed Assassin's Creed III and most had beaten multiple titles in the franchise; 3 identified as Latino and the rest as White; purposive sampling of avid players from a survey of ~1,000 students (54 respondents)
study_characteristics.study_design: qualitative interview study (semistructured interviews, narrative inquiry, inductive thematic analysis following Creswell's data analysis spiral)
study_characteristics.game_type: commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) narrative action-adventure video game
study_characteristics.game_name: Assassin's Creed (franchise, primarily Assassin's Creed III)
study_characteristics.aim: To examine how students' perceptions of historical peoples and time periods may be influenced by the depictions they encounter in the narrative video game Assassin's Creed, with particular attention to describing the ways students received and processed historical characters and stories in the games

eligibility.concerns: The study examines out-of-classroom gameplay without formal instructional integration; it focuses on unmediated student engagement with a commercial game rather than a designed educational gamification intervention. The game was not used in a classroom setting but rather studied for its influence on students' historical perceptions.

rq1.conceptualization: The study does not define gamification explicitly. Instead, it conceptualizes the use of a commercial narrative video game (Assassin's Creed) as a medium through which students independently engage with historical content. The focus is on how the game's narrative structure, character embodiment, immersive historical settings, and interactive storytelling foster historical empathy and perspective-taking. The game is treated as a site of informal historical learning rather than a formal gamification intervention.
theoretical_frameworks: Barton and Levstik's (2004) two-part definition of historical empathy as perspective recognition and care
Gee's (2011) theory of narrative video games as tools for sense making, perspective taking, and empathy
Wolf's (2001) linear and branching narrative structures in video games
Rosenzweig and Thelen's (1998) framework on popular uses of history

rq2.key_outcomes: Students described (1) a sense of immediate access to history contrasting with school-based memorization learning; (2) a sense of human connection to people in the past through both fictional and historical characters; (3) increased perception of multiple perspectives in history (e.g., British Loyalist perspective, Native American perspective during American Revolution); (4) willingness to allow the games to rewrite their beliefs about history and reshape their identities (e.g., revised views of George Washington, the Crusades, slavery, and Catholic Church history); (5) theorizing about historical accuracy with high trust in game designers. However, students tended to miss opportunities for critical engagement, evidencing uncritical trust in Ubisoft's portrayals and risk of presentism.
rq2.engagement_results: Students demonstrated high affective engagement with the game. They contrasted positive emotional associations from gameplay with disengagement from memorization-based school history. Students described visceral feelings of being 'put into' history, feeling terror during the Boston Massacre scene, developing empathy for enslaved people through character embodiment, and experiencing emotional connections that prompted identity reflection. 11 of 14 participants reported conducting online searches inspired by the games.

game_design_elements: Narrative/storyline (linear and branching structures combined)
Character embodiment/avatar (playing as historical and fictional characters)
Immersive historical environments (visually and aurally detailed settings)
Cutscenes (cinematic interludes advancing the plot)
Missions (required and optional 'side quests')
Role-playing (first-person perspective taking)
Historical figures as NPCs (non-player characters)
Open world exploration of historical settings
Multiple perspectives embedded in narrative
technological_platforms: Console and PC video game (Assassin's Creed franchise by Ubisoft, 2007-2018)
instructional_strategies: No formal instructional integration; study examined unmediated out-of-classroom gameplay
Semistructured interviews used as reflective tools post-gameplay
Comparison of game-based and school-based learning experiences
Students independently conducted online searches to verify game content
rq3.content_integration: The Assassin's Creed series is set in various historical time periods (primarily the American Revolution in Assassin's Creed III, but also the Crusades, Renaissance Italy, French Revolution, and others). Historical content is integrated through narrative plotlines intertwining fictional characters with real historical events and figures (e.g., George Washington, Benjamin Franklin, Samuel Adams, Pope Alexander VI). The game presents alternate perspectives (e.g., Native American viewpoint via Connor/Ratonhnhake:ton) and depicts everyday life alongside major historical events. A 'discovery tour' educational mode was also announced for later titles.

implementation_barriers: School administrator reluctance to allow video game research due to negative perceptions of gaming and concerns about violence (particularly given school shooting context)
Franchise name 'Assassin's Creed' connoting gratuitous violence to adults
M for Mature (17+) rating limiting classroom applicability
Time constraints (each major title takes 30-60 hours to complete)
Financial expense of game hardware and software
Access difficulties: researcher was denied access to public mixed-gender schools
Gender imbalance: study limited to all-male private school sample
methodology_limitations: Convenience sample limited to one private Catholic boys' school in the Midwest
All-male participant group; no female perspectives captured
Single interview per participant (school-imposed limitation)
Purposive sampling of avid players only; results do not reflect students with more cursory engagement
Self-reported data relying on retrospective accounts of gameplay experiences
No classroom observation or assessment of actual historical knowledge gains
Qualitative design without control or comparison group
Limited racial/ethnic diversity (3 Latino, 11 White participants)
negative_effects: Students tended to miss opportunities for critical engagement with their visceral sense of immersive experience
Risk of presentism: students felt seamless connection to the past without problematizing the gap between their emotions and those of historical people
Uncritical trust in game designers' historical accuracy and neutrality
Students allowed the game to rewrite their historical beliefs without seeking outside corroborating evidence
Blurring of boundaries between game characters and actual historical figures
Entertainment-driven narrative may amplify or occlude certain aspects of history based on market demands
Students who dismissed games as non-educational (like Adam) missed opportunities for robust critical engagement
mitigation_strategies: Author recommends fostering critical investigation into gameplay experiences
Author recommends teacher-guided debrief and critical analysis of game portrayals
Author suggests developing ways to help students recognize constructed nature of game media
Author recommends integrating affective engagement (care) with cognitive perspective-taking in history instruction
Author recommends teaching historical empathy as both perspective recognition and care to bridge school and out-of-school historical experiences
Author notes the importance of making students aware that historians have techniques for investigating the ambiguities raised by multiple perspectives

domain1.q1_evidence: The study used a convenience sample from a single private Catholic boys' school due to access difficulties. The researcher was denied access to public mixed-gender schools. Purposive sampling was then employed, selecting only avid Assassin's Creed players who had completed the game. Selection criteria were clearly described but inherently biased toward enthusiastic male players at one specific institution.
domain1.q2_evidence: The sample is not representative of a broader student population: all 14 participants were male, from one private Catholic school in the Midwest, predominantly White (11 White, 3 Latino), and were self-selected avid gamers. The author acknowledges these limitations and notes results do not reflect students with more cursory engagement.

domain2.q3_evidence: The study used established qualitative methods: semistructured interviews (Kvale, 1996; Weiss, 1994), narrative inquiry (Chase, 2011), and Creswell's (2009) data analysis spiral. Triangulation was achieved through researcher gameplay memos, supplemental Ubisoft materials, and online fan-created materials. The interview protocol is provided as an appendix, enabling transparency and replication.
domain2.q4_evidence: Analysis followed a rigorous inductive approach: individual coding per transcript, Josselson's hermeneutic approach, open coding (Charmaz, 2010), constant-comparative coding, and axial coding collapsed into themes. The analytical process was well-documented and aligned with established qualitative research methods.

domain3.q5_evidence: The findings are well-supported by rich, detailed participant quotes and are consistently interpreted through Barton and Levstik's theoretical framework. However, the author is clearly sympathetic to the educational potential of the games, which may have influenced interpretation. The author does acknowledge negative aspects (lack of critical engagement, presentism risk) alongside positive ones.
domain3.q6_evidence: The author explicitly discusses limitations including the all-male convenience sample, single-school setting, purposive sampling of avid players only, school-imposed single-interview restriction, and inability to generalize. The discussion section addresses both benefits and dangers of the game's influence on historical understanding.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study employs rigorous qualitative methods with a well-documented analytical process and strong theoretical framework. The main risk of bias stems from the highly non-representative sample (14 male students from one private Catholic school, all avid gamers) and the inherent limitations of convenience sampling driven by access constraints. Data collection tools and analysis methods are sound, and limitations are transparently discussed. The interpretive lens is generally balanced, acknowledging both positive empathetic outcomes and concerns about uncritical engagement.

pdf_filename: Battle Card, Card Game for Teaching the History of the Incas Through Intelligent Techniques.pdf

bibliographic.title: Battle Card, Card Game for Teaching the History of the Incas Through Intelligent Techniques
bibliographic.venue: SAI 2022 - Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems (LNNS)

study_characteristics.sample_description: Schoolchildren between the ages of 10 and 12 at the primary level who participated in interviews and pre-test/post-test surveys to evaluate the video game
study_characteristics.study_design: Design-based research with acceptance testing (pre-test/post-test surveys and interviews with schoolchildren)
study_characteristics.aim: To develop a card game called Battle Card based on the Inca empire that teaches history of the Incas through artificial intelligence algorithms, and to identify the influence of a video game as a pedagogical tool in student learning

eligibility.concerns: The study is primarily a software engineering/game development paper with limited formal educational evaluation. The sample size is not explicitly reported. The evaluation relies mainly on game quality metrics and informal satisfaction surveys rather than rigorous educational outcome measures.

rq1.conceptualization: The study conceptualizes the card game as an interactive and effective way to learn history, replacing the traditional memorization model. Each card represents an Inca historical figure with attributes (name, description of historical role, power values, element type). The game contextualizes students about the period's most significant events and characters. History education through games is framed as promoting patriotism and making learning dynamic rather than boring.
theoretical_frameworks: Quality criteria for serious games (Caserman et al., referencing serious game part, game part, and balance)
Game quality metrics framework (Amacifuen Cerna - pedagogical and technological metrics for measuring quality of online games)

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Game quality metrics: Effectiveness 71.8% (target effectiveness X=83.33%, goal completeness X=0.83); Efficiency 60% (finish time X=7 min, efficiency relative to user level X=0.6); Flexibility 0% (accessibility X=0); Safety 100%; Fault tolerance 90%; Satisfaction 80%
rq2.statistical_results: Satisfaction survey results: 80% found the game attractive; 60% clearly understood the dynamics of the game; 100% of schoolchildren commented they would play it again. Performance test: game loading time 5.386 seconds. Unit tests: 3 specs, 0 failures.
rq2.key_outcomes: The game was evaluated through unit tests (all passed), performance tests (5.386s loading time), and acceptance tests using game quality metrics. Satisfaction surveys with schoolchildren showed positive reception: 80% found it attractive, 60% understood the dynamics, and 100% would play again. The overall results showed educators and specialists could use Battle Cards as a pedagogical tool in student learning.
rq2.engagement_results: 80% of schoolchildren found the game attractive; 100% stated they would play it again; students suggested improvements to graphic design and visual effects, indicating engagement with the game

game_design_elements: Card-based battle mechanics (each card represents an Inca historical figure)
Three card element types (water, fire, ice) with rock-paper-scissors style advantages
Four power attributes per card (attack and defense values)
Three progressive difficulty levels corresponding to Inca geographic regions (coast, mountain, jungle)
Decreasing available cards per level (6, 5, 3) to increase difficulty
Score tracking system
Player vs. AI opponent structure
State machine for card behavior (deck, on board/idle, on hold/selected, attack, attacked, destroyed)
Historical character names and descriptions on cards (e.g., Sinchi Roca, Manco Capac, Lloque Yupanqui)
Battle rules between card types
technological_platforms: Phaser.io (JavaScript game framework for desktop and mobile platforms)
instructional_strategies: Embedding historical content within card characters and their descriptions
Contextualizing Inca history through game levels named after geographic regions of the Tahuantinsuyo (coast, mountain, jungle)
Progressive difficulty to maintain engagement and challenge
Player vs. AI gameplay to simulate strategic thinking about historical figures
In-game instructions explaining card types, battle rules, and level progression
rq3.content_integration: Historical content is integrated directly into the game cards: each card features an Inca historical figure (e.g., Sinchi Roca, Manco Capac, Lloque Yupanqui) with their name, a brief historical description of their role (in Spanish), and game attributes. The three game levels correspond to the natural regions of the Tahuantinsuyo (the Inca empire): coast, mountains, and jungle, linking game progression to geographic/historical knowledge of the Inca civilization.

implementation_barriers: Flexibility metric scored 0% - no alternative forms of interaction are available beyond the default, limiting accessibility
Game interface and card design need improvement according to student feedback
Visual effects require enhancement based on user feedback

No multiplayer option available (only player vs. AI)

No control group or comparative experimental design
Evaluation relies on game quality metrics rather than formal learning outcome assessments
No standardized pre-test/post-test measuring historical knowledge gains
Satisfaction surveys are informal and lack psychometric validation

mitigation_strategies: Suggested future work: improve card design and appearance
Suggested future work: develop for mobile devices (Android and iOS)
Suggested future work: add a virtual assistant to help explain the game

Suggested future work: add more rivals and online play functionality

Suggested future work: add more difficulty levels

domain1.q1_evidence: No explicit selection criteria for participants are described. The paper mentions schoolchildren between ages 10 and 12 at the primary level were involved in interviews and surveys, but does not explain how they were selected or recruited.
domain1.q2_evidence: Sample size is not reported. No information about the school, class, or demographic characteristics of participants. No discussion of whether the sample is representative of the target population.

domain2.q3_evidence: The study uses game quality metrics (from Amacifuen Cerna, 2017) to evaluate the game, not validated educational measurement instruments. Satisfaction surveys are described informally without reporting the instrument, number of items, or psychometric properties. Pre-test and post-test surveys are mentioned but results are not reported in detail.
domain2.q4_evidence: Analysis is limited to simple percentages from game quality metrics and satisfaction survey responses. No statistical tests are applied. No formal analysis of pre-test/post-test data is presented despite mentioning these surveys were conducted.

domain3.q5_evidence: The paper concludes that educators and specialists could use Battle Cards as a pedagogical tool based on satisfaction survey results and game quality metrics, but there is no direct evidence of learning outcomes. The leap from 80% satisfaction to pedagogical effectiveness is not well justified.
domain3.q6_evidence: The paper acknowledges several limitations through its future work section: need for improved card design, lack of mobile platform support, absence of multiplayer, and need for better AI algorithms. However, methodological limitations of the evaluation are not explicitly discussed.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study has high risk of bias across all domains. It is primarily a software development and game design paper rather than a rigorous educational research study. The participant selection is undocumented, sample size is unreported, evaluation instruments lack validation, analysis methods are rudimentary (simple percentages with no statistical testing), and conclusions about pedagogical value are drawn from satisfaction data rather than measured learning outcomes. The pre-test/post-test data that was reportedly collected is not presented in the results.

pdf_filename: Building a virtual Roman city teaching history through video game design.pdf

bibliographic.title: Building a virtual Roman city: teaching history through video game design
bibliographic.venue: Journal of Classics Teaching

study_characteristics.sample_description: 45 third-year university students enrolled in a History course about the city in the Roman world at York University, Toronto, Canada. 17 out of 45 authorised their response papers for use in the study; 30 out of 45 provided course evaluation feedback, of which 22 commented on the Virtual City Project.
study_characteristics.study_design: qualitative case study
study_characteristics.game_type: student-designed 3D virtual environment / VR simulation using game engine
study_characteristics.game_name: Virtual City Project (custom project built in Unity 3D with Rome Fantasy Pack asset package)
study_characteristics.aim: To assess the pedagogical efficacy of constructionist approaches to teaching students about Roman architecture using VR and video game design technology, and to address the technical and pedagogical challenges of using game design software in the classroom.

eligibility.concerns: The study focuses on constructionist game design (students designing/building in a game engine) rather than playing a pre-made educational game. It is a qualitative case study with no control group or quantitative outcome measures. The gamification element is through the use of game design technology (Unity 3D) and VR rather than traditional gamification mechanics like points or badges.

rq1.conceptualization: The study frames the approach through Seymour Papert's constructionism -- 'learning-by-making' -- where students actively design and construct digital artifacts (3D Roman buildings) using video game design software (Unity 3D) rather than passively consuming instructional material. The approach uses game design technology as a pedagogical tool for constructionist learning in history education, specifically combining VR presentation with the design process. The author distinguishes constructionism from instructionism and positions game design as a medium for building knowledge through experience.

rq2.key_outcomes: Qualitative findings based on student response papers (17/45), course evaluations (22/30 commented on the project), classroom observations, and analysis of the 3D buildings produced. Most groups (9 out of 10) successfully integrated research content into their 3D building designs. All groups were able to use Unity 3D without catastrophic failures. Students showed incremental improvement in technical proficiency over the six-hour design sessions. Course evaluation feedback was overwhelmingly positive: students described the project as 'stimulating', 'interesting', 'fun', 'engaging', and 'creative'. One student called it 'probably the most fun assignment I have done during my time at university'. Multiple students recommended keeping the project as a permanent course component. Only one student found it 'not fleshed out enough to be worthwhile'. Some groups exceeded expectations by creating custom objects and importing external textures beyond the prefabricated asset package.
rq2.engagement_results: Strongly positive student engagement. Of the 22 course evaluation comments about the Virtual City Project, nearly all were positive. Students reported high levels of enjoyment, found the combination of technology and history stimulating, and multiple students recommended the project be continued in future iterations. Students reported that the hands-on design process helped them learn more about their assigned structures than traditional methods would have.

game_design_elements: 3D environment construction using prefabricated architectural components
Virtual reality (VR) immersive presentation and navigation
Collaborative group-based design
Research-informed design decisions
Asset manipulation (textures, materials, lighting, primitive objects)
Constructionist learning-by-making approach
technological_platforms: Rome Fantasy Pack asset package (by Quantum Theory)
instructional_strategies: Constructionist learning-by-making
Group-based collaborative research and design (10 groups of ~4-5 students)
Three-week research phase followed by design phase
Four-hour crash course tutorial on Unity 3D
Six hours of in-class design sessions over three weeks
Individual student response papers reflecting on design decisions and challenges
VR group presentations with class discussion
Contextualised fictional scenario (Roman frontier city in North West Europe with local conditions)
rq3.content_integration: Students researched specific Roman public building types (temple, portico, triumphal arch, aqueduct, bath complex, basilica, macellum, elite house, brothel, tavern), then constructed 3D digital reconstructions based on their research. The research phase was specifically designed to ensure content integration before design began. Buildings were then assembled into a coherent Roman city centre with appropriate urban planning (two main roads meeting at a public square). The fictional scenario required buildings to be appropriate to local climate and political conditions of a frontier town, adding historical reasoning to design choices.

implementation_barriers: Steep learning curve of professional-grade Unity 3D game engine for history students with no prior technical experience
Limited asset package: key architectural elements (e.g., apsidal pieces, specific Roman features) were missing from the Rome Fantasy Pack
Insufficient in-class time devoted to design sessions (only six hours over three weeks); 16 of 17 respondents requested more time
Difficulty aligning and connecting architectural pieces seamlessly
Group work logistics: only one computer per group, limiting individual hands-on participation
Instructor needed specialized technical knowledge in both game design and coding
Instructor had to perform all computer coding for the final VR program personally
VR presentation limited to one headset at a time with the rest of class viewing via 2D projection
methodology_limitations: Small qualitative sample: only 17 of 45 student response papers were authorised for use
No control group or comparative condition with traditional teaching methods
No quantitative outcome measures or pre/post testing of knowledge retention
Essay-based assessment regime did not lend itself to quantification of learning outcomes
Cannot determine whether this approach is better for knowledge retention than traditional research-based projects
Single case study at one institution with one cohort
Self-selection bias in response papers and course evaluations
The generic nature of the asset package prevented students from building specific historical structures, limiting specificity of historical learning
negative_effects: One group (portico) completely ignored the research component and built a structure that did not match their assignment
Some groups produced historically inaccurate hybridised architectural elements (e.g., tetrastyle instead of hexastyle temple)
One group incorporated anachronistic historical rationale for their triumphal arch design
Design element came at the expense of time for case-specific historical research
Students could only build generic representations rather than specific historical structures
Technical focus potentially distracted from historical content learning
mitigation_strategies: Allocate more in-class time for design sessions in future iterations
Provide more comprehensive Unity 3D tutorials (e.g., include vertex snapping function)
Assess the research component before students begin designing to ensure content integration
Consider using simpler design platforms like Minecraft: Education Edition to reduce technical barriers
Add more accessible tutorial material or longer instructional sessions
Include computer programming and coding elements as coding literacy grows among students
Retain Unity 3D despite steep learning curve for its benefits in transferable technical skills and interdisciplinary learning

domain1.q1_evidence: The study used a convenience sample of students enrolled in a specific third-year history course at York University. There were no explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria for participant selection. Only 17 of 45 students authorised their response papers for research use, creating potential self-selection bias. Course evaluation responses (30/45) were also voluntary.
domain1.q2_evidence: Single institution (York University, Toronto), single course, single cohort (Fall 2018). The sample of 45 students in a Roman history course at a Canadian university is not representative of broader higher education populations. The author was also the instructor/designer of the experiment, introducing potential bias.

domain2.q3_evidence: Data collection relied on qualitative sources: anonymised student response papers, course evaluation comments, classroom observations, and analysis of 3D buildings. No validated instruments, rubrics, or standardised assessments were used. No pre/post knowledge tests were administered. The assessment was essay-based and not designed for quantification.
domain2.q4_evidence: Analysis was primarily descriptive and interpretive, with no systematic qualitative coding methodology described. The author selected specific buildings and student quotes to discuss without describing a systematic analytical framework. No inter-rater reliability or member checking was reported. The author was both the instructor and researcher, creating potential conflicts of interest in interpretation.

domain3.q5_evidence: The author presents both positive and negative findings, including the group that completely failed to integrate research content (portico group), anachronisms in the triumphal arch group's rationale, and one student's negative evaluation. The conclusions are measured and acknowledge that it is hard to determine whether the approach is better for knowledge retention than traditional methods.
domain3.q6_evidence: The author explicitly discusses multiple limitations: the steep learning curve of Unity 3D, the generic nature of the asset package preventing specificity, the trade-off between design time and content-focused research time, the inability to quantify learning outcomes, and the challenge of determining whether the approach is superior to traditional methods. Future improvements are proposed.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: While the study is transparent about its limitations and presents balanced findings, the overall risk of bias is high due to the absence of validated measurement instruments, lack of a control group, small and self-selected qualitative sample (17/45 authorised papers), no systematic analytical methodology, and the dual role of the author as both instructor/designer and researcher. The study provides valuable descriptive insights but limited evidence for causal claims about pedagogical efficacy.

pdf_filename: Changing Students' Perceptions of a History Exploration Game Using Different Scripts.pdf

bibliographic.title: Changing Students' Perceptions of a History Exploration Game Using Different Scripts
bibliographic.venue: Proceedings of the 30th International Conference on Computers in Education (ICCE 2022), Asia-Pacific Society for Computers in Education
bibliographic.publisher: Asia-Pacific Society for Computers in Education

study_characteristics.sample_description: A large sample of elementary and middle school learners playing the history game Jo Wilder and the Capitol Case. The total sample across all five latent classes was N=2417 (184+546+489+665+533). Students played the game in a variety of contexts.
study_characteristics.study_design: Quasi-experimental with latent class analysis
study_characteristics.game_type: Point-and-click history adventure game (digital, narrative-driven exploration game)
study_characteristics.game_name: Jo Wilder and the Capitol Case
study_characteristics.aim: To explore different profiles of engagement among students playing a history game and to examine whether minor game dialogue changes (different scripts varying in humor and snark) affect learners' perceptions of game elements such as character likeability, humor, and enjoyment of history

eligibility.concerns: The study focuses on engagement profiles and perceptions rather than direct learning outcomes. It examines gamification elements (narrative scripts, character dialogue) within a history education game, which aligns with the review scope.

rq1.conceptualization: The study conceptualizes games as powerful tools for learning in formal and informal educational contexts. It frames engagement through the lens of engagement profiles -- typologies of learner groups based on their goals, motivations, and preferences when playing digital games. The study does not provide an explicit definition of gamification but treats the history game as a complete game-based learning environment, emphasizing how game design elements (dialogue scripts, character traits, humor, narrative tone) shape learner engagement and attitudes toward history.
theoretical_frameworks: Engagement profiles / player typology (Latent Class Analysis)
E-Game Flow Scale (Fu, Su, & Yu, 2009) for measuring immersion
Reysen Likability Scale (Reysen, 2005) for character likeability
Multidimensional Sense of Humor Scale (Thorson & Powell, 1993) for perceived humor
Three-Dimensions of Student Attitude Towards Science (TDSAS; Zhang & Campbell, 2011) adapted for attitudes toward history
Player states vs. player traits debate

rq2.quantitative_metrics: 16-item Likert survey measuring four constructs: (1) immersion, (2) character likeability, (3) perceived humor, (4) attitudes toward history. Latent Class Analysis (LCA) with model fit statistics (AIC, BIC, VLMR, BLRT, Entropy). Odds ratios for script effects and reading level effects on class membership.
rq2.statistical_results: K=5 LCA model selected (AIC=97602, BIC=98181, VLMR=0.048, BLRT<0.01, Entropy=0.861). Script effects: Humor No Snark script -- players more likely in 'Liked It All' vs 'Didn't Like Jo' (OR=1.519); Snark No Humor script -- 'Didn't Like Jo' vs 'Didn't Like History' (OR=1.660), 'Didn't Like Jo' vs 'Liked It All' (OR=1.820), 'Liked It All' vs 'Not Very Funny' (OR=1.506). Reading level effects: strong readers more likely in 'Liked It All' vs 'Didn't Like Any' (OR=2.362), and other comparisons ranging from OR=1.377 to OR=1.715. Benjamini & Hochberg post-hoc correction applied.
rq2.comparative_methodology: Four script conditions compared: (1) Initial Design (Snark + Humor), (2) No Snark (Humor only), (3) No Humor (Snark only), (4) No Humor No Snark. Latent class membership proportions compared across conditions using 3-step procedure in MPlus. Reading level included as a covariate.
rq2.key_outcomes: Five distinct player engagement profiles identified: 'Didn't Like Anything' (N=184, 7%), 'Didn't Like Jo' (N=546), 'Didn't Like History' (N=489), 'Liked It All' (N=665, 28%), and 'Not Very Funny' (N=533). Removing humor or snark from the game script shifted some students' engagement profiles. Removing either humor or snark from the base script made players more open to positive evaluations of history learning, though at the cost of worsened attitudes toward the main character Jo. Higher reading level was associated with greater overall game enjoyment across all groups.
rq2.engagement_results: Students generally enjoyed the game, with 'Liked It All' being the largest group (28%) and 'Didn't Like Any' the smallest (7%). Script changes primarily affected the malleable middle groups ('Not Very Funny', 'Didn't Like History', 'Didn't Like Jo') rather than extreme groups ('Liked It All' and 'Didn't Like Anything'). The Snark No Humor script produced the most significant shifts in group membership.

game_design_elements: Narrative dialogue scripts (varying snark/sarcasm and humor/wordplay)
Character personality traits (reluctant/snarky vs. enthusiastic/positive protagonist)
Humor and jokes in character dialogue
Point-and-click exploration mechanics
Historical artifact investigation
Linear narrative structure with free exploration of locations
Inspectable items and character conversations
Embedded Likert survey at four gameplay checkpoints
technological_platforms: Jo Wilder and the Capitol Case (2019) -- digital point-and-click adventure game
MPlus statistical software for Latent Class Analysis
instructional_strategies: Narrative-driven history exploration through a child protagonist
Historical inquiry through artifact investigation
Character-driven engagement with history content
Adaptive game design through modifiable dialogue scripts
Self-report survey embedded within gameplay to measure engagement
rq3.content_integration: History content is integrated through a narrative in which the player character Jo helps her historian grandfather determine the story of two artifacts for a Capitol exhibit. Players investigate historical artifacts, explore locations, and engage in character conversations that reveal historical clues. The game's dialogue scripts serve as the primary vehicle for both history content delivery and engagement, with the tone of the dialogue (snarky/humorous vs. serious/neutral) directly affecting students' attitudes toward history as a subject.

implementation_barriers: Text-heavy game nature may disadvantage weaker readers, reducing accessibility and enjoyment
Changing character traits (removing humor/snark) to improve history attitudes came at the cost of worsened player attitudes toward the main character

Players with pre-existing negative attitudes toward educational games or history ('Didn't Like Anything' group) were not affected by script changes, suggesting some engagement barriers are trait-based rather than state-based
Reading comprehension level significantly affects game engagement, making the game less effective for lower-level readers
methodology_limitations: Self-report survey data may not fully capture actual engagement or learning
Exploratory study -- some trends did not hold up after Benjamini & Hochberg post-hoc correction for multiple comparisons
The study examines perceptions and engagement profiles but does not measure actual history learning outcomes
Cannot definitively determine whether engagement profiles represent player states (context-dependent) or traits (persistent dispositions)
Script changes altered 20-40% of total game dialogue, making it difficult to isolate which specific dialogue changes drove the effects
negative_effects: Removing humor or snark improved history attitudes but worsened player attitudes toward Jo as a character -- the 'snarky' Jo was perceived as mean by some players
In the Initial Design script (with both humor and snark), Jo's character traits may have reinforced players' existing negative attitudes toward history learning
Lower reading level students were disproportionately placed in the 'Didn't Like Anything' group, indicating the text-heavy game may alienate struggling readers
mitigation_strategies: Personalized and adaptive game design that modifies dialogue, character traits, and tone based on individual player profiles
Ensuring game content is worded at appropriate reading levels and is culturally responsive to the target student population
Using engagement profiles as a tool for adaptive learning systems to optimize individual engagement
Modifying salient game qualities (character appearances, mannerisms, humor) to suit individual players

domain1.q1_evidence: The study uses a large sample of elementary and middle school students (N=2417) playing the game in a variety of contexts. Students were assigned to different script conditions. Selection criteria for participants are implicitly defined by who played the game, though explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria are not detailed.
domain1.q2_evidence: The sample is large, but details about how participants were recruited, demographic breakdown, school types, and whether the sample is representative of the broader population of elementary/middle school students are not provided. The 'variety of contexts' is mentioned but not specified.

domain2.q3_evidence: The 16-item Likert survey was developed and piloted, drawing items from established validated scales: E-Game Flow Scale (Fu et al., 2009), Reysen Likability Scale (Reysen, 2005), Multidimensional Sense of Humor Scale (Thorson & Powell, 1993), and TDSAS (Zhang & Campbell, 2011). The LCA methodology follows established guidelines (Samuelsen & Raczynski, 2013; Nylund-Gibson & Choi, 2018).
domain2.q4_evidence: Latent Class Analysis with systematic model selection (K=2 through K=6) using multiple fit statistics (AIC, BIC, VLMR, BLRT, Entropy). The 3-step procedure in MPlus was used appropriately to include covariates without influencing model structure. Benjamini & Hochberg post-hoc correction was applied for multiple comparisons. The authors transparently report trends that did not survive post-hoc correction.

domain3.q5_evidence: Findings are interpreted consistently with the data. The authors carefully distinguish between effects that survived post-hoc correction and those that did not. The discussion of player states vs. traits is balanced, acknowledging evidence for both interpretations.
domain3.q6_evidence: The authors discuss the trade-off between improved history attitudes and worsened character perceptions, the importance of reading level, and the implications for adaptive design. The exploratory nature of the study is acknowledged. However, the lack of direct learning outcome measures is not explicitly flagged as a limitation.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study employs a large sample, validated survey instruments adapted from established scales, rigorous latent class analysis methodology with systematic model selection and appropriate statistical corrections. The authors are transparent about non-significant trends and thoughtful in their interpretation. Main concerns are the lack of detailed participant demographics/recruitment information and the absence of direct learning outcome measures, but overall methodological quality is sound for an exploratory engagement study.

pdf_filename: Code Book The development of an Adventure Action Game for History Instruction and the Evaluation of Flow State, Learning Performance and Gender Difference.pdf

bibliographic.title: Code Book©- The development of an Adventure Action Game for History Instruction and the Evaluation of Flow State, Learning Performance and Gender Difference
bibliographic.venue: Proceedings of the 22nd International Conference on Computers in Education (ICCE 2014)
bibliographic.publisher: Asia-Pacific Society for Computers in Education

study_characteristics.sample_description: 38 college students from one institute of technology in Taiwan; 11 males and 27 females, aged 19-22 years old
study_characteristics.study_design: pre-experimental (one-group pretest-posttest)
study_characteristics.aim: To develop a first-person adventure action game (Code Book) for history learning, explore learners' flow state in history learning through this action game, evaluate learners' learning performance, and analyze gender differences

eligibility.concerns: Short conference paper (3 pages) with limited methodological detail; single-group design without control group limits causal inference

rq1.conceptualization: Game-based learning (GBL) applied to history education through a custom-developed first-person adventure action game. The game integrates historical content (Opium Wars, 1840-1842) into a WWII espionage narrative with role-playing, puzzle-solving missions, battle scenarios, and scaffolded historical information prompts. Learners play as a secret agent searching for confidential files in a German Army headquarters.

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Pre-test and post-test scores (5 history questions); flow questionnaire (23 items, 5-point Likert scale with two dimensions: flow antecedents and flow experience); Cronbach's alpha = 0.93
rq2.statistical_results: Paired-samples t-test: pretest M=1.32 (SD=1.25) vs posttest M=2.68 (SD=1.45), t=-5.33, p<0.001. Flow antecedents M=3.63 (SD=0.67); Flow experience M=3.73 (SD=0.59). Gender differences: flow antecedents t=0.12, p=0.906; flow experience t=-0.29, p=0.774; pretest t=1.30, p=0.201; posttest t=0.85, p=0.400 (all non-significant)
rq2.comparative_methodology: Within-subjects comparison (pretest vs posttest); between-subjects comparison by gender (male n=11 vs female n=27)
rq2.key_outcomes: Significant improvement in history knowledge after game-based learning (p<0.001). Learners reached high flow state (all dimension means above median 3.00). No significant gender differences in flow state or learning performance, suggesting the game is suitable for both genders.
rq2.engagement_results: High flow state achieved: flow antecedents M=3.63, flow experience M=3.73 (both above median 3.00). Highest flow antecedent sub-dimensions: feedback (M=3.68) and playability (M=3.68). Highest flow experience sub-dimensions: concentration (M=3.80) and time distortion (M=3.79), indicating high learner attention and immersion.

game_design_elements: Role-playing (playing as a secret agent)
Missions and quests (finding confidential files, escaping headquarters)
3D first-person perspective
Battle and combat scenarios
Puzzle-solving missions
Narrative/storyline (WWII espionage theme with Opium Wars history)
Scaffolding prompts with historical information
Clues hidden behind history knowledge
Challenging scenarios (chasing and escaping from enemies)
Immediate feedback
technological_platforms: NTUST MEG (National Taiwan University of Science and Technology Multimedia Entertainment and Games research team)
instructional_strategies: Role-playing pedagogy - learners assume the identity of a secret agent
Scaffolding - historical information provided as prompts alongside game files
Embedded assessment through history knowledge clues needed to complete missions
Pre-test and post-test assessment design
rq3.content_integration: Historical content about the Opium Wars (1840-1842, a diplomatic event in China) is integrated into a WWII espionage narrative. Players must find and analyze historical information embedded in books and confidential files hidden in different locations within a German Army headquarters. Historical knowledge clues are required to accomplish missions and progress through the game.

implementation_barriers: Short gameplay session (25 minutes) may limit depth of learning
Small sample size (n=38) from a single institution limits generalizability
Unbalanced gender distribution (11 males vs 27 females)
Participants were mostly from multimedia design discipline, potentially biasing comfort with 3D game environments
methodology_limitations: No control group - single-group pretest-posttest design limits causal inference
Short conference paper format provides limited methodological detail
Only 5 questions used for the knowledge test
Flow measured only via self-report questionnaire
No delayed post-test to assess retention
Sample from one institute of technology in Taiwan limits external validity
negative_effects: Initial hypothesis that males would show higher involvement in 3D first-person action game was violated - no significant gender difference found (though this is presented as a positive finding)
mitigation_strategies: Used validated flow scale (Kiili, 2006) translated and revised by Hou & Chou (2012) with high reliability (Cronbach's alpha = 0.93)
Included both battle and puzzle-solving missions to appeal to diverse player preferences
Knowledge test questions designed by a history expert
Authors suggest future research with larger-scale experiments and behavioral pattern analysis

domain1.q1_evidence: No explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria for participants beyond being college students from one institute of technology. Convenience sampling from a single institution.
domain1.q2_evidence: Sample of 38 students from one institute of technology in Taiwan with unbalanced gender (11 males, 27 females). Most participants from multimedia design discipline, not representative of general college population. No randomization or control group.

domain2.q3_evidence: Flow questionnaire based on validated Kiili (2006) scale, translated and revised by Hou & Chou (2012), with reported Cronbach's alpha of 0.93. Knowledge test designed by a history expert with 5 items.
domain2.q4_evidence: Appropriate use of paired-samples t-test for pre-post comparison and independent t-tests for gender comparison. However, limited to basic statistical analyses with no effect sizes reported. Only 5 questions on the knowledge test may limit measurement sensitivity.
