domain3.q5_evidence: Interpretations generally consistent with data. The violation of their gender hypothesis is honestly discussed. However, the strong conclusion about learning effectiveness is drawn from a design without a control group, which is not fully acknowledged as a limitation.
domain3.q6_evidence: Some limitations acknowledged implicitly (sample composition from multimedia design discipline). Future research directions mentioned (larger-scale experiments, behavioral pattern analysis). However, key limitations such as lack of control group, small sample size, and short intervention duration are not explicitly discussed as study limitations.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: High risk of bias primarily due to the single-group pre-experimental design without a control group, small convenience sample (n=38) from one institution, unbalanced gender distribution, and participants predominantly from multimedia design backgrounds. While validated instruments were used and basic statistics were appropriate, the lack of a control group and limited sample severely constrain the internal and external validity of the findings. The short conference paper format (3 pages) also means important methodological details may be missing.

pdf_filename: DESIGN OF A SMARTART CLASSROOM IN ART HISTORY A LEARNING EXPERIENCE WITH SELF-REGULATED SERIOUS GAMES.pdf

bibliographic.title: Design of a SmartArt Classroom in Art History: A Learning Experience with Self-Regulated Serious Games
bibliographic.venue: Proceedings of INTED2019 Conference (13th International Technology, Education and Development Conference)

study_characteristics.sample_description: University students from multiple undergraduate programs at the University of Burgos: History and Heritage Degree, Media Communication Degree, Tourism Degree, and non-regular students in university extracurricular courses
study_characteristics.study_design: Design-based research (system design and description, no empirical evaluation with participants)
study_characteristics.game_type: Serious game / graphic adventure videogame with gamification elements
study_characteristics.aim: To design a Virtual and Intelligent Classroom called SmartArt, adaptable to different types of students interested in learning the History of Art, using self-regulated serious games integrated with Moodle

eligibility.concerns: This is primarily an art history education study rather than general history education. The study is a design paper describing the SmartArt system without empirical evaluation data from actual participants. It focuses on Classical Greek Sculpture as the content domain. No sample size or empirical results are reported from a formal study with students.

rq1.conceptualization: The authors conceptualize gamification through the lens of serious games, describing it as a gamified learning structure that uses digital tools to facilitate interactive learning through simulation with embedded learning aids. They link gamification with Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) and Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS). They reference Clark (1970) and identify four basic principles of serious games: experimentation/learning by doing, interaction and immediate feedback, reducing fear of error to build meaningful learning, and transferring the main role to the player. The paper treats serious games and gamification as closely related but does not provide a standalone explicit definition of gamification.
theoretical_frameworks: MIX Taxonomy of Instructional Experience (Margulieux, McCracken, Catrambone 2016)

rq2.quantitative_metrics: No original quantitative data reported. The authors cite prior research (Gallego-Durán et al. 2014) finding that gamified teaching explains 72% of the variance in learning outcomes, simulators explain 62%, and quiz/puzzle games explain 45%.
rq2.statistical_results: No original statistical results. Referenced finding: gamified teaching explains 72% of the variance in learning outcomes (from cited meta-analysis by Gallego-Durán et al. 2014).
rq2.key_outcomes: This is a design paper presenting the SmartArt virtual classroom. No empirical outcomes from actual implementation are reported. The paper claims, based on literature review, that the combination of serious games with SRL increases motivation, creativity, and deep learning. The design is intended to facilitate self-regulated learning of art history content.

game_design_elements: Avatar/animated character guides (teacher avatar and historical figure Phidias)
Graphic adventure narrative structure
Mini-games and quizzes (clue games, word games, crossword puzzles, sorting/matching tasks)
Three difficulty levels (Beginner, Intermediate, Advanced)
Process-oriented feedback with justification for success/failure
Prior knowledge assessment
Interactive glossary
Evaluation rubrics with Likert scale (1-5, Excellent to Not Acceptable)
Collaborative gamified tasks (team-based clue matching)
Individual gamified tasks (sorting clues on a board)
Educational forum debate as gamified consolidation activity
Sequential task structure with successive approximations to goal
technological_platforms: Moodle (UBUVirtual - University of Burgos virtual platform)
instructional_strategies: Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) with metacognitive strategies
Flipped Learning methodology
Process-oriented feedback (redirecting to correct content upon error)
Prior knowledge activation and analysis
Successive approximations to learning goals
Collaborative learning through interactive forum discussions
Evaluation rubrics serving both assessment and instructional functions
Self-regulated inquiry questions at each learning milestone
Metacognitive strategy scaffolding: task orientation, planning, monitoring, and reflection
rq3.content_integration: The SmartArt classroom integrates art history content (specifically Classical Greek Sculpture focusing on Ancient and Medieval Ages) through a narrative-driven graphic adventure. Historical figure Phidias serves as an avatar guiding students through learning milestones about Greek sculptors (Miron, Policleto, Fidias, Praxiteles, Escopas, Lisipo). Content is embedded in interactive activities: matching sculptor characteristics with names, crossword puzzles about classical sculpture, collaborative clue-based team activities, and a consensual glossary. The content is presented through hypermedia resources integrated into the Moodle platform alongside the serious game.

implementation_barriers: Designing serious games requires a delicate narrative design accompanied by precise technical design
Need to avoid problems inherent to the development of large computer games (authors designed own graphic adventure to mitigate this)
Mere use of automatic tutoring in LMS does not ensure effectiveness without careful design and monitoring
Adaptation needed for different student populations with varying levels (regulated vs non-regulated students)
methodology_limitations: No empirical evaluation with actual participants is reported
No sample size or participant data provided
Paper presents only the design without implementation results
No pre/post-test or control group comparison
Effectiveness claims are based on cited literature rather than original data
Content limited to one specific topic (Classical Greek Sculpture) without evidence of generalizability
mitigation_strategies: Used own graphic adventure design to avoid complexity of developing a large computer game
United mini-games under a single storyline to maintain coherence
Included process-oriented feedback rather than product-oriented feedback to enhance SRL
Included evaluation rubrics to provide both evaluative and instructional guidance
Designed three difficulty levels to accommodate different learner proficiency

domain1.q1_evidence: No participant selection criteria are described. The study is a design paper that describes the SmartArt system without reporting any empirical study with participants. Target populations are mentioned (undergraduate students in History and Heritage, Media Communication, Tourism, and extracurricular courses) but no actual sample was recruited or studied.
domain1.q2_evidence: No sample was actually recruited. The paper describes the intended target audience but provides no data on actual participants or their representativeness.

domain2.q3_evidence: No measurement instruments were used to collect empirical data. The design includes evaluation rubrics with a Likert scale (1-5), but these are presented as part of the system design rather than as validated research instruments. No learning outcome measures, motivation scales, or other assessment tools are described or validated.
domain2.q4_evidence: No data analysis methods are described because no empirical data were collected. The claims about effectiveness (e.g., 72% variance explained) are drawn from cited meta-analysis literature (Gallego-Durán et al. 2014), not from original analysis.

domain3.q5_evidence: The conclusions present the design features as beneficial without empirical evidence from the SmartArt system itself. Claims about increased motivation, creativity, and deep learning are extrapolated from general literature on serious games and SRL rather than demonstrated through the presented system.
domain3.q6_evidence: No limitations of the study or the design are discussed. The paper does not acknowledge the absence of empirical testing or the limitations of presenting a design without evaluation data.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: This is a design paper that describes the conceptual and technical architecture of the SmartArt virtual classroom for art history education. It provides no empirical data, no participant sample, no measurement instruments, and no original analysis. All effectiveness claims are derived from cited literature rather than from evaluation of the proposed system. The study does not discuss any limitations. While the design itself is detailed and well-grounded in educational theory (SRL, ITS, Flipped Learning), the absence of any empirical evaluation makes it impossible to assess the actual effectiveness of the intervention, resulting in high overall risk of bias.

pdf_filename: Designing a Role-play Game for Learning Taiwan History and Geography.pdf

bibliographic.title: Designing a Role-play Game for Learning Taiwan History and Geography
bibliographic.venue: 2010 IEEE International Conference on Digital Game and Intelligent Toy Enhanced Learning (DIGITEL)

study_characteristics.sample_description: No empirical study with participants was conducted; this is a game design and development paper. The game content targets primary and secondary education students learning social science (history and geography of Taiwan).
study_characteristics.study_design: design and development research (no empirical evaluation reported)
study_characteristics.game_name: Southern Taiwan Anti-Japanese War RPG (built with Oblivion game engine)
study_characteristics.aim: To develop a 3D role-play digital game based on the anti-Japanese war history and geography of Southern Taiwan during the Qing dynasty, aiming to enhance learning effectiveness and motivation for Taiwanese history and geography.

eligibility.concerns: This is a design-only paper with no empirical evaluation conducted. The authors state that usability evaluation and educational experiments (pre/post-tests, questionnaires, focus group interviews) are planned for future work. No learning outcomes data are reported.

rq1.conceptualization: The paper conceptualizes digital game-based learning through role-playing games as an approach where learners are immersed in historical contexts and content, with entertainment, challenge, rules, and interactive feedback serving as drivers of learning motivation. Games are positioned as tools that transform traditional lecture-type education into learner-based models, promoting self-directed learning, problem-solving, critical thinking, and creative thinking. The paper draws on experiential learning theory and flow theory to frame how game-based learning works.

rq2.key_outcomes: No empirical outcomes are reported. The paper is a design and development study only. The authors expect that the game will enhance learning effectiveness and motivation for Taiwan history and geography. Future work is planned to include pre- and post-tests for learning achievement, questionnaires for learning motivation, learning attitudes, and satisfaction, plus focus group interviews.

game_design_elements: Role-playing with character customization (race, face, hair, eyes, age, complexion)
Seven progressive game stages based on historical war locations (Wan Tan, Dong Gang, Wan Luan, Ping Tung, Chao Jhou, Da Wu Shan, Hou Bi Lin)
Historical narrative and storyline based on anti-Japanese war in Qing dynasty
NPC interactions and dialogue system
Combat/martial art fighting system
Character growth and experience progression
Interactive map allowing navigation between stages
Narrations and animations linking game stages
Learning content shown during loading screens
Approximately 20 character types (Taiwanese, Hakka, aboriginal tribes, Japanese people/soldiers, volunteer troops)
Character personality parameters triggering different situations
Property and equipment systems
technological_platforms: Oblivion game engine (The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion)
3ds Max (for 3D architectural modeling and character costume design)
instructional_strategies: Experiential learning through immersive 3D historical environments
Problem-based learning through game challenges and tasks
Authentic historical settings modeled after real architecture and geography
Alignment with social science learning objectives of primary and secondary education
Narrative-driven learning through historical war storyline
Micro-learning content embedded in loading screens
Active exploration and discovery of historical locations
rq3.content_integration: The game integrates Taiwan history and geography content by recreating the anti-Japanese war of Southern Taiwan during the Qing dynasty. Seven real historical locations are modeled as game stages using the Qian Long Taiwan Map. Real architecture is faithfully recreated in 3D (e.g., Wan-Jin Catholic Cathedral). The game world replicates real-world area ratios, land shapes, heights, and vegetation. Learning objectives cover natural environment, cultural heritage, historical development from Paleolithic to Modern Age, social/cultural/economic/political development, Japanese Colonial period, and social life of Taiwan. All tasks align with the social science capability index of schools.

implementation_barriers: Complexity of integrating learning materials into games requiring script writing, production techniques, character design, environment modeling, and knowledge management
Need to balance entertainment and educational value (serious games often sacrifice entertainment)
No empirical validation has been conducted yet to confirm effectiveness
methodology_limitations: No empirical evaluation conducted; effectiveness claims are entirely aspirational
No participant data or sample reported
No usability testing reported
Future evaluation plan described but not executed
Game design decisions are not validated through user testing
mitigation_strategies: Planned future usability evaluation of the game
Planned pre- and post-tests checked and modified by social science teachers
Planned questionnaires covering learning motivation, attitudes, and satisfaction
Planned focus group interviews for qualitative data
Both quantitative and qualitative data collection planned for future work

domain1.q1_evidence: No participants were recruited or studied. This is purely a design paper with no empirical component. No selection criteria for participants are described.
domain1.q2_evidence: No sample was obtained. The target population (primary and secondary students) is mentioned only in terms of game content alignment with curriculum objectives, but no actual participants were involved.

domain2.q3_evidence: No data collection instruments were used. The paper describes future plans for pre/post-tests, questionnaires, and focus group interviews, but none were actually administered.
domain2.q4_evidence: No data analysis was performed. No quantitative or qualitative results are reported. All claims about learning effectiveness and motivation are expectations, not findings.

domain3.q5_evidence: The paper frames its expectations about effectiveness as if they are supported by the design alone, without any empirical evidence. The claims about enhancing learning effectiveness and motivation are not grounded in data from this study.
domain3.q6_evidence: The authors do acknowledge that empirical evaluation is future work, and they describe specific plans for usability testing, pre/post-tests, questionnaires, and interviews. However, they do not explicitly discuss design limitations.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: This is a game design and development paper with no empirical evaluation whatsoever. No participants were recruited, no data were collected, and no results are reported. All claims about learning effectiveness and motivation are aspirational expectations. While the game design is described in detail and future evaluation plans are outlined, the complete absence of empirical evidence means the study cannot support any conclusions about the effectiveness of the game for learning history and geography. The risk of bias is high across all domains due to the lack of any empirical methodology.

pdf_filename: Designing and evaluating a mobile educational game Void Broken 2.0 for history instruction.pdf

bibliographic.title: Designing and evaluating a mobile educational game "Void Broken 2.0" for history instruction
bibliographic.venue: Proceedings of the 27th International Conference on Computers in Education (ICCE 2019)
bibliographic.publisher: Asia-Pacific Society for Computers in Education

study_characteristics.sample_description: Sixty-six high school freshmen (24 boys and 42 girls) from northern Taiwan, with an average age of 16.26 years, recruited via convenience sampling from the researcher's lecture classes. They had never taken formal courses about the Qing Dynasty content used in the experiment.
study_characteristics.study_design: single-group pre-experimental pretest-posttest design
study_characteristics.aim: To design an educational game for Chinese Qing Dynasty history learning based on Theory of Cognitive Development (Piaget), and to evaluate whether the game improves history learning performance, whether students show high evaluations, and whether gender differences exist in learning performance or game evaluation.

eligibility.concerns: No control group; pre-experimental design limits causal claims. Short intervention (50 minutes of gameplay).

rq1.conceptualization: The study conceptualizes game-based learning for history education through Piaget's Theory of Cognitive Development. The game integrates cognitive schema, assimilation, accommodation, and equilibrium components into the educational game design. Historical figures and events form the cognitive schema; matching characters to events based on relations constitutes the adaptation process; accommodation occurs when students revise incorrect relations; assimilation occurs when cognitive schema changes through acquiring new knowledge; equilibrium is reached when students master the matching without errors.

rq2.quantitative_metrics: History learning performance measured via pretest-posttest relation matching items (48-point total); Game evaluation questionnaire using 5-point Likert scale covering perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and game elements (Cronbach's alpha = .90).
rq2.statistical_results: Paired-samples t-test: Posttest M=13.62 (SD=5.66) vs. Pretest M=7.88 (SD=4.38), t=9.58, p<.001. Average progress score was 5.74 points (max possible progress = 18). Game evaluation: Overall M=4.29 (SD=0.53); Perceived Usefulness M=4.29 (SD=0.58); Perceived Ease of Use M=4.14 (SD=0.70); Game Elements M=4.41 (SD=0.63). Gender differences (independent-samples t-test): No significant difference in history learning performance (t=-1.98, p=.052); Significant difference in overall game evaluation (t=2.35, p=.022), perceived usefulness (t=2.83, p=.006), and perceived ease of use (t=2.09, p=.041) favoring males; No significant difference in game elements evaluation (t=1.10, p=.276).
rq2.comparative_methodology: Pretest-posttest comparison within a single group using paired-samples t-test; gender comparison using independent-samples t-test.
rq2.key_outcomes: Students' history learning performance improved significantly after playing Void Broken 2.0. All game evaluation dimensions scored above the median (3.0), indicating the game was perceived as useful, easy to use, and satisfying in terms of game elements. Male students perceived the game as more useful and easier to use, but no significant gender differences were found in learning performance or game elements evaluation.
rq2.engagement_results: Overall game evaluation mean was 4.29 out of 5.0 (SD=0.53), well above the median of 3.0. Game elements evaluation was highest at M=4.41 (SD=0.63). Students were reported to be very active during gameplay and many wanted to play the full version in the future.

game_design_elements: Card-based deck building (50 historical figure cards)
Matching mechanics (3x3 grid battle board with timeline and status conditions)
Difficulty levels (easy, medium, hard with varying card requirements and guardian monster HP)
Battle/challenge system (5 historical event battles with guardian monsters)
Bonus frames (dual-condition activation for extra power)
Information acquisition mechanics (character biographies and event descriptions)
Ancient China map interface for battle selection
Deck building before battles (8 or 16 cards depending on difficulty)
Score/power system against guardian monsters
Round-based gameplay with limited rounds
instructional_strategies: Cognitive Development Theory integration (schema, assimilation, accommodation, equilibrium)
Relation matching between historical characters and events
Trial-and-error learning through iterative card placement
Cooperative small group gameplay (groups of 2-3 students, 32 groups total)
Information acquisition through in-game character biographies and event descriptions
Progressive difficulty levels to scaffold learning
Pretest-gameplay-posttest sequence embedded in 90-minute session
rq3.content_integration: Historical content from the Qing Dynasty (A.D. 1644-1911) was integrated based on domestic high school curriculum guidelines. Fifty important historical figures were designed as in-game card decks with four status categories (Royal Family, Political Minister, General Military, Foreign Forces or Anti-Government Elements). Five major historical events served as game battles: Taiping Kingdom of Heaven, Self-Strengthening Movement, First Sino-Japanese War, Nien Rebellion, and Siege of the International Legations. Relations between figures and events were categorized as participant, contemporary, or irrelevance based on historical accuracy of timelines and involvement.

implementation_barriers: Limited experimental time constrained the game to 5 events and 3 difficulty levels (full version has more content)
Game design may be biased toward certain game groups, particularly male students who perceived it as more useful and easier to use
Requires preloaded mobile devices for each student group
Students needed researcher intervention for technical problems (e.g., unexpected game quits)
methodology_limitations: No control group (single-group pre-experimental design) limits causal inference
Convenience sampling from researcher's own lecture classes threatens external validity
Short intervention period (50 minutes of gameplay) may not reflect long-term learning effects
Whether high-level cognitive processes are facilitated by the game remains unknown
Collaboration and problem-solving processes during gameplay were not measured
No data triangulation methods used (e.g., system operation records, discussion data)
negative_effects: Gender bias in perceived usefulness and ease of use favoring male students
Female students rated the game lower on usefulness and ease of use, possibly due to less familiarity with game designs and operations
mitigation_strategies: Authors suggest future integration of other methods for data triangulation (system operation records, discussion data)
Authors suggest analyzing students' high-level cognitive behaviors to better understand the cognitive thinking process
Despite gender differences in perception, learning performance and game element evaluations showed no significant gender difference, suggesting the game is useful for all genders

domain1.q1_evidence: The study clearly describes the target population (high school freshmen in northern Taiwan), the sampling method (convenience sampling from researcher's lecture classes), inclusion criteria (no prior formal courses on Qing Dynasty content), and provides detailed participant demographics (N=66, 24 boys/42 girls, average age 16.26).
domain1.q2_evidence: Convenience sampling from the researcher's own lecture classes severely limits representativeness. The sample is drawn from a single school in northern Taiwan and may not be representative of high school students more broadly. No randomization or justification for sample size is provided.

domain2.q3_evidence: History learning performance was measured with a researcher-developed pretest/posttest using relation matching items aligned with game content (48-point scale). The game evaluation questionnaire was adapted from Hou and Chou (2011) with established reliability (Cronbach's alpha = .90; prior use showed reliability of .783). The 5-point Likert scale covered perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and game elements with established theoretical grounding (Davis, 1989; Prensky & Thiagarajan, 2001).
domain2.q4_evidence: Appropriate statistical tests were used: paired-samples t-test for pretest-posttest comparison and independent-samples t-test for gender comparisons. Results are reported with means, standard deviations, t-values, and p-values. Effect sizes are not reported, which is a minor limitation.

domain3.q5_evidence: Interpretations generally align with results. The authors correctly note that the pre-experimental design limits causal claims. However, they make some causal-sounding statements ('the Void Broken 2.0 can help students learn more') despite the lack of a control group. The discussion of gender differences is balanced and appropriate.
domain3.q6_evidence: The authors acknowledge several limitations: the unknown facilitation of high-level cognitive processes, unexplored collaboration/problem-solving processes, and the need for data triangulation. However, they do not explicitly discuss the major threats to validity from the pre-experimental design (no control group) or convenience sampling, nor do they discuss potential testing effects or the short intervention duration.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: While the study uses appropriate measurement tools and statistical analyses (Domain 2: Low), the single-group pre-experimental design with no control group and convenience sampling from the researcher's own classes pose substantial threats to internal and external validity (Domain 1: High). The lack of explicit discussion of these major design limitations and occasional over-interpretation of causal effects add further concerns (Domain 3: Some concerns). The overall risk of bias is rated as High primarily due to the study design limitations.

pdf_filename: 3D Game-Based Approach to Learning Ancient Malay Heritage's History.pdf

bibliographic.title: 3D Game-Based Approach to Learning Ancient Malay Heritage's History
bibliographic.venue: 2023 IEEE 14th Control and System Graduate Research Colloquium (ICSGRC)

study_characteristics.sample_description: 19 play testers (school children aged 10 to 17 years old) volunteered for the playtesting and evaluation session. A separate needs-analysis survey was conducted with 183 secondary school students taking History subjects (78% male).
study_characteristics.study_design: descriptive
study_characteristics.game_name: Laksamana (3D game based on Hikayat Hang Tuah)
study_characteristics.aim: To develop a 3D third-person perspective game highlighting Ancient Malay culture and history (specifically Hikayat Hang Tuah and the history of Malacca under Sultan Mansur Shah) for learning purposes for school children, and to examine how pupils view history through a game-based approach.

eligibility.concerns: Small sample size (n=19 for evaluation). Primarily a design-and-development study with limited formal evaluation methodology. No control group comparison with statistical analysis. Qualitative evaluation is informal (observation and verbal questioning).

rq1.conceptualization: The study conceptualizes game-based learning (GBL) as students achieving learning objectives by playing games that blend instructional information and games with little or no supervision by the teacher (citing Prensky). The paper frames GBL as an approach where digital games serve as instruments for supporting and fostering contextual learning, with the 3D game environment allowing players to experience historical settings and learn history through gamification. The study uses GBL and gamification somewhat interchangeably, focusing on immersive 3D game experiences as a vehicle for history education.
theoretical_frameworks: ADDIE Model (Analyze, Design, Develop, Implement, Evaluate)

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Verbal quiz of 10 questions after reading session and after playtesting session. Average game completion duration measured. Survey with 183 respondents on perceptions of 3D game-based history learning (yes/no questions).
rq2.statistical_results: Reading session: highest score was 3 out of 10 questions correct; 3 out of 19 completed reading but had difficulty answering. Playtesting session: all 19 participants completed the game; average duration 13 minutes; highest score 9 out of 10 questions correct. Survey results: 71% found it easier to play 3D games and understand the story; 94% agreed 3D games can create interest to learn history; 85% agreed 3D game visualizes ancient Malay heritage better than textbook images; 77% agreed playing game can relate with the history of Hikayat Hang Tuah.
rq2.comparative_methodology: Within-subjects informal comparison: same group of 19 participants completed a reading session (textbook content) and a playtesting session. Performance on verbal quiz compared informally (highest score 3/10 for reading vs 9/10 for game).
rq2.key_outcomes: Students performed substantially better on verbal history questions after playtesting the 3D game (highest 9/10) compared to after reading textbook content (highest 3/10). Students showed more engagement and interest with the game compared to reading. The animation in the game related to history taught in school, interactions enhanced interest, and challenges provided motivation.
rq2.engagement_results: Students read textbook content in monotone and were less interested in reading the whole content. In contrast, school children seemed to love playing the 3D game based on their feedback. The interaction in the game enhanced interest in children to keep playing and gaining knowledge. The challenges in the game gave motivation to complete the game.

game_design_elements: Third-person perspective gameplay
3D immersive historical environment
Character combat system
Cutscenes for narrative storytelling
Tutorial session
Game levels with objectives/challenges
Inventory system
Character skills
Object interaction
Sound effects and background music
Semi-realistic art style
Victory screen
Pause menu with options (sound, graphics)
technological_platforms: Adobe Photoshop - concept art and UI
instructional_strategies: Experiential learning through 3D virtual environment exploration
Narrative-driven learning adapted from historical literary source (Hikayat Hang Tuah)
Game-based learning (GBL) with blended instructional content
Visual immersion in historical setting for contextual learning
Challenge-based motivation to complete objectives
rq3.content_integration: History content is integrated through the game's storyline adapted from the book 'Hikayat Hang Tuah' (published 1908), set in 15th century Malacca during the reign of Sultan Mansur Shah. The 3D environment recreates the ancient Malay era including Malay villages, Istana Melaka (Malacca Palace), buildings, and interiors of the period. Players experience the story of Hang Tuah, Malacca's greatest warrior, through cutscenes and gameplay. Facts from the History school subject are included with modifications in the game including plot twists, character appearance, and environments. The semi-realistic art style was purposely chosen to accurately reflect the historical background.

implementation_barriers: Resources of the history of the warrior of Melaka are quite scarce and have numerous changes
Characters and stories in the video game may not be as accurate as anticipated due to limited historical sources
Making a video game is a lengthy process that should be completed in a group to save time
Traditional elderly and adults still believe that games will impart bad influence on younger generations
Students currently have no interest in studying history and dislike reading
methodology_limitations: Small evaluation sample (n=19 play testers)
No formal control group with statistical comparison
Evaluation based on informal verbal questioning and observation rather than validated instruments
No pre-test/post-test design with standardized assessment
Survey and playtesting evaluation methods lack rigor
Reading session and playtesting session comparison is informal and not controlled for confounding variables
mitigation_strategies: Future work proposed to conduct comparative analysis assessing effectiveness of 3D game-based learning vs. traditional methods
Future work to develop and evaluate appropriate assessment methods and tools for measuring learning effectiveness
Future work to add more variety and skill on character attributes and expand the storyline

domain1.q1_evidence: The paper states 'A group of participants are recruited for two sessions' and 'A total of 19 play testers are volunteered to participate' but does not specify any inclusion/exclusion criteria for participant selection beyond age range (10-17 years old) and being school children.
domain1.q2_evidence: The 19 play testers 'volunteered to participate' but no information is provided about how they were recruited, from which school(s), or whether they represent the target population of Malaysian secondary school students. The separate survey had 183 respondents chosen 'randomly' with invitations sent through email, all being 'students in secondary school and taking History subjects.'

domain2.q3_evidence: The evaluation used informal verbal questioning ('asked to do so' about the game's plot) with 10 questions, but the paper does not describe whether these questions were validated or how they were developed. No validated assessment instruments were used. The needs-analysis survey used simple yes/no questions in Google Form without reported validity or reliability.
domain2.q4_evidence: The paper reports only descriptive findings from observation and verbal quiz (e.g., 'highest score is 9 out of 10 questions are correct', 'average duration is 13 minutes') without any statistical analysis. The comparison between reading session (highest 3/10) and playtesting session (highest 9/10) is informal with no statistical tests applied.

domain3.q5_evidence: The paper concludes 'this video game can be used to help educate history' based on informal observations and verbal responses, but the evidence presented (comparison of highest scores between reading and playtesting) is limited and the interpretation may overstate what the informal evaluation supports.
domain3.q6_evidence: The paper acknowledges that 'The characters and stories in the video game may not be as nice as anticipated because the resources of the history of the warrior of Melaka are quite scarce' and proposes future comparative analysis and development of 'appropriate assessment methods and tools.' However, the paper does not explicitly discuss the methodological limitations of the small sample size, lack of validated instruments, or the informal nature of the evaluation.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study has high overall risk of bias due to: (1) no clear participant selection criteria and volunteer-based convenience sampling with only 19 participants; (2) absence of validated assessment instruments, relying instead on informal verbal questioning and behavioral observation; (3) no statistical analysis of results, with only descriptive comparisons between reading and playtesting sessions; (4) no control group or rigorous experimental design; (5) limited discussion of methodological limitations. The study is primarily a design-and-development paper with informal evaluation rather than a rigorous empirical study.

pdf_filename: Designing Computer Simulation Game for Learning the History of the Kingdom of Majapahit.pdf

bibliographic.title: Designing Computer Simulation Game for Learning the History of the Kingdom of Majapahit
bibliographic.venue: Conference (exact venue not specified in paper; published November 2014)

study_characteristics.education_level: Primary/secondary education (Indonesian curriculum context; game also designed with undergraduate student involvement)
study_characteristics.sample_description: No empirical evaluation with participants was conducted. Undergraduate students at Universitas Kristen Petra served as visual artists creating game assets, but no formal user study or testing with learners is reported.
study_characteristics.study_design: Design-based research (game design and development, first stage only; no empirical evaluation)
study_characteristics.game_name: Unnamed Majapahit simulation game (no formal title given)
study_characteristics.aim: To design a computer simulation game for learning the history of the Kingdom of Majapahit (13th-14th century Java, Indonesia), using archaeological studies to create historically accurate visual reconstructions and gameplay scenarios based on real historical events.

eligibility.concerns: This is a design paper (stage 1 of a two-stage project) describing game concept, design methodology, and asset creation. No empirical evaluation of learning outcomes or user testing with students is reported. The second stage (prototype development and evaluation) was planned but not yet completed at time of publication.

rq1.conceptualization: Computer games are conceptualized as an e-learning tool that can build student interest in history by providing intriguing facts as narrative merged within gameplay, engaging students with imaginative virtual worlds and simulation of real-world environments and hypothetical situations. The game is positioned as a supplementary learning tool to be used beyond the classroom, enabling students to voluntarily add study time through multitasking (learning while playing). The authors draw on Gee's five principles of game-based learning (active and creative learning, design learning, semiotic learning, semiotic domains, and metalevel thinking) and Francis's four models for game-based learning (situated learning in virtual environments, overt instructions and reflective discussions, practical media production, and critical framing).
theoretical_frameworks: Gee's five basic principles of learning in games (active and creative learning, design learning, semiotic learning, semiotic domains, learning metalevel thinking of semiotic domains)

Francis's four models for game-based learning in formal education (situated learning in virtual environment, overt instructions and reflective discussions, practical media production, critical framing)
Gentile's perspective on video games designed for learning purposes
Benjamin's concept of authenticity in relation to time and space

rq2.key_outcomes: No empirical evaluation was conducted. The paper presents a design-phase project only. Expected outcomes described conceptually include: increased student interest in Majapahit history, ability to challenge known conceptions through experimentation and observation, emotional engagement with historical narrative, development of analytical thinking through strategy gameplay, and providing students with a different perspective compared to course books.

game_design_elements: Turn-based strategy gameplay with AI opponent
Historical narrative structure divided into 3 dramatic stages (Beginning: 1292-1319 AD, Golden Era: 1320-1389 AD, Fall: 1390-1406 AD)
Two levels of play (global strategic map level for territorial expansion via military/diplomacy, and tactical battle level for military engagements)
Player choice between military conquest and diplomatic agreement strategies
Archaeologically-based visual reconstruction of characters, environments, and architecture
Main and supporting character classifications (narrative: protagonist/antagonist; gameplay: playable/NPC)
Character visual design based on archaeological artifacts, relief carvings, statues, and historical records
Game environments based on archaeological research (natural and man-made environments)
Multiple architectural styles (old Javanese, old Majapahit, new Majapahit)
Infographics, images (still and moving), text, and UI as visual elements
Narrative-driven gameplay providing context and motivation for player actions
technological_platforms: 3D modeling for game characters and environments
instructional_strategies: Experience-based learning through gameplay (analyze challenges, devise strategies, test, implement, draw conclusions)
Virtual reconstruction for observational learning of historically accurate environments
Narrative-driven learning transforming historical facts into interactive story
Simulation of historical events with variable outcomes encouraging experimentation
Strategy-based problem solving requiring analysis and critical thinking
Situated learning in virtual environment (Francis model)
Critical framing through historical scenario engagement
rq3.content_integration: Historical content is deeply integrated into both gameplay mechanics and visual design. The game narrative follows the actual chronological history of Majapahit (1292-1406 AD). Game scenarios are based on real historical events, territorial maps reflect actual kingdom boundaries from archaeological research, character designs are based on archaeological studies of carvings, relief, statues, and historical records (clothing, fashion, social stratification). Building architecture follows documented old Javanese, old Majapahit, and new Majapahit styles. Natural environments are based on present-day Trowulan geography. The game allows alternative historical outcomes through player choices while maintaining relevance to historical facts.

implementation_barriers: Time constraints of formal education system make classroom integration of computer games difficult (50 minutes to 1 hour standard class duration is insufficient)
Commercial games not designed for classroom time frames
Game can only be applied beyond the classroom as supplementary learning
Difficulty implementing emotional-approach-based learning within the mechanized structure of formal education
Incomplete historical records of Majapahit require subjective interpretation to fill gaps
Authenticity cannot be fully achieved due to temporal distance (Benjamin's concept) — players cannot truly experience the past
methodology_limitations: Paper presents only the first stage (design); no prototype evaluation or empirical testing conducted
Visual reconstruction relies on fragmentary archaeological evidence requiring subjective interpretation
Facial features of characters based on illustrator's subjective preferences rather than archaeological evidence
Source references rarely found intact, requiring degrees of subjective interpretation
No complete historical document of Majapahit exists to validate accuracy
Second level of gameplay (battle mode) was still under development at time of writing
negative_effects: Research indicates gameplay with excessive violence and/or distorted gender representation can negatively affect player behavior, especially at early age (cited from Gentile)
Commercial games do not provide means for players to reflect on learning activities — players become too focused on play
Virtual reconstruction may not provide enough room for imagination
mitigation_strategies: Designing gameplay specifically for learning purposes rather than using commercial games
Integrating Francis's four models (situated learning, overt instructions/reflective discussions, practical media production, critical framing) to maintain educational relevance
Using archaeological studies as basis for visual design to maintain historical accuracy
Guiding players' perception to remain relevant with historical facts through narrative and visual stimuli
Positioning game as beyond-classroom supplement rather than trying to fit within class time constraints

domain1.q1_evidence: No empirical study was conducted; there is no participant selection, sampling, or eligibility criteria described. The paper is purely a game design description.
domain1.q2_evidence: No sample of participants was studied. Undergraduate students were involved as visual artists for asset creation, but there is no learner evaluation sample.

domain2.q3_evidence: No measurement instruments or data collection tools were used. No assessment of learning outcomes, engagement, or usability was conducted.
domain2.q4_evidence: No data analysis was performed. The paper presents design rationale and game concept without any empirical data or systematic analysis of effectiveness.

domain3.q5_evidence: Claims about the game's potential benefits (increasing interest, emotional engagement, analytical thinking) are speculative and not supported by empirical evidence. Conclusions are aspirational rather than evidence-based.
domain3.q6_evidence: The paper does acknowledge several limitations: difficulty of integrating games in formal education time constraints, incompleteness of historical records requiring subjective interpretation, the inherent impossibility of achieving full historical authenticity, and the need for further research on implementation within formal education.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: This is a design-phase paper presenting game concept, methodology, and visual asset development for a Majapahit history simulation game. No empirical evaluation, user testing, or learning outcome assessment was conducted. All claims about educational benefits are theoretical/aspirational. The study represents Stage 1 of a two-stage project, with the evaluation stage (Stage 2) not yet completed. While the design rationale is well-articulated and grounded in educational game design theory (Gee, Francis, Gentile), the absence of any empirical evidence makes the risk of bias for any effectiveness claims very high.

pdf_filename: Development of a game for History Course of Secondary School Students.pdf

bibliographic.title: Development of a game for History Course of Secondary School Students
bibliographic.venue: ICETAS 2017 (International Conference on Engineering, Technology and Applied Science)

study_characteristics.sample_description: Eight history course teachers from three schools in Hyderabad, Sindh, Pakistan participated in classroom observations, preliminary interviews, and cognitive walkthrough evaluation. Three schools (A: 37 students, B: 18 students, C: 30 students in 8th grade) were observed.
study_characteristics.study_design: Qualitative design-based research (classroom observation, preliminary interviews, prototype development, and cognitive walkthrough evaluation with think-aloud technique)
study_characteristics.game_type: Digital game-based learning (DGBL) prototype - desktop application
study_characteristics.aim: To develop a game prototype for history-based courses for secondary school students that improves engagement and learning by providing an interactive alternative to traditional lecture-based teaching

eligibility.concerns: The study focuses on game prototype development and formative evaluation (cognitive walkthrough with teachers only), not on measuring student learning outcomes. No student-based experiment was conducted. The game is a DGBL prototype rather than a gamification application per se, though it incorporates gamification elements like practice tests, feedback emojis, and performance tracking.

rq1.conceptualization: The study conceptualizes the game as a digital game-based learning (DGBL) tool that combines educational content with interactive game elements. It is framed as a technological intervention for history education that supplements traditional lecture-based teaching by incorporating multimedia content, text-to-speech, practice tests with varied question types, emoji-based feedback, navigation features, and performance reporting. The authors see games as interactive tools that provide challenges and entertainment to achieve educational goals.

rq2.key_outcomes: Qualitative outcomes from cognitive walkthrough with 8 teachers: (1) The game environment start screen was perceived as attractive and engaging; (2) Sound clips and text-to-speech were found very helpful for learning and memorizing content; (3) Variety of practice test question types gained teacher attention and interest; (4) Overall evaluation of game was satisfactory and accepted by teachers; (5) Teachers confirmed the prototype could help engage and motivate students. No quantitative student learning outcome data was collected.
rq2.engagement_results: Teachers reported that the game prototype environment was attractive and increased interest to play it. Participants found the pause/stop feature and text-to-speech helpful for understanding content. The practice test variety was appreciated for gaining attention and interest. However, excessive animations were found distracting and hindered focus on content. Teachers confirmed the prototype addresses the identified need for an interactive, non-lecture-based approach to history teaching.

game_design_elements: Login/registration system
Topic selection interface
Lecture content with multimedia (images and text)
Text-to-speech audio for content delivery
Practice test with multiple question types (best answer, select all, picture-sound matching)
Emoji-based feedback (happy emoji for correct, sad emoji for wrong, thinking emoji for pending)
Shuffled answer options for repeated practice
Student performance tracking and statistics reports
Navigation controls (forward, backward, pause, stop, exit)
Topic switching capability during lectures
Unlimited practice test attempts
instructional_strategies: Multimedia-based content presentation (images + text + audio)
Self-paced navigation with pause/stop/replay controls
Formative assessment through practice tests with immediate feedback
Multiple question formats to address different cognitive levels
Performance tracking and reporting for teacher monitoring
Content based on 8th grade Social Studies book topics (Allama Iqbal, Muslim Invasion in the Sub-continent, Import and Export of Pakistan)
rq3.content_integration: Three topics from the 8th grade Social Studies book were integrated into the game prototype: 'Allama Iqbal', 'Muslim Invasion in the Sub-continent', and 'Import and Export of Pakistan'. Content was presented through topic-relevant images with textual content, accompanied by text-to-speech audio narration that elaborates on the written text and provides examples and meanings of difficult words. The content was developed based on teacher input from preliminary interviews about what should be included in the technological intervention.

implementation_barriers: Traditional lecture-based teaching dominates history classrooms with minimal student involvement
History content perceived as dry, tough, and difficult to memorize by students
Schools use only board and marker with no technological resources
Teachers find it very difficult to maintain student attention and engagement
Too many dates and names in history content confuse students
No existing educational games found online for this specific history content
methodology_limitations: Only teachers participated in cognitive walkthrough evaluation, not actual students
Small sample of 8 teachers from 3 schools in one city (Hyderabad, Pakistan)
No quantitative measurement of learning outcomes or student performance
No controlled experiment or comparison with traditional teaching
Prototype stage only - not a fully developed or deployed game
Qualitative data only from think-aloud technique during cognitive walkthrough
Limited to 3 history topics from 8th grade Social Studies
negative_effects: Excessive character-wise animations were distracting and annoyed participants
Too many animations made content appear slower and hindered effective readability
Text appearing on screen with too many animations prevented focus on content
Animation speed was perceived as too slow
mitigation_strategies: Incorporated all teacher suggestions from cognitive walkthrough into improved prototype
Changed school names to appear as a dropdown list to prevent spelling mistakes
Added navigation buttons for front and back screens
Suggested replacing character-wise animation with line/paragraph-wise text display
Recommended using icons instead of emojis to represent correct/incorrect answers
Plan to conduct future experiments with actual students in real classroom environment

domain1.q1_evidence: The study does not provide clear eligibility criteria for school or participant selection beyond convenience. Three schools were described as 'randomly selected' from Hyderabad but no randomization procedure is described. Teachers were identified with help of school management, introducing potential selection bias.
domain1.q2_evidence: Only 3 schools from one city (Hyderabad, Sindh, Pakistan) and 8 teachers participated. This is a very small, geographically limited sample. No students were included in the evaluation. The schools observed had between 18-37 students in 8th grade, all using only board and marker with lecture-based teaching.

domain2.q3_evidence: Classroom observation was direct observation by the researcher with no structured observation protocol described. Preliminary interviews used open-ended questions but no validated instrument. Cognitive walkthrough followed Wharton et al.'s method with think-aloud technique, which is a recognized usability evaluation method, but it was applied only to teachers, not to the target student population. No learning outcome measures were used.
domain2.q4_evidence: Data analysis methods are not clearly described. Qualitative data from observations, interviews, and cognitive walkthrough are presented descriptively with no systematic coding or thematic analysis framework described. Interview findings are presented in tabular form but without rigorous qualitative analysis methodology. No triangulation of data sources is formally discussed.

domain3.q5_evidence: The conclusions claim the cognitive walkthrough 'has been proved very effective' and the game evaluation is 'satisfactory and accepted by teachers,' but these conclusions are based only on qualitative teacher feedback during a prototype walkthrough. The paper does not distinguish between teacher perceptions and actual effectiveness for student learning. Claims about engagement and learning improvement are not supported by student data.
domain3.q6_evidence: The paper acknowledges in the conclusion that 'it is important to measure the impact of game on learning of students' and states the researcher 'intends to perform different experiments with students in real time classroom environment.' However, no formal limitations section is included, and the significant methodological limitations (no student participants, no learning measures, small sample, single city) are not explicitly discussed as limitations.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study presents a prototype development process with formative evaluation by teachers only. There are no student learning outcomes measured, no controlled comparison, no validated assessment instruments, no systematic qualitative analysis methodology described, and a very small sample from a single geographic location. The conclusions overstate findings relative to the evidence. While the design-based approach with classroom observation, teacher interviews, and cognitive walkthrough is reasonable for early-stage prototype development, the study has high risk of bias across all domains when evaluated as evidence for the effectiveness of gamification in history education.

pdf_filename: Development of Educational Game for Indonesian History Lesson Focusing on Indonesia Pre-Literacy Relics 'Prehistoria' for Grade X High School Student.pdf

bibliographic.title: Development of Educational Game for Indonesian History Lesson Focusing on Indonesia Pre-Literacy Relics 'Prehistoria' for Grade X High School Student
bibliographic.venue: 2020 International Conference on Computer Engineering, Network and Intelligent Multimedia (CENIM 2020)

study_characteristics.sample_description: 5 respondents who completed the survey (4 from 10th grade, 1 from 12th grade); additional users played the game and contributed playtime data recorded on the server
study_characteristics.study_design: Design and development research with post-play survey using 5-point Likert scale questionnaire
study_characteristics.game_type: Puzzle-adventure digital educational game (2D, WebGL browser-based)
study_characteristics.aim: To create a puzzle-adventure type digital game that can help educate Grade X high school students about the Indonesian pre-literacy period, developed with Unity and deployed via WebGL, aligned with Indonesia's revised 2013 national curriculum

eligibility.concerns: Very small sample size (n=5 respondents); no pre-post test of learning outcomes; primarily a game development study with limited evaluation of educational effectiveness; COVID-19 pandemic prevented controlled face-to-face testing

rq1.conceptualization: The study frames the work as gamification of Indonesian History education, conceptualizing it as using educational games (a subset of serious games) as a medium of education alongside existing methods. Educational games are defined as serious games used in education, while serious games are games designed, developed, and used outside of entertainment purposes. The gamification approach involves creating a curriculum-aligned digital game (puzzle-adventure) that integrates historical content from the pre-literacy period into gameplay mechanics.
theoretical_frameworks: Serious games framework (games designed outside entertainment purposes)
Curriculum-aligned game design (Indonesia's revised 2013 national curriculum)
Game-based learning as supplementary educational medium

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Object recognition rates by respondents (e.g., Cave Painting recognized by all 5, Trilobites by only 1); Age recognition rates (Megalithic by 3, Paleozoic by only 1, one respondent recognized no ages); Average gameplay completion time of 254.36 seconds across 5 levels
rq2.statistical_results: Descriptive statistics only (frequency counts and averages). Average play time per level: Level 1 = 38.96s, Level 2 = 63.2s, Level 3 = 60s, Level 4 = 64.1s, Level 5 = 28.1s. Total average game time = 254.36 seconds. 60% recognized puzzle genre, 40% recognized adventure genre. No inferential statistics reported.
rq2.key_outcomes: The game was successfully developed and is playable in approximately 4-5 minutes. Many ancient objects were well-recognized by respondents (e.g., Cave Painting by all 5 respondents, Menhir and Planting by 4). However, some objects (Trilobites, Cephalaptis, Ax, Moko) were recognized by only 1 respondent. Age recognition was problematic, with one respondent not recognizing any historical age. The survey identified multiple usability issues including difficult-to-use arrow movement controls, disruptive UI, hard-to-understand health and toggle status features, and a strong need for a tutorial.
rq2.engagement_results: Enemy challenge was rated as adequate (3 of 5 respondents rated it 'Good'). Difficulty perception varied widely among respondents. 4 of 5 respondents said a tutorial would benefit the game. UI was perceived as disruptive by 3 of 5 respondents. Arrow movement was perceived as very difficult to use by 3 of 5 respondents.

game_design_elements: Level progression across 5 historical periods (Paleozoic, Mesolithic, Neolithic, Megalithic, present day)
Photo capture mechanic (photographing historical objects at target spots)
Health system (HP bar decreasing upon enemy contact)
Inventory system (collecting photographed objects)
Two enemy types (patrolling ancient humans and chasing assassins)
Fog of war map system (areas revealed as player explores)
Arrow movement controls (directional navigation)
Toggle status HUD visibility
Puzzle elements (finding objects, navigating maps)
Adventure elements (time travel narrative, exploration)
Level-based difficulty scaling
instructional_strategies: Curriculum synergy with Indonesia's revised 2013 national curriculum (Erlangga 10th Grade Indonesian History textbook)
Experiential learning through time travel narrative (exploring historical periods firsthand)
Object discovery and identification (photographing ancient relics and artifacts)
Progressive historical period exploration (Paleozoic through Megalithic)
Contextual learning through map environments designed to represent different historical ages
Information display when photographing objects (showing object name and details)
rq3.content_integration: Historical content from the pre-literacy period of Indonesian history is directly integrated into the gameplay. Each of the five game levels corresponds to a specific historical age (Paleozoic, Mesolithic, Neolithic, Megalithic, and present day). Players collect photographs of period-specific artifacts and relics (e.g., Trilobites and Cephalaptis for Paleozoic; hunting tools, Kjokkenmoddinger, cave paintings for Mesolithic; axes, pickaxes for Neolithic; Menhir, Nekara, Moko, Sarcophagus for Megalithic). Content was selected directly from the Erlangga 10th Grade Indonesian History textbook to align with the national curriculum.

implementation_barriers: COVID-19 pandemic prevented face-to-face controlled testing environment due to government restrictions
Very small sample size (only 5 respondents) limiting generalizability
Performance/loading speed issues with WebGL deployment
UI perceived as disruptive by majority of respondents
Arrow movement controls found very difficult to use by majority
Several game features (Health, Toggle Status) poorly understood by respondents
Adventure elements not well-recognized by respondents (only 40%)
Map coloring did not effectively indicate which historical age/period the player was in
Some historical objects and ages not well-recognized despite being in-game
methodology_limitations: Very small sample size (n=5 respondents) with no power analysis
No control group or pre-post test design to measure actual learning outcomes
No validated assessment instrument for measuring historical knowledge acquisition
Convenience sampling (4 students from 10th grade, 1 from 12th grade)
Survey-based evaluation only with 5-point Likert scale; no objective learning measures
COVID-19 restrictions prevented controlled experimental conditions
Limited to a single textbook as curriculum reference (Erlangga publisher)
No comparison with other teaching methods or tools
Descriptive statistics only; no inferential statistical analysis
negative_effects: One respondent could not recognize any historical age from the game
Several historical objects recognized by only 1 of 5 respondents (Trilobites, Cephalaptis, Ax, Moko)
UI disruption during gameplay reported by majority of respondents
Arrow movement controls perceived as very difficult, potentially hindering learning experience
Toggle Status feature almost unrecognized (only 1 of 5 respondents)
Health feature difficult to understand despite being a core mechanic
mitigation_strategies: Authors recommend adding a tutorial to help players understand game features and mechanics
Recommend improving adventure elements to increase recognition
Suggest optimizing game loading performance
Propose improving clarity of historical objects in the game
Recommend making features easier to understand
Suggest adding more content within the pre-literacy period
Propose future full human-machine interaction and content testing

domain1.q1_evidence: No clear inclusion/exclusion criteria for participant selection. Only 5 respondents were used (4 from 10th grade, 1 from 12th grade), with no explanation of how they were selected or recruited. The 12th-grade student is outside the target population (10th grade).
domain1.q2_evidence: Sample of 5 respondents is extremely small and unlikely to be representative of the target population (Grade X high school students in Indonesia). No demographic information beyond grade level is provided. COVID-19 restrictions prevented proper controlled testing.

domain2.q3_evidence: The survey questionnaire was custom-designed with no reported validation. It uses a mix of binary yes/no questions, 5-point Likert scales, and open recognition questions. No reliability or validity metrics are reported for the instrument. The 5-point Likert scale is referenced but the questionnaire itself was not validated.
domain2.q4_evidence: Only descriptive statistics (frequency counts and simple averages) are reported. No inferential statistics, no effect sizes, no confidence intervals. The average formula is presented but applied only to gameplay time data. No validated analysis framework for educational effectiveness is used.

domain3.q5_evidence: The authors present results that are broadly consistent with the data shown in their tables. They acknowledge negative findings (poor object/age recognition, UI problems, control difficulties). However, the claim of 'potential for educational use' in the abstract is not strongly supported by the survey data, which shows significant recognition failures.
domain3.q6_evidence: The authors include a dedicated 'Limitation and Future Works' section acknowledging COVID-19 constraints, limited scope (Indonesian History only), tool limitations, and identifying specific areas for improvement. They also discuss limitations within the Discussion section, noting problems with object recognition, age recognition, UI, and controls.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study has high overall risk of bias primarily due to: (1) extremely small sample size of only 5 respondents with no justification or power analysis; (2) no validated measurement instruments; (3) no control group or pre-post design to assess actual learning outcomes; (4) only descriptive statistics with no inferential analysis; (5) convenience sampling with one participant outside the target population; and (6) COVID-19 preventing proper controlled testing conditions. The study is primarily a game development and usability report rather than a rigorous evaluation of educational effectiveness.

pdf_filename: Digital game-based learning (DGBL) model and development methodology for teaching history.pdf

bibliographic.title: Digital Game-based learning (DGBL) model and development methodology for teaching history
bibliographic.venue: WSEAS Transactions on Computers

study_characteristics.sample_description: 582 Form Four students and 15 teachers from five local secondary schools in Selangor, Malaysia; additional interviews with four history teachers
study_characteristics.study_design: mixed-methods (preliminary needs analysis via questionnaire and interview, document analysis, and literature review leading to model proposal)
study_characteristics.game_type: digital game-based learning (DGBL) courseware / educational game
study_characteristics.game_name: DGBL-ID model (proposed framework; no specific game name - prototype to be developed using Virtools for 3D educational game)
study_characteristics.aim: To propose a DGBL model for History educational game design and a development methodology (DGBL-ID) that combines Instructional Design (ID) and game development processes for teaching history

eligibility.concerns: This is primarily a model/framework proposal paper rather than an empirical evaluation of a finished game. The empirical component is a preliminary needs analysis survey, not an intervention study testing game effectiveness. The proposed game prototype had not yet been developed or evaluated at the time of publication.

rq1.explicit_definition: DGBL is a paradigm which utilizes the game as a medium for conveying the learning contents, it is all about leveraging the power of computer games to captivate and engage endusers for a specific purpose, such as to develop new knowledge and skills. DGBL is also defined as an application which uses the characteristics of video and computer games to create engaging and immersive learning experiences for delivering specified learning goals, outcomes and experiences.
rq1.conceptualization: The authors conceptualize DGBL as combining pedagogy and digital game components. The pedagogy side includes learning goal setting, learning theory setting, educational psychology, country curriculum needs, patriotism and moral value, and memorization and forgetting theory. The digital game side includes game story's background, rules, immersive elements, enjoyment, multimedia technology, feedback, challenge/competition, and reward/award. Student engagement and cooperation bridge both components.
theoretical_frameworks: Memorization and Forgetting Theory (Davidovitch et al.)
Simulation-Games Instructional Systems Design Model (SG-ISD, referenced)
Games for Activating Thematic Engagement (GATE, referenced)

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Preliminary survey results: 79% of students have problems learning history; 70.6% find it difficult to memorize historical facts; 44.5% have no interest due to boring textbooks; 92% of students have experienced playing digital games; 83.6% like to play games; 69.5% stated playing digital games brings advantages. Failing percentage in history for SPM examination was 25.6% (2005), rising to 34.3% (2006). STPM failing percentage was 45.11% (2005).
rq2.statistical_results: Descriptive statistics only (percentages from survey). No inferential statistics. No pre/post intervention comparison as the game was not yet developed.
rq2.key_outcomes: The study identifies key problems in history learning (difficulty memorizing facts, lack of interest, boring teaching methods) and demonstrates student readiness for game-based learning. It proposes a DGBL model and DGBL-ID development methodology but does not yet report learning outcomes from an actual game intervention.
rq2.engagement_results: Survey findings indicate high student engagement with digital games in general: 92% have played digital/electronic games, 83.6% like to play games. Students prefer racing (67.2%), adventure (62.1%), and fighting games (55.9%). Key requirements for GBL history courseware include illustrating historical facts clearly (70.6%), increasing students' interest (66.7%), and learning history via entertained experience (65.5%).

game_design_elements: Game story's background (historical events with date, location, time)
Rules (clear instructions and regulations)
Immersive environment
Enjoyment
Feedback (instant learning response)
Multimedia technology (2D/3D animations, graphical environment, imitative sound)
Challenge and competition (adaptive difficulty levels)
Reward/Award (motivation to continue game play)
Role playing
Game levels with progressive difficulty
Narrative and storytelling
Cooperation among students
technological_platforms: 3D Studio Max or Maya (for character modeling)
instructional_strategies: Inquiry-based learning
Narrative-based learning
Problem solving
Constructivism
Adaptive learning based on individual ability
Synchronous/central game sessions (classroom-based, face-to-face)
Integration with national curriculum (KBSM - Integrated Curriculum for Secondary School)
Patriotism and moral values embedding
rq3.content_integration: The DGBL model integrates history content through two main components: pedagogy (learning goal setting, learning theory, educational psychology, curriculum needs, patriotism/moral values, memorization/forgetting theory) and digital games (story background, rules, immersive elements, enjoyment, multimedia, feedback, challenge/competition, rewards). The DGBL-ID development methodology has five phases: (1) Analysis - requirement/problem analysis, student characteristics, learning objectives, game idea, teaching environment; (2) Design - instructional design and game design including delivery method, teaching strategy, storyboard, multimedia elements, gameplay, art design, game levels; (3) Development - lesson plans, teaching resources, game prototype using Virtools; (4) Quality Assurance - play testing, alpha testing, beta testing, content verification against syllabus; (5) Implementation and Evaluation - launching on CD in school computer lab, usability and effectiveness evaluation.

No existing history courseware used in Malaysian schools at the time of the study
Conflict on how to merge Instructional Design and game development effectively
Still difficult to integrate games into formal education curriculum
Lack of teaching aid/material and not proficient in Malay Language (teacher-reported barriers)
methodology_limitations: The proposed DGBL model and DGBL-ID methodology had not yet been empirically validated at the time of publication
The game prototype was not yet developed or tested
The preliminary analysis was conducted only in five secondary schools in Selangor, limiting generalizability

Existing development methodologies reviewed had shortcomings: (a) do not explain instructional part clearly, (b) methodology is just a linear process without iterative development, (c) some phases or activities are not clear
After quality assurance phase, the methodology does not go back to design phase but only modifies within development phase, which could limit major redesign
Descriptive survey data only; no experimental or quasi-experimental evaluation of effectiveness
negative_effects: Students perceived history as a dead, boring subject with no commercial value
Difficulty in memorizing facts is the main problem (70.6% of students)
Declining pass rates in history examinations (SPM failing percentage increased from 25.6% in 2005 to 34.3% in 2006)
Students' negative attitudes toward history indirectly caused decrease in passing percentage
mitigation_strategies: Proposed DGBL approach as alternative to foster history learning through entertained experience
Proposed combining instructional design and game development into unified DGBL-ID methodology to address gaps in existing approaches
Included quality assurance phase with play testing, alpha testing, and beta testing to ensure error-free prototype
Incorporated iterative improvement within development phase
Designed model to include both pedagogy and game components to ensure educational effectiveness alongside engagement
Planned usability and effectiveness evaluation with target users (Form Four history students)

domain1.q1_evidence: The study clearly describes respondents: 582 Form Four students and 15 teachers from five local secondary schools in Selangor, with additional interviews of four history teachers. The document analysis covers SPM performance reports from 2002-2005. However, sampling method (convenience vs. random) is not explicitly stated.
domain1.q2_evidence: The sample is drawn only from five secondary schools in Selangor, Malaysia, which limits representativeness to the broader Malaysian secondary school population or to other countries. No justification for school selection is provided.

domain2.q3_evidence: The study uses questionnaires and interviews for the preliminary needs analysis, but no information is provided about the validation, reliability, or piloting of these instruments. The survey instruments are not described in detail.
domain2.q4_evidence: Analysis is limited to descriptive percentages from the survey. No inferential statistics are reported. The main contribution (DGBL model and DGBL-ID methodology) is based on literature review and the needs analysis but has not been empirically tested. No formal analytical framework is described for the document analysis or literature review.

domain3.q5_evidence: The findings from the preliminary analysis are used consistently to justify the proposed model components. However, the leap from survey results to model design involves subjective interpretation, and the authors do not discuss alternative interpretations of their findings.
domain3.q6_evidence: The paper acknowledges shortcomings in existing development methodologies but does not explicitly discuss limitations of its own study design, survey methodology, or the preliminary nature of the proposed model. No discussion of threats to validity or generalizability of findings.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study presents a theoretical model (DGBL) and development methodology (DGBL-ID) for history educational games, supported by a preliminary needs analysis survey. However, several significant concerns exist: (1) the proposed model and methodology were not empirically validated at the time of publication; (2) survey instruments lack reported validity/reliability; (3) sample is limited to one region of Malaysia; (4) analysis is purely descriptive; (5) study limitations are not discussed. While the model components are well-articulated and grounded in literature review, the absence of empirical validation of the proposed framework significantly limits the strength of evidence.

pdf_filename: Educational Computer Game for learning History Impact on learners’ level of knowledge and learners’ satisfaction.pdf

bibliographic.title: Educational Computer Game for learning History: Impact on learners' level of knowledge and learners' satisfaction
bibliographic.venue: 2019 7th International Conference on ICT & Accessibility (ICTA)

study_characteristics.education_level: Secondary school (average age 18-20, from different schools in Kairouan)
study_characteristics.sample_description: 36 volunteer participants from different schools in Kairouan, Tunisia. Divided into two groups: control group (20 participants, 15 male, 5 female, avg age 20) using traditional learning, and experimental group (16 participants, 13 male, 3 female, avg age 18) using the educational computer game.
study_characteristics.study_design: Quasi-experimental with pre-test/post-test control group design
study_characteristics.game_type: Educational computer game (2D action game, browser-based)
study_characteristics.aim: To introduce an educational computer game called 'LAST MISSION' designed for learning the history of World War 1 and World War 2, and to investigate whether its use has a positive effect on learners' level of knowledge and learners' satisfaction.
