risk_of_bias.overall_justification: High overall risk of bias due to: (1) limited and non-representative sample from a single district; (2) no description of instrument validity or reliability; (3) only descriptive statistics with no inferential analysis; (4) no actual GBL intervention implemented or evaluated - the study is a needs analysis and design proposal only; (5) no discussion of study limitations; (6) the proposed GBL model is not validated. The study provides useful preliminary data on problems in history learning and student readiness for GBL but does not constitute strong evidence for the effectiveness of game-based learning in history education.

pdf_filename: Game based technology to enhance the learning of history and cultural heritage.pdf

bibliographic.title: Game based technology to enhance the learning of history and cultural heritage
bibliographic.venue: ACM Conference on Advances in Computer Entertainment Technology (ACE 2009)

study_characteristics.sample_description: More than a hundred users with very diverse cultural backgrounds, including families, elderly people, and students
study_characteristics.study_design: descriptive
study_characteristics.aim: To present a game engine-based application where virtual environments and interactions promote learning the history of three European archaeological sites (Lokroi, Glauberg, Biskupin)

eligibility.concerns: Primarily a system/design description paper with only brief mention of user testing. No formal empirical evaluation reported beyond 'positive feedback' from 100+ users. Borderline for inclusion as it lacks formal outcome measures.

rq1.conceptualization: Game technology conceptualized as a means to support the learning process within Cultural Heritage sites through realistic virtual environments, discovery-based exploration of Points of Interest (POIs), and interactive navigation metaphors that amplify the role of discovery in learning.

rq2.key_outcomes: System tested by more than 100 users with diverse backgrounds; received positive feedback. No formal quantitative or qualitative outcome data reported.

game_design_elements: 3D virtual environment exploration
Hotspot-based Points of Interest (POIs) with multimedia content
Discovery-based information gathering
Environmental effects (fog, sky, water, particles)
Interactive navigation metaphors
instructional_strategies: Discovery-based learning through hotspot exploration
Multimedia content integration (video, images, 3D models, text)
Immersive virtual reconstruction of archaeological sites
rq3.content_integration: Three archaeological sites (Lokroi/Magna Graecia in Italy, Glauberg in Germany, Biskupin in Poland) were virtually reconstructed with a video game visual style. Historical information organized as Points of Interest containing multimedia material becomes accessible through exploration and discovery.

methodology_limitations: No formal evaluation methodology described
Only reports 'positive feedback' without quantitative or systematic qualitative data
Short paper format limits methodological detail

domain1.q1_evidence: No participant selection criteria described. Paper only states 'tested by more than a hundred users with very diverse cultural backgrounds.'
domain1.q2_evidence: Users described as having 'very diverse cultural backgrounds' including 'families, elderly people, students' but no formal sampling strategy described.

domain2.q3_evidence: No data collection instruments described. Paper only mentions 'positive feedback' without specifying how feedback was collected or measured.
domain2.q4_evidence: No data analysis methods described. Results limited to a single sentence about positive feedback.

domain3.q5_evidence: The claim of 'positive feedback' cannot be verified as no data is presented to support it.
domain3.q6_evidence: No limitations of the study or system evaluation are discussed.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: High risk across all three domains due to absence of formal evaluation methodology, no participant selection criteria, no validated data collection tools, no described analysis methods, and no discussion of limitations.

pdf_filename: Game-based augmented reality learning of Sarawak history in enhancing cultural heritage preservation.pdf

bibliographic.title: Game-based augmented reality learning of Sarawak history in enhancing cultural heritage preservation
bibliographic.venue: Indonesian Journal of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science
bibliographic.publisher: IAES (Institute of Advanced Engineering and Science)

study_characteristics.education_level: Not specified (general participants, no restriction on age or job position)
study_characteristics.sample_description: Twenty participants invited to evaluate the game-based AR features through dedicated gameplay durations and answering a distributed questionnaire; no restriction on job position or age, but required basic understanding of English
study_characteristics.study_design: Prototype development and evaluation using questionnaire-based usability and functional testing with GameFlow scale analysis
study_characteristics.game_type: Augmented reality game-based learning (location-based, multiplayer, collaborative treasure hunt)
study_characteristics.aim: To enhance AR technology in game-based cultural heritage and history preservation in Sarawak, supplement gamified experiences in learning James Brooke's history, design an AR game prototype, develop it with collaborative learning elements, and evaluate it for enhancing cultural heritage preservation

eligibility.concerns: The study focuses on cultural heritage preservation through history learning rather than formal history education in a classroom setting; sample is general participants rather than students in a history course; no control group or pre-post comparison

rq1.conceptualization: Game-based AR is conceptualized as a gamified approach to history learning where AR technology is combined with game elements (treasure hunt, hints/clues, quiz challenges, scoreboards, collaborative multiplayer) to create engaging and interactive experiences for cultural heritage preservation. The game-based AR is designed in the form of gamified features that disclose fun elements and increase AR learning experiences.
theoretical_frameworks: Flow theory (flow antecedents and flow experiences)

rq2.quantitative_metrics: GameFlow Scale measuring flow dimensions: Challenge (mean 3.85-4.50, SD .7609-.8751), Feedback (mean 4.10-4.20, SD .7182-.7678), Playability (mean 4.35-4.40, SD .5871-.6806), Concentration (mean 3.95-4.15, SD .8870-.9333), Control (mean 4.05-4.55, SD .5130-.8256), Knowledge (mean 4.45-4.75, SD .4442-.6048). Flow antecedents reliability alpha = .0286; Flow experiences reliability alpha = .6527; Control reliability alpha = .6471; Knowledge reliability alpha = .4590
rq2.statistical_results: Cronbach's alpha reliability estimates: Flow antecedents = .0286 (low/poor); Challenge = .1428 (poor); Feedback = .4631; Playability = .4456; Flow experiences = .6527 (generally good reliability); Concentration = .5616; Control = .6471 (reasonable); Knowledge = .4590. Mean scores ranged from 3.85 to 4.75 on a 5-point scale.
rq2.key_outcomes: Participants felt mediocre about the challenge and knowledge factors of the prototype. The GameFlow scale found that challenge and knowledge factors have low reliability. The design of game challenge is the major factor improving flow experience, but flow antecedents show poor reliability. Knowledge factor has room for improvement and is more relatable to the study objective. The study highlights enhancement of cultural heritage preservation through AR game-based experiences learned from James Brooke's history in Sarawak.
rq2.engagement_results: Usability testing measured five factors: Knowledge (items about improving history knowledge, understanding hints, wanting to learn more), Autonomy (understanding game walkthrough, distance indicator use, sense of control), Immersion (not noticing time passing, emotional investment in scores/titles, game absorption), Challenge (hints helping with quizzes, increasing difficulty, suitable difficulty), and Social Interaction (cooperating with teammates, ease of joining, collaboration improving skills). Mean scores generally above 4.0 on a 5-point scale suggest positive engagement.

game_design_elements: AR markers/tracking (hint cards, quiz cards)
Location-based GPS distance indicator
Multiplayer collaborative mode (Photon PUN networking)
Treasure hunt exploration mechanic
Hints and clues system
Quiz challenge (multiple-choice questions via AR)
Scoreboard system (records top 4 players)
Navigation system (splash screen, main menu, lobby selection)
Popup tutorial
Player titles and rankings based on quiz percentage
Lobby system (host creates, guest joins with room ID)
technological_platforms: Vuforia AR SDK (marker tracking and database)
instructional_strategies: Collaborative learning through multiplayer interaction
Location-based exploration of historical landmarks
Gamified treasure hunt to discover historical facts about James Brooke
Progressive hint unlocking tied to historical content
Quiz-based knowledge assessment integrated into gameplay
Associative, cognitive, and situational learning methods
rq3.content_integration: Historical content about James Brooke (White Rajah of Sarawak, reigned 1841-1868) is integrated through AR hint cards containing historical facts scattered across physical locations. Each hint relates to different historical facts about Sarawak's James Brooke, including extra information presented as hint sentences. Players explore the field to find hidden hint cards using GPS distance indicators, scan them with AR to reveal superimposed 3D historical content, and then complete quiz challenges to assess their learning about Sarawak history and cultural heritage.

implementation_barriers: GPS locating service accuracy and range errors between device and target
AR marker scanning requires bright environment and appropriate marker surface size
Multiplayer networking requires both players to stay within the same lobby for data synchronization
Participants need basic understanding of English to use the prototype
Static hint card content limits replayability and knowledge depth
Game difficulty distribution needs improvement for reasonable assessment
methodology_limitations: Small sample size (n=20) with no restriction on job position or age
No control group or pre-post experimental comparison
Low Cronbach's alpha reliability for flow antecedents (.0286) and challenge (.1428) dimensions
Knowledge factor reliability is low (.4590)
No demographic stratification in analysis
Evaluation based on self-reported questionnaire data only
negative_effects: Participants felt mediocre about the challenge and knowledge factors
Challenge factor has the lowest and most considerable gap between reliability dimensions
Flow antecedents show poor reliability value, making the assumption about game challenge improving flow experience doubtful
mitigation_strategies: Design hint cards in more interactive ways with more informative knowledge content
Implement multiple AR tracking targets to provide more hint options during scene exploration
Design cards with interactive minigames that grant rewards or achievements
Retrieve question bank and hints from database rather than static content for varied gameplay
Distribute questions and hints with more reasonable difficulties for each game phase
Reconsider a more reasonable assessment of game difficulties

domain1.q1_evidence: No clear inclusion/exclusion criteria for participants beyond basic English proficiency. The study states the collection of results was not based on respondents' job position or age, suggesting convenience sampling without defined eligibility criteria.
domain1.q2_evidence: Only 20 participants with no demographic restrictions or stratification. No information about how participants were recruited or whether they represent any target population. The sample may not be representative of intended users of history education games.

domain2.q3_evidence: The GameFlow Scale from Kiili's model was used, which is an established instrument. However, the Cronbach's alpha values were very poor for several dimensions: flow antecedents (.0286), challenge (.1428), feedback (.4631), playability (.4456), and knowledge (.4590). These values fall well below acceptable reliability thresholds (typically >.70), questioning the validity of measurements in this specific application.
domain2.q4_evidence: Analysis is limited to descriptive statistics (means, standard deviations) and Cronbach's alpha reliability estimates. No inferential statistics, no significance testing, and no effect sizes are reported. The authors acknowledge low reliability but still draw conclusions from these unreliable measurements.

domain3.q5_evidence: The authors acknowledge that flow antecedents show poor reliability and that the assumption about game challenge improving flow experience is 'doubtful.' However, they still conclude the study highlights enhancement of cultural heritage preservation without sufficient empirical evidence to support this claim given the measurement limitations.
domain3.q6_evidence: Some limitations are discussed implicitly (low reliability scores, mediocre participant feelings about challenge/knowledge). The conclusion section proposes improvements, acknowledging areas of weakness. However, there is no formal limitations section, and the small sample size and lack of experimental design are not explicitly discussed as limitations.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study has high risk of bias due to: (1) convenience sampling of only 20 participants with no clear selection criteria or demographic controls; (2) extremely poor reliability scores for key measurement dimensions (flow antecedents alpha = .0286, challenge alpha = .1428), questioning the validity of the evaluation instrument as applied; (3) no experimental design (no control group, no pre-post comparison); (4) only descriptive statistics with no inferential analysis; (5) conclusions about cultural heritage preservation enhancement are not well-supported by the empirical evidence presented. The study is primarily a prototype development and initial usability evaluation rather than a rigorous empirical assessment of learning outcomes.

pdf_filename: Games for Teaching and Learning History A Systematic Literature Review.pdf

bibliographic.title: Games for Teaching and Learning History: a Systematic Literature Review
bibliographic.venue: CEUR Workshop Proceedings

study_characteristics.country_of_application: Not applicable (systematic literature review with no specific country of application)
study_characteristics.sample_description: 78 studies for RQ1-3 (narrowed to 11 COTS-focused studies for RQ4) identified from Scopus database search conducted in March 2022. Initial search yielded 255 records, screened to 125, then refined to 78 after applying inclusion and exclusion criteria. Studies document game-based educational projects for teaching geography and/or history in secondary education.
study_characteristics.study_design: Systematic literature review
study_characteristics.game_type: Multiple types reviewed: educational games designed ad hoc (63 projects), Commercial Off-the-Shelf games (COTS, 11 projects), and student-designed games (4 projects)
study_characteristics.game_name: Not applicable (review covers multiple games including Sim City, Minecraft, Age of Empires, Civilization, Pokemon Go, Spore, Valiant Hearts, Dominations, Second Life, Kodu, and many ad hoc educational games)
study_characteristics.aim: To identify educational projects where games have been used to teach geography and history in secondary education, examining: (RQ1) what kind of academic works document these projects, (RQ2) what kind of games are used, (RQ3) main methodological approaches, and (RQ4) the extent to which impact of COTS-based projects is measured.

eligibility.concerns: This is a systematic literature review, not a primary empirical study. It synthesizes 78 studies on games for teaching geography and history in secondary education. It does not involve direct implementation or empirical data collection with learners. Additionally, it covers geography and history combined, not exclusively history education. The review explicitly excludes literature reviews from its own included studies.

rq1.conceptualization: The authors define video games as 'artistic products, created with a ludic intention, which provide an artificial system accepted by the players who interact with it in a new complex experience that depends mainly on the emotional dimension' (citing Oceja, 2020). They distinguish between educational games (created ad hoc), Commercial Off-the-Shelf games (COTS), and student-designed games. The paper does not provide an explicit definition of gamification per se, but frames its scope around game-based learning in history/geography education.
theoretical_frameworks: Behaviorism (games as opportunity for reward-based responses)
Cognitivism (Malone and Lepper, 1987 - intrinsic motivations for learning)
Constructivism (players building knowledge through interaction with digital environments and other players)
Constructionism (Papert, 1993 - students designing their own games)
Sociocultural approaches (Gee, 2014 - emphasizing activities around the game, teacher role, conversations, context over explicit educational content)

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Descriptive statistics on included studies: 43 conference papers vs 35 journal articles; 63 projects used educational games, 11 used COTS, 4 involved students designing games. For COTS projects (n=11), most measured educational impact: 3 quantitative, 3 qualitative, 4 mixed methods, 1 not measured.
rq2.statistical_results: No meta-analytic statistics performed. The review presents frequency counts and descriptive summaries. For individual COTS studies reviewed: Sim City improved spatial intelligence (quasi-experimental, T-test); Minecraft increased motivation significantly (ANOVA) and improved content knowledge (pre-post assessments); Age of Empires showed greater learning achievement (mixed methods pretest/posttest); Civilization increased motivation (ANOVAs and inferential statistics) but conceptual maps showed lower motivation; Pokemon Go enhanced learning attitudes (qualitative observations); Spore/Valiant Hearts improved perceived topic knowledge, learning motivation, acceptance towards video games (mixed methods, one-group pre-post).
rq2.comparative_methodology: Comparison between academic journals (n=35) and conference proceedings (n=43). Comparison between three approaches: educational games (n=63), COTS (n=11), and student-designed games (n=4). Table 2 compares 11 COTS-based projects across COTS game used, whether impact was measured, variables assessed, methodology, and results.
rq2.key_outcomes: Most projects use educational games created ad hoc rather than COTS. Conference proceedings outnumber journal articles (43 vs 35). Very few projects (n=11) use COTS despite evidence of their benefits. Student-designed game projects are particularly scarce (n=4). Most COTS projects attempted to measure educational impact with diverse methodologies and generally positive results. Educational games are often not rigorously evaluated for their educational impact.
rq2.engagement_results: Several individual COTS studies reported increased motivation and positive attitudes: Minecraft studies showed increased motivation significantly and most students enjoyed the experience; Age of Empires found boys were significantly more motivated; Civilization study found increased motivation when using games vs. traditional class but lower motivation when using conceptual maps; Pokemon Go effectively enhanced students' attitudes toward learning; Spore/Valiant Hearts improved perceived topic knowledge, learning motivation, and acceptance towards video games; Second Life showed teachers perceived children acquired new skills.

game_design_elements: Educational games designed ad hoc (63 of 78 projects)
Commercial Off-the-Shelf (COTS) games (11 projects)
Student-designed games (4 projects)
Pre-game and post-game activities as critical design elements
Concept maps integrated with game use
Dialogic mediation by teachers
Rubrics and didactic instruments for assessment
instructional_strategies: Game-based learning (GBL) with educational games
Problem-based learning (PBL) combined with games (e.g., Minecraft and Kodu)
Sociocultural approaches emphasizing teacher role and surrounding activities over explicit game content
Constructionist approaches (students designing their own games)
Edutainment approaches using educational games for content/skill practice
Design-based research
Mixed methods combining quantitative and qualitative assessment
Interpretive-type research structured in phases (search, preparation, design, implementation, evaluation)
rq3.content_integration: Games are used to teach history and geography content in secondary education. Most projects (63 of 78) use educational games designed specifically to deliver curriculum content. COTS games are used less frequently (11 of 78) but leverage existing commercial titles with historical/geographical settings. The review notes from the sociocultural perspective that the explicit educational content of COTS is not the most important element; rather, conversations, activities, teacher mediation, and pre/post-game activities around the game experience are critical for learning outcomes.

implementation_barriers: Shortage of teachers using COTS despite evidence of educational benefits
Most educational games are created ad hoc and rarely implemented or rigorously evaluated
Educational impact is rarely measured rigorously in game-based education projects
Gap between educational research and real educational practice ('failure of educational research' per Miller, 1999)
Dominance of conference proceedings over journal articles may limit visibility and impact
Lack of quality assessment tools applied to game-based learning studies
Very few projects allow students to design their own games (only 4 of 78)
Educational games (edutainment) are often superficial and far from games students normally play
Explicit educational content in games can contaminate student experience, making it feel artificial
methodology_limitations: Single database search (Scopus only); Web of Science and other databases not included
Search limited to English-language publications
Combined geography and history as single subject, which may miss discipline-specific nuances
No quality appraisal of individual studies included in the review
No meta-analysis performed; only descriptive statistics
PRISMA methodology adapted with modifications (no duplicate removal since single database, two different sample sizes for different RQs)
Grey literature not systematically searched
No inter-rater reliability reported for screening decisions
No PROSPERO registration mentioned
negative_effects: Using conceptual maps with Civilization showed lower motivation compared to traditional class
Educational games often perceived as artificial rather than playful by learners (edutainment critique)
Superficial quality of many educational games compared to commercial games students normally play
mitigation_strategies: Authors recommend applying quality scales such as PEDro to assess rigor of future studies
Suggest expanding reviews to search for specific games and grey literature for a more detailed picture
Recommend exploring constructionist approaches where students design their own games using free tools (Scratch, Unity)
Emphasize importance of teacher training and professionalization for game-based learning (teacher efficacy, pedagogical issues, school culture)
Highlight need for design-based research approaches (Reeves, 2000)
Suggest both digital and physical game design as accessible options for teachers
Advocate for greater use of COTS games with teacher mediation following sociocultural approaches

domain1.q1_evidence: Clear inclusion and exclusion criteria are stated. Inclusion: works documenting game-based educational projects, focusing on teaching/learning history/geography, focusing on secondary education. Exclusion criteria explicitly listed: book chapters, model design, books, not secondary education, not geography/history, not focusing on games, not implemented, not in English, teacher perceptions on GBL, critical reviews, literature reviews. Boolean search string provided. PRISMA-style flow diagram (Figure 1) shows numbers at each stage (255 -> 125 -> 78 -> 11).
domain1.q2_evidence: Only Scopus was searched; no other databases (WOS, ERIC, etc.) were used. Authors themselves acknowledge Scopus can be outscored by Web of Science in coverage. Search limited to English publications only. Grey literature not included. Single search timepoint (March 2022). Authors note that many more projects exist than are captured in academic literature, suggesting significant coverage gaps.

domain2.q3_evidence: No quality appraisal or risk of bias assessment was conducted on included studies. Authors explicitly note this limitation and recommend applying quality scales such as PEDro in future research. Data extraction appears limited to basic categorization (publication type, game type, measurement approach) without a formal coding framework or extraction form.
domain2.q4_evidence: Analysis is purely descriptive (frequency counts, bar charts, tables). No meta-analysis, vote counting with statistical weighting, or formal synthesis method is applied. Table 1 lists all 78 included studies; Table 2 systematically summarizes the 11 COTS studies across key dimensions (game, measurement, variables, methodology, results). The synthesis approach is appropriate for a scoping/mapping review but limited for drawing robust conclusions.

domain3.q5_evidence: Findings are presented clearly and consistently with the data shown in tables and figures. The four research questions are addressed systematically. Discussion appropriately contextualizes findings within broader literature on game-based learning, referencing sociocultural theory, edutainment critique, and constructionism.
domain3.q6_evidence: Some limitations are acknowledged (single database, suggestion for quality appraisal in future work, need to search grey literature). However, there is no formal limitations section; limitations are dispersed across the conclusion/discussion. Important limitations not explicitly discussed include: lack of inter-rater reliability for screening, no PROSPERO registration, potential language bias, and implications of combining geography and history as a single unit.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: This systematic literature review has significant methodological limitations: reliance on a single database (Scopus), no quality appraisal of included studies, purely descriptive analysis without meta-analysis, and limited discussion of limitations. While the search strategy and inclusion/exclusion criteria are clearly stated with a PRISMA-style flow diagram, the narrow search scope and absence of critical appraisal substantially limit the reliability and comprehensiveness of the findings. As a secondary study (literature review), it does not meet eligibility criteria for inclusion as a primary empirical study.

pdf_filename: Gamification and the History of Art in Secondary Education A Didactic Intervention.pdf

bibliographic.title: Gamification and the History of Art in Secondary Education: A Didactic Intervention
bibliographic.venue: Education Sciences

study_characteristics.education_level: Secondary education (Compulsory Secondary Education / ESO, ages 12-17)
study_characteristics.sample_description: 47 secondary education students (from an initial 52) divided into two groups/classes (22 and 25 students upon reaching 4th ESO) from different study centers. 53% female, 47% male. Average age 12 years at start and 17 at end. Some students had special educational needs (2 in one group, 3 in the other). Convenience sampling, non-probabilistic. None had prior systematic experience with gamification methodologies.
study_characteristics.study_design: Longitudinal qualitative study (4 academic years: 2017/2018 to 2020/2021, applied in 1st, 2nd, and 4th year of ESO)
study_characteristics.game_type: Multiple gamification strategies (discovery learning, narrative gamification, challenge-based learning, rewards, escape room, break out, gamified evaluation tools)
study_characteristics.game_name: Custom didactic intervention with three themed phases: 'Explorers of the Ancient Art' (1st ESO), 'Virtual Museum' (2nd ESO), 'Monuments Mission' (4th ESO); Kahoot used for evaluation games
study_characteristics.aim: To assess the suitability of gamification methodologies to improve the teaching-learning processes of Art History skills in Secondary Education, analyzing academic results, students' vision of art history, and their assessment of different gamification strategies

eligibility.concerns: The study focuses specifically on Art History content within the broader Geography and History subject. It is a primary empirical study with gamification intervention in a history-related educational context.

rq1.explicit_definition: The paper quotes a definition from Marin and Hierro (2013): 'Gamification is a technique, a method and a strategy at the same time. It starts from the knowledge of the elements that make games attractive and identifies, within a specific activity, task or message, in a Non-game environment, those aspects that can be converted into a game or ludic dynamics. All this to achieve a special involvement, on the part of the users, encourage a change in their behavior or transmit a message or content. That is to say, create a significant and motivating experience.' (p. 14)
rq1.conceptualization: Gamification is conceptualized as structuring the teaching-learning process using the rules of games to influence motivation and connection with the process. It is distinguished from simply using games in education. The author views gamification as an active methodology with high motivational power that can generate links between students and skills, break with traditional classroom visions, transform teacher-student roles, and provide rules to articulate learning connections.
theoretical_frameworks: Gamification as active methodology for social sciences education

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Average grades compared between general Geography and History subject and Art History gamified assessment: 1st ESO: general 6.21 vs Art History 6.85; 2nd ESO: general 6.18 vs Art History 7.52; 4th ESO: general 6.48 vs Art History 8.23. Learning outcomes from diary sources: Memorize Artistic Styles (1st: 52%, 2nd: 62%, 4th: 67%), Memorize Authors (1st: 36%, 2nd: 86%, 4th: 52%), Memorize Works of Art (1st: 72%, 2nd: 82%, 4th: 79%). Positive vision of art history: 44.7% explicit references and 27.3% very explicit/abundant presence across 536 textual sources.
rq2.statistical_results: No inferential statistics reported. Results are based on qualitative analysis of 536 textual sources (learning diary entries) across three intervention phases (168 entries in 1st ESO, 230 in 2nd ESO, 138 in 4th ESO) and comparison of average grades. Art History grades progressively increased across academic years while general grades remained stable.
rq2.comparative_methodology: Within-subjects longitudinal comparison: (1) comparison of average grades in general Geography and History subject vs. gamified Art History assessment tools across three academic years; (2) longitudinal tracking of same students across four academic years to observe evolution of learning outcomes and attitudes
rq2.key_outcomes: Positive effect on learning Art History skills with progressive improvement over time. Art History grades consistently higher than general subject grades and increasing across years. Growth in motivation for studying Art History. Progressive development of positive vision about art history (from 11.5% with no references to positive vision to 27.3% with very explicit abundant presence). Generally positive assessment of gamification strategies, though with uneven evaluations across different strategies.
rq2.engagement_results: Favorable assessments of gamification strategies by students: Discovery learning (68% favorable in 1st ESO), Narrative gamification (71% in 1st, 65% in 2nd, 81% in 4th ESO), Use of rewards (91% in 1st, 88% in 2nd, 72% in 4th ESO), Break Out (92% in 2nd ESO), Escape Room (66% in 4th ESO), Assessment games (77% in 1st ESO). Students reported high engagement with narrative elements and rewards. Some strategies like Escape Room and Break Out generated mixed feelings including stress and nervousness in some students.

game_design_elements: Narrative framework (gamified narratives contextualizing learning in historical periods)
Challenges (missions and objectives students must complete)
Rewards (stamps, passports, thank-you letters, puzzle pieces, diplomas)
Discovery learning (exploration missions)
Micro-projects (research and presentation tasks)
Escape Room (final evaluation activity in 4th ESO)
Break Out (digital evaluation game in 2nd ESO)
Evaluation games (Kahoot-based assessment)
QR codes (linking phases of intervention)
Learning diaries (reflective assessment tool)
Group work and collaboration
Progressive unlocking of activities through rewards
instructional_strategies: Longitudinal didactic intervention across multiple academic years
Narrative-based contextualization of art history periods
Challenge-based learning with progressive difficulty
Learning by discovery with exploration missions
Micro-project-based learning (research, reproduction, presentation of art works)
Gamified evaluation replacing traditional assessment
Learning diary for reflective practice
Group collaboration with individual accountability
Integration of film and multimedia as narrative triggers (The Monuments Men)
Virtual museum creation as collaborative product
rq3.content_integration: Art History content was systematically integrated across three years of the Spanish ESO curriculum: 1st ESO covered Prehistory and Ancient Age art (cave paintings, ziggurats, pyramids, sphinxes, Greek temples, Roman monuments); 2nd ESO covered Medieval and Modern art (Romanesque, Islamic, Gothic, Renaissance, Baroque); 4th ESO covered Modern and Contemporary art (19th century styles). The gamification narrative connected the three phases, with each year building on the previous one. Content was delivered through micro-projects where students researched specific works of art, their characteristics, and historical context, then presented their findings.

implementation_barriers: Art History content is relegated to a secondary position within the Geography and History subject in the Spanish curriculum
Lack of specific hours dedicated to Art History teaching
Excessive amount of curricular content and prioritization of other content
Structural limitations in content distribution of the Social Sciences subject that do not depend on teacher intervention
3rd year of ESO had to be excluded because its curriculum contained no Art History content
Student attrition over 4-year longitudinal study (from 52 to 47 students due to failures or center transfers)
Convenience sampling limits generalizability
methodology_limitations: Didactic intervention was only applied once in this study, so results cannot be compared with other applications
Inability to reorganize content distribution of the Social Sciences subject
No control group for comparison
Qualitative methodology only - no inferential statistical analysis
Non-probabilistic convenience sampling
Data unavailable due to privacy concerns
Need for replication to consolidate results
negative_effects: Some gamification activities (Break Out, Escape Room) generated feelings of being overwhelmed, stressed, or shutdown in some students
Unfavorable evaluation of evaluation games: stress and nervousness during timed competitive games like Kahoot
Escape Room caused anxiety about time progression in some students
Uneven assessment of different motivation strategies - not all strategies worked equally well for all students
Risk of excessive competitiveness from individual rewards (mitigated by group rewards)
Risk of demotivation for not achieving objectives
mitigation_strategies: Inclusion of group rewards alongside individual rewards to reduce excessive competition
Use of multiple different gamification strategies to address varied student preferences
Learning diary for ongoing reflective self-assessment rather than single high-stakes evaluation
Longitudinal design allowing adjustment across academic years
Combination of various gamification methods tailored to each course level
Authors recommend taking negative emotional reactions into account for subsequent applications

domain1.q1_evidence: The study clearly describes the sample selection: 47 secondary education students from two groups at the ESO stage, convenience non-probabilistic sampling. Inclusion was based on enrollment in the specific courses where Art History content is taught (1st, 2nd, and 4th ESO). The 3rd year was explicitly excluded with justification (no Art History content). Student demographics are reported (gender distribution, age, academic results, special needs).
domain1.q2_evidence: Convenience sampling from only two class groups at different study centers. Sample of 47 students is small and not randomly selected. The author acknowledges this is a limitation and that results cannot be generalized without replication. No information on how the two centers were selected.

domain2.q3_evidence: Data collection relied on student learning diary entries (536 textual sources) analyzed qualitatively using WebQDA software. The categorization structure was based on research objectives. However, no established validated instruments were used; the learning diary structure was designed by the researcher. Grade comparisons used standard academic assessment. No inter-rater reliability was reported for the qualitative coding.
domain2.q4_evidence: Qualitative content analysis using WebQDA with a categorization structure based on three aspects: learning results, student vision of art, and assessment of gamification strategies. Results are presented with percentages from the categorization. However, no inferential statistics are used for grade comparisons, no control group exists, and the researcher who designed and implemented the intervention also conducted the analysis, raising potential researcher bias.

domain3.q5_evidence: Results are generally presented consistently with the data shown in tables and figures. The progressive improvement in grades and positive vision of art history are supported by the data. However, the interpretation tends toward positive framing, and the lack of a control group means improvements cannot be definitively attributed to gamification rather than other factors (maturation, teacher effect, repeated exposure).
domain3.q6_evidence: The author explicitly discusses limitations: the intervention was applied only once, results cannot be compared with other applications, inability to reorganize subject content distribution, structural difficulties, and the need for replication. The negative effects of some strategies (stress from Escape Room and Break Out) are also acknowledged.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: While the study provides rich qualitative data from a well-structured longitudinal intervention, several methodological concerns lower confidence in the findings: (1) small convenience sample with no random selection; (2) no control group for comparison; (3) researcher-designed non-validated instruments; (4) no inter-rater reliability for qualitative coding; (5) the researcher designed, implemented, and evaluated the intervention, introducing potential bias; (6) only descriptive statistics with no inferential analysis for grade comparisons. The longitudinal design across 4 years is a strength, and limitations are acknowledged, but the overall risk of bias remains high.

pdf_filename: Gamification, Pandemic and Learning the History of Ideas. Experiments in the Context of Core Curriculum.pdf

bibliographic.title: Gamification, Pandemic and Learning the History of Ideas. Experiments in the Context of Core Curriculum
bibliographic.venue: RIED-Revista Iberoamericana de Educación a Distancia

study_characteristics.sample_description: 23 students across four courses of the Core Curriculum subject 'Contemporary Civilization' (a history of Western philosophy from Plato to Freud) at Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez in Chile. First-year students from law, psychology, journalism, commercial engineering, and civil engineering programs.
study_characteristics.study_design: Qualitative autoethnographic research (teacher-researcher autoethnography with ethnographic recording of student interventions)
study_characteristics.game_type: Serious games (custom-designed tabletop/role-playing games conducted via Zoom)
study_characteristics.game_name: Multiple serious games: El Juego de Giges, El Juego de la Caverna, El Juego del Concilio, El Juego de Urticario Crudelis, El Juego del Colono, El Juego de los Sueños, El Juego del Contrato, El Juego del Manifiesto, El Juego de los Espectros, Decisión Final
study_characteristics.aim: To examine the rationale and results of a gamification experiment based on serious games in the context of teaching the history of ideas (Western philosophy from Plato to Freud) during the COVID-19 pandemic, investigating how games develop essential skills for critical comprehension of the history of ideas including hermeneutic and intersubjective reasoning, historical imagination, sense of contingency, and contextualization ability.

eligibility.concerns: The study focuses on the history of ideas/philosophy rather than history in the strict disciplinary sense, though it is framed within humanities education and involves historical thinking skills. The study is qualitative with no control group or quantitative measures.

rq1.conceptualization: The authors conceptualize gamification through the lens of serious games drawing on classical play theory. They reference Huizinga (2005), Bally (1973), and Fink (2016) to understand games as creating fictional worlds based on imagination with internal logical coherence and aesthetic harmony. Games involve the creation of a para-identity where the player assumes a role distinct from ordinary social identities, engaging in a self-conscious fictional activity. The game is characterized as essentially a ritual — a dramatized action socializing a universe of symbols and norms — that creates a bounded playground space and a suspension of ordinary chronological time. The authors use the term 'serious games' (juegos serios) following López Raventós (2016), distinguishing their approach from mere gamification elements, and emphasize the cognitive and epistemological powers of play.
theoretical_frameworks: Bally's theory of play as expression of freedom
Fink's philosophy of play as symbol of the world
Hermeneutic tradition (fusion of horizons, historical consciousness)
Seixas (2017) on historical consciousness and historical thinking
Froeyman (2016) on ethical turn in historiography
Autoethnographic methodology (Adams, Ellis, Holman Jones, Bochner)

rq2.key_outcomes: The study reports qualitative outcomes from autoethnographic field notes across 10 serious games played over 80 sessions. Key findings include: (1) Games developed 'historical consciousness' — the ability to reflect critically on historical time and understand the otherness of past societies. (2) Students developed hermeneutic and intersubjective reasoning by establishing conceptual mediations with historical characters. (3) Games fostered historical imagination — the ability to construct abstract concepts and fictional scenarios from diverse experiences. (4) Students developed a sense of contingency — understanding that philosophical ideas are not universal truths but mental constructions within specific spatiotemporal coordinates. (5) Games promoted contextualization ability — students learned to situate authors' thought in precise spatiotemporal coordinates. (6) The fictional para-identity of gameplay created a 'radical otherness' that allowed students to think beyond their usual values and worldviews. (7) Games served as epistemic rituals breaking pandemic monotony and the productivist time of virtual education. (8) Group identifications formed during games translated into real friendships, overcoming pandemic isolation.
rq2.engagement_results: Students became highly engaged with the game activities. In the Juego de los Sueños, after the first session students spontaneously requested a winner be declared and asked for explanations about which team's solution best reflected Descartes' philosophy, showing that victory and quality of reflection mattered equally. Students broke the solipsism of the pandemic through game-based group identification. The games functioned as 'pure events' that disrupted the cadence of quarantines and virtual deliveries, adding narrativity to the courses.

game_design_elements: Decision-making by groups (toma de decisiones por grupos)
Dilemma games (juego de dilemas)
Role-playing (juego de rol)
Tribunal/trial simulation (juego de tribunal)
Team debate (juego de equipos de debate)
Imagination and guessing games with uchronic thinking (juego de imaginación y adivinanza; pensamiento ucrónico)
Vital decisions by teams (juego de decisiones vitales por equipos)
Team competition
Para-identity/character assumption
Fictional scenarios connected to contemporary issues
technological_platforms: Zoom (video conferencing platform for all sessions)
instructional_strategies: Autoethnographic teaching and research methodology
Pre-assigned readings from philosophical canon texts (one book every week and a half)
Three participatory sessions per book with professor as coordinator
Connection of philosophical texts to contemporary everyday dilemmas and current affairs in Chile, Latin America, and the world
Group-based collaborative gameplay (teams of 5-6 students)
Hermeneutic strategies for game development in class
Post-game reflection and evaluation
Recording of spoken interventions (sounds) and written interventions (chats/texts) in each session
Final game (Decisión Final) as summative assessment comparing all 21 philosophers studied
rq3.content_integration: Each serious game was directly tied to specific philosophical texts from the syllabus covering Western philosophy from Plato to Freud. Games required students to apply the ideas from the assigned readings to fictional scenarios that connected historical philosophical concepts to contemporary issues. For example, El Juego de Giges required applying Plato's concept of justice to a modern dilemma about Ukrainian refugees; El Juego de la Caverna used Plato and Aristotle's theories to reorganize society in a post-apocalyptic future; El Juego del Contrato placed students as French Revolution characters negotiating a constitution based on Rousseau's Social Contract. The content integration was deep — game evaluation criteria assessed mastery of the philosophical texts and the ability to apply historical ideas to present-day contexts.

implementation_barriers: COVID-19 pandemic forced all sessions online via Zoom, creating distance that disincentivized student intervention and interest
Virtualization of teaching posed challenges for highly participatory Core Curriculum sessions
Students' faces were rarely visible during Zoom sessions (cameras off), making interaction more difficult
The pandemic eliminated physical meeting spaces, created a destabilized sense of time, and increased neoliberal academic productivism pressures
Humanities teaching was particularly harmed by the pandemic context
methodology_limitations: Autoethnographic method limits findings to the teacher-researcher's professional experience perspective
No quantitative data or control group — findings are purely qualitative
Limitations are tied to the pedagogical-didactic interest of the research, as objectives included provoking new teaching-learning formats
Results are based on field diary notes and recordings, subject to researcher interpretation
Small sample size (23 students across 4 course sections)
negative_effects: In El Juego del Contrato, many teams could not reach agreements when reconciling their characters' particular objectives with a general will, discarding solutions from Rousseauian theory of popular sovereignty
Some students were implicitly confronted with choosing between uncomfortable complex truths and comfortable self-serving virtual reality of social media 'likes' and safe spaces
mitigation_strategies: Gamification was adopted specifically as a response to the challenges of virtualized teaching during the pandemic
Games were designed to create engagement and break the monotony of pandemic distance learning
The serious game format created ritual-like 'pure events' that disrupted the alienating cadence of quarantine
Group-based gameplay fostered social connections that helped overcome pandemic isolation
Authors argue the approach should be systematized for use in post-pandemic contexts as well

domain1.q1_evidence: The study focuses on a specific, well-defined context: four courses of Contemporary Civilization at Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez, Chile, with 23 students over 80 sessions from March 2020 to December 2021. The selection is clearly defined by the institutional context.
domain1.q2_evidence: The sample of 23 students is from a single university in Chile, taking a specific Core Curriculum course. There is no discussion of how representative this sample is of broader student populations. The unique pandemic context and the specific institutional setting (Core Curriculum model adopted from Columbia University) limits generalizability.

domain2.q3_evidence: Data collection relies entirely on autoethnographic field notes and ethnographic recordings (spoken and written student interventions). While the authors reference established autoethnographic methodologies (Adams, Ellis, Holman Jones, Bochner), no validated instruments or standardized assessment tools were used. The evaluation of game outcomes is based on the teacher-researcher's subjective interpretation of field diary notes.
domain2.q4_evidence: Analysis is qualitative, based on the construction of a chronological narrative from field notes organized around four objectives. There is no systematic coding methodology described, no inter-rater reliability, and no triangulation with other data sources beyond the teacher-researcher's perspective. The authors acknowledge their limitations are tied to the autoethnographic approach.

domain3.q5_evidence: The findings are consistently interpreted within the theoretical framework of play theory (Huizinga, Bally, Fink) and hermeneutic tradition. The authors present rich qualitative descriptions of each game's outcomes. However, the interpretation is uniformly positive with limited critical examination of potential negative outcomes or failures.
domain3.q6_evidence: The authors briefly acknowledge limitations of the autoethnographic method (findings tied to teacher-researcher perspective, pedagogical-didactic interest). However, the discussion of limitations is relatively thin — there is no discussion of confirmation bias, observer effect, or the inherent limitations of the teacher evaluating their own pedagogical intervention.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study presents a rich qualitative autoethnographic account of gamification in history of ideas education during the pandemic. However, several factors contribute to high risk of bias: (1) the teacher-researcher is both the designer/implementer of the games and the sole evaluator of outcomes, with no independent assessment; (2) no validated measurement instruments were used; (3) analysis lacks systematic methodology (no coding scheme, no inter-rater reliability); (4) findings are uniformly positive with minimal critical self-examination; (5) small, non-representative sample from a single institution; (6) no comparison group or pre-post measures. While the autoethnographic approach is methodologically legitimate, the lack of triangulation and the dual role of the researcher as both participant and evaluator create substantial risk of bias.

pdf_filename: Gamifying History Designing and Implementing a Game-Based Learning Course Design Framework.pdf

bibliographic.title: Gamifying History: Designing and Implementing a Game-Based Learning Course Design Framework
bibliographic.venue: Teaching & Learning Inquiry

study_characteristics.sample_description: 15 students in a third-year history seminar course on the Black Death at the University of Waterloo (a large public research institution in Ontario, Canada). 14 participants provided insight; 12 agreed to have their data used. 11 were enrolled in the Faculty of Arts, 1 in the Faculty of Math. Six identified as female, six as male. The course was an elective open to students from any Faculty.
study_characteristics.study_design: Mixed-methods (pre-/post-questionnaires, two focus groups, and two in-class observations by a third-party research assistant)
study_characteristics.game_type: Game-based learning course design framework (gamified course structure with embedded role-playing game)
study_characteristics.game_name: Custom game-based learning course design framework applied to a Black Death history course (includes a two-week role-playing game component)
study_characteristics.aim: To analyze the development and implementation of a game-based learning course design framework structured around four core gamified elements (narrative assignment design, learner discovery, team-based collaboration and competition, and choice through quests), and to evaluate how it functions as a teaching approach and whether it increases student engagement.

eligibility.concerns: Small sample size (n=15, with only 12 consenting to data use). Single institution, single course implementation. The study focuses on a game-based learning course design framework rather than a standalone digital game, but it incorporates gamification elements and game-based learning principles into history education.

rq1.explicit_definition: The authors distinguish between gamification and game-based learning: 'gamification referring to the addition of game-based elements—such as points and leaderboards, conflict, or competition (Whitton 2014)—onto an already established learning activity or assessment. Game-based learning, then, is the integration of game-based principles into the design of a learning activity or assessment.' They also define engagement as 'a learner's active participation in not only class and team discussions, but also in one's willingness to go above and beyond in the course, completing additional assignments... or accessing external material that is not being assessed.'
rq1.conceptualization: The authors conceptualize game-based learning as distinct from gamification. While gamification adds game elements onto existing activities, game-based learning integrates game principles into the design itself. Their framework merges existing course design frameworks with game-based learning principles to structure an entire course. The four core elements of their framework—narrative assignment design, learner discovery, team-based collaboration and competition, and choice through quests—are intended to benefit student engagement rather than directly improve grades. The framework draws inspiration from task-based learning (Willis 1996) and backward course design (Wiggins and McTighe 2005).
theoretical_frameworks: Community of Inquiry framework (Garrison, Anderson, and Archer 2000)
Mapping of game mechanics to learning mechanics (Arnab et al. 2015)

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Pre- and post-questionnaires measuring student perceptions of teaching approaches. Table 2 presents percentages of students who found certain teaching approaches helpful: Lectures (89% extremely helpful), Large class discussions (45% extremely helpful), Small group discussions (33% extremely helpful), Group work (22% extremely helpful), Individual work (33% extremely helpful), Demonstrations (56% extremely helpful), Technology enabled learning (44% extremely helpful). 90% of students selected lectures as the most helpful learning type in the pre-questionnaire, while group work was rated least helpful.
rq2.statistical_results: No formal statistical tests were reported. Findings are primarily qualitative with descriptive percentages from questionnaires. 80% of pre-questionnaire students chose the course for the topic/time period interest; 20% for scheduling. Six of 12 participating students completed at least one optional side-quest. By end of semester, all respondents ranked the role-playing game as the most engaging course element.
rq2.comparative_methodology: Pre-/post-questionnaire comparison of student perceptions before and after the gamified course. The study compared student stated preferences (e.g., for lectures) with observed in-class behavior (e.g., engagement during team activities). No control group was used.
rq2.key_outcomes: Team-based nature and embedded gameplay elements were most effective at improving engagement. The two-week role-playing game was universally ranked as the most engaging part of the course. Students expressed strong interest in historical empathy through role-play. Initial confusion about gamified terminology (assignments, format/schedule, creature names) declined substantially over time. Students who stated they preferred lectures were observed to be consistently engaged during team-based activities. Extrinsic rewards (team prize of a plushie) had limited motivational impact; the team-based competition itself was more motivating. Side-quests had inconclusive engagement results—some students found them motivating while others needed stronger incentivization.
rq2.engagement_results: Engagement increased through team-based collaboration and competition, with students reporting a heightened sense of belonging and willingness to exceed expectations. The role-playing game component generated the highest engagement. Students were least engaged during team presentations to other teams. Observations showed students stopped taking detailed notes within 10 minutes but remained consistently engaged during collaborative activities. By end of course, students wished there had been more team-based game activities and expressed desire for more gamified elements.

game_design_elements: Narrative assignment design (overarching Plague Hospital narrative throughout the course)
Learner discovery (problem-based, learner-driven resolution rather than instructor-supplied solutions)
Team-based collaboration and competition (Plague Hospitals competing via points/metrics)
Choice through quests (optional side-quests for bonus team points)
Points system (Potions for positive, Poisons for negative, represented by physical pins)
Team flags and visual displays in classroom
Game manual (reimagined syllabus)
Assignment cards (printed on a deck of playing cards)
Character sheets for role-playing game (biography, objectives, win/loss conditions)
Two-week role-playing game (town council members facing the Black Death)
Team identity creation (naming Hospitals, selecting team colours)
Respawning monsters (ability to redo assignments)
Debriefing sessions after role-playing game
Celebration of learner successes
technological_platforms: Non-digital / physical classroom implementation (no specific technology platform; physical cards, pins, flags)
instructional_strategies: Task-based learning approach
Team-based seminar structure (teams of 4-5 students)
Weekly collaborative learning tasks during two contact hours
Independent research in third contact hour
Problem-based learning (starting with a core historical problem)
Role-playing game (two-week immersive activity)
Learner choice in assignment selection
Pre-/post-questionnaires for reflection
Focus groups for feedback
Debriefing sessions after game activities
Individual final paper synthesizing team research
rq3.content_integration: The framework was applied to a third-year history course on the Black Death at the University of Waterloo. Historical content was deeply embedded in all game elements: the overarching narrative cast students as Plague Physicians in Plague Hospitals; assignments were framed as quests and adventures related to the Black Death; the role-playing game had students take on characters as medieval town council members facing plague; character sheets included historical biographies and supplemental readings. The course maintained weekly readings and research components while wrapping them in game-based framing. The framework's six-step process (core problem, learning outcomes, engaging narrative, build teams, provide choice, celebrate success) ensured historical learning objectives were met through gamified delivery.

implementation_barriers: Initial student confusion about gamified terminology and course structure (assignment names, format/schedule, creature names in the monster guide)
Students' preconceived preference for lectures conflicting with active learning approaches
Small sample size limiting generalizability (n=12 with consent for data use)
Results from a single institution only
Resource and logistical support requirements may be unrealistic for some instructors or institutions
Game-based nature of course was unknown to students when enrolling, creating initial surprise
Extrinsic rewards (team prizes) proved insufficiently motivating
Side-quests lacked sufficient incentivization for all students
methodology_limitations: Very small sample size (n=15 class, n=12 consenting participants)
Single course implementation at one institution
No control group for comparison
Engagement operationalized only within this class context, not as a pre-existing construct
Reliance on self-reported data alongside limited observations (only two observation sessions)
Student stated preferences (lectures) contradicted observed behavior (engagement in team activities), complicating interpretation
No formal statistical analysis reported
negative_effects: Initial confusion and trepidation among students confronted with unconventional teaching paradigm
Some students felt the gamified elements became less prominent as the course progressed
Group presentations to other teams were perceived as the least engaging activity
Some students did not find side-quests sufficiently motivating without tangible rewards
Ambiguity of the team prize reduced its motivational impact
Students initially viewed the team-based format negatively, associating it with generic 'group work'
mitigation_strategies: Instructor provided a separate traditional course outline alongside the gamified syllabus (game manual) to reduce confusion
Confusion about gamification declined substantially over time as students became accustomed to the framework
Building team identity through naming, colours, and flags helped overcome negative perceptions of group work
The framework is designed to be adaptable to different disciplines, class sizes, and institutional contexts
Authors suggest considering allowing students to 'opt out' of an assessment by completing enough side-quests, thus making side-quests more rewarding
Authors recommend not swaying from gamified course direction despite initial student resistance

domain1.q1_evidence: The study clearly describes participants: 15 students in a third-year elective history seminar at the University of Waterloo, with 14 providing insight and 12 consenting to data use. Inclusion was straightforward—all enrolled students were eligible. Ethics clearance was obtained (ORE: 23218).
domain1.q2_evidence: Very small sample (n=15 class, n=12 with consent). Single elective course at one institution. Students self-selected into the course for topic interest, not for gamification. The sample is not representative of broader student populations. 11 of 12 from Faculty of Arts, only 1 from Math.

domain2.q3_evidence: Multiple data collection methods were used (pre-/post-questionnaires, two focus groups, two classroom observations). Coding followed open coding process (Strauss and Corbin 1990) with six primary codes and sub-codes checked by multiple researchers. However, no validated instruments are referenced for the questionnaires, and the observation protocol is described only briefly.
domain2.q4_evidence: Qualitative analysis used open coding with researcher verification. Descriptive percentages are reported from questionnaires but no formal statistical analysis was conducted. The mixed-methods approach is appropriate for the exploratory research questions, but the lack of quantitative rigor limits the strength of conclusions.

domain3.q5_evidence: Findings are presented in a nuanced manner. The authors note contradictions between stated student preferences (lectures) and observed behavior (engagement in team activities). They acknowledge that engagement results for side-quests were inconclusive. They distinguish clearly between different aspects of the framework and their effectiveness.
domain3.q6_evidence: The authors explicitly acknowledge: small sample size (n=12), single institution, need for future research across disciplines and class sizes, resource and logistical challenges for adoption, and the ambiguous impact of extrinsic rewards. They note the answer to whether the framework increases engagement 'remains unclear' and call for further study.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study has a well-designed mixed-methods approach with transparent reporting and thoughtful discussion of limitations. However, significant concerns arise from the very small, non-representative sample (n=12-15), single-institution design, lack of validated measurement instruments, absence of a control group, and no formal statistical analysis. The qualitative findings are rich and consistently interpreted, but the generalizability of results is severely limited. The authors are appropriately cautious in their conclusions.

pdf_filename: Grand Theft Longboat Using Video Games and Medievalism to Teach Medieval History.pdf

bibliographic.title: Grand Theft Longboat: Using Video Games and Medievalism to Teach Medieval History
bibliographic.venue: Historia Ludens: The Playing Historian

study_characteristics.sample_description: Third-year undergraduate students taking the 'History and Myth: Writing and Re-writing the Middle Ages' module at the University of Huddersfield (BA in History), running since 2013. A 20-credit module over 12 weeks. Individual student pitch examples discussed but no formal sample described.
study_characteristics.study_design: descriptive
study_characteristics.game_name: Student-designed medieval video game pitches (e.g., Grand Theft Longboat, Antioch: Searching for Salvation, The Golden Legend, Hanged Drawn OR Quartered)
study_characteristics.aim: To describe a university module where students analyze medieval and modern medieval narratives (video games, films, TV) and create their own original medieval video game/film/TV pitches, combining history education with creative game design as pedagogy.

eligibility.concerns: This is a reflective practitioner account of a teaching module, not a formal empirical study. No systematic data collection or analysis. Students design game pitches but do not create functioning games. The gamification element is the use of video game design as a pedagogical tool for history learning.

rq1.conceptualization: Game-based learning is conceptualized through the lens of game design as pedagogy: students engage with medieval history by analyzing existing video games set in the Middle Ages and by designing and pitching their own original medieval video games. The approach treats video games as historical narratives that parallel medieval chronicle writing, emphasizing the value of fiction, speculation, and 'filling in the gaps' in historical understanding. Games are seen as tools for exploring 'history from below', the inner psyche of historical figures, and alternative historical outcomes.
theoretical_frameworks: Kapell and Elliott's 'Playing with the Past' framework (2013)

rq2.key_outcomes: No formal evaluation conducted. The author reports informal observations: 'the majority of students have shown a very good if not excellent understanding of the aim of exercise, displaying high levels of both creativity and effort in their pitches'; 'module feedback from students is consistently very positive in terms of what students feel they have gained both intellectually, and in terms of enjoyment.' Student quote: 'This module represented a very creative way to look at history... The pitch and essay are also a really different way of being assessed and make it a lot more fun.'
rq2.engagement_results: Students reported high engagement and enjoyment. The author notes students 'exceeded my expectations in demonstrating the potential of video games as a medium for representing authentic versions of the Middle Ages and enabling engagement with medieval history.' Students exercised 'greater initiative and autonomy' compared to a previous traditional module.

game_design_elements: Student-designed game pitches (10-minute oral presentations)
Open-world exploration (GTA-style, inspired by Red Dead Redemption, Saints Row)
Action RPG elements (Skyrim, Dragon Age, Fable inspired)
Graphic adventure with puzzle solving (Broken Sword inspired)
Decision-making and branching narratives
Character-driven historical exploration
Alternative history scenarios ('what if' gameplay)
technological_platforms: No specific technology platform required — students pitch conceptual game designs
instructional_strategies: Students as game designers (constructionist approach)
Analysis of existing medieval video games and media
Integration of primary source analysis with creative design
Historiographical methodology applied to game narratives
Peer presentation and feedback (pitches delivered to cohort)
Reflective self-assessment within 24 hours of pitch
2000-word analytical essay on medievalism in media
Interdisciplinary approach combining history and media studies
rq3.content_integration: Medieval history content is integrated through a dual approach: (1) weekly seminars covering topics such as Joan of Arc, Robin Hood, King Arthur, Vikings, the Crusades, the Borgias, Mongols, and the Gothic Middle Ages, analyzed through both primary sources and modern media representations; (2) student game pitches must be grounded in historical research, drawing on primary sources and secondary scholarship, while using game design to explore how and why the Middle Ages are represented in particular ways. The key concept is 'intellectual profit' — students must justify what their game would help audiences understand about the Middle Ages that a traditional book could not.

implementation_barriers: Students do not actually create functioning games — only pitches/concepts
Module limited to one university (University of Huddersfield)
Relies on students being experienced gamers for game pitch element
No formal assessment of whether game design activity improves historical understanding beyond traditional methods
methodology_limitations: No formal research methodology — reflective practitioner account
No systematic data collection or analysis
No control group or comparison with traditional teaching
Sample characteristics and size not described
Student feedback quoted selectively without systematic collection
Author is both the module creator and the chapter author (potential bias)

domain1.q1_evidence: No participant selection criteria described. The chapter discusses examples from students who took the module over multiple years since 2013 but provides no information about how many students participated, their demographics, or how the featured examples were selected.
domain1.q2_evidence: The study is set at a single UK university (University of Huddersfield). Note 3 mentions students occasionally come from Erasmus exchanges. The module is available to BA History students and those on joint degrees. The featured student examples may not be representative of the full range of student work.

domain2.q3_evidence: No data collection instruments are described. The author references 'module feedback from students' being 'consistently very positive' but does not describe the feedback instrument. One student quote is provided but the collection method is unspecified. The chapter relies entirely on the author's informal observations and selective examples.
domain2.q4_evidence: No data analysis methods are described. The chapter presents anecdotal examples of student pitches with the author's interpretive commentary. There is no systematic coding, thematic analysis, or quantitative analysis of student outcomes.

domain3.q5_evidence: The author's conclusions ('a very successful and productive means of approaching primary sources and historiographical debate') are supported only by selective anecdotal evidence. The claim that students showed 'very good if not excellent understanding' lacks systematic evidence. However, the detailed pitch examples do illustrate sophisticated student engagement with historical content.
domain3.q6_evidence: The author does not explicitly discuss limitations of the study or module evaluation. However, the chapter is positioned as a reflective practitioner account rather than formal research, and the author acknowledges the module is still evolving. No mention of negative feedback or unsuccessful pitches.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: High risk of bias across all domains due to absence of formal research methodology. The chapter is a reflective practitioner account with no systematic data collection, no validated instruments, no described analysis methods, and selective presentation of student examples. While it provides rich qualitative description of the module design and student outputs, it cannot be considered empirical evidence of effectiveness.

pdf_filename: History on the Game Board The Use of Board Games in Polish History Education.pdf

bibliographic.title: History on the Game Board: The Use of Board Games in Polish History Education
bibliographic.venue: Public History Review

study_characteristics.education_level: High school and university (history teacher training)
study_characteristics.sample_description: 53 high school students surveyed during workshops on social life in communist Poland (anonymous survey with 4 open-ended questions); 37 university history students surveyed before and after playing Twilight Struggle (2021-2022); 20 in-depth interviews with final-year university students on game-based learning methods
study_characteristics.study_design: Mixed methods: pre-post anonymous surveys with open-ended questions, in-depth qualitative interviews, and classroom observation/practitioner report
study_characteristics.game_name: Kolejka, Reglamentacja, Mis Wojtek, Niepodlegla, Twilight Struggle
study_characteristics.aim: To describe popular board game titles used in history education in Poland, present examples of their educational use and student feedback, and indicate the applications of board games in the academic training of future history teachers

eligibility.concerns: This is primarily a practitioner report with descriptive survey data rather than a controlled empirical study. The author is both the instructor and researcher, and no formal experimental design or statistical testing is employed. The surveys use open-ended questions with frequency counts rather than validated instruments.

rq1.conceptualization: Board games are conceptualized as tools of public history that make historical periods experiential and emotionally engaging. The article frames board games as a form of historical reenactment that confronts players with cognitive challenges similar to those experienced by people in historical periods. Games are seen as facilitating experiential learning, historical empathy, and atmosphere reconstruction rather than mere content delivery. The author positions board games as a bridge between public history (popular, engaging) and school history education (perceived as boring and encyclopedic).
theoretical_frameworks: Public history as framework for informal/experiential history education
Historical empathy development through game-based emotional engagement
Psychology of learning for instruction (Driscoll & Burner)

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Kolejka survey (53 students): Pre-game, 100% gave no answers to questions about communist-era economy/products. Post-game: 87% (46 students) listed minimum 4 associations with People's Poland economy; most common associations were queues 100% (53), poverty 94% (50), ration cards 90% (48), speculator 85% (45). 100% (53) named at least 3 era-specific products; vinegar 96% (51), alcohol 90% (48), chocolate-like product 80% (42). Emotions: fear/anxiety 18% (13), frustration 16% (8). Historical empathy: 80% (48) could identify specific feelings about people in that era. Twilight Struggle interviews (20 final-year students): 100% intend to use game-based learning in their work; 95% say they will use Twilight Struggle specifically.
rq2.comparative_methodology: Pre-post survey design for the Kolejka workshop: students answered identical questions before and after the game session. No control group. The dramatic shift from 0% knowledge pre-game to high percentages post-game is reported descriptively without statistical testing.
rq2.key_outcomes: Substantial knowledge gains about communist-era Poland after playing Kolejka (from zero knowledge to detailed associations). Strong development of historical empathy (80% could articulate feelings about historical people's experiences). Emotional engagement including frustration, anger, joy, sympathy, and helplessness mirroring historical experiences. Near-universal intent among future teachers to adopt game-based methods (100% of 20 interviewed final-year students). Students reported games made abstract historical periods tangible, helped reconstruct historical atmosphere, and facilitated retention of facts, dates, and causal relationships. Intergenerational bonding through games about People's Poland era.
rq2.engagement_results: Students expressed high excitement and satisfaction with game-based learning. Frequent student comments: 'This is how I can learn history', 'This kind of history is not boring.' Students reported emotional responses including frustration, helplessness, anger, and joy during Kolejka gameplay. Post-game interviews revealed students found game-based history 'a great example of historical reconstruction on the board.' For Twilight Struggle, students noted that 'facts, dates, numbers and people formed a coherent story' and they felt they 'went back in time and relived history.' Students autonomously sought additional information via smartphones during games.

game_design_elements: Historically authentic product cards with archival photographs (Kolejka: 60 original communist-era products)
Queue cards reflecting real historical social mechanisms (e.g., party connections, mother with child priority)
Archival photographs of historical scenes embedded in game materials
Historical narrative instructions written in era-appropriate language/propaganda style
