Cooperative mechanics for nation-building themes (Niepodlegla)
Card-driven mechanics linking historical events to game actions (Twilight Struggle: character, organization, doctrine, war, event cards)
Geographic board maps representing historical territorial realities
Photographs of historical leaders placed on game boards/cards
Historical insert booklets accompanying games with contextual information
Dual-language versions for international accessibility (Mis Wojtek in Polish and English)
Two difficulty variants — basic and advanced (Niepodlegla)
Negotiation and resource allocation mechanics (Reglamentacja: coupon exchange within timed rounds)
'History on the cards' comprehensive companion chapter (Twilight Struggle: 16 pages of card-by-card historical descriptions)
technological_platforms: Twilight Struggle digital app (faithful reproduction with original Cold War-era audio recordings of leaders' speeches)
YouTube and Spotify for supplementary historical audio/music content during gameplay
Online tournament platform for Mis Wojtek international school competitions
instructional_strategies: Pre-game and post-game surveys to assess knowledge change
Student-led facilitation: a student at each table acts as content coordinator, decider, and speculator introducing historical narrative
Small group format (5 players per table) to encourage critical thinking, analysis, synthesis, and evaluation
Parallel atmosphere enhancement: listening to period music during gameplay
Post-game group discussion of conclusions with comparative analysis against textbook content
Integration into formal lesson structure (90-minute double lesson units)
School board game tournaments and playoffs as motivational framework
International online tournaments connecting Polish schools worldwide
Mentoring classes in board games with students prior to independent workshops
Comparative analysis of game historical content with Polish school textbook content (Twilight Struggle)
rq3.content_integration: Games are tightly integrated with Polish national curriculum history topics. Kolejka and Reglamentacja cover everyday life in communist Poland (People's Republic of Poland 1980s), a topic in the final cycle of elementary school curriculum. Mis Wojtek covers WWII and the Polish II Corps route through the Middle East to Italy. Niepodlegla covers 1910-1920 and Poland's independence, tied to the centennial anniversary. Twilight Struggle covers Cold War history (1945-1989) which maps to both elementary and secondary school universal history curriculum. The author uses these games in university courses on history didactics, public history, media culture, and cultural studies, training future teachers to integrate them into their professional practice.

implementation_barriers: History education in Polish schools has a poor reputation among students — perceived as difficult and boring simultaneously
Communist period topics are covered late in the curriculum and often skipped or treated superficially due to time constraints
Students had zero prior knowledge of communist-era economy and daily life before the game intervention (100% blank responses pre-game)
Higher entry threshold for more complex games like Niepodlegla compared to simpler titles like Kolejka
Twilight Struggle requires more than two hours to play, limiting use in standard lesson periods
Gap between popular public history engagement and formal school history education
Need for teacher training in game-based methods — current university programs do not systematically include this
Declining student interest in history as a subject choice for graduation exams and university major
methodology_limitations: Author is simultaneously the instructor, game facilitator, and researcher — no independent observation or assessment
No control group for comparison in any of the survey or interview data
Anonymous survey with open-ended questions only — no validated measurement instruments
Small sample sizes (53 for Kolejka survey, 37 for Twilight Struggle surveys, 20 for in-depth interviews)
No formal statistical analysis of results — only descriptive frequency counts and percentages
Primarily a practitioner/descriptive report rather than a rigorous empirical study
Student opinions collected as anecdotal evidence — potential social desirability bias
No longitudinal follow-up to assess knowledge retention over time
negative_effects: Emotional distress noted in game instructions: 'the game may cause negative emotions in emotionally sensitive people' including tears, helplessness, and 'symptoms of gratuitous malice'
Students experienced frustration and anger during Kolejka gameplay
Fear/anxiety reported by 18% of students; frustration by 16%; sadness, fatigue, and stress by over 10%
mitigation_strategies: Using humor and era-appropriate satirical language in game instructions to balance emotional intensity
Student facilitators at each table provide historical context and narrative framing to guide the experience
Post-game debriefing discussions to process emotions and connect experiences to historical understanding
Offering two difficulty variants (basic and advanced) for complex games to match student readiness
Atmosphere enhancement through period music and multimedia to deepen rather than trivialize the emotional experience
Mentoring classes to prepare students before leading independent workshops

domain1.q1_evidence: The study involves convenience samples: 53 students participating in workshops led by the author, 37 university history students in the author's courses, and 20 final-year students selected for in-depth interviews. No selection criteria, sampling method, or inclusion/exclusion rationale is described. Interview participants appear self-selected from the author's own students.
domain1.q2_evidence: All participants are from the author's own classes/workshops at a single institution (University of Silesia in Katowice) or a single high school. No information on demographics, response rates, or how representative these samples are of broader Polish student or teacher-trainee populations. The high school is described only as 'a high school' with no further details.

domain2.q3_evidence: Surveys used non-validated, author-created open-ended questions (4 questions for Kolejka, before/after knowledge questions for Twilight Struggle). No psychometric properties reported. No established instruments for measuring historical knowledge, historical empathy, or engagement were used. The 20 in-depth interviews lack a described protocol or systematic coding scheme.
domain2.q4_evidence: Analysis consists entirely of descriptive frequency counts and selected student quotations. No statistical tests, no qualitative coding methodology described, no inter-rater reliability. The transition from raw interview/survey data to reported results is opaque. Student quotes are presented as illustrative but selection criteria for which quotes to include are not described.

domain3.q5_evidence: The author interprets all findings positively without considering alternative explanations. The dramatic pre-post knowledge change (0% to 87%+) could partly reflect the novelty effect, the 4-hour workshop duration, or demand characteristics rather than game-specific effects. The 100% intent to use game-based learning among interviewed students (who self-selected into the author's mentoring program) is presented as evidence of game effectiveness rather than potentially reflecting selection bias or social desirability.
domain3.q6_evidence: No limitations section is included in the paper. The author does not discuss any methodological weaknesses, potential biases from her dual role as instructor-researcher, absence of control groups, small sample sizes, or generalizability concerns. The paper reads as an advocacy piece for board game use rather than a balanced empirical investigation.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study has high risk of bias across all domains. It is fundamentally a practitioner report with descriptive survey data rather than a rigorous empirical study. Key concerns include: (1) convenience sampling from the author's own classes with no selection criteria; (2) non-validated measurement instruments (author-created open-ended questions); (3) no control group or comparison condition; (4) no statistical analysis; (5) dual role of the author as instructor and researcher introducing bias; (6) exclusively positive interpretation of all findings with no consideration of alternative explanations; and (7) complete absence of a limitations discussion. While the descriptive data and student quotes provide interesting practitioner insights into board game use in Polish history education, the methodological rigor is insufficient for drawing causal conclusions about effectiveness.

pdf_filename: HistoryLand: a Serious Game for History Learning in Primary Education.pdf

bibliographic.title: HistoryLand: a Serious Game for History Learning in Primary Education
bibliographic.venue: Unknown (conference/workshop proceedings)

study_characteristics.sample_description: 34 fifth-grade Greek students (15 males and 19 females) aged 11 to 12 years old, from a primary school class on Modern History
study_characteristics.study_design: One-shot pre-post questionnaire study (no control group)
study_characteristics.aim: To explore the impact of the HistoryLand game on students' immersion, collaboration, knowledge improvement, and enjoyment when used as a complementary tool for teaching Modern History in Greek primary education

eligibility.concerns: Short pilot study with no control group; one-shot design raises novelty effect concerns acknowledged by the authors; prototype game (work-in-progress)

rq1.conceptualization: The study frames HistoryLand as a 'serious game' for game-based learning, designed as a complementary tool for teaching Modern History. It follows the model for serious educational games proposed by Annetta (2010). The game combines individual card-collection gameplay with collaborative story composition, integrating a conversational agent for scaffolding discussions. The conceptualization positions games as motivating and engaging learning environments that complement traditional instruction rather than replacing it.
theoretical_frameworks: Annetta (2010) framework for serious educational game design
Collaborative learning (dyad-based story composition with conversational agent scaffolding)

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Likert-scale questionnaires (1-5) measuring four dimensions: Enjoyment (Cronbach alpha=0.893, M=4.41, SD=0.37), Immersion (Cronbach alpha=0.813, M=4.18, SD=0.64), Collaboration (Cronbach alpha=0.947, M=4.73, SD=0.67), and Knowledge improvement (Cronbach alpha=0.903, M=4.59, SD=0.26). Pre-post comparison using Wilcoxon Signed-ranks tests and Spearman rank correlation coefficients.
rq2.statistical_results: Three significant pre-post differences: (1) Pedagogical value of computer-based activities: Z=-1.97, p=0.04, r=-0.24 (pre M=2.84, SD=1.46; post M=3.41, SD=1.42); (2) Concentration levels/distraction: Z=-2.61, p=0.00, r=-0.32 (game M=2.38, SD=1.59 vs typical lesson M=3.25, SD=1.52); (3) Preference for group work: Z=-3.57, p=0.00, r=-0.43 (pre M=3.65, SD=1.54; post M=4.65, SD=0.92). Significant correlations: immersion-enjoyment r=0.914, p=0.000; immersion-knowledge improvement r=0.793, p=0.000; collaboration-knowledge improvement r=0.887, p=0.000.
rq2.comparative_methodology: Pre-post questionnaire comparison using Wilcoxon Signed-ranks test (non-parametric, as normality and homogeneity of variance criteria were not satisfied). No control group comparison.
rq2.key_outcomes: Students perceived the game favorably across all four dimensions (enjoyment, immersion, collaboration, knowledge improvement), with all mean scores above 4.0 on a 5-point scale. Students rated computer-supported learning activities as significantly more useful after playing the game. Distraction levels during the game were significantly lower than during typical History lessons. Preference for collaborative group work significantly increased after the game activity.
rq2.engagement_results: Enjoyment M=4.41 (SD=0.37); Immersion M=4.18 (SD=0.64); students felt highly involved in the game (M=4.85, SD=0.49); forgot about time passing (M=4.73, SD=0.78); the game grabbed attention (M=4.76, SD=0.76)

game_design_elements: Item card collection mechanics (historical facts/figures on cards)
Three progressive levels representing historical periods (Balkan Wars, WWI, WWII)
Lives system (three chances per level to find the correct card)
Dynamic scoring based on number of mistakes
Collaborative story composition phase (dyads combining collected cards)
Conversational agent providing guidance and scaffolding discussions
Avatar-based interface with themed game environment
technological_platforms: Online game deployed in school computer lab
instructional_strategies: Individual gameplay phase followed by collaborative phase
Card identification requiring historical period discrimination (finding irrelevant card)
Collaborative story writing about a historical event (Asia Minor Campaign)
Scaffolded peer discussion via conversational agent
Game as complement to traditional classroom instruction (not replacement)
Integration with existing curriculum (Modern History course content)
rq3.content_integration: The game content is directly integrated with the Greek primary school Modern History curriculum. Three levels cover the Balkan Wars, World War I, and World War II. The collaborative phase focuses on the Asia Minor Campaign (1922). Students must apply prior classroom knowledge to identify cards and compose historically accurate stories, reinforcing content discussed in class.

implementation_barriers: Prototype/work-in-progress status of the game limits generalizability
Limited game content covering only select historical periods
Requirement for school computer lab infrastructure
One-shot study design constraining evidence strength
methodology_limitations: No control group for comparison
Small sample size (N=34) from a single class
One-shot design (single 90-minute session) does not allow assessment of long-term effects
Self-reported questionnaire data only (no objective learning outcome measures such as test scores)
Potential novelty effect acknowledged by authors
Non-parametric statistics needed due to violation of normality and homogeneity of variance assumptions
negative_effects: Some students reported distraction during game play (M=3.82, SD=1.54 for 'I cannot recall any distraction')
Variable awareness of surroundings during immersion (M=3.35, SD=1.59)
Potential novelty effect may inflate positive perceptions
mitigation_strategies: Authors plan to conduct a more robustly designed in-depth study over an extended period to address novelty effect concerns
Future work planned to extend analysis of conversational agent effectiveness
Plans to enrich game content to include more historical periods

domain1.q1_evidence: No explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria for participants. All students from a single primary school class were included (convenience sampling). No information about how or why this particular class was selected.
domain1.q2_evidence: Sample of 34 students from a single Greek primary school class. No discussion of representativeness. Single school, single class, single country limits generalizability significantly.

domain2.q3_evidence: Pre- and post-task questionnaires with Likert scales. Internal consistency reported for post-task dimensions (Cronbach alpha ranging 0.813-0.947, all acceptable). However, no validated instrument cited; questionnaire based on Sisson (2011) for comparison dimensions. No objective learning measures (e.g., knowledge tests) used.
domain2.q4_evidence: Appropriate non-parametric statistics used (Wilcoxon Signed-ranks test, Spearman correlation) given violated normality assumptions. Descriptive statistics reported. However, analysis relies entirely on self-report data with no triangulation from objective measures. Effect sizes reported (r values).

domain3.q5_evidence: Conclusions are generally consistent with the data presented. Authors appropriately describe findings as 'preliminary' and 'pilot'. However, some conclusions about knowledge improvement are based solely on self-report rather than measured learning outcomes.
domain3.q6_evidence: Authors explicitly acknowledge the novelty effect concern, the need for a more robustly designed study, and the preliminary nature of their findings. They outline concrete plans for future research to address limitations.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study has high risk of bias primarily due to its study design (one-shot pilot with no control group, convenience sample of 34 students from a single class). While the questionnaire instruments show acceptable reliability and appropriate non-parametric statistics are used, the reliance entirely on self-report measures without objective learning assessments, combined with the small convenience sample and single-session design susceptible to novelty effects, contribute to an overall high risk of bias. The authors commendably acknowledge these limitations.

pdf_filename: A game for learning history on mobile devices.pdf

bibliographic.title: A game for learning history on mobile devices
bibliographic.venue: Education and Information Technologies

study_characteristics.sample_description: Students in the 2nd cycle of the Portuguese Educational System (5th and 6th grade), aged 10 to 12. Of 649 total respondents, 508 played games on mobile devices (298 male, 210 female, average age 11.2 years). Survey conducted between May and November 2013.
study_characteristics.study_design: design_based
study_characteristics.aim: To present a mobile game designed to support teaching and learning of Portuguese History (Republic Implantation in 1910) for 6th grade students, informed by research on students' game preferences and Gee's learning principles.

eligibility.concerns: The paper is primarily a design-based study describing the game design process and student survey on game preferences. It does not include a formal evaluation of learning outcomes from the game itself, only the survey informing the design.

rq1.conceptualization: The paper conceptualizes games as systems with rules, obstacles, and choices where the player learns through failures (citing Gee 2007). Games are seen as powerful mechanisms for teaching formal contents through fun and learning in every move. The study draws on Gee's learning principles and game mechanics to structure game-based learning for history. The paper focuses on mobile game-based learning rather than gamification per se, treating the custom mobile game as an educational tool integrating game mechanics with historical content.
theoretical_frameworks: Game mechanics and game design fundamentals (Salen and Zimmerman 2004)

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Survey data on game preferences: 84.6% of students wanted to use games to learn course content. Top game types for classroom use: Adventure (66.0%), Action (59.1%), Sport (50.5%). Game characteristics for keeping players playing included graphic effects/animations (79.9% male, 70.0% female), gameplay (78.2% male, 59.9% female), characters (74.2% male, 79.5% female). Difficulty preferences: Moderate (40.8%), Easy (22.4%), Very Easy (16.9%), Hard (12.2%), Very Hard (7.7%). Average play time: 4.4 hours/week (males 5.5h, females 2.8h).
rq2.statistical_results: Descriptive statistics only (frequencies and percentages). No inferential statistical tests reported. Gender differences in game preferences were described but not statistically tested in this paper.
rq2.key_outcomes: The study produced a detailed understanding of Portuguese students' mobile game preferences and habits that informed the design of the '1910' history game. Key findings: male students prefer longer, competitive games (GTA, CS, PES, Minecraft) while female students prefer casual games (Pou, Subway Surfers). Students strongly endorsed using games for learning school content (84.6%). Eight of Gee's 36 learning principles were identified in the most popular games and applied to the game design: Psychosocial Moratorium, Committed Learning Principle, Amplification of Input, Achievement Principle, Practice Principle, Regime of Competence, Intuitive Knowledge, and Affinity Group Principle.
rq2.engagement_results: Students showed high receptivity to using games in course activities. They valued repetition of tasks for cognitive/motor skill development and identification with game characters. The paper notes students are receptive and like games that allow development of cognitive skills or motor dexterity.

game_design_elements: Points/coins for correct answers
Levels/episodes organized by historical periods (1890, 1908, 1910, 1911)
Leaderboard (top five scores of classmates)
Progression unlocking (completing tasks unlocks next historical event on timeline)
Role-playing as a journalist character in 1890
Quests/missions (investigating facts/events for newspaper articles)
Achievement/reward system (more points for harder tasks)
Notebook for recording historical facts
Avatar with fictionalized character identity
Penalty system (losing half points for incorrect answers)
Repeat/retry mechanism for episodes
instructional_strategies: Narrative-driven learning through role-playing as a journalist
Historical content integration through episodic storytelling across key dates
Multiple activity types: drag-and-drop, multiple choice, jigsaw puzzles, matching, fill-in-the-blanks
Progressive difficulty across episodes
Application of Gee's learning principles (Psychosocial Moratorium, Committed Learning, Amplification of Input, Achievement, Regime of Competence, Intuitive Knowledge, Affinity Group)
Teacher monitoring via web dashboard with student results in Excel
Game notebook as review/study tool collecting historical information
Flexible use: in-class or as homework with subsequent classroom discussion
rq3.content_integration: The game covers the Republic Implantation in Portugal (1910), a topic in the 6th grade Portuguese History curriculum. Historical content is integrated through four episodic periods (1890, 1908, 1910, 1911) with authentic historical photographs and events. The player assumes the role of a journalist in 1890 Lisbon who investigates historical events for newspaper articles, encountering the political crisis, the regicide of 1908, the revolution of 1910, and the new republic's measures in 1911. Activities include selecting correct words for articles, choosing photographs, solving jigsaw puzzles, identifying secret society members, quizzes about historical places, coloring the national flag, and matching national anthem verses.

implementation_barriers: Difficulty integrating games into rigid school curricula
Teachers need training/expertise to use games in education
Financial barriers (cost of games and dedicated equipment in schools)
Technical barriers (lack of dedicated equipment in schools)
Need for interdisciplinary teams (game designers, programmers, artists, historians, educationalists)
Mobile devices for personal use can cause distraction, especially for low-achieving students
Non-response bias due to school and student self-selection in survey participation
methodology_limitations: The paper presents a design study without formal evaluation of the game's learning effectiveness
Survey sample is not fully representative (most respondents from northern Portugal)
Self-selection bias in survey participation
No pre-test/post-test or control group comparison for learning outcomes
Descriptive statistics only; no inferential statistical analysis of gender differences or other comparisons
Some games mentioned by students are not age-appropriate (PEGI 16/18 games played by 10-12 year olds)
negative_effects: Mobile devices for personal use can cause distraction for low-achieving students (citing Beland and Murphy 2015)
Some students play age-inappropriate games with violent content
mitigation_strategies: Using mobile devices addresses barriers of dedicated school equipment by allowing anytime/anywhere play
Teacher role designed into the game system (creating class groups, monitoring progress, accessing results)
Game designed for both in-class and homework use to maximize flexibility
Survey validated by field experts and approved by National Board of Education
Design informed by actual student preference data rather than assumptions

domain1.q1_evidence: The study targets a clearly defined population: 5th and 6th grade students in the 2nd cycle of the Portuguese Educational System, aged 10-12. All schools were invited to participate through the Ministry of Education website and email.
domain1.q2_evidence: N=508 game-playing students from 649 respondents. However, the authors acknowledge most respondents were from northern Portugal and the sample includes non-response bias due to school and student self-selection. The sample is described as 'representative in relation to the target population' but this claim is weakened by the acknowledged self-selection bias.

domain2.q3_evidence: An online survey was used, validated by experts in the field and approved by the National Board of Education (Direção Geral de Educação) of Portugal. The survey explored four dimensions: student characterisation, game habits, game preferences, and preferences for learning school content through games.
domain2.q4_evidence: Only descriptive statistics (frequencies and percentages) are reported. No inferential statistical tests were conducted to validate observed differences (e.g., gender differences in game preferences). The analysis of Gee's learning principles in popular games is qualitative and based on the researchers' interpretation.

domain3.q5_evidence: The findings from the survey are consistently linked to the game design decisions. The identification of Gee's learning principles in popular games is systematically applied to the design of the '1910' game. The connection between student preferences and design choices is clearly articulated.
domain3.q6_evidence: The authors acknowledge the self-selection bias and geographic concentration of the sample. However, they do not discuss the limitation that the game was not formally evaluated for learning effectiveness, nor do they discuss the limitations of using only descriptive statistics. The paper presents the game design without evidence of its actual educational impact.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study presents a well-structured design-based research approach with a validated survey instrument and clear connection between findings and game design. However, key limitations include: (1) self-selection bias in the survey sample with geographic concentration in northern Portugal, (2) only descriptive statistics without inferential analysis, (3) no formal evaluation of the designed game's learning effectiveness, and (4) partial discussion of limitations. The study is methodologically sound as a design study but lacks empirical evidence of the game's educational impact.

pdf_filename: History-Themed Games in History Education Experiences on a Blended World History Course.pdf

bibliographic.title: History-Themed Games in History Education: Experiences on a Blended World History Course
bibliographic.venue: ResearchGate Preprint

study_characteristics.sample_description: Undergraduate students enrolled in a 5 ECTS free elective course (ARCD301 - Playing with The Past) at Abdullah Gul University, Kayseri, Turkey, whose major program is not a history program. The course ran four times between 2015 and 2018.
study_characteristics.study_design: qualitative observational study
study_characteristics.game_type: commercial off-the-shelf strategy video games (grand strategy)
study_characteristics.game_name: Crusader Kings II, Europa Universalis IV, Hearts of Iron IV (also Civilization IV and Empire Total War in early iterations)
study_characteristics.aim: To experiment on how to integrate history-themed strategy video games into a blended world history course to achieve higher understanding of the contemporary social, political, economical, and technological context of historical eras, and to report observations on student experiences and learning outcomes.

eligibility.concerns: This is primarily a descriptive course design paper with qualitative observations rather than a rigorous empirical study. No formal sample size is reported, no control group, and no standardized outcome measures. Assessment is based on instructor observations of blog posts, in-class discussions, and a survey (details not provided).

rq1.conceptualization: The study conceptualizes history-themed games as strategy video games with detailed historical models that can serve as supportive tools in history courses. Following a 'history as a process' philosophy, the games allow students to experiment with social, political, economical, and technological norms of historical eras, providing an 'immersion process' (citing Radetich et al.) that improves understanding of historical settings. The approach is blended learning combining classical lecture and discussion (L&D) sessions with game experience sessions.

rq2.comparative_methodology: The authors compared three game series over multiple course iterations (2015-2018): Civilization series, Total War series, and Paradox Grand Strategy series. In the first two years they used one game from each series (Civilization IV, Crusader Kings II, Empire Total War). Based on observations, Grand Strategy games provided the most comprehensive experience due to level of detail, high historical accuracy, and versatility, leading them to switch entirely to Grand Strategy games in later iterations.
rq2.key_outcomes: Five key qualitative learning outcomes were observed: (1) In-depth geographical knowledge - students internalized concepts of strategic and economic importance through interactive world maps; (2) Increased awareness of interaction between various societal issues - students became aware of complex interactions between economic, religious, technological, political, and cultural elements; (3) Experience-based immersive learning - students reported a critical immersive component with trial-and-error methodology allowing internalization of historical interactions; (4) Discussion over modeling decisions - students critically engaged with and debated the game's modeling choices (e.g., Eurocentric trade networks, westernization mechanic); (5) Contextualizing key events and major developments - students shifted from modern viewpoints to historical perspectives, understanding events as part of greater processes.
rq2.engagement_results: Students who could not achieve assigned goals in game-based assignments self-incentivized to try again with different tactics and decisions, even though success or failure was explicitly stated as unimportant. This self-motivated repetition created high personal motivation and further increased immersiveness. Students also spontaneously initiated critical discussions about game modeling decisions.

game_design_elements: Interactive world map with geopolitical components
Character-driven feudal system simulation (CK2)
Title and dynasty hierarchical system
Vassal-liege opinion mechanics (-100 to 100 scale)
Casus belli requirement for war declaration
Religious mechanics (Catholic-Pope relations, Sunni Islam decadence)
Westphalian nation-state simulation (EU4)
Standing army system replacing levy system
Technology tree with three categories (administrative, diplomatic, militaristic) and 32 levels
Institutions mechanic (Feudalism, Renaissance, Colonization, Printing Press, Global Trade, Manufactories, Enlightenment)
Fixed unidirectional trade network system
Country-specific historical events and mission trees
Political ideology system (democratic, fascist, communist, non-aligned) in HoI4
World tension mechanic
Strategic resources trade system (oil, aluminum, tungsten, rubber, chromium, steel)
Logistics and naval convoy system
Emergent gameplay from interacting mechanics
technological_platforms: Crusader Kings II (Paradox Interactive) - medieval ages (869-1453)
Europa Universalis IV (Paradox Interactive) - early modern to industrial age (1444-1812)
Hearts of Iron IV (Paradox Interactive) - early to mid 20th century (1910-1948 with Great War mod)
Sid Meier's Civilization IV (Firaxis Games) - used in early iterations
Empire Total War (Creative Assembly) - used in early iterations
The Great War mod for HoI4 (extends period to 1910)
instructional_strategies: Blended learning with classical lecture and discussion (L&D) sessions combined with game experience sessions
Modular course structure covering three historical ages: middle ages, early modern age, modern age
Two-week modules: one week L&D, one week game experience
Guided game sessions (3-5 hours) with specific nation/scenario options and goals
Weekly 300-500 word blog post reflections comparing game experiences with lecture content
Term project: 2000-3000 word article based on 15-20 hour extended gameplay as a chosen nation/dynasty with historical research
Midterm exam with counterfactual history 'what if' scenarios
Progressive game introduction across three Grand Strategy titles following historical periodization
In-class discussions over game modeling decisions and historical accuracy
rq3.content_integration: The course integrates world history content across three ages: Middle Ages (Christian and Islamic worlds, feudal vs. Iqta systems, crusades, Great Schism, Sunni-Shia split), Early Modern Age (Mongol aftermath, three Muslim empires, Renaissance, Reformation, colonization, Enlightenment, imperialism), and Modern Age (Industrial Revolution, WWI, interwar period, WWII). Each historical period is paired with a corresponding Grand Strategy game whose mechanics model the specific socio-political systems of that era. Students compare and contrast game experiences with historical sources in written assignments.

implementation_barriers: Requires effort to set up the blended course structure
Some games have steep learning curves (e.g., Victoria II was excluded due to complicated mechanics and unpolished UI)
Course schedule constraints limited the number of games that could be used
Games may contain Eurocentric design biases (e.g., EU4 institutions mechanic, fixed trade network favoring Western Europe)
Students whose major is not history may have varying baseline knowledge
methodology_limitations: No formal sample size reported
No control group or comparison condition
No standardized quantitative outcome measures
Observations are based on qualitative assessment of blog posts, in-class discussions, and a survey whose details are not provided
Assessment of learning outcomes relies primarily on instructor observations and essay quality
The study is descriptive and experiential rather than rigorously empirical
Preprint not published in a peer-reviewed venue
negative_effects: Games contain Eurocentric modeling choices (institutions appear in Europe first, trade routes flow toward Western Europe, former 'westernization' mechanic)
Some game modeling decisions are only partially successful emulations of historical systems (e.g., Islamic bishopric/mosque representation)
Risk that students may internalize game biases as historical facts if not critically discussed
Success/failure dynamics in game-based assignments can create pressure despite being explicitly stated as unimportant
mitigation_strategies: Critical in-class discussions about game modeling decisions and their historical accuracy
Switching from the overtly Eurocentric 'westernization' mechanic to the improved 'institutions' mechanic
Comparing game experiences with primary and secondary historical sources in written assignments
Explicitly stating that success or failure in game assignments is not graded
Iterative course improvement over four years by testing different game series and selecting the most suitable ones
Using multiple games with different modeling foci to provide more comprehensive perspectives

domain1.q1_evidence: No clear inclusion/exclusion criteria for participant selection. The course is a 5 ECTS free elective targeted at non-history majors, but no details on how many students enrolled, demographic characteristics, or whether any selection criteria were applied. The study ran four times (2015-2018) but does not specify which iterations are being reported on or how students were recruited.
domain1.q2_evidence: The sample consists only of students at a single Turkish university (Abdullah Gul University) who self-selected into an elective course, which limits generalizability. No information on sample size, demographics, or representativeness is provided.

domain2.q3_evidence: Learning outcomes are assessed through blog posts (300-500 words), a term project (2000-3000 words), and a midterm exam with counterfactual history questions. A survey is mentioned but no details are provided about its design, validation, or results. No standardized assessment instruments were used. The quality of written essays is subjectively evaluated by instructors.
domain2.q4_evidence: No formal data analysis methods are described. The findings section ('Observations of the Student Experiences') presents qualitative observations organized thematically but without systematic coding, inter-rater reliability, or any quantitative analysis. No survey results are reported despite mentioning a survey was conducted.

domain3.q5_evidence: The authors present only positive observations without any negative or null findings. The interpretation appears to be strongly influenced by the authors' role as course designers and instructors, creating potential confirmation bias. Claims about learning outcomes are not supported by systematic evidence.
domain3.q6_evidence: The paper does not contain a dedicated limitations section. The conclusion briefly acknowledges that 'it requires some effort to set up such a blended world history course' but does not discuss methodological limitations, threats to validity, or limitations of the observational approach.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study presents a descriptive account of a blended history course using strategy video games but lacks methodological rigor. There is no defined sample size, no control group, no standardized measures, no formal data analysis, and no discussion of limitations. The findings are based entirely on informal instructor observations without systematic data collection or analysis. While the course design and game mechanic descriptions are detailed and informative, the evidence for learning effectiveness claims is weak. The publication is a preprint without peer review.

pdf_filename: How a Serious Game Supports Elementary School History Classes in Teaching About the Bombardment of Copenhagen in 1807.pdf

bibliographic.title: How a Serious Game Supports Elementary School History Classes in Teaching About the Bombardment of Copenhagen in 1807
bibliographic.venue: Joint International Conference on Serious Games (JCSG 2023), Lecture Notes in Computer Science (LNCS 14309)

study_characteristics.sample_description: 22 pupils aged 13-14 from a Danish elementary school, split into two classes: experimental group (11 pupils, 4 male and 7 female) and control group (11 pupils, 6 male and 5 female)
study_characteristics.study_design: quasi_experimental
study_characteristics.game_name: Bombardment of Copenhagen 1807 (custom serious game built in Unity Engine 2021)
study_characteristics.aim: To investigate whether a serious game can be engaging and improve learning outcomes about the history of the Copenhagen Bombardment in 1807 for Danish elementary school pupils in the 7th grade

rq1.explicit_definition: Previous definitions have emphasized that serious games are applications that are not designed exclusively for fun or that are intended to be more than entertainment.
rq1.conceptualization: The study conceptualizes serious games as educational tools that use narrative engagement, clear goals, and intuitiveness to communicate learning objectives tied to the school curriculum. The game transforms historical textbook content into an interactive 3D environment with NPCs providing historical information.

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Knowledge test with 6 curriculum-aligned questions; user-engagement questionnaire (8 items on 5-point Likert scale) covering focused attention, perceived usability, and aesthetic appeal
rq2.statistical_results: Experimental group answered questions correctly to a much higher degree than control group. Q1: Exp 82% vs Con 9% (diff 73%); Q5: Exp 90% vs Con 20% (diff 70%); Q6: Exp 60% vs Con 0% (diff 60%). However Q2: Exp 0% vs Con 20% (diff -20%). Engagement questionnaire: highest mean score Q2.2 (intuitiveness, Mean: 4.00, SD: 0.943); Q2.3 narrative clarity (Mean: 3.60, SD: 1.174); Q1.2 purpose clarity (Mean: 3.45, SD: 0.820).
rq2.comparative_methodology: Quasi-experimental comparison between experimental (gaming) group and control (analogue textbook reading) group, with both groups taking the same 6-question knowledge test
rq2.key_outcomes: The experimental gaming group showed substantially higher understanding of specific learning objectives compared to the control group on most questions (73%, 70%, and 60% advantages on Q1, Q5, Q6 respectively). The game was perceived as intuitive and the narrative was clear.
rq2.engagement_results: Interviews revealed mainly positive perceptions across feedback, immersion, teaching, and motivation themes. 8 positive vs 3 negative statements for feedback; 6 positive vs 5 negative for immersion; 8 positive vs 3 negative for teaching. Students found it 'more fun than the traditional teaching in history class' but some felt 'the game was overloaded with information.'

game_design_elements: Narrative engagement
NPC-guided storytelling
Collectible notes (4 notes to collect)
Visual feedback on progress
3D exploration environment
Clear goals tied to curriculum
Historical reconstruction of Copenhagen
technological_platforms: Unity Store asset packs for 3D models
instructional_strategies: Curriculum-aligned content co-designed with history teacher
Teacher involvement in game development
Same textual content as analogue textbook embedded in game
Post-game knowledge testing
Semi-structured interviews for qualitative feedback
rq3.content_integration: The game takes place in a 3D reconstruction of Copenhagen with canals, bridges, harbors, buildings, and a church tower. Players follow NPC guidance to collect and read four notes containing the exact same text as the analogue textbook used by the control group. Historical information about the Bombardment is delivered through NPC interactions and collectible notes.

implementation_barriers: Difficulty conducting perfect research evaluation with pupils aged 13-14 in elementary school due to logistics, time constraints, gatekeepers, legislation
Lack of a proper post-test and baseline assessment
Technical issues and resource constraints
Voiceover-only information delivery proved ineffective for Q2
methodology_limitations: Small sample size (only 22 pupils, 11 per group)
Uncertain whether early teens could cope cognitively with a 5-point Likert scale
Randomization was impractical in fieldwork context
No pre-test to establish baseline knowledge
Individual variation in responses to the computer game not accounted for
Could be unethical to randomize pupils in the same class
negative_effects: Some pupils found the game overloaded with information making it hard to remember
Some pupils missed the traditional way of reading and answering questions
Engagement challenges from balancing clear goals vs discoverability and difficulty
Information conveyed only through voiceover (Q2) was not effectively learned
mitigation_strategies: Include improved multimedia learning framework combining words, voiceover, narrative, and sound effects
Include more emphasis on minimizing cognitive overload
Make the game purpose clearer at the beginning
Include a list of tasks for players to reference while playing
Need much higher number of participants and baseline/control groups in future research

domain1.q1_evidence: The participants in this study were pupils from a Danish elementary school aged 13 or 14. One class functioned as a control group... The control group consisted of 11 pupils (six male and five female). The other class (experimental group) also consisted of 11 pupils (four male and seven female).
domain1.q2_evidence: Very small sample of only 22 pupils from a single school, not randomized. Both classes are from the same school, with the same curriculum, but had each a different history teacher. The sample is a convenience sample with no randomization.

domain2.q3_evidence: The questionnaire was inspired by the user-engagement scale (UES) short form and consisted of eight items on a 5-point Likert scale. The knowledge test was made in collaboration with the teacher and had six questions. However, no reliability or validity metrics are reported for any instruments. Authors acknowledge uncertainty about whether early teens could cope cognitively with a 5-point Likert scale.
domain2.q4_evidence: We analyzed the user-engagement questionnaire using cumulative frequency, following a mean and standard deviation for each question. The knowledge tests were also analyzed by cumulative frequency... All the interviews were analyzed via traditional coding following four steps: organizing, recognizing, coding, and interpretation.

domain3.q5_evidence: The results revealed higher understanding of specific learning objectives in the experimental gaming group compared to the control group. The authors note the Q2 exception and explain it was due to voiceover-only delivery. Interpretations are consistent with the data presented in Tables 1-3.
domain3.q6_evidence: A major limitation for this study is whether the early teens understood the questions asked and could cope cognitively with a 5-point Likert scale. In addition, randomization is often impractical for evaluating serious games in a fieldwork context... First, a much higher number of participants is needed, and baseline and control groups should be included in the research design.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: While the study has clear participant selection criteria (Domain 1 q1) and appropriate interpretation with acknowledged limitations (Domain 3), the very small convenience sample of 22 students from a single school with no randomization (Domain 1 High) and lack of validated instruments (Domain 2 Unclear) result in an overall High risk of bias.

pdf_filename: How Much Life do I Lose from the Plague Educational Board Games as Teaching Tools in Archaeology and Ancient History Courses.pdf

bibliographic.title: How Much Life do I Lose from the Plague? Educational Board Games as Teaching Tools in Archaeology and Ancient History Courses
bibliographic.venue: Public Archaeology

study_characteristics.sample_description: University students enrolled in the 'Ancient Medicine' course at the School of Archaeology and Anthropology, Australian National University, during the Southern Hemisphere spring semester of 2010. Students formed teams of 3-6 members to design board games. Eleven final games were submitted.
study_characteristics.study_design: case_study
study_characteristics.game_name: Multiple student-designed board games including Ankh - The Game of Life and Ying Yang: A Journey Through Ancient Chinese Medicine
study_characteristics.aim: To describe the development, implementation, assessment, debriefing and outcomes, and potential uses of a university student-driven educational gaming project, as a major assessment item in an archaeology course entitled 'Ancient Medicine'

eligibility.concerns: The study focuses on archaeology/ancient medicine rather than purely history education, but it covers ancient history content (Egyptian medicine, Chinese medicine, medieval plague, etc.) and is relevant to history education through game-based learning.

rq1.explicit_definition: Abt (1987: 9) defines them as games that have 'an explicit and carefully thought-out educational purpose and are not intended to be played primarily for amusement, but that does not mean they are not, or should not, be entertaining.'
rq1.conceptualization: The study conceptualizes educational board games as student-driven design projects where students themselves create the games as a form of active, constructivist learning. The processual nature of educational games is emphasized: designing, testing, and iterating on games is itself a learning activity. Board games are positioned as a cost-effective, low-tech alternative to digital games.
theoretical_frameworks: Bogost's persuasive games and procedural rhetoric
Gee's four-step learning process in games
Prensky's binary categorizations for learning games

rq2.comparative_methodology: No formal comparative methodology. Assessment centred around three specific criteria: (1) overall success of the game itself; (2) individual and team member participation evaluations; (3) a game overview document. Standard departmental class and teacher evaluation forms were also used.
rq2.key_outcomes: Overall, from the quality of the final games produced, it is clear that students took their tasks quite seriously and were getting enough out of the project to view it as much more than just another assignment. Student feedback was diverse, but overwhelmingly positive. The educational board gaming project achieved very positive feedback in standard departmental evaluations.
rq2.engagement_results: Students took tasks quite seriously and viewed the project as much more than just another assignment. Student feedback was diverse, but overwhelmingly positive. The distinctiveness and success of the project was even noted by the local university media as something that might be emulated.

game_design_elements: Board game mechanics (dice rolling, movement, cards)
Educational content integration (knowledge questions)
Thematic design around historical medical systems
Chance elements and strategic decision-making
Player progression through game spaces
Alpha and beta play testing iterations
Team-based collaborative design
instructional_strategies: Student-driven game design as assessment
Team-based collaborative learning
Multiple iterative play testing rounds
Role delegation within teams (research, artwork, mechanics, quality assurance, project manager)
Peer evaluation through cross-team play testing
Game overview document and poster presentation
rq3.content_integration: Students researched historical medical systems (Egyptian, Chinese, Greek, Roman, medieval European medicine) and designed board games that required players to gain and retain knowledge of ancient medicine themes. Games were evaluated on whether a player had to gain and retain knowledge of the ancient medicine theme underpinning the story and rhetoric. For example, Ankh - The Game of Life required knowledge of Egyptian medicine to avoid illness squares, and Ying Yang integrated Chinese symbolism and medical theory into its pentagonal board design.

implementation_barriers: Time constraints - overcoming time constraints in constructing games over one semester
Some students felt meeting high expectations detracted from their ability to complete all assignments for all classes
Personality conflicts within teams needed resolution in consultation with the teacher
Web-based discussion forum went almost entirely unutilized
Only one instructor (DH) had direct experience in educational game theory, design and testing
methodology_limitations: No formal quantitative assessment of learning outcomes
No pre-post comparison or control group
Pilot project with only one semester of data
Assessment criteria were holistic rather than measuring specific learning gains
Only descriptive/qualitative evidence of effectiveness
negative_effects: A few students felt personally that meeting high expectations was detracting too much from their ability to complete assignments for all classes
Personality conflicts within teams when friends teamed up, leaving other teams comprised of strangers
Clarifying and adjusting rules, spell-checking question cards, and polishing mechanics were time-consuming
mitigation_strategies: Scheduled structure of the semester with strict time intervals for each design stage
Decreased number of formal play-testing sessions in subsequent iterations (2012 and 2014)
Allowed individually created conference-quality poster as alternative when interpersonal conflicts could not be resolved
Created crib sheet with general descriptions of game design roles
Quick reference guide collated from real-world commercial and educational examples

domain1.q1_evidence: The participants are described as students enrolled in the 'Ancient Medicine' course at Australian National University. However, no specific selection criteria, sample size, or demographic details are provided beyond the course enrollment context.
domain1.q2_evidence: The sample is the entire class of students enrolled in the course, which is appropriate for a case study. However, no information is given about how many students were enrolled or whether they are representative of any broader population. Teams ranged from 'four to six' members and eleven final games were submitted.

domain2.q3_evidence: No validated research instruments were used. Assessment was based on three criteria: overall success of the game, individual/team participation evaluations, and a game overview document. Standard departmental class and teacher evaluation forms were mentioned but not described. No reliability or validity evidence provided.
domain2.q4_evidence: No formal data analysis methods are described. The paper provides a descriptive narrative account of the project and general impressions ('overwhelmingly positive,' 'very impressed by the quality') without systematic data analysis procedures.

domain3.q5_evidence: The authors' interpretations are consistent with the descriptive account provided. They present the project as a successful pilot with positive outcomes while acknowledging that it was a pilot and had limitations. Claims about student engagement are supported by examples of the games produced.
domain3.q6_evidence: The time-constraint criticism was dealt with in subsequent iterations. Only one instructor had direct experience in educational game theory. The paper acknowledges time constraints, personality conflicts, and the challenges of only having one hour of contact time per week over a four-month semester.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: While the study provides a rich descriptive account of the project and interpretations are consistent with the evidence (Domain 3 Low), the lack of validated research instruments (Domain 2 q3 No), absence of formal data analysis methods (Domain 2 q4 No), and unclear participant selection and representativeness (Domain 1 Unclear) result in an overall High risk of bias. This is primarily a descriptive case study without rigorous empirical measurement.

pdf_filename: Indonesian History Educational Card Game Gamification of the Process of Learning to Increase Interest in History among Children..pdf

bibliographic.title: Indonesian History Educational Card Game: Gamification of the Process of Learning to Increase Interest in History among Children
bibliographic.venue: Journal of Game, Game Art and Gamification

study_characteristics.sample_description: 60 students from grades 5-6 (ages 9-12) at Mahatma Gandhi School and SD Santo Lukas and others in Jakarta, Indonesia. Additional qualitative data from 3 interviews (elementary school teacher, board game developer, young mother) and informal game testing with children from 4th to 10th grade and several adults.
study_characteristics.study_design: mixed_methods
study_characteristics.game_name: Indonesian History Educational Card Game (prototype card game about the VOC colonization era)
study_characteristics.aim: To spark interest and curiosity in children to make them research more about Indonesian history, to retell history in a more visual manner which is more attractive to children, and to make history more interesting by using gamification as an interactive teaching method

eligibility.concerns: This is more of a design project with informal evaluation rather than a rigorous empirical study. The survey is a needs analysis rather than an effectiveness evaluation of the game itself.

rq1.explicit_definition: Gamification is a method of applying game mechanics to engage and motivate people more to complete their task voluntarily. People has a natural desire for competition, achievement, status and collaboration. Gamification is a great method to motivate people to put a greater performance.
rq1.conceptualization: Gamification is conceptualized as the application of elements in game (rules, objectives, competition, etc) into other activities to engage users. The study also draws on game element theory by Lennart Nacke (players, objectives, rules, resources, conflict) and Salen & Zimmerman's definition of games. The card game is positioned as a way to make history 'fun and enjoyable' for children who find textbooks boring.
theoretical_frameworks: A Theory of Fun for Game Design (Raph Koster)
The Art of Game Design (Jesse Schell)

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Survey with 15 questions measuring attitudes toward history, reading habits, game preferences, and interest in educational games among grade 5-6 students
rq2.statistical_results: Only 22% (13 people) of respondents said they like history; 35% dislike history; 43% feel neutral. 58% (35 people) are interested in a game to help learn history in class; 35% are not sure; 7% are not interested. 72% like playing games; 88% have played board/card games before.
rq2.key_outcomes: The survey established a need for gamified history learning. Informal game testing showed: younger students (4th-6th grade) found it somewhat difficult to get answers correct; older students (up to 10th grade) found it noticeably much easier and had fun prompting younger ones to join. Adults had difficulty with correct answers (lessons mostly forgotten) but had fun playing and trying to remember.
rq2.engagement_results: 58% of respondents expressed interest in a history learning game. Informal testing showed the card game generated enthusiasm across age groups. Older students 'seemed to have much fun' and prompted younger ones to join. One adult described it as 'an enjoyable way to learn.' The card game was described as offering a 'more visual manner' and 'dynamic, colorful and expressive visuals' compared to text-heavy history books.

game_design_elements: Educational card game format
Trivia/question-answer mechanics
Visual historical illustrations
Child-friendly colorful design
Multiplayer social interaction
instructional_strategies: Needs analysis survey before game design
Expert interviews (teacher, game developer, parent)
Content drawn from Indonesian IPS elementary school textbook
Focus on VOC colonization era history
Prototype testing with diverse age groups
rq3.content_integration: The card game content focuses on Indonesian history during the colonization period, specifically the VOC (Dutch East India Company) era. Historical content was taken from Indonesian Ilmu Pengetahuan Sosial (IPS) elementary school textbook. The game retells history in a more visual manner using dynamic, colorful and expressive visuals rather than old photographs, making historical events more children-friendly.

implementation_barriers: Low student interest in history (only 22% like the subject)
Teachers rarely use games in class (43% report teachers rarely use games)
History is not a standalone subject but part of IPS (social studies)
Limited access to smartphones/tablets for some students (15% have no access)
Indonesian board/card game market is developing but mostly uses imported games
methodology_limitations: No formal experimental evaluation of the card game's effectiveness
Game testing was informal with no standardized measurement
Survey was a needs analysis, not an effectiveness evaluation
No pre-post test comparison
Small and informal game testing sample with no systematic documentation
No control group
negative_effects: Younger students (4th-6th grade) found it somewhat difficult to get correct answers because material is either not taught in their school or not taught as thoroughly
Adults found some historical questions much more difficult to answer than others, indicating uneven difficulty
mitigation_strategies: Using more interesting illustrations such as cartoons that children are already familiar with
Recommending game use not only in schools but also home learning environment
Allowing students to play in their free time to extend learning beyond classroom

domain1.q1_evidence: The author conducted a survey amongst 60 students from grade 5 to 6. The survey is taken at Mahatma Gandhi School and SD Santo Lukas and others.
domain1.q2_evidence: The sample of 60 students is from specific schools in Jakarta. No information about how schools were selected or whether the sample is representative of the broader target population. The game testing was done with 'several children of varying ages' with no specified sampling strategy.

domain2.q3_evidence: The survey questionnaire has 15 questions but no validation or reliability information is provided. The game testing used no standardized assessment tools - results are reported as informal observations ('they found it somewhat difficult,' 'seemed to have much fun').
domain2.q4_evidence: Data analysis consists only of reporting simple percentages from the survey. No formal analysis methods are described for the interview data or game testing observations. No statistical analysis is performed.

domain3.q5_evidence: The conclusions that history interest is low among children and that gamification could help increase interest are consistent with the survey data showing only 22% liking history but 58% interested in a learning game. The game testing observations support the claim that the card game generated engagement.
domain3.q6_evidence: No limitations section is included in the paper. The authors do not discuss methodological limitations, potential biases in their survey, or the informal nature of their game testing. The paper reads more as a design project report than a research study.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study has High risk of bias due to: no validated instruments (Domain 2 q3 No), no formal data analysis methods (Domain 2 q4 No), and no discussion of limitations (Domain 3 q6 No). The study is primarily a design project with a needs analysis survey and informal prototype testing rather than a rigorous empirical evaluation.

pdf_filename: Investigating elementary students' epistemological beliefs, game preference by applying game-based learning to a history course.pdf

bibliographic.title: Investigating elementary students' epistemological beliefs, game preference by applying game-based learning to a history course
bibliographic.venue: Proceedings of the IEEE International Conference on Advanced Materials for Science and Engineering (IEEE-ICAMSE 2016)

study_characteristics.sample_description: 112 fifth grade students in an elementary school in Taiwan who participated in a four-week digital history game learning activity
study_characteristics.study_design: survey-based quantitative study using structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM)
study_characteristics.game_type: digital history game (custom-designed educational game integrating historical events)
study_characteristics.game_name: Not explicitly named; a custom-designed digital game integrating historical events for elementary history course
study_characteristics.aim: To extend the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) by incorporating epistemological beliefs to explore factors related to game-based learning user behaviors, specifically examining how epistemological beliefs influence game preferences and intention to use digital games for history learning

eligibility.concerns: The study focuses on acceptance and preference factors (TAM model) rather than directly measuring learning outcomes in history; it is a short conference paper (3 pages) with limited methodological detail

rq1.conceptualization: Game-based learning is conceptualized as the use of digital games to enhance the learning experience while maintaining a balance between content and games. The study frames it through the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), focusing on perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, epistemological beliefs, game preferences, and behavioral intention to use. The game integrates historical events and requires students to search for clues and ask key persons for assistance.
theoretical_frameworks: Digital game acceptance framework (Bourgonjon et al. 2010)

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Path coefficients from PLS-SEM analysis: H1 (Ease of use -> usefulness) = 0.34*, SE=0.225; H2 (Ease of use -> preference) = 0.21*, SE=0.020; H3 (Usefulness -> preference) = 0.32*, SE=0.025; H4 (Sophisticated beliefs -> preference) = 0.31*, SE=0.036; H5 (Preference -> intention) = 0.38*, SE=0.132. All significant at p<.05.
rq2.statistical_results: All five hypotheses were confirmed. Perceived ease of use significantly predicted usefulness (0.34) and preference (0.21). Usefulness significantly predicted preference (0.32). Sophisticated epistemological beliefs significantly predicted preference (0.31). Preference significantly predicted intention to use (0.38).
rq2.key_outcomes: All TAM hypotheses were confirmed. Perceived usefulness had the strongest influence on game preference among TAM variables. Sophisticated epistemological beliefs positively affected preference for digital games. Preference for digital games positively influenced behavioral intention to use digital game-based learning. Student-centered game-based learning can better attract students than traditional teacher-centered methods.
rq2.engagement_results: Game-based learning in history was found to involve a higher level of learning activities and engagements, supported by reference to Cozar-Gutierrez & Saez-Lopez (2016). The role of game features in fostering students' learning and motivation was also confirmed.

game_design_elements: Historical event integration into game narrative
Clue-searching mechanics
Key person/NPC interaction for assistance
Multiple viewpoints and resources for open-ended exploration
Assignment-based progression
technological_platforms: Custom digital game (platform not specified beyond screenshots showing a 2D/isometric computer game)
instructional_strategies: Student-centered learning through game-based exploration
Four-week structured history course integration
Open-ended exploration with multiple viewpoints and resources
Assignment-driven gameplay requiring clue searching and NPC interaction
rq3.content_integration: The digital game was designed to integrate historical events from the elementary history curriculum in Taiwan. Students explored historical content by searching for clues and interacting with key persons within the game environment, providing multiple viewpoints and open-ended exploration of history topics over a four-week period.

implementation_barriers: Traditional teacher-centered history instruction in Taiwan creates passive learners who lack analytical skills
Relationships between epistemological beliefs and learning processes in game-based learning have received surprisingly little scholarly attention
Pedagogical principles alone cannot constitute an interesting and attractive game that motivates people to play
methodology_limitations: Relatively small sample size acknowledged by authors (reason for using PLS over other SEM methods)
Very short conference paper (3 pages) with limited methodological detail
No control group or pre-post comparison design
No direct measurement of learning outcomes or knowledge gains
Survey-based self-report data only
Limited description of the digital game itself and its specific historical content
No reliability or validity statistics reported for measurement instruments
mitigation_strategies: Educators should recognize and enhance students' epistemological beliefs when implementing game-based learning
Using extended TAM model that incorporates epistemological beliefs to better understand acceptance factors

domain1.q1_evidence: No inclusion/exclusion criteria described for participant selection. The study mentions 112 fifth graders but provides no details on how or why these students were selected, whether participation was voluntary, or how the school was chosen.
domain1.q2_evidence: Single elementary school in Taiwan with no discussion of representativeness. No demographic details beyond grade level. No information on response rate or whether all invited students participated.

domain2.q3_evidence: No reliability or validity statistics (Cronbach's alpha, factor loadings, AVE, CR) are reported for any measurement instruments. The paper states items were based on prior literature (TAM, epistemological beliefs) but provides no specifics about the instrument items, adaptation process, or psychometric properties.
domain2.q4_evidence: PLS-SEM was used with SmartPLS 2.0, which is an appropriate method for small samples. Path coefficients and significance levels are reported. However, model fit indices, R-squared values, effect sizes, and measurement model evaluation (convergent/discriminant validity) are not reported.

domain3.q5_evidence: Results are interpreted in line with the hypotheses and supported by relevant literature citations. However, claims about game-based learning effectiveness in history are partly drawn from cited literature rather than the study's own empirical findings, which only measured acceptance and preference, not learning outcomes.
domain3.q6_evidence: No explicit limitations section. The only acknowledged limitation is the small sample size (mentioned as justification for using PLS). No discussion of threats to validity, generalizability concerns, or suggestions for future research to address methodological shortcomings.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study has high overall risk of bias due to: (1) no description of participant selection criteria or representativeness; (2) no reported psychometric properties for measurement instruments; (3) no model fit indices or measurement model evaluation beyond path coefficients; (4) no limitations discussion; and (5) being a very short conference paper (3 pages) that lacks the detail needed to fully assess methodological rigor. The study measures acceptance/preference rather than actual learning outcomes, and conflates its acceptance findings with claims about learning effectiveness.

pdf_filename: Jingnan Campaign-Using Game-Based Assessment with the Mechanism of Strategy Games for History Teaching System Development and Learning Evaluation.pdf

bibliographic.title: Jingnan Campaign©-Using Game-Based Assessment with the Mechanism of Strategy Games for History Teaching: System Development and Learning Evaluation
bibliographic.venue: 2015 IIAI 4th International Congress on Advanced Applied Informatics

study_characteristics.sample_description: Twenty-nine college students from northern Taiwan (18 males, 11 females)
study_characteristics.study_design: pre-experimental (single group pre-post test with survey)
study_characteristics.aim: To develop a game-based history assessment system integrating strategy game mechanisms with scaffolding theory, and to investigate learners' technology acceptance, flow state, and learning achievement

eligibility.concerns: Very short paper (2 pages); limited methodological detail; small sample size with no control group

rq1.conceptualization: Game-based assessment applied to history teaching, integrating simulated historical campaign context with strategy game mechanisms. The game combines situated learning with game elements such as commanding armies, answering history questions through a 'Jiaozhen' (challenge) mechanism, intelligence clues as scaffolding, and multiple-choice assessments embedded within gameplay. The approach leverages game feedback, repetitive practice, and trials to strengthen motivation and achievement.

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Pre-post test (36 multiple-choice items on Jingnan Campaign history knowledge, Cronbach's alpha = 0.79); Flow state scale (Cronbach's alpha = 0.91, two dimensions: flow antecedent and flow experience); Technology acceptance model questionnaire (Cronbach's alpha = 0.79, two dimensions: perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use)
rq2.statistical_results: Paired t-test on pre-post test: t = 7.72, p < .05 (significant progress in history knowledge). Post-test correlated with flow antecedent: r = 0.39, p = .037. Post-test correlated with entire flow state: r = 0.37, p = .047. Regression: entire flow state significantly explained variance of post-test (beta = 0.39, p < .05). No significant gender differences in technology acceptance, flow state, or learning achievement.
rq2.comparative_methodology: Single group pre-post test comparison (no control group); gender comparison (no significant differences found)
rq2.key_outcomes: Significant learning achievement gains after using the game-based assessment system; positive perceptions of perceived usefulness (mean above median of 3); perceived ease of use slightly below median (M = 2.87); flow state positively associated with learning achievement and explained its variability to a certain extent
rq2.engagement_results: Perceived usefulness and flow state means were above the median (3 points), indicating positive engagement. Flow state was significantly positively correlated with learning achievement. Perceived ease of use did not reach the median, possibly due to learners' lack of experience with strategy games.

game_design_elements: Strategy game mechanics (commanding armies in battle)
Jiaozhen (challenge) mechanism - question-answer duels between generals when armies meet
Intelligence clues as scaffolding for answering questions
Multiple-choice questions embedded in gameplay
Immediate corrective feedback (correct answer boosts morale; wrong answer results in attack by opponent)
Repetitive practice and retry opportunities (replay levels on failure)
Simulated historical campaign context (Jingnan Campaign, Ming Dynasty civil war)
technological_platforms: Custom-developed game system by Mini Educational Game Group of National Taiwan University of Science and Technology (http://www.ntustmeg.net)
instructional_strategies: Situated learning in historical context
Scaffolding through intelligence clues that guide reasoning rather than rote memorization
Game-based assessment integrating learning and evaluation
Immediate feedback on correct/incorrect answers
Higher-order cognitive thinking promoted through analysis of intelligence clues
rq3.content_integration: The game is set in the context of the Jingnan Campaign, a civil war in the early Ming Dynasty in China. Historical content about the campaign is drawn from a database and presented as short descriptions shouted by generals during the Jiaozhen challenge. Intelligence clues related to the historical content are provided as scaffolding. The pre-post test contained 36 multiple-choice items specifically about Jingnan Campaign history, designed by two history professionals.

implementation_barriers: Perceived ease of use did not reach the median (M = 2.87), suggesting the game interface/mechanics may be difficult for some learners
Learners' lack of experience with strategy games may hinder ease of use
Very limited empirical research on game-based assessment for history instruction
methodology_limitations: Small sample size (n = 29)
No control group (single group pre-post design)
Short paper with limited methodological detail
No discussion of effect sizes
Gender imbalance (18 males, 11 females) though no significant gender differences found
Participants from a single region (northern Taiwan) limiting generalizability
negative_effects: Perceived ease of use below median suggests usability challenges
mitigation_strategies: Authors suggest future research to investigate whether game experience influences ease of use
Authors suggest exploring learners' behavioral patterns during gameplay

domain1.q1_evidence: No clear selection criteria described beyond 'college students from northern Taiwan.' No inclusion/exclusion criteria specified. Recruitment method not detailed.
domain1.q2_evidence: Small convenience sample of 29 students from a single region in Taiwan. No discussion of how participants were selected or whether they are representative of any broader population.

domain2.q3_evidence: Flow state scale adopted from established instruments (Kiili, 2006; Hou & Chou, 2012) with Cronbach's alpha = 0.91. Technology acceptance model questionnaire based on Davis (1989) with alpha = 0.79. Pre-post test designed by two history professionals with alpha = 0.79.
domain2.q4_evidence: Paired t-test, correlation, and regression analysis are appropriate for the design. However, with n = 29, statistical power is limited. No effect sizes reported. The very short paper format limits reporting of analytical details.

domain3.q5_evidence: Results are briefly reported and interpretations are generally consistent with findings. However, the extremely brief format (2 pages) prevents thorough interpretation. Claims about flow state affecting learning are based on modest correlations (r = 0.37-0.39).
domain3.q6_evidence: Very minimal discussion of limitations. The paper does not explicitly acknowledge the lack of a control group, small sample size, or threats to validity. Only brief suggestions for future research are provided.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: High risk of bias due to: (1) no control group making it impossible to attribute learning gains solely to the game-based assessment; (2) very small sample size (n=29) with convenience sampling; (3) extremely brief paper (2 pages) providing insufficient methodological detail; (4) no discussion of study limitations or threats to validity; (5) no effect sizes reported. While measurement instruments show acceptable reliability, the overall study design and reporting are weak.

pdf_filename: Learning About the Past Through Digital Play History Students and Video Games.pdf

bibliographic.title: Learning About the Past Through Digital Play: History Students and Video Games
bibliographic.venue: Handbook of Digital Public History (De Gruyter)

study_characteristics.sample_description: Over 200 history students who responded to a survey about their perceptions of learning about history through playing video games; respondents were self-selecting student gamers
study_characteristics.study_design: qualitative survey with speculative design fiction
study_characteristics.game_type: commercial historical video games (various genres including strategy, RPG, action-adventure)
study_characteristics.game_name: Various (Assassin's Creed series mentioned prominently; also strategy games set in medieval periods)
study_characteristics.aim: To examine history students' perceptions of their learning about the past through playing video games, and to understand students' roles as active agents in learning about the past through virtual play rather than as passive consumers of digital products
