eligibility.concerns: The study focuses on informal/leisure gameplay of commercial historical video games rather than formal classroom gamification interventions; it is a survey-based qualitative study about perceptions of learning rather than a controlled experiment measuring learning outcomes

rq1.conceptualization: The study does not provide an explicit definition of gamification. Instead, it conceptualizes the use of historical video games as a form of digital play through which students learn about history. The authors frame historical gaming as active engagement with the past through ludic structures, narrative, and agency within simulated historical environments. They also describe a university module (MD 348211 - Playing the Past: making history in digital spaces 01) that incorporates historical game-based learning including RPG elements, strategy gameplay, VR, game design/modding, and collaborative play.
theoretical_frameworks: Player agency and subjectivity in digital games (Charles 2009)
Historical game accuracy and authenticity (Copplestone 2017; Stirling and Wood 2021)
Self-Determination Theory / motivational model of video game engagement (Przybylski, Rigby, and Ryan 2010)
Speculative design fiction / design fiction prototyping (Sterling; Dunne and Raby 2013)
Narrative approaches to qualitative data analysis (Atkinson and Delamont 2005; Clandinin and Connelly 2000; Bold 2011)

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Table 2.1 presents frequency data from survey responses (n=213): Learn something (154), Try to find out more (148), Play another game (124), Talk to someone (93), Change the way you play the game (85), Visit a forum (47), Visit a place (43), Other (10). Follow-up on how gamers tried to find out more: online research (149), books (87), Wikipedia (86). 40% of respondents said they changed the way they played the game.
rq2.key_outcomes: Students perceived historical video games as powerful tools for learning about history. Key findings: (1) Motivation - students reported intrinsic motivation through agency, empowerment, and immersion in historical settings; interest in specific historical periods was sparked or deepened. (2) Experience - aesthetics, social interaction, choice/agency, and challenge were vital factors for positive gaming experience; games encouraged collaborative and social learning. (3) Learning - students reported learning historical information, engaging in historical/counterfactual thinking, understanding systemic contexts, and being motivated to conduct additional research outside the game. Gameplay extended beyond information acquisition to engagement in processes of historical thinking.
rq2.engagement_results: Students reported high engagement through: sense of agency and empowerment ('The plot arc gives a real sense of empowerment'), deep engagement with historical characters/polities, immersion in authentic historical environments, social/collaborative gameplay, replay value through different historical scenarios, and motivation to research topics beyond the game world (online research, books, Wikipedia, visiting places)

game_design_elements: Player agency and choice in historical scenarios
Counterfactual/alternative history pathways
Historical accuracy and authenticity in game environments
High-quality visual aesthetics and graphics
Music and atmospheric elements
In-game encyclopaedias for historical information
Narrative and storyline set in historical periods
Strategy and resource management mechanics
RPG role-playing as historical characters
Re-playability with different outcomes
Game modding capabilities
Side quests with historical content
Collaborative/multiplayer elements
Challenge and difficulty progression
technological_platforms: VR rooms (mentioned in context of university module)
instructional_strategies: Speculative design fiction as pedagogical framing
University module combining gameplay with reflective learning (learning diaries, blog posts, quick voice memos)
Game design/modding as learning activity
Collaborative and team-based gameplay
Encouraging students to research historical topics beyond the game
Assessment based on engagement and reflection rather than traditional exams
Using student survey responses to inform module design
rq3.content_integration: Historical content is integrated through authentic historical settings, characters, events, and processes embedded within game narratives and mechanics. Games simulate historical environments (e.g., medieval Italy, Ancient Rome) allowing students to experience and interact with historical contexts. The university module described uses a week-long gameplay experience across different game types (first-person, strategy, collaborative) combined with reflective writing and game design activities. Students engage with historical content through active play, decision-making within historical scenarios, and counterfactual exploration.

implementation_barriers: Self-selecting sample - respondents were already enthusiastic gamers and positive about gaming
Student perception that gaming modules are not 'proper' History
Limited capacity on module (cap of 40 students)
Tension between games as entertainment vs. educational tools
Games create an 'illusion of agency' rather than true historical understanding
Historical accuracy concerns - games are 'not very accurate' representations of the past
Pathways in games are often restricted and can reinforce established or hegemonic interpretations
Need for institutional support (e.g., 24-hour learning center access, VR equipment, game engine partnerships)
methodology_limitations: Self-selecting survey sample leads to overwhelmingly positive responses about gaming
Qualitative survey data limits generalizability
No control group or comparative condition
No direct measurement of actual learning outcomes - relies on self-reported perceptions
The speculative design fiction methodology is exploratory and generative rather than conclusive
Fiction was 80% participant voices and 20% narrative voice, introducing authorial interpretation
Study focuses on perceptions rather than objectively measured knowledge gains
negative_effects: Risk of reinforcing colonialist and hegemonic ideologies through game narratives
Games can direct gamers toward specific interpretations of the past, particularly in strategy games
Potential for games to create illusion of agency rather than genuine historical understanding
Some students may view gaming modules as not academically rigorous
mitigation_strategies: Using speculative design fiction to imagine alternative futures for history education
Combining gameplay with reflective activities (learning journals, voice memos, blog posts)
Including game design/modding to develop critical understanding of game construction
Incorporating multiple game types and collaborative activities
Drawing on user-centered approaches to understand student perspectives
Assessment designed around engagement and reflection

domain1.q1_evidence: The study uses a self-selecting convenience sample of student gamers who chose to respond to the survey. The authors explicitly acknowledge that 'respondents to our survey were self-selecting and, as such, were unsurprisingly positive about the experience of playing video games.' No formal inclusion/exclusion criteria for participants are described beyond being history students who play video games.
domain1.q2_evidence: The sample of 213 respondents represents only students who are already enthusiastic gamers. The authors acknowledge this limitation. The sample is drawn from a single university context in the UK, limiting representativeness. No demographic breakdown is provided beyond being history students.

domain2.q3_evidence: The survey instrument is not described in detail. The study mentions survey questions with predefined response options (Table 2.1) and free-text responses, but no information is provided about instrument validation, piloting, or reliability. The speculative design fiction approach is a creative methodology but lacks standardized evaluation criteria.
domain2.q4_evidence: The authors describe their thematic analysis approach: they separately coded the dataset, identified themes, came together to review and cross-check codes and emerging themes, and extracted representative quotes. They were transparent about the fiction being 80% participant voices and 20% narrative voice. The analytical approach follows established qualitative methods (Atkinson and Delamont; Clandinin and Connelly).

domain3.q5_evidence: The findings are consistently presented across three themes (motivation, experience, learning) that align with the research aims. Survey data (Table 2.1) and qualitative quotes support the interpretations made. The speculative design fiction is clearly distinguished from the analytical discussion.
domain3.q6_evidence: The authors explicitly acknowledge the self-selecting nature of their sample and the overwhelmingly positive responses this produced. They discuss the paradox of gamers being 'tightly constrained in their ability to experience the past' while still finding gaming valuable. Limitations of the speculative design fiction approach are partially acknowledged through its framing as exploratory and generative.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: While the qualitative analysis and interpretation are conducted with reasonable methodological rigor, the study has significant limitations in its sampling approach (self-selecting enthusiastic gamers), lack of validated instruments, absence of direct learning outcome measurement, and limited generalizability from a single UK university context. The speculative design fiction methodology is innovative but makes it difficult to separate empirical findings from creative interpretation. The study provides valuable qualitative insights into student perceptions but cannot support strong causal claims about the effectiveness of historical video games for learning.

pdf_filename: Learning Chinese History through Digital Game.pdf

bibliographic.title: Learning Chinese History through Digital Game
bibliographic.venue: 2010 IEEE International Conference on Digital Game and Intelligent Toy Enhanced Learning (DIGITEL)

study_characteristics.sample_description: 428 secondary school students (58% male, 42% female; 90% aged 12-14, 10% aged 15-18) and their teachers from 3 secondary schools in Hong Kong who used the game as a teaching tool. An additional preliminary survey of 40 students (37 males, 3 females aged 15-20) was also conducted.
study_characteristics.study_design: Case study with survey-based evaluation
study_characteristics.aim: To present a case study of digital game-based learning in a history class, examining how a digital game about the three Mongolian conquests is designed, produced, applied in the classroom, and what impacts and feedback teachers and students provide.

eligibility.concerns: The study uses descriptive survey data without a control group or statistical testing. The methodology is relatively informal for a research study.

rq1.conceptualization: The authors conceptualize digital game-based learning as using digital games as effective tools for 21st century education. They frame digital games as transforming traditional classrooms into constructivist environments that produce improved skills in question formulating, hypothesis generation, and problem solving. Games are seen as matching the learning characteristics of the new generation: speed, parallel information processing, active engagement, quick adaptation, problem solving, and immediate reward.

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Survey responses from 428 students: 83% liked the game; 74% said the game gave them better learning motivation; 70% reported they learned history from the game; 81% liked the game-based learning approach; 62% thought computer games are a good way to learn. Play count data: full version played 6336 times; 1st conquest 1329 times; 2nd conquest 395 times; 3rd conquest 353 times.
rq2.statistical_results: Descriptive statistics only (percentages from survey responses). No inferential statistical tests were performed.
rq2.key_outcomes: Students reported positive perceptions of game-based learning for history. The majority felt the game improved their learning motivation (74%), that they learned history content from the game (70%), and that they liked this game-based learning approach (81%). Teachers reported positive changes in students' learning attitudes, noting students were more interested and concentrated in class. Teachers indicated they would continue adopting the game-based approach.
rq2.engagement_results: 83% of students liked the game. Students commented that 'it attracts me to play', 'it is nice to learn in a happy way', 'we like games, so education mixing games is good', and 'it is easier for me to learn through games'. Teachers observed students were more interested and concentrated during lessons. The game was played over 6336 times in one year on the HKEdCity platform.

game_design_elements: Strategy-based gameplay (army building, recruiting soldiers, feeding, training, assigning tasks)
Historical narrative integration (three Mongolian conquests)
Role-playing as army commander
Save game feature for continuity across sessions
Supplementary after-game historical materials
Multiple conquest levels/scenarios
Interactive battle gameplay
technological_platforms: Supplementary website with background information and teaching plans
Computer room deployment (one computer per student)
instructional_strategies: Teacher-game designer collaboration for content alignment
15-20 minute game sessions per lesson
Post-game teacher-led recap and debriefing
Student discussion of in-game experiences
Supplementary historical reading materials
Suggested teaching plans for teachers
Reflective questions and activities for after-game discussions
After-game assessment and reinforcement
rq3.content_integration: Historical content about the three Mongolian conquests is integrated directly into the game flow. Players build armies based on real Chinese and Western history. Historical information about the Mongolian conquests is brought up during gameplay according to the game narrative. A supplementary website provides detailed historical background, people, and places involved in the conquests. Teachers provided the content information which game designers and programmers then implemented into the game mechanics.

implementation_barriers: History curriculum syllabus does not cover all historical content teachers wish to share
Traditional classroom methods (read from textbook) fail to engage students
Need for computer room with one computer per student
Technical support requirements for schools
One-year production period needed for game development
Funding requirements (Incentive Scheme for Developing Instructional Software from HKSAR Education Bureau)
methodology_limitations: No control group or comparison condition
Survey-based evaluation only with no pre/post testing
No inferential statistics or rigorous quantitative analysis
Self-reported data only from students and teachers
Small number of participating schools (3 secondary schools)
Authors acknowledge that more detailed and formal researches are needed
Preliminary survey had unbalanced gender ratio (37 males, 3 females out of 40)
negative_effects: 17% of students reported they did not learn history from the game
13% of students were not sure if they learned history from the game
After-game assessment and reinforcement found to be essential, suggesting learning does not occur automatically from play alone
Drop-off in play counts across conquests (6336 full, 1329 first, 395 second, 353 third) suggests declining engagement
mitigation_strategies: Teacher-led recap and debriefing after each game session to reinforce learning
After-game assessment and reinforcement to strengthen memory
Supplementary historical reading materials provided alongside the game
Reflective questions and activities for post-game discussions
Free technical support provided to schools
Game made freely available on educational platform (HKEdCity)

domain1.q1_evidence: No explicit eligibility or selection criteria described for the participating schools or students. The 3 secondary schools appear to have been selected based on convenience (teachers who co-operated with the authors). The preliminary survey sample of 40 had highly unbalanced gender representation (37 males, 3 females).
domain1.q2_evidence: Only 3 secondary schools in Hong Kong participated. No discussion of how representative these schools are of the broader population. The sample is limited to Hong Kong, making generalizability limited.

domain2.q3_evidence: The survey instrument is not described in detail and there is no mention of validation or reliability testing. Questions appear to be simple yes/no/not sure format, which limits the depth of data collected. No standardized learning outcome measures were used.
domain2.q4_evidence: Analysis consists only of descriptive percentages from survey responses. No inferential statistical analysis was performed. No pre-post comparison, no control group. The authors acknowledge the need for more detailed and formal research.

domain3.q5_evidence: The interpretations generally align with the survey data presented, though the authors tend to emphasize positive findings. The declining play counts across conquest levels are not discussed as a potential concern. The authors appropriately note that after-game assessment is essential for learning.
domain3.q6_evidence: The authors acknowledge that 'more detailed and formal researches are needed in this area' but do not provide a systematic discussion of limitations. There is no explicit limitations section. Potential biases in self-reported data are not discussed.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study presents a case study with significant methodological limitations: no control group, no standardized outcome measures, no inferential statistics, convenience sampling of only 3 schools, and reliance entirely on self-reported survey data with simple yes/no/not sure questions. While it provides useful descriptive insights into a game-based learning implementation for Chinese history, the evidence quality is limited by the informal research design. The authors themselves acknowledge the need for more rigorous research.

pdf_filename: Learning Cultural Heritage History in Muzium Negara through Role-playing Game.pdf

bibliographic.venue: International Journal of Advanced Computer Science and Applications (IJACSA)

study_characteristics.sample_description: 32 respondents, majority aged 21-25 years old, 23 out of 32 (71.9%) were male. Recruited via convenience sampling method.
study_characteristics.study_design: Design-based research with post-implementation survey evaluation
study_characteristics.aim: To design and develop a role-playing game (RPG) set in Muzium Negara (National Museum of Malaysia) to enhance students' interest, motivation, and knowledge on the cultural and historical heritage of Malaysia, and to evaluate its enjoyment level using the eGameFlow model.

eligibility.concerns: The study focuses primarily on game design/development with a relatively small survey evaluation (n=32) using convenience sampling. It measures enjoyment rather than direct learning outcomes. The sample consists of young adults rather than formal secondary school students, though the content targets the Malaysian History curriculum.

rq1.conceptualization: The study conceptualizes gamification through game-based learning, specifically using the RPG genre to learn historical content in a virtual museum setting. Game-based learning is described as 'an exciting and effective way of learning when adequately constructed using learning principles as a goal.' The RPG genre is characterized as providing players with roles that advance through playing and storytelling experiences, involving good storylines and interactions with objects or characters. The authors link RPGs to constructivism (hands-on experimentation) and sociocultural learning theory (adoption of new social roles).

rq2.quantitative_metrics: eGameFlow model survey with 7 dimensions (social interaction excluded): Concentration (mean=4.13), Goal Clarity (mean=4.16), Feedback (mean=4.10), Challenge (mean=4.12), Autonomy (mean=4.63), Immersion (mean=4.23), Knowledge Improvement (mean=4.31). Overall average mean = 4.24 out of 5 (84.8%).
rq2.statistical_results: Descriptive statistics only. Total average mean across all eGameFlow dimensions was 4.24 (84.8%). Highest-rated dimension was Autonomy (4.63); lowest was Feedback (4.10). Individual items ranged from 3.67 (online support for challenges, H4) to 4.84 (sense of control over menu A1, knowing next step A8, sense of control over game A9).
rq2.key_outcomes: 84.8% of participants experienced enjoyment while playing the game. The game was identified to efficiently increase knowledge on knowing and memorizing history content in the museum. Autonomy scored highest (4.63), indicating players felt strong sense of control. Knowledge Improvement scored 4.31, suggesting the game enhanced players' knowledge about Malaysia's history.
rq2.engagement_results: Concentration mean=4.13; Immersion mean=4.23 (players reported forgetting time, becoming unaware of surroundings, feeling emotionally involved). Challenge mean=4.12. Overall engagement was positive with 84.8% enjoyment rating.

game_design_elements: Role-playing (player controls a fictional character)
Narrative structure based on Freytag's pyramid (Exposition, Rising Action, Climax, Falling Action, Conclusion)
Virtual museum exploration with interactive artefacts
Multiple game levels corresponding to museum galleries (Prehistoric Era, Malay Kingdom, Colonial Era, Malaysia Today)
Non-player characters (NPCs) providing missions and guidance
Cut-scenes for character and mission introduction
Pop-up details with historical information about artefacts
Clear goals and missions to complete each level

Player autonomy (menu control, strategy freedom, decision-making)
Challenge progression across levels
technological_platforms: Unity (cross-platform game engine for environment and scene development)
Blender (open-source 3D creation suite for museum and artefact models)
instructional_strategies: Game-based learning through RPG genre
Virtual museum-based learning (supplementing classroom-based learning)
Narrative-driven learning with historical storyline
Experiential learning through interaction with virtual artefacts
Exploration-based learning across four historical gallery themes
Immersive learning through 3D virtual environment
rq3.content_integration: Historical content is integrated directly from the four main galleries of Muzium Negara (National Museum of Malaysia): Prehistoric Era (evolution of earth's surface to earliest Malaysian inhabitants, Palaeolithic stone tools, Hindu-Buddhist temple relics from Lembah Bujang), Malay Kingdoms (first Malay Kingdoms, Malacca Malay Kingdom in 15th century), Colonial Era (Portuguese, Dutch, British, and Japanese administration and effects), and Malaysia Today (struggle for independence, formation of new nation, transformation since 1957). Players explore virtual galleries, interact with artefacts that display detailed historical information, and complete missions in imaginary worlds corresponding to each historical era.

implementation_barriers: Geographical location barriers prevent students from visiting the actual museum
Museum policies may restrict student access
Student commitments limit museum visit opportunities
Single-player only (no multiplayer functionality at time of study)
Game not yet available in console version
Need for collaboration with Muzium Negara for more detailed and quality historical information
methodology_limitations: Small sample size (n=32) using convenience sampling
No control group or comparative experimental design
Only descriptive statistics reported (means), no inferential statistics
Social interaction dimension excluded from evaluation due to single-player design
Evaluation focused on enjoyment rather than actual learning outcomes or knowledge gains
Respondents were young adults (17-25) rather than the target secondary school population
No pre-test/post-test design to measure actual knowledge improvement
Gender imbalance in sample (71.9% male)
negative_effects: Some distraction from tasks was noted (item C4 'No distraction from task' scored lowest in Concentration at 3.93)
Online support for overcoming challenges was rated lowest overall (H4 = 3.67)
Immediate feedback on actions was rated relatively low (F2 = 3.81)
Difficulty scaling with skill improvement was rated below average for its dimension (H8 = 3.94)
mitigation_strategies: Future plans to add multiplayer functionality for increased interactivity and social interaction
Plans to develop a console version for broader accessibility
Plans to collaborate with Muzium Negara for more accurate and detailed historical content
Used Agile Development Methodology with iterative Scrum framework to allow frequent requirement changes and improvements
Applied eGameFlow model to systematically identify areas needing improvement

domain1.q1_evidence: The study used convenience sampling to recruit 32 young adults aged 17-25. No clear inclusion/exclusion criteria were specified beyond the age range. No information about how participants were recruited or selected. The target population (secondary school students who need to pass SPM History) differs from the actual sample (young adults, mostly university-age).
domain1.q2_evidence: Sample of 32 respondents with strong male bias (71.9% male). The sample is not representative of the target population of Malaysian secondary school history students. Convenience sampling limits generalizability. No demographic stratification or discussion of representativeness.

domain2.q3_evidence: The eGameFlow model (Fu, Su & Yu, 2009) is a validated and well-established scale for measuring learners' enjoyment of e-learning games. The instrument has been used in prior research. The 7 dimensions measured (excluding social interaction) are clearly described with specific questionnaire items provided in full detail (Table III).
domain2.q4_evidence: Only descriptive statistics (means) were reported. No measures of variability (standard deviation, confidence intervals) were provided. No inferential statistical tests were conducted. No reliability measures (e.g., Cronbach's alpha) were reported for the adapted instrument. The 84.8% enjoyment figure is simply the overall mean (4.24/5) converted to a percentage, without statistical rigor.

domain3.q5_evidence: The study claims the game 'efficiently increases knowledge' but this was measured only through self-reported survey items (Knowledge Improvement mean=4.31), not through actual knowledge assessment. The conclusion that 84.8% experienced 'enjoyment' conflates an average Likert scale score with a percentage of agreement. The abstract and conclusion make broad claims about enhancing interest, motivation, and knowledge that go beyond what the survey evaluation actually measured.
domain3.q6_evidence: The study does not include a limitations section. There is no discussion of the small sample size, convenience sampling bias, lack of control group, gender imbalance, or the gap between the sample (young adults) and the intended target population (secondary school students). Future work mentions are limited to adding multiplayer and collaborating with the museum, without acknowledging methodological limitations.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study presents high risk of bias across all three domains. The sample selection relies on convenience sampling with a small, non-representative sample (n=32) that does not match the target population. While a validated instrument (eGameFlow) was used, the analysis is limited to descriptive means without variability measures, reliability testing, or inferential statistics. The interpretation overstates findings by claiming knowledge improvement based solely on self-reported enjoyment surveys rather than actual learning assessments, and no limitations are discussed. The study is primarily a design-and-development paper with a minimal evaluation component.

pdf_filename: Learning History by Playing a Mobile City Game.pdf

bibliographic.title: Learning History by Playing a Mobile City Game
bibliographic.venue: DaI

study_characteristics.sample_description: Approximately 500 pupils from 3 secondary schools in Amsterdam. Twenty classes of about 25 pupils each participated in Pilot 2. Ten classes played the mobile history game (experimental condition) and ten classes followed regular project-based lessons (control condition). Pupils were aged 13 or 14 years, from both pre-university education and vocational secondary education tracks.
study_characteristics.study_design: Quasi-experimental with mixed methods (quantitative and qualitative)
study_characteristics.aim: To generate insights into the practicalities and the effects of mobile game-based learning in secondary education on the development of pupils' engagement in learning (motivation for history), historical knowledge, and collaborative skills.

eligibility.concerns: The paper reports primarily preliminary results from Pilot 2; most quantitative data had not yet been analyzed at the time of publication. Pilot 1 had only one class and was primarily usability-focused.

rq1.conceptualization: The study conceptualizes game-based learning through Gee's (2005) principles of digital pedagogy for game-based learning, organized into three sections: empowerment of the learner (co-design, customize, identity, distributed knowledge), the learning task as a problem-solving task (well-order problems, pleasantly frustrating, cycles of expertise, information on demand and just-in-time, fish tanks, sandboxes, skills as strategies), and the learning process as a process of understanding (system thinking, meaning as action image). The game Frequency 1550 is framed as a mobile city game supporting situated learning where knowledge is unbound from a specific context to foster transfer to new problems and domains.
theoretical_frameworks: Shaffer's epistemic frames and professional practice approach (2004, 2006a, 2006b)
Narrative framework for structuring learning contents (Hug 2005)

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Pre- and post-tests for motivation for history, historical knowledge of medieval Amsterdam, attitude towards collaborative learning, and ability/credits in history. Quantitative data planned to be analyzed using multilevel multivariate regression analyses. However, at the time of publication, knowledge tests had not been analyzed yet.
rq2.statistical_results: No statistical results reported; results are described as preliminary. The quantitative data from Pilot 2 had not yet been fully analyzed at the time of writing.
rq2.comparative_methodology: Quasi-experimental design with experimental condition (10 classes playing Frequency 1550) and control condition (10 classes receiving regular project-based lessons on the medieval history of Amsterdam). Measures taken before intervention, during intervention, immediately after, after 1 week, and after 2 months.
rq2.key_outcomes: Preliminary results show high pupil motivation and active engagement in playing and learning about medieval Amsterdam. Pupils were on-task most of the day despite normally having short attention spans. Pupils reported the game was more fun than regular history lessons. Guides reported small knowledge gains (e.g., pupils realizing not every tower is a church). Pupils from pre-university education performed better than those from vocational secondary education. Collaborative skills were developed through the game's team-based structure requiring communication between city teams and HQ teams.
rq2.engagement_results: Pupils were very enthusiastic about the game, both at HQ and in the city. Children who normally could not focus for more than 10 minutes were now working concentrated for hours. Most pupils were engaged to complete assignments and on-task most of the day. Qualitative data showed that technical problems caused motivation to decrease, but not always. Pupils at HQ reported they liked HQ even more than walking in the city, as they had a better overview and more control.

game_design_elements: Points system (366 Days of Burghership to earn citizenship)
Competition between teams (confrontations to take away points)
Team-based collaboration (teams of four pupils with two roles: city team and HQ)
Narrative/storyline (medieval bailiff contacting present via UMTS network)
Role-playing (pupils take on identities as beggars or merchants)
Location-based assignments (18 assignments across 6 sectors)
Virtual bombs/rats (to disrupt other teams' communication)
Power-ups (monk's habit for invisibility)
Video clips from medieval characters at specific locations
Sector-based progression (must complete assignments to unlock new sectors)
Win condition (first team to acquire burghership keeps the Holy Host)
technological_platforms: Laptops with Internet connection at HQ
Game server at the Waag Society's lab
GPS-based medieval map of Amsterdam displayed on gamephone
instructional_strategies: Situated learning in authentic historical locations in Amsterdam
Collaborative learning with distributed team roles (city team and HQ team)
Location-based media assignments requiring research and historical reenactment
Introductory video clips providing historical context for each assignment
Plenary reflection sessions after game days
Integration of out-of-school (city) and in-school (HQ) learning
Multimodal content delivery (video clips, maps, text assignments)
rq3.content_integration: Historical content about medieval Amsterdam is deeply integrated into the game. The city of Amsterdam is divided into six thematic sectors (labour, trade, religion, rules and government, knowledge, defence). Pupils explore real historical locations while receiving video clips from medieval characters providing historical information. Assignments require pupils to demonstrate knowledge of medieval Amsterdam through location-based media tasks, answering specific history questions, and researching and reenacting historical situations. The game transforms the modern city into a medieval playground where students learn by physically visiting and interacting with historically significant sites.

implementation_barriers: Technical problems with GPS not sending correct position information
Videophone connection loss requiring frequent restarts (10 minutes each time)
Slow transfer of video clips and pictures causing delays
Small screen of gamephone was difficult to read in sunlight
Game had already been delayed due to technical and organizational problems before the pilot started
Assignment difficulty level did not always match pupil ability levels across different education tracks
Some teachers could not administer post-tests due to scheduling near summer vacation
Miscommunication about test administration procedures between researchers and teachers
The paper-based version of the game had to be used on the first day because the technical version was not finished yet
methodology_limitations: Pilot 2 data mostly not analyzed at the time of publication; only preliminary qualitative results reported
No comparison with control condition presented in the paper
Knowledge tests not analyzed yet
Incomplete data collection: some classes did not receive all planned tests
Pilot 1 involved only one class from one school, limiting generalizability
Self-reported motivation data not yet available
negative_effects: Technical problems diminished motivation of pupils, especially on the first day of Pilot 1
Some pupils had difficulty differentiating between fictional story elements and real historical source material
Some pupils thought there was too much emphasis on the learning part, which spoiled the fun
Scenario complexity made it difficult for some pupils to understand the game's goal and mission
Virtual rats/bombs cutting off communication for 10 minutes was overly demotivating
Pupils from vocational secondary education needed additional teacher/guide support and struggled more with assignments
Environmental factors (hot weather, noisy locations like Dam Square) interfered with gameplay
mitigation_strategies: Game was redesigned between Pilot 1 and Pilot 2 based on evaluation feedback
Back-story was simplified and narrative framework about the Miracle of Amsterdam was removed
Game duration reduced from two days to one day based on feedback
Assignments content and difficulty levels were adjusted
Sectors were explicitly labeled with thematic names for clearer structure
Suggestion to change virtual rats from cutting connection to reducing points instead
Suggestion to improve screen visibility and reduce technical difficulties
Suggestion to better match assignments to pupil levels

domain1.q1_evidence: The study clearly describes two pilots. Pilot 2 uses a quasi-experimental design with 20 classes from 3 schools in Amsterdam, with 10 classes in experimental and 10 in control condition. Inclusion criteria are implicitly defined by school/class selection.
domain1.q2_evidence: The sample is limited to 3 secondary schools in Amsterdam. Pupils are aged 13-14. No information on how schools were selected or whether they are representative. The diversity of the sample (pre-university vs. vocational tracks) is noted but creates uneven assignment difficulty matching.

domain2.q3_evidence: The paper describes planned data collection instruments (tests, observation forms, logbooks, evaluation meetings, essays, track & tracing) but does not report on validity or reliability of any measures. Knowledge tests and motivation tests are mentioned but not described in detail. Most quantitative data were not yet analyzed at publication time.
domain2.q4_evidence: The paper mentions planned multilevel multivariate regression analyses and thick descriptions for qualitative data, but actual analyses presented are limited to preliminary qualitative observations and impressions from evaluation meetings. No statistical analyses are reported. The narrative method of inquiry from Pilot 1 is described but its application is brief.

domain3.q5_evidence: The authors present generally positive conclusions about pupil motivation and engagement but acknowledge these are preliminary. They note uncertainty about learning effects and motivation changes. However, strong positive conclusions about the game's potential are drawn despite limited analyzed data. The paper concludes the game supports Gee's game-based learning principles without fully testing this claim.
domain3.q6_evidence: The authors openly discuss technical problems, data collection failures (missing tests in some classes), scheduling issues, assignment-pupil level mismatches, and the fact that most data have not been analyzed. They acknowledge that Pilot 1 had limitations and detail specific needed improvements.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study presents primarily preliminary qualitative results from a quasi-experimental design where the quantitative data had not been analyzed at the time of publication. No statistical results are reported, validity and reliability of instruments are not discussed, the sample is limited to three schools in one city, and data collection was incomplete due to logistical and organizational problems. While the study design is appropriate and limitations are transparently discussed, the lack of completed analysis and reported outcomes represents a high risk of bias for drawing conclusions about learning effects.

pdf_filename: A Pilot Evaluation of a Virtual Reality Educational Game for History Learning.pdf

bibliographic.title: A Pilot Evaluation of a Virtual Reality Educational Game for History Learning
bibliographic.venue: European Conference on Games Based Learning (ECGBL)

study_characteristics.sample_description: Twenty-eight (28) primary school students who participated in the context of an exhibition focused on game-based learning for Primary Schools at the city of Kavala in Greece. The game targeted 3rd grade students in Greek schools. During the game, students had to complete at least three trials over approximately 15 minutes.
study_characteristics.study_design: descriptive
study_characteristics.aim: To present a virtual reality (VR) game for history learning and examine the results of a pilot study evaluating students' attitudes and experience towards the VR game, specifically examining whether students assess it as interesting and engaging, authentic and expressive, and effective and useful.

eligibility.concerns: The study is a pilot evaluation with a small sample (n=28) and no control group. It measures only perceived learning and attitudes, not actual learning outcomes. The study took place during an exhibition rather than in a regular classroom setting.

rq1.conceptualization: The paper conceptualizes the intervention as a virtual reality (VR) game for history learning that combines game-based learning with immersive VR technology. The game uses interactive, explorative experiences to move away from traditional book-based education into immersive game-based learning experiences. The VR game is framed as a tool to promote historical thinking skills by letting users participate actively in the learning process and learn through the acquisition of experience rather than through passive exploration. The paper does not provide an explicit definition of gamification but treats the VR game as a serious game integrating educational content with game mechanics (trials, puzzles, quizzes, narrative storytelling, progression).
theoretical_frameworks: Storification in history education (Akkerman et al., 2009)
Reality Judgment and Presence Questionnaire (Banos et al., 2000)

rq2.quantitative_metrics: 23-item 7-point Likert scale questionnaire measuring seven variables: Pragmatic Quality (M=5.03, SD=1.61, alpha=.71), Hedonic Identity (M=5.06, SD=1.85, alpha=.91), Hedonic Stimulation (M=5.56, SD=1.76, alpha=.91), Focus (M=5.71, SD=1.30, alpha=.87), Autotelic Experience (M=5.82, SD=1.47, alpha=.89), Perceived Learning (M=5.32, SD=1.68, alpha=.86), Reality Judgment (M=5.50, SD=1.14, alpha=.77).
rq2.statistical_results: Spearman's correlation between reality judgement and other variables: reality judgement correlated significantly with focus (r=.70, p<.001), autotelic experience (r=.69, p<.001), and perceived learning (r=.45, p<.05). Reality judgement correlated significantly with all variables except Hedonic Identity. Individual items: focused on tasks (M=5.82, SD=1.3), experience left feeling great (M=5.64, SD=1.87), prefer to learn history with similar environments (M=5.30, SD=1.83), would learn faster this way (M=5.48, SD=1.89), felt part of virtual world (M=5.96, SD=1.26), felt as active participant of narrated story (M=5.56, SD=1.22).
rq2.key_outcomes: Students' general assessment of the VR game was positive across all measured dimensions. They considered the game as simple, innovative, valuable, inspiring, challenging, practical, predictable and appropriate for learning about history. Students reported strong focus during gameplay and high sense of presence in the virtual environment. The correlation analysis revealed that making the learning environment feel more real was crucial for its success, as reality judgement was significantly correlated with focus, autotelic experience, and perceived learning.
rq2.engagement_results: Students were focused on tasks during the entire game duration (Focus M=5.71, SD=1.30). They reported high autotelic experience (M=5.82, SD=1.47), feeling great about the experience (M=5.64, SD=1.87). Students felt present in the virtual environment: felt part of the virtual world (M=5.96, SD=1.26), considered themselves active participants in the narrated story (M=5.56, SD=1.22). Focus group discussions confirmed students were excited, impressed with the 3D virtual environment, and felt immersed. Students reported the instructional design managed to hide formal learning processes under the umbrella of the VR game.

game_design_elements: Six sequential trials/levels with progression (must complete one to advance to next)
Quizzes with multiple-choice questions (5 per trial, must get at least 4/5 correct to proceed)
Puzzles (virtual jigsaw puzzles revealing myth-related images)
Constructive feedback after each quiz response
Narrative storytelling (character narrates myths with image slider)
Role-playing (player takes role of ancient Greek hero)
Exploration of virtual Acropolis environment
Challenge/trial structure based on Greek mythology
Retry mechanism (repeat quiz step if fewer than 4 correct answers)
technological_platforms: Available free on Google Play Store (Greek and English editions)
instructional_strategies: Discovery learning through virtual environment exploration
Digital storytelling (character narrates myths with synchronized images)
Game-based learning with hermeneutics (puzzle solving to discover meaning of myth-related images)
Self-assessment through interactive quizzes with constructive feedback
Structured sequence: engagement, narrative-based learning, hermeneutics, assessment (based on DPE framework)
Immersive presence in historical site (virtual Acropolis)
Revision trial (6th trial revises all previous myths)
rq3.content_integration: The game covers five Greek myths from the 3rd grade Greek primary school history curriculum: Gods and Titans, Hercules, Theseus, Jason and the Argonauts, and the Odyssey. Each myth corresponds to a trial set within the virtual Acropolis. Students explore the virtual archaeological site, listen to a character narrate the myth with synchronized images, solve a puzzle that reveals a myth-related image requiring interpretation, and complete a quiz to consolidate understanding. The sixth trial functions as a revision of all previous myths. The game is designed to complement (not replace) classroom history learning.

implementation_barriers: Short duration of learning experience (approximately 15 minutes) limits the amount of interactive learning content
VR applications for history focus more on realistic approximation of archaeological sites than on instructional interactions promoting historical thinking
Need for smartphone and Google Cardboard hardware (though low cost)
Historical limitations of VR in education: installation cost, headset weight/fit, simulator sickness, poor instructional design of virtual learning environments
Lack of a coherent framework for designing virtual reality apps for history learning
methodology_limitations: Pilot study with small sample size (n=28)
No control group or experimental comparison
Only perceived learning was measured, not actual learning effectiveness
Study took place in an exhibition context, not a regular classroom setting
No analysis of different phases of the underlying learning mechanism or their separate contributions to learning outcomes
Short duration of the learning experience (approximately 15 minutes)
Non-normal data distribution (Spearman's correlation used instead of Pearson's)
No demographic details of participants beyond being primary school students
mitigation_strategies: Game designed as complementary activity within more integrated instructional intervention
Free availability on Google Play Store reduces cost barriers
Low-cost Google Cardboard used instead of expensive VR headsets
Game developed using free programs and technologies (Unity 3D, Blender)
Authors plan future research targeting actual learning effectiveness with the Trials of the Acropolis app
Authors aim to advance the app to include all three storification modes (receivers, constructors, participants)

domain1.q1_evidence: The target population is described as primary school students (3rd graders), but the actual participants were 28 students at an exhibition focused on game-based learning in Kavala, Greece. No specific selection or inclusion criteria are described. It is unclear how these 28 students were recruited or whether they were representative of the target population of 3rd graders.
domain1.q2_evidence: The sample of 28 students was a convenience sample drawn from exhibition attendees rather than a systematic sample of 3rd grade students. No demographic characteristics (age, gender distribution) are reported. The exhibition context means participants were likely self-selected or parent-selected, potentially introducing bias toward students already interested in technology and games.

domain2.q3_evidence: The questionnaire items were derived from established instruments: AttrakDiff (Hassenzahl & Monk, 2010) for pragmatic and hedonic quality, Flow State Scale (Jackson & Marsh, 1996) for autotelic experience and focus, and Reality Judgment and Presence Questionnaire (Banos et al., 2000) for presence measures. Cronbach's alpha values ranged from .71 to .91, indicating acceptable to good internal consistency across all seven variables.
domain2.q4_evidence: Descriptive statistics (means, standard deviations, min/max) and Spearman's correlations were appropriately used given the non-normal data distribution. Focus group discussions complemented the quantitative data. However, the analysis is limited to descriptive and correlational findings without inferential tests for differences.

domain3.q5_evidence: The findings are interpreted consistently with the data presented. The authors connect questionnaire results to focus group comments, and the conclusions about positive attitudes, focus, and presence are supported by the reported means and correlations. The authors appropriately note that the correlation between reality judgement and other variables suggests that making the environment feel real is crucial for success.
domain3.q6_evidence: The authors acknowledge the key limitation that only perceived learning was measured rather than actual learning effectiveness. They also note the short duration of the experience. However, they do not discuss the small sample size as a limitation, the convenience sampling from an exhibition context, the lack of a control group, or the limited generalizability of findings. Future research directions are mentioned but the methodological limitations are only partially addressed.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study has a high risk of bias in participant selection (small convenience sample of 28 students from an exhibition context with no demographic details or selection criteria), but uses validated instruments with acceptable reliability (Domain 2). The interpretation is generally consistent with the data though limitations are only partially discussed. The primary weakness is the lack of actual learning outcome measurement and the non-representative sample. As a pilot evaluation study, these limitations are acknowledged but significant. The overall risk is Moderate because the validated instruments and transparent reporting of results partially offset the sampling concerns.

pdf_filename: Learning History Through Computer Game Authoring.pdf

bibliographic.title: Learning History Through Computer Game Authoring
bibliographic.venue: The 8th International Conference on Computer Science & Education (ICCSE 2013)

study_characteristics.sample_description: Five college new faces (freshmen), four males and one female, with no prior experience in computer game authoring, who voluntarily participated in the RPG authoring workshop
study_characteristics.study_design: qualitative case study with interviews and open-ended discussion
study_characteristics.aim: To explore the feasibility of using RPGMaker as a game authoring tool for creating historical RPGs to foster history learning, and to examine participants' learning experiences and user experience with the authoring tool

eligibility.concerns: Very small sample size (n=5); qualitative study with no control group; uses game authoring (constructionist) approach rather than game playing, which is a broader interpretation of gamification

rq1.conceptualization: The study conceptualizes learning history through computer game authoring as a constructionist approach where learners create 2D RPGs about historical events using authoring tools. Rather than playing games, students design and build games that embed historical content, thereby engaging deeply with historical facts, events, characters, and narratives. The approach leverages the popularity of computer games among youth to make history learning more enjoyable and engaging.
theoretical_frameworks: Learning by design / learning through making

rq2.key_outcomes: Four out of five participants completed their historical RPGs. Qualitative findings from open-ended discussions and interviews showed: (1) participants found learning history through RPG authoring more enjoyable than traditional methods; (2) participants reported being more engaged with the subject matter; (3) participants viewed the method as innovative and practically engaging; (4) the interaction between participants during presentation and discussion led to different perspectives toward historical events, fostering historical thinking; (5) participants changed their initial storyboard plans during authoring because they generated more ideas during the process, indicating deep engagement with content.
rq2.engagement_results: Participants reported positive engagement. Sample comments included: 'I like the latter method; it makes learning history become more enjoyable', 'I am more engaged to the subject being learned', and 'I see it is an innovative way in learning history. It could practically engage me to the topic that I have to learn.' Participants promoted group work and peer collaboration during the workshop.

game_design_elements: Role-playing game (RPG) genre
Character design with historical attributes (motives, background, characteristics, missions)
Interactive dialogues embedding historical facts
Map/environment design reflecting historical settings
Plot planning with protagonists and antagonists
Combat/battle mode
Weather change function for historical climate realism
Storyboard planning and narrative construction
Tile sets for visual environment creation
technological_platforms: RPGMaker 2003 (by Enterbrain, Inc.) - 2D RPG authoring tool
instructional_strategies: Constructionism-based workshop (8 sessions, 60-75 minutes each, one session per week)
Structured game authoring workshop with sequential phases: group discussion, tool introduction, subject matter study, character/game design, plot planning, RPG authoring, presentation
Collaborative learning through group discussion and peer feedback
Subject matter research using Internet, textbooks, and videos
Storyboard sketching before digital authoring
Presentation and peer review of completed RPGs
Researcher available as facilitator throughout the workshop
rq3.content_integration: Participants researched historical topics using multiple sources (Internet, textbooks, videos), established storylines based on findings, designed characters reflecting historical figures with culturally appropriate attributes, transformed historical facts into interactive game dialogues, designed game environments matching historical settings, and used weather functions to match historical climates. The process of creating the game required deep engagement with historical content, and discussions at the end of sessions promoted different perspectives on historical events.

implementation_barriers: Limited time for sessions - participants suggested more time was needed to complete RPGs
One out of five participants did not complete the RPG within the workshop timeframe
Low resolution game display produced by RPGMaker lowered participant motivation
2D graphics were less appealing - two participants preferred 3D RPG over 2D RPG for realism
Default RPGMaker villains (monsters, vampires) were irrelevant to real-world historical contexts, requiring import of custom character sets
Traditional storyboard planning could not fully reflect interactive dialogues and battle modes that appear in the RPG
Computer game authoring is inherently complex, traditionally requiring programming and mathematics skills
Limited research exists on feasibility of game authoring tools for history learning specifically
methodology_limitations: Very small sample size (n=5) limits generalizability
No control group or comparative condition
Qualitative data only - no quantitative measures of learning outcomes
Participants were self-selected volunteers enthusiastic about game authoring, introducing selection bias
No pre-test/post-test assessment of historical knowledge gains
Short-term workshop study (8 weeks) with no follow-up on long-term retention or transfer
Single group of college freshmen - results may not generalize to other age groups or educational levels
negative_effects: Low resolution display of RPGMaker lowered some participants' motivation
Preference for 3D over 2D suggests potential dissatisfaction with tool limitations
Participants deviated from planned storyboards during authoring, which could be seen as both creative flexibility and planning inefficiency
mitigation_strategies: Participants imported custom character sets to replace irrelevant default villains
Participants helped each other resolve obstacles during the workshop (peer support)
Researcher was available as facilitator throughout the workshop to help with technical problems
Authors suggest amending the conceptual framework to accommodate changes during the RPG authoring phase
Authors suggest exploring incorporation of game authoring method into classroom curriculum

domain1.q1_evidence: The study clearly describes the target population (college freshmen with no prior game authoring experience) and provides demographic details (4 males, 1 female). However, the selection was based on voluntary participation of enthusiastic students, which introduces selection bias.
domain1.q2_evidence: Sample of only 5 self-selected volunteers who were enthusiastic about game authoring is not representative of the broader student population. The small convenience sample severely limits generalizability.

domain2.q3_evidence: Data collection relied on open-ended discussions and interviews at the end of the workshop. No validated instruments or standardized measures were used. No pre-test/post-test design. No quantitative assessment of learning outcomes. The interview questions (shown in Table I) are basic and not validated.
domain2.q4_evidence: The analysis methods are not clearly described. The paper presents sample comments from participants but does not describe a systematic qualitative analysis methodology (e.g., thematic analysis, coding procedures). Results are presented descriptively without rigorous analytical framework.

domain3.q5_evidence: The conclusions about learning benefits are drawn from a very small qualitative dataset without systematic analysis. Claims about engagement and enjoyment are based on a few sample quotes. The study does not distinguish between enjoyment of the game authoring activity itself and actual history learning outcomes.
domain3.q6_evidence: The paper briefly acknowledges some issues (time constraints, 2D vs 3D preferences, low resolution display) but does not formally discuss methodological limitations such as sample size, lack of control group, or absence of learning outcome measures. The paper does not include a dedicated limitations section.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study has high overall risk of bias due to: (1) very small, self-selected convenience sample (n=5); (2) no validated instruments or quantitative measures of learning; (3) no control group or comparative design; (4) lack of systematic qualitative analysis methodology; (5) conclusions about learning benefits not adequately supported by the evidence presented; (6) limited discussion of methodological limitations. While the study provides useful exploratory insights into game authoring for history education, the evidence quality is low.

pdf_filename: Mobile games to foster the learning of history at archaeological sites.pdf

bibliographic.title: Mobile games to foster the learning of history at archaeological sites
bibliographic.venue: Proceedings of IEEE VL/HCC 2007 Symposium on Visual Languages and Human-Centric Computing

study_characteristics.sample_description: Four middle school students (11-12 years old) from the middle school 'Michelangelo' in Bari, Italy, who had previously played the traditional (non-digital) excursion-game during a school visit to the archaeological site of Egnathia. Divided into two groups of two for the pilot usability evaluation.
study_characteristics.study_design: qualitative pilot usability study
study_characteristics.game_type: mobile excursion-game (treasure hunt-style educational game on cellular phones)
study_characteristics.game_name: Una giornata di Gaio ad Egnathia (Gaius' Day in Egnathia)
study_characteristics.aim: To design and evaluate a mobile phone-based system that supports middle school students learning history at archaeological sites through game-play, implementing a digital version of the excursion-game developed by Historia Ludens

eligibility.concerns: Very small sample size (4 students); pilot usability study conducted in a university laboratory rather than at the actual archaeological site; primarily a system design paper with limited empirical evaluation of learning outcomes

rq1.conceptualization: The paper conceptualizes gamification as 'edutainment' -- education in the form of entertainment -- specifically through mobile game-play that uses a treasure hunt structure (excursion-game) to stimulate understanding of history at archaeological sites. The approach combines the excitement of chase and solving puzzles with freely exploring a place and discovering its hidden secrets. Game elements include missions, role-playing (impersonating a Roman family), an oracle hint system, place codes/visual tags, 3D reconstructions as rewards, competition between groups, and a debriefing phase.
theoretical_frameworks: Excursion-game pedagogy (developed by Historia Ludens, based on simulation gaming)

rq2.key_outcomes: The pilot usability evaluation provided qualitative design feedback rather than measured learning outcomes. Students preferred audio-enhanced game over silent version, indicating greater engagement. Students identified usability issues: absence of feedback during system delays, unclear functionalities during 3D-reconstruction exploration, and need for digital map on the phone to complement the paper-based map. The authors note that 'the joy and learning efficiency must be established using a more systematic on-site empirical evaluations.' Preliminary studies confirmed the belief that game-play engages students and permits an effective and exciting visit.
rq2.engagement_results: Students preferred audio which created greater engagement. The game-play was reported to engage students and permit an effective and exciting visit of the archaeological sites, enhancing the overall students' experience, though this was based on preliminary pilot observations rather than formal measurement.

game_design_elements: Missions/quests (sequential mission-based gameplay)
Role-playing (each group impersonates a Roman family)
Treasure hunt structure (exploring and discovering places)
Oracle hint system (in-game help mechanism)
Place codes and visual tags (location-based interaction)
3D reconstructions as rewards ('God's gifts' upon completion)
Competition between groups
Audio feedback and sound cues
Group navigator role (group leader)
Debriefing phase with replay of winning group's performance
Logfile tracking (mission execution time, oracle usage)
technological_platforms: Cellular phones (J2ME-capable with memory card slot)
Memory cards containing game software and 3D data
Optional digital camera for visual tag recognition
Game Master notebook with Bluetooth/card reader for debriefing
instructional_strategies: Excursion-game methodology (treasure hunt at archaeological site)
Collaborative learning in small groups (4-5 players per group)
Contextual inquiry for user-centered design
Debriefing phase for reflection, generalization, and conceptualization of learned information
3D visualization of reconstructed monuments to compare with existing ruins
Physical exploration combined with digital interaction
Map-based spatial learning (marking places on site map)
rq3.content_integration: Historical content is integrated through narrative role-playing: students impersonate a Roman family (Gaius' family) that has arrived in the ancient city of Egnathia. Missions are contextualized around activities of daily Roman life (e.g., finding a furnace where a potter needs assistants). The oracle provides historically-grounded hints that support both gameplay and learning of historical content. After missions, 3D reconstructions designed in collaboration with archaeologists allow students to compare original appearance of structures with existing ruins. The debriefing phase consolidates historical knowledge through discussion and replay.

implementation_barriers: Limited 3D rendering performance on cellular phones of that era
Archaeological site administrations often unable to afford special hardware infrastructure
Need for on-site evaluation not yet conducted at time of publication
System requires J2ME-capable phones with memory card slots, which may not be universally available
No data transmission during gameplay limits real-time features
methodology_limitations: Very small sample size (only 4 students in pilot evaluation)
Evaluation conducted in university laboratory, not at actual archaeological site
Participants had already played the traditional excursion-game, introducing familiarity bias
No formal measurement of learning outcomes or knowledge acquisition
No control group or comparative design
Authors acknowledge that a more accurate/systematic study is needed
mitigation_strategies: Using visitors' own cellular phones to reduce infrastructure costs
Memory card-based approach eliminates need for network infrastructure at the site
Learner-Centered Design methodology with iterative evaluation to address usability issues
Collaboration with domain experts (Historia Ludens, archaeologists, teachers) to ensure content quality
Contextual inquiry to collect data about actual user activities
Plans for systematic on-site empirical evaluation in spring 2007

domain1.q1_evidence: No clear selection criteria for participants. The four students were selected because they had previously played the traditional excursion-game at Egnathia, but no justification is given for this specific sample or why only four students were included.
domain1.q2_evidence: Sample of 4 students is extremely small and not representative of the target population of middle school students. Students were pre-selected based on prior experience with the traditional game, which introduces familiarity bias and limits generalizability.

domain2.q3_evidence: No standardized or validated assessment instruments were used. The evaluation focused on qualitative usability feedback rather than learning outcomes. No pre-test/post-test design, no validated questionnaires, and no formal data collection instruments are described.
domain2.q4_evidence: No formal analysis methods described. Results are reported as informal observations and student preferences (e.g., preference for audio). No systematic qualitative analysis methodology is mentioned.

domain3.q5_evidence: The conclusions about engagement and effectiveness ('game-play will engage students and permit an effective and exciting visit') go beyond what the pilot study data can support. The authors claim their belief has been 'confirmed by the preliminary pilot studies' but the studies only evaluated usability, not engagement or learning effectiveness.
domain3.q6_evidence: The authors clearly acknowledge that the pilot evaluation was not intended to evaluate overall user experience, that a more accurate study would be required, and that 'joy and learning efficiency must be established using a more systematic on-site empirical evaluations.' They explicitly note the lab-based setting is a limitation.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study has a high overall risk of bias due to its nature as a preliminary design/pilot study with only 4 participants evaluated in a laboratory setting rather than the actual archaeological site. There are no validated measurement instruments, no formal analysis methods, no control group, and no systematic assessment of learning outcomes. The authors themselves acknowledge these limitations and frame the work as preliminary, with plans for more rigorous evaluation. The conclusions about effectiveness go somewhat beyond what the limited pilot data can support.

pdf_filename: Online Interactive Game-Based Learning in High School History Education Impact on Educational Effectiveness and Student Motivation.pdf

bibliographic.title: Online Interactive Game-Based Learning in High School History Education: Impact on Educational Effectiveness and Student Motivation
bibliographic.venue: Fourth International Conference on Ubi-Media Computing

study_characteristics.sample_description: Thirty students from Taichung Municipal Dongshan Senior High Class 719; based on pretest average score 90, nineteen higher-scoring students formed the control group (high achievers) and eleven lower-scoring students formed the experimental group (low achievers). Four-week experiment.
study_characteristics.study_design: quasi-experimental with pretest-posttest nonequivalent control group design
study_characteristics.game_type: online interactive quiz-based game / web-based competition game
study_characteristics.aim: To investigate whether using IGLS as an ancillary tool in junior high history teaching enhances students' learning motivation and academic performance in Taiwan history

eligibility.concerns: Small sample size (n=30, with only 11 in experimental group). Non-random group assignment based on pretest scores (high vs. low achievers) rather than random allocation, which introduces selection bias. The groups are not equivalent at baseline by design.

rq1.conceptualization: The study conceptualizes game-based learning through the lens of Digital Game-Based Learning (DGBL), referencing Prensky's framework. IGLS is an online interactive quiz game system composed of three elements: quiz game module, item generation module, and learning management module. The system integrates competition, collaboration, and knowledge sharing through online community learning mechanisms. Prensky's six key elements for digital game-based learning are referenced: (1) rules, (2) goals or objectives, (3) outcomes and feedback, (4) conflict/competition/challenge and opposition, (5) interaction, (6) representation and story.
theoretical_frameworks: Keller's ARCS motivation theory (Attention, Relevance, Confidence, Satisfaction)

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Paired sample t-test on pretest and posttest scores for Taiwan history (Vol. 1) with 400 multiple-choice questions. Likert Five-Point Scale questionnaire for motivation and satisfaction.
rq2.statistical_results: Experimental group (low achievers): pretest mean=84.1818, posttest mean=91.4545, t(10)=significant at p=.010. Control group (high achievers): pretest mean=94.0263, posttest mean=96.2105, p=.061 (not significant). Experimental group improvement was -7.27 vs control group improvement of -1.68. Questionnaire results: Strongly agree 61.82%, Agree 27.27%, Neutral 10.91%, Disagree 0%, Strongly disagree 0%, grand mean 4.51 out of 5. Over 90% of students approved the system's attraction to participation and intention.
rq2.comparative_methodology: Pretest-posttest comparison between experimental group (using IGLS) and control group (traditional instruction). Pretest result of Taiwan history used as covariance, learning method as independent variable, post test as dependent variable.
rq2.key_outcomes: IGLS significantly improved academic performance for the experimental group (low achievers) at p<.05. The control group showed no significant improvement. IGLS especially provides low achievers with confidence and positive attitude. Over 90% of students showed positive motivation toward using the system. The system enhanced participation, performance improvement, ease of learning, interest in history, and suitability for history learning.
rq2.engagement_results: Interface satisfaction: mean scores ranged from 4.55 to 4.82 (easy to handle: 4.64, content clearly expressed: 4.73, buttons easy to click: 4.82, convenience of design: 4.55). Functionality satisfaction: records help with learning 4.55, group competition helps 4.55, online version helps 4.55, message board makes communication easier 4.09, handle situation in group competition 4.45. Motivation improvement: game arouses participation 4.55, improves performance 4.64, eases presence in learning 4.64, attracts interest in history 4.64, system suitable for learning history 4.36.

game_design_elements: Quiz/question-based competition
Team-based gameplay (2 vs 2, 3 vs 3, etc.)
Hit points system (100 HP per team, reduced by correct opponent answers)
Random item generation (multiple choice with random options, match items, random argument computational problems)
Score charts and performance records
Online and stand-alone play modes
Chat rooms for knowledge sharing
Learning management module for teacher monitoring
Free grouping for community formation
technological_platforms: Web-based online platform (IGLS - Interactive Game-based Learning System)
Accessible via Internet after school hours
instructional_strategies: Online community learning with peer cooperation and competition
Knowledge sharing through chat rooms and group interaction
Teacher as manager monitoring learner progress through learning management module
Ancillary tool supplementing regular classroom instruction
Self-evaluation through score review charts
Collaborative and competitive learning patterns
rq3.content_integration: IGLS includes content from seven graders' sociology textbook 'Taiwan history (Vol.1)'. Topics covered include prehistory, international competition, Cheng's governance, and earlier stage of Ching dynasty's occupation. The quiz items are drawn from both IGLS's content and Taiwan history textbook Vol. 1, totaling 400 multiple-choice questions.

implementation_barriers: Risk of digital learning turning into game addiction, which reduces learning motivation
Need for Internet access outside school for continued use
Balancing entertainment and educational value in digital game-based learning
Traditional teacher-centered instruction being replaced requires pedagogical shift
methodology_limitations: Very small sample size (n=30 total; only 11 in experimental group)
Non-random group assignment based on pretest scores (high vs. low achievers), creating non-equivalent groups
Short experimental duration (four weeks / one month)
No random assignment - groups differ systematically at baseline
Control group consisted of high achievers while experimental group consisted of low achievers, making direct comparison problematic
Questionnaire only administered to experimental group, not control group
Limited to one class in one school in Taichung, Taiwan
negative_effects: If digital learning turns into games addiction, it may bring down learners' motivation (cited from Mitchell and Savill-Smith)
Focusing too much on playing games instead of learning itself is a risk
mitigation_strategies: Teacher monitoring through learning management module to track student progress
Integration of collaboration, feedback, and assessment into game design (Johnson and Johnson recommendation)
Using Prensky's six key elements to balance game design with educational objectives
Teacher reminders to use system regularly after school

domain1.q1_evidence: Selection criteria are partially described - students from one class in one school. However, group allocation was based on pretest scores (above/below average of 90), not random assignment. This creates systematically different groups by design.
domain1.q2_evidence: Only 30 students from a single class (Class 719) at one school in Taichung, Taiwan. Non-random purposive sampling with no discussion of representativeness. The experimental group (low achievers, n=11) and control group (high achievers, n=19) are fundamentally different populations.

domain2.q3_evidence: Academic performance measured by 400 multiple-choice questions drawn from IGLS content and Taiwan history textbook. Likert Five-Point Scale questionnaire for satisfaction and motivation was discussed with professor and program designers for content validity. Standard instruments were used.
domain2.q4_evidence: Paired sample t-test was used to compare pretest and posttest within each group, which is appropriate. However, the study uses pretest as covariance but groups are fundamentally non-equivalent (high vs. low achievers). The ANCOVA approach is mentioned but not properly reported. Descriptive statistics for questionnaire are basic (means and SDs only).

domain3.q5_evidence: The study claims IGLS benefits academic performance, but the comparison between a group of low achievers and high achievers is inherently flawed - low achievers naturally have more room for improvement (regression to the mean). The conclusion that IGLS 'especially provides low achievers with confidence' conflates the experimental design with a finding about differential effects.
domain3.q6_evidence: The paper does not discuss any limitations of the study design, the small sample size, the non-random assignment, or the non-equivalence of groups. No threats to validity are acknowledged.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study has serious methodological limitations including very small sample size (n=30 total, n=11 experimental), non-random group assignment creating fundamentally non-equivalent groups (low achievers vs. high achievers), no discussion of limitations, and interpretations that do not adequately account for regression to the mean and baseline differences. The quasi-experimental design as implemented does not support the causal claims made.

pdf_filename: Playhist Play and learn history Learning with a historical game vs an interactive film.pdf

bibliographic.title: Playhist: Play and Learn History. Learning with a Historical Game vs An Interactive Film
bibliographic.venue: Conference Paper (associated with FP7 EXPERIMEDIA Project)

study_characteristics.sample_description: Visitors to the Foundation of the Hellenic World (FHW) in Athens, Greece, randomly assigned to two groups (Group A: control, interactive film; Group B: experimental, serious game). Exact sample size not reported in this paper as it describes the experimental design prior to full data collection.
study_characteristics.study_design: Randomized controlled experiment (two-group comparison: control group watching interactive film vs experimental group playing serious game)
study_characteristics.aim: To investigate whether 'learning by playing' concept is valid for history museums and cultural centers by comparing a 3D interactive and collaborative serious game about Ancient Greece with an interactive film, measuring Quality of Experience (QoE) and Quality of Learning (QoL)
