eligibility.concerns: This paper primarily describes the experimental design and system architecture of PLAYHIST rather than reporting final empirical results. It is a design-and-protocol paper with planned metrics but without reported quantitative outcome data.

rq1.conceptualization: The authors conceptualize gamification through the lens of 'learning by playing' — transforming traditional interactive cultural heritage films into interactive and collaborative serious games within a museum/virtual reality environment. They frame it as introducing gamification concepts into historical content to improve visitor learning in museums and cultural centers. The game uses missions, mini-games, scenarios, points/punctuation, ranking, competition, avatar customization, and collaborative tasks to engage learners with historical content.
theoretical_frameworks: Game-based learning / serious games for cultural heritage
Cognitive and motivational effects of serious games (referencing Wouters et al. 2013 meta-analysis)

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Planned metrics include: Quality of Experience (QoE) measured via user satisfaction questionnaires and automatic ECC module data; Quality of Learning (QoL) measured via questionnaires about historical content (historical dates reflected in the interactive film or serious game); Quality of Service (QoS) measured via system performance metrics (rendered virtual scenes per second, delay between real-time motion capture and character animation). No final quantitative results are reported in this paper.
rq2.comparative_methodology: Two-group randomized comparison: Group A (control) watches the existing interactive film at FHW; Group B (experimental) plays the 3D serious game developed with Unity3D. Both groups are assessed using the same QoE and QoL questionnaires for direct comparison.
rq2.key_outcomes: The paper describes the planned experimental design but does not report final outcome data. The authors conclude theoretically that serious games for cultural heritage are particularly suited to the affective domain, that empathy with game characters helps understanding of historical events, cultures, and heritage, and that 3D Virtual Worlds have the potential to expand knowledge of foreign cultures by presenting information in a visual context.
rq2.engagement_results: Not reported (planned to be measured via QoE questionnaires and ECC module automatic data collection)

game_design_elements: Missions and objectives (main goal: erect a votive stele along the Sacred Way)
Mini-games with educational objectives per scenario
Three progressive scenarios/levels (Lion Harbour, North Agora, Sacred Way)
Points/punctuation system with ranking
Competition (winner has most points in least time)
Avatar customization (using webcam to personalize character)
Collaborative multiplayer interaction (up to 4 players)
Expert role (museum person interacts via Kinect motion capture as in-game character)
Time-based challenges
Feedback tools
technological_platforms: Tholos (3D dome-shaped Virtual Reality theatre/museum with 130 seats at FHW)
EXPERIMEDIA platform components (ECC, SCC, AVCC, PCC, 3DCC)
instructional_strategies: Learning by playing in cultural heritage context
Scenario-based learning with historical educational objectives per mini-game
Collaborative group activities with assigned roles
Expert-guided learning (museum expert interacts in real-time as game character to advise players)
Immersive virtual reality environment recreating ancient city of Miletus
Task-based learning (players complete tasks to progress and learn historical content)
rq3.content_integration: The game is directly aligned with existing FHW interactive film content about Ancient Miletus. Historical content is integrated through three scenarios with specific educational objectives: Lion Harbour (learn about types of goods sold in the Agora), North Agora (learn about the exchange and buy/sell system in the Agora of Miletus), and Sacred Way (learn about annual festivities in honour of Apollo and votive steles). Players travel to the virtual city of Miletus as it was two thousand years ago, exploring buildings and completing historically-grounded missions.

implementation_barriers: Technical challenges with Tholos render machines (Linux version too old for Unity3D, requiring architecture redesign to single main machine with three graphic outputs)
Achieving correct curved-surface projection in Tholos dome required creating a 3-virtual-camera structure in Unity3D with matrix transformations
Integration of broad range of EXPERIMEDIA software components across five areas (experiment, social, audio visual, pervasive, 3D content)
Development and integration across three different environments (visitor's Android environment, expert's desktop, Playhist core)
methodology_limitations: Paper describes experimental design but does not report empirical results — outcomes are planned but not yet measured at time of publication
No sample size specified
No details on participant demographics or selection criteria beyond 'visitors to FHW'
Validation metrics (QoE, QoL) described at high level without detailed instrument specifications or psychometric properties
No power analysis or statistical analysis plan described
mitigation_strategies: Architecture redesign from Tholos render machines to single main machine to overcome OS compatibility issues
Custom 3-virtual-camera structure with matrix transformation to handle Tholos dome curved surface projection
Use of established EXPERIMEDIA project infrastructure and components to support experimentation

domain1.q1_evidence: No explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria for participants. The study mentions 'visitors to the FHW' will be randomly assigned to two groups, but no selection criteria, recruitment methods, or eligibility requirements are described.
domain1.q2_evidence: No sample size is specified. No demographic information about participants is provided. Museum visitors may not be representative of any defined target population. No information on how many visitors were recruited or what the expected sample size would be.

domain2.q3_evidence: Two questionnaires (Q1 for QoE, Q2 for QoL) are mentioned but not described in detail. No validated instruments are referenced. No information on reliability or validity of the measurement tools. The ECC module will collect automatic data but the specific metrics are not clearly defined.
domain2.q4_evidence: No statistical analysis methods are described. The paper describes planned metrics (QoE, QoL, QoS) but provides no information on how data will be analyzed or what statistical tests will be used.

domain3.q5_evidence: No empirical results are reported, so interpretation cannot be assessed. The conclusions are theoretical assertions about serious games for cultural heritage rather than evidence-based findings from the described experiment.
domain3.q6_evidence: No limitations are discussed. The paper does not acknowledge that it presents a design/protocol without results, nor does it discuss potential threats to validity of the planned experiment.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The paper is fundamentally a system design and experimental protocol description rather than a completed empirical study. No empirical data or results are reported. Participant selection criteria, sample size, measurement instruments, and analysis methods are all inadequately described. No limitations are discussed. The conclusions drawn are theoretical rather than evidence-based. All three domains present high risk of bias due to the absence of reported empirical findings.

pdf_filename: Reliving History with Reliving the Revolution Designing Augmented Reality Games to Teach the Critical Thinking of History.pdf

bibliographic.title: Reliving History with "Reliving the Revolution": Designing Augmented Reality Games to Teach the Critical Thinking of History
bibliographic.venue: Chapter XIII in an edited book (Idea Group Inc.)

study_characteristics.education_level: Mixed (graduate students, educators, and high school students aged 13-17)
study_characteristics.sample_description: Pilot study: two trials with a mix of graduate students and educators. Redesign trial: eight individuals ranging in age from 13 to 17, all attending local and regional high schools.
study_characteristics.study_design: Design-based research with iterative prototyping, qualitative case study with pre- and post-game surveys, videotaped and in-person observations, and content analysis of debates, game discussions, and notes
study_characteristics.aim: To design and evaluate an augmented reality game that engages students in interpretive, collaborative, and problem-solving activities to teach the critical thinking skills of history, specifically around the Battle of Lexington (April 19, 1775)

eligibility.concerns: The bibtex key says 'Gibson2023' but the actual author is Karen Schrier and the year is 2007. This is a design-based study focused on an AR history education game with iterative testing rather than a controlled experiment.

rq1.conceptualization: The study conceptualizes the AR game as a location-based game that uses wireless handheld devices (PDAs) to provide virtual game information in a physical environment. Gamification is framed through the lens of educational AR gaming that integrates role-playing, collaborative problem-solving, evidence collection, and debate within a historically authentic setting. The game is designed to embed learning within play so that educational content is 'inherent to' the game experience rather than separate from it.
theoretical_frameworks: Historical inquiry and critical thinking frameworks (Hoge, 2003; National Center for History, 1994)
Games-To-Teach design principles (Squire, Jenkins, & The Games-To-Teach Team, 2003)

rq2.comparative_methodology: Comparison between Pilot study design and Redesign trial through iterative design process; pre- and post-game surveys on game play, attitudes toward history, and knowledge of the Revolutionary War
rq2.key_outcomes: RtR motivated discovery, enthusiasm, reflection, collaboration, teamwork, problem solving, interpretation, analysis, and consideration of alternative views of history. Participants engaged with historical content, felt immersed in the Battle of Lexington, and practiced historical thinking skills including questioning sources, identifying biases, creating hypotheses, and drawing inferences. The Redesign trial showed improvements: participants were less overwhelmed, more directed by mini-objectives/checkpoints, and more motivated to collaborate inter-role. Participants reported the game felt novel and authentic, and they took the 'serious game' very seriously. They reflected on their own interpretations, questioned preconceived notions about the Battle of Lexington, and related historical understanding to broader social issues.
rq2.engagement_results: Participants enjoyed being at the actual historic site and using PDAs to integrate virtual information with a real-world context. The game felt novel and authentic. Walking around was 'more engaging and more interactive.' Participants found particular pleasure in kinesthetic learning and discovering information embedded in the environment. They preferred this to sitting in a classroom. The collaborative aspect was highly valued - participants could share ideas, engage in mini-debates, and reflect more deeply on evidence. Some Pilot participants felt overwhelmed by information overload, but Redesign participants with mini-objectives thrived in the nonlinear environment.

game_design_elements: Overarching goal (determining who fired the first shot at the Battle of Lexington)
Role-playing (four historic roles: Prince Estabrook, John Robbins, Ann Hulton, Philip Howe)
Mini-objectives/secret missions as checkpoints
Non-player characters (NPCs) providing testimonials and documents
Evidence collection and item gathering
Time constraints (two 30-35 minute periods plus debate)
Collaborative pair play
Nonlinear exploration and navigation
Two time periods (before and after the Battle)
Debate/reflection period
Physical nametags for role identification
Location-triggered content via GPS
technological_platforms: MIT Teacher Education Laboratory AR game editor system
instructional_strategies: Situated learning in authentic historical location (Lexington Common, Massachusetts)
Collaborative learning through pair play and group debate
Role-playing with distinct perspectives and biased information
Iterative design with prototyping and testing cycles
Evidence-based historical inquiry and hypothesis formation
Integration of physical and virtual worlds for multimodal learning
Scaffolded complexity through mini-objectives
Reflection and debate to consolidate learning
Multiple perspectives on historical events to challenge master narratives
Teacher/mentor-supported activity embedded in broader history curriculum
rq3.content_integration: Historical content is deeply integrated into the game mechanics. Participants investigate the Battle of Lexington (April 19, 1775) by collecting testimonials from virtual historic figures (NPCs) at GPS-triggered locations on the actual Lexington Common. Each of the four roles receives different, slightly biased historical accounts. The game content - testimonials, documents, and item descriptions - was crafted as a mix of artistry and historic precision based on the author's immersion in Lexington's history. Two time periods (before and after the battle) provide different NPC information. The physical buildings and sites serve as portals for virtual historical content, creating connections between real monuments and virtual narratives.

implementation_barriers: Limited budget ($0) and limited resources (single designer/researcher/tester/educator)
Technical limitations of the River City AR game system (participants could not actively interact with NPCs in their roles)
Difficulty balancing discovery and familiarity in game design
Information overload for some participants during Pilot study
Verbal time limit reminders were insufficient; visual countdown clock needed
Some Pilot participants forgot they were playing a historic role
Open-ended design felt unfocused for some participants who wanted more linear progression
Participants sometimes needed targeted questions and scaffolding to guide debate and encourage reflection
The debate made RtR feel less like a 'game' to some participants
Dependence on GPS technology and handheld devices
Need for instructor/mentor support - the game is not a standalone educational solution
methodology_limitations: Small sample sizes in both Pilot and Redesign trials
Redesign trial limited to 8 high school students aged 13-17
No control group or formal experimental design
Qualitative results primarily based on observations and participant statements rather than standardized assessments
Single designer acting as researcher, tester, and educator introduces potential bias
Pre- and post-game survey results not reported with quantitative detail
Limited generalizability due to specific historical site requirement (Lexington Common)
negative_effects: Some participants felt overwhelmed by the amount of information and detail in the Pilot study
Some Pilot participants forgot their historic roles during gameplay
Some participants desired a more linear game structure and felt the open-ended design was unfocused
Little feedback on progress during evidence collection made some participants unsure of their status
The debate component made the experience feel less game-like for some participants
mitigation_strategies: Redesign added role-specific mini-objectives/secret missions as checkpoints to provide direction
Redesign incorporated more inter- and intra-pair collaboration throughout
Role-specific content was enhanced with language, tone, and style to reinforce role characteristics
Physical nametags provided to emphasize role identity
Prince Estabrook role was redesigned with limited NPC access but unique testimonials to emphasize his status
Nonlinear world with well-placed boundaries and sufficient direction balanced player agency with pedagogical goals
Future recommendation to add visual/audio countdown clock for time constraints

domain1.q1_evidence: No formal selection criteria for participants are described. The Pilot study used 'a mix of graduate students and educators' and the Redesign trial used 8 high school students aged 13-17 from 'local and regional high schools,' but the selection/recruitment process is not specified.
domain1.q2_evidence: Sample is small and convenience-based. The Pilot used graduate students/educators (not the target K-12 population), and the Redesign used only 8 high school students. Neither sample is representative of broader student populations.

domain2.q3_evidence: Data collection included pre- and post-game surveys, videotaped and in-person observations, and content analysis of debates and discussions. However, no validated instruments are identified. Survey results are not reported quantitatively. The tools appear researcher-developed without reported validation.
domain2.q4_evidence: Analysis is primarily qualitative with selective participant quotes. No systematic coding methodology is described. No inter-rater reliability is reported. The single researcher serving as designer, tester, and educator introduces significant potential for bias in data interpretation.

domain3.q5_evidence: Findings are presented thematically with supporting participant quotes and are generally consistent with the described observations. However, negative findings (e.g., information overload, role confusion) are discussed alongside positive ones, which shows some balance. The interpretation sometimes relies heavily on selected participant quotes without quantitative support.
domain3.q6_evidence: The author discusses several limitations and challenges openly, including problems with the Pilot study, participants feeling overwhelmed, role identity issues, and the need for teacher scaffolding. The iterative design approach inherently involves identifying and addressing problems. Next steps and future improvements are also discussed.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: This is a design-based research study with small, non-representative samples, no control group, and a single researcher serving multiple roles (designer, researcher, educator). While the study provides rich qualitative insights into AR game design for history education and honestly discusses challenges encountered, the lack of validated instruments, systematic analysis methods, and quantitative reporting limits the reliability of the findings. The iterative design approach is appropriate for its goals but limits generalizability.

pdf_filename: Replaying History: Engaging Urban Underserved Students in Learning World History Through Computer Simulation Games.pdf

bibliographic.title: Replaying History: Engaging Urban Underserved Students in Learning World History Through Computer Simulation Games
bibliographic.venue: Proceedings of the 6th International Conference on Learning Sciences (ICLS 2004)

study_characteristics.sample_description: 18 students at a Media and Technology Charter School in a large Northeastern city, designed for inner-city youth. The class was comprised entirely of students who had failed ninth grade the previous year and were being held back. Roughly 75% were African-American, 15% were Latino, and 10% were of European descent. Five of these students participated in a one-week, 15-hour extension camp at the end of the unit.
study_characteristics.study_design: Qualitative case study within a design experiment methodology
study_characteristics.aim: To examine what classroom practices emerge and how learning occurs when Civilization III is used as the basis for learning about world history in a Humanities enrichment course in an inner-city school

eligibility.concerns: Purely qualitative study with no quantitative outcome measures; pre and post tests were designed but students refused to complete the pre-test, making quantitative comparisons impossible

rq1.conceptualization: The study conceptualizes using a commercial simulation game (Civilization III) as a tool for learning history. Engagement in gameplay is framed as a complex process of appropriation and resistance, recruiting students' identities and intentions. The game is positioned as a rich semiotic system requiring mastery of geographic facts, historical concepts, and interrelationships among geographical, political, economic, and historical systems. Learning through the game transforms history from memorizing facts to exploring emergent properties of a simulated system.
theoretical_frameworks: Design experiment methodology (Barab & Squire; Brown, 1992; Cobb et al., 2001)
Motivation framework of fantasy, control, challenge, and curiosity (Cordova & Lepper, 1996)
Identity resources and cultural tools (Wertsch, 1998; de Certeau, 1984)

rq2.key_outcomes: Students developed deeper understandings of relationships among history, geography, economics, and politics through gameplay. Key learning outcomes included: (1) understanding interconnections between geography, economics, and political systems; (2) developing multi-factor causal explanations for historical phenomena such as colonization (population density, strategic resources, relations with other civilizations, access to trade networks); (3) learning geographic facts (locations of Egypt, Nova Scotia, Greenland); (4) understanding the role of natural resources in civilization development; (5) ability to construct and test historical hypotheticals (e.g., reversing European colonization of the Americas); (6) recognizing that 'you can't separate geography from economics from politics.' Learning was highly interpretive, driven by students' own goals and mediated by classroom discourse. Powerful systemic-level understandings emerged through gameplay for some students (e.g., Tony) only after approximately 30 hours of play.
rq2.engagement_results: Engagement was a complex process of appropriation and resistance. Many students initially rejected the activity (days 1-4), finding Civilization III too complex. By day 4, when students realized they could use the game to 'replay history' and explore hypothetical scenarios, they began to appropriate it. Identity was central to engagement - students were most engaged when the game allowed them to express ideas they believed in or investigate questions tied to their identities (e.g., African-American students wanting to reverse colonization and make the Americas African). Motivation was multi-dimensional, occurring at the intersection of personal goals, fantasies, the possibility space of the simulation, desire to learn world history, and social pressure. Failure in the game drove recursive cycles of problem-solving that led to frustration but also engagement and learning.

game_design_elements: Historical simulation with deep geographic, political, and economic systems
Turn-based strategy gameplay
Civilization building and management
Resource management and trade
Diplomatic relations and alliances
Military strategy and conflict
Technology research trees
Maps, charts, and graphs as in-game analytical tools
Multiple civilizations with unique characteristics
Failure and restart mechanics driving recursive learning cycles
instructional_strategies: Design experiment with iterative refinement
Instructor-researcher as participant-observer
Drawing connections between game world and real-world map on the board
Just-in-time lectures connecting game events to historical content
Using historical narratives as explanatory devices for understanding game events (e.g., causes of World War I)
Encouraging historical hypotheticals ('What if you reverse colonization?')
Student journals documenting gameplay decisions
Post-gameplay reflection and presentation to other classes
Extension camp for deeper engagement (one week, 15 hours)
Framing game as tool for replaying and exploring history
rq3.content_integration: Civilization III was used as the basis for an interdisciplinary world cultures course over a six-week period (three times per week, 45 minutes per class). The game served as a platform for exploring world history topics including colonization, the rise and fall of civilizations, geographic determinism, trade networks, and political systems. Teachers made explicit links between game events and historical curriculum by drawing world maps on the board showing where students' in-game civilizations corresponded to real locations. Historical narratives were introduced as explanatory devices for understanding game mechanics (e.g., causes of WWI). Students explored hypothetical historical scenarios (e.g., 'Why did the Europeans colonize the Americas as opposed to the reverse?') and developed multi-factor causal models for historical phenomena like colonization.

implementation_barriers: Students initially rejected the activity and the game (days 1-4), similar to how they rejected school-based history education generally
Civilization III was perceived as very complex and too difficult to learn
Students did not initially see how the game could help them in school or real life
Even gamer students took several days to appropriate the game as a learning tool
Time constraints limited the partnering teacher's ability to fully integrate the game into instruction
Students refused to complete pre-tests (even under threat of grade reduction), making quantitative assessment impossible
The game was not designed as an educational tool, requiring significant pedagogical scaffolding
Space allotments prevented inclusion of the full case study in the paper
methodology_limitations: Qualitative case study design limits generalizability
Small sample size (18 students, with 5 in the extension camp)
No pre-test/post-test comparison possible due to student refusal
Participant-observer role of the researcher may introduce bias
Single classroom context in a specific charter school serving underserved students
Six-week intervention period with only three sessions per week may be insufficient
Systemic-level understanding emerged only after ~30 hours of play, raising scalability concerns
Full case study omitted due to space constraints, limiting the evidence presented
negative_effects: Initial frustration and resistance from students who saw the game as too complex
Students frequently perceived early failures as bad game design rather than learning opportunities
Some students became embittered by failure, attributing causes externally
The game at times was frustrating or even uninteresting for some students
Risk of students developing materialist or geographically deterministic readings of history (e.g., 'great man' theory)
mitigation_strategies: Teachers drew connections between in-game civilizations and real-world map to scaffold understanding
Just-in-time lectures and historical narratives were used to contextualize game events
Suggesting historical hypotheticals (e.g., reversing colonization) to recruit student identity and interest
Helping students construct narratives for unfolding play that brought knowledge of geography or history as tools for gameplay
Extension camp provided additional time for deeper engagement and learning
Triangulation of data through observations, interviews, journals, and document analysis

domain1.q1_evidence: The study clearly defines its context: a Media and Technology Charter School in a large Northeastern city serving inner-city youth. The sample of 18 students who had failed ninth grade is explicitly described. The case study approach (Stake, 1995) is appropriate for the research questions. The three research questions are clearly stated.
domain1.q2_evidence: The sample is a single classroom of 18 students who had all failed ninth grade, in a specific charter school context. This is a highly specific population (urban underserved, retained students) that is not representative of typical history classrooms. The study acknowledges this is a particular context but does not discuss external validity or generalizability limitations explicitly.

domain2.q3_evidence: Data collection included observations, transcribed interviews, student journals, and student artifacts - appropriate qualitative methods. Nine participants received semi-structured interviews with performance tasks. However, the planned pre and post tests were abandoned because students refused to take the pre-test. The constant comparative method (Glaser & Strauss, 1967) was used for analysis. Data triangulation from multiple sources strengthens validity.
domain2.q4_evidence: The constant comparative method was applied to approximately 300 pages of primary data. Two researchers analyzed data independently and verified patterns informally. Analysis focused on emergent themes and patterns. However, the first researcher served as instructor-researcher and participant-observer, creating potential bias. Inter-rater reliability is not formally reported. The full case study was omitted due to space constraints, limiting readers' ability to assess the evidence base.

domain3.q5_evidence: Findings are richly described with extensive student quotes and detailed narratives. The interpretations about appropriation, identity, and learning through failure are well-supported by the presented evidence. However, the study emphasizes positive outcomes and engaged students (particularly Tony) while giving less attention to students who remained disengaged. The framing of the game as a colonial simulation was largely student-driven, which is acknowledged.
domain3.q6_evidence: The study acknowledges that engagement was complex and not universally positive - the game was 'at times engaging, and at times frustrating (or even uninteresting).' It notes that systemic understanding required approximately 30 hours of play. However, the study does not explicitly discuss generalizability limitations, researcher bias from the dual instructor-researcher role, or the implications of the failed pre/post-test design. The Educational Implications section is relatively brief.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study provides rich qualitative data from a well-designed case study using established methods (Stake, 1995; Glaser & Strauss, 1967). Data triangulation from multiple sources (observations, interviews, journals, artifacts) strengthens validity. However, several concerns exist: (1) the dual instructor-researcher role creates potential bias; (2) the very small, non-representative sample (18 retained 9th graders at a specific charter school) limits generalizability; (3) the failure of the pre/post-test design eliminates any quantitative evidence of learning outcomes; (4) the full case study was omitted for space, limiting the evidence base; and (5) limitations and researcher positionality are not thoroughly discussed. Overall, the study offers valuable exploratory insights but with methodological constraints typical of early design-based research in game-based learning.

pdf_filename: Storiﬁcation in History education A mobile game in and about medieval Amsterdam.pdf

bibliographic.title: Storification in History education: A mobile game in and about medieval Amsterdam
bibliographic.venue: Computers & Education

study_characteristics.sample_description: 216 students aged 12-16 years (most 13 years old) from 5 different secondary schools, spread over 10 school classes, ranging from lower secondary professional education to pre-university education. Divided into 54 groups of 4-5 students each.
study_characteristics.study_design: qualitative case study with mixed methods (content analysis of game design, observations, coach observation forms with Likert scales, group interviews, media box/log analysis)
study_characteristics.aim: To evaluate how narrative (storification) was designed and applied in a mobile History game, analyzing three types of storification (receiving, constructing, participating in a story) and their effects on student engagement.

eligibility.concerns: The study focuses more on narrative/storification processes than gamification per se, but the game-based learning approach with points, competition, and collaborative game mechanics qualifies it as gamification in history education.

rq1.conceptualization: The study conceptualizes game-based learning through the lens of 'storification' — narrative organization that transforms human experience into story lines by making sense via narrative organization. Three types are identified: receiving a story (spectator), constructing a story (director), and participating in a story (actor). Games are viewed as narrative learning environments that help students link characters, tools, and causation through meaningful temporal and sequential connections.

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Coach observation forms used 5-point Likert scales: average score 3.52 for HQT engagement in Internet surfing; average score 4.23 for HQT engagement in solving assignments. Multiple-choice questions answered correctly on first attempt 75% of cases, requiring max 3 attempts in only 5%. Open-text questions answered correctly in one attempt 81% of cases (60% if considering typing/grammar errors). HQT-CT collaboration question: 48.3% answered 'regularly' (4 on 5-point scale). 60% of students recorded Montelbaanstower from wrong perspective. 100% of students enacted sayings; 30% combined literal enactment with symbolic meaning.
rq2.key_outcomes: The game evoked a mixture of three types of storification that differently affected students' engagement. Participating in the story evoked high activity but less awareness of the whole story. Constructing the story triggered awareness of the whole story. Receiving the story was least engaged with by students (they often skipped background texts). Both constructing and participating positively affected engagement compared to receiving. HQTs (directors/constructors) were more motivated and concentrated throughout gameplay than CTs (actors/participants). Students generally focused more on completing assignments than understanding the broader narrative.
rq2.engagement_results: Students were very active and motivated in making video recordings and enacting sayings. HQTs were more busy, motivated, and concentrated throughout game play compared to CTs. CTs experienced loss of control and overview of the game. Students paid more attention to procedures and technology than to the story line during introductions. Students generally did not read background texts carefully, scrolling to assignments instead.

game_design_elements: Narrative/story-based structure (back story, area introductions, diary entries)
Location-based assignments (orientation, imagination, symbolic)
Role differentiation (City Team walkers and Head Quarter Team coordinators)
Team competition (collecting 'days' as points; team with most days wins)
Collaborative group structure (4-5 students per group)
Medieval map as navigation tool
Video and text messages as narrative delivery
Media box as story board / coordination tool
Three assignment types per area (orientation, imagination, symbolic)
Six thematic areas (labor, trade, religion, rules and government, knowledge, defense)
Perspective-taking tasks (walking pilgrim route, enacting historical sayings)
Photo and video creation tasks
technological_platforms: Video phones for communication and media capture
Computers with Internet connection (for Head Quarter Teams)
Digital media box environment (website for collecting materials)
instructional_strategies: Storification (narrative organization as learning mechanism)
Location-based learning (walking through actual medieval Amsterdam sites)
Collaborative learning (CT and HQT interdependency)
Perspective-taking (acting as historical characters)
Constructivist approach (students as story authors/directors/actors)
Role-playing (becoming a Burgher of medieval Amsterdam)
Multimedia creation (photos, videos of historical reenactments)
Information seeking tasks (Internet research for historical context)
rq3.content_integration: The game 'Frequentie 1550' was designed around the history of medieval Amsterdam (late medieval era). Students explored six thematic areas of the old city (labor, trade, religion, rules and government, knowledge, defense), each with location-specific historical content delivered through video diary entries, text messages with background information, and assignments requiring interaction with actual historical sites, buildings, and artifacts. The narrative connected students to a Burgher character trying to become a citizen by staying 366 days.

implementation_barriers: Students often did not pay attention to background texts and story elements, focusing instead on completing assignments
Technical problems with video phones: small screens, sun glare making reading difficult
GPS/map issues: dots not appearing correctly, CTs appearing at wrong locations on maps
Medieval map did not represent current Amsterdam accurately (missing streets, water), causing navigation confusion
Map orientation was inverted (north-south reversed), causing additional confusion
Communication difficulties between HQT and CT teams (18 coaches reported explicit difficulties)
Timing conflicts: phone ringing during video recording tasks
Some students unfamiliar with Internet search strategies (Wikipedia, keyword searching)
CTs had limited overview of overall game narrative compared to HQTs
Distractions in the city environment (people, traffic, shops) broke narrative immersion for CTs
methodology_limitations: Qualitative case study design limits generalizability
No control group or pre-post measurement of learning outcomes
No formal assessment of historical knowledge acquisition
Reliance on observation notes and coach reports (subjective)
Analysis based on content analysis of game design and process, not standardized measures
Interrater agreement procedure described but specific reliability statistics not reported
Single game played on single day per school - limited exposure
Differences between game days (10 days across different schools) not systematically analyzed
negative_effects: CTs experienced loss of control and limited narrative overview during gameplay
Students mixed historical back story with fictional elements, suggesting shallow historical understanding
Perspective-taking was not always understood or successfully executed by students
Historically relevant narrative was sometimes lost due to city distractions and focus on task completion
Flow experience was disrupted for CTs by long walking and waiting times between assignments
mitigation_strategies: Teams switched roles (CT/HQT) in the second half of the day so all students experienced both perspectives
Two different roles (CT and HQT) were created to maintain both involvement in the whole story and meaningful experience of narrative elements
Introductory video clips were sent when entering each new area to orient students
Both medieval and modern Amsterdam maps were provided to HQTs for navigation
Closing group presentation allowed students to share and reflect on collected media

domain1.q1_evidence: The study clearly defines the case: 216 students from 5 secondary schools, 10 school classes, playing the Frequentie 1550 game. The inclusion context is well described.
domain1.q2_evidence: Students ranged from lower secondary professional to pre-university education across 5 schools, providing some diversity. However, all schools were in Amsterdam and selection criteria for schools are not described. Convenience sampling is implied.

domain2.q3_evidence: Multiple data sources were used (researcher observations, coach observation forms with Likert scales, group interviews, media box logs). However, the observation instruments were not validated instruments; they were designed for this study. The Likert-scale items are described but psychometric properties are not reported.
domain2.q4_evidence: Content analysis followed grounded theory approach (Strauss & Corbin, 1998). Three researchers performed analysis and negotiated until agreement. Interrater agreement procedure was followed. Quantitative data from observation forms reported as frequencies and averages.

domain3.q5_evidence: Results are systematically presented according to the three storification types (receiving, constructing, participating) with clear tables summarizing design vs. actual play. Interpretations are well-supported by multiple data sources.
domain3.q6_evidence: The conclusion discusses the tension between participation and overview but does not include a formal limitations section. Methodological limitations such as lack of control group, no formal learning assessment, and generalizability issues are not explicitly addressed.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study provides rich qualitative data from multiple sources and follows systematic analytical procedures. However, it lacks validated measurement instruments, has no control group, does not formally assess learning outcomes, and does not include a limitations section. The study design is appropriate for its exploratory aims but limits the strength of conclusions about educational effectiveness.

pdf_filename: Student-Made Games to Learn the History of Mathematics.pdf

bibliographic.title: Student-Made Games to Learn the History of Mathematics
bibliographic.venue: PRIMUS: Problems, Resources, and Issues in Mathematics Undergraduate Studies

study_characteristics.sample_description: Prospective secondary mathematics teachers enrolled in a history of mathematics course at the University of Delaware during Spring 2008 and Spring 2009. Most were undergraduate secondary mathematics education majors; approximately one-third chose to incorporate games into their 45-minute lessons.
study_characteristics.study_design: descriptive case study / practitioner report (no formal evaluation)
study_characteristics.game_type: student-designed board games and computer-based adaptations of popular games (BINGO, Integer Flash, Jeopardy, team competitions)
study_characteristics.game_name: Multiple student-created games: Math BINGO, numeration system team competition, Integer Flash adaptation, Computer Jeopardy (multiple variants), and others
study_characteristics.aim: To describe how college students (prospective secondary math teachers) designed and used their own adaptations of popular board and computer games to learn the history of mathematics, and to identify factors for successful use of games in this context.

eligibility.concerns: This study is about using games to teach the HISTORY OF MATHEMATICS (a mathematics education course), NOT about teaching history as a subject/discipline. The subject matter is mathematical content (fractions, numeration systems, negative numbers, cubic equations, linear equations, algebraic symbolism) viewed through a historical lens. The games are used within a mathematics course, not a history course. The students are prospective mathematics teachers, not history students. The 'history' component is the history of mathematical concepts and methods, which falls under mathematics education rather than history education as defined in the systematic review's scope.

rq1.conceptualization: Games are conceptualized as student-designed adaptations of popular commercially available board games and television game shows (e.g., BINGO, Jeopardy, card games) used as a mechanism for incorporating history of mathematics content into peer-taught lessons. The emphasis is on student creation and adaptation of games rather than instructor-designed gamification.
theoretical_frameworks: No explicit theoretical framework cited; draws on general principles of game-based learning in mathematics education (Johnson & Rising 1972; Bright, Harvey & Wheeler 1985; Randel et al. 1992)

rq2.key_outcomes: No formal evaluation was conducted. The authors report qualitative observations: students actively and enthusiastically participated in games during class; students made best efforts to get correct answers; games contributed to students learning history of mathematics facts and ideas more effectively than rote memorization; students felt motivated and interested in the history of mathematics; students felt better prepared for future teaching. The instructors informally evaluated game success in promoting desired learning.
rq2.engagement_results: Students actively and enthusiastically participated in the games. All students actively participated in team-based activities. Students sometimes got 'overly enthusiastic.' Students enjoyed competing individually or in teams. The competition strategy was seen as a great way to engage students.

game_design_elements: Competition (team-based and individual)
Rewards (candy, verbal praise, points)
Punishments for wrong answers (e.g., being voted off team)
Elements of chance (dice rolls, card draws)
Point systems (Jeopardy-style point values)
Clear rules and instructions
Attractive physical materials
Time constraints (games kept short to maintain interest)
technological_platforms: Physical board games and card games
Downloaded BINGO templates from the Internet
instructional_strategies: Student-designed games (learners as game creators)
Peer teaching (45-minute lessons presented to classmates)
Content review before gameplay
Post-game discussion and comments
Group work and team competition
Integration of game into a broader lesson with presentation and practice problems
Written self-reflection papers after lessons
rq3.content_integration: Games were integrated as part of student-led 45-minute lessons on assigned mathematical topics viewed through a historical lens. Content included: fractions (BINGO), ancient numeration systems (team competition), negative numbers (Integer Flash), electronic computers and binary arithmetic (Jeopardy), cubic equations and Chinese/Indian methods (Jeopardy), history of linear equations and methods of false position (Jeopardy), and historical algebraic notation (Jeopardy). Questions blended mathematical problem-solving with historical facts about mathematicians and mathematical methods.

implementation_barriers: Class presentations were not formally evaluated, making it difficult to measure learning outcomes rigorously
Time constraints of 45-minute lessons limited game duration
Some games risked becoming too loud or excited, requiring ground rules
Difficulty of historical mathematical language required group work to manage complexity
methodology_limitations: No formal evaluation of learning outcomes was conducted
Purely descriptive account based on instructor observations and student reflections
No control group or comparison condition
No pre/post assessment of knowledge gains
Sample limited to two semesters at one university
Approximate one-third participation rate in game design (self-selected, not randomized)
negative_effects: Risk of excessive noise and excitement disrupting learning environment
Some students included slightly embarrassing punishments for wrong answers (e.g., being voted off team)
mitigation_strategies: Ground rules established before each game
Loss of points for breaking rules or getting too loud
Games kept relatively short to maintain interest
Post-game discussion to reinforce learning
Follow-up activities such as additional readings to emphasize learning responsibility

domain1.q1_evidence: No explicit selection criteria for study participants. The study describes students in a specific course at one university during two semesters (Spring 2008 and Spring 2009). Only approximately one-third of students chose to use games, representing a self-selected subset with no formal inclusion/exclusion criteria.
domain1.q2_evidence: Sample is limited to prospective secondary mathematics teachers at the University of Delaware. No discussion of representativeness or generalizability to other populations. All student names are pseudonyms, and examples are selectively presented.

domain2.q3_evidence: No validated measurement instruments were used. Data consists entirely of instructor observations and student self-reflection papers. The authors explicitly acknowledge that 'the class presentations were not formally evaluated.'
domain2.q4_evidence: No systematic data analysis methods described. The paper is a descriptive practitioner report presenting selected examples of student-designed games. No coding scheme, no systematic analysis of reflections, no quantitative measures.

domain3.q5_evidence: Conclusions about effectiveness ('games contribute to students' learning history of mathematics facts and ideas in ways more effective than those using other approaches') are not supported by any formal evidence or comparison. The interpretation goes beyond what the descriptive evidence can support.
domain3.q6_evidence: The authors do acknowledge that 'the class presentations were not formally evaluated' and use hedging language ('we think the design and use... had several benefits'). However, limitations are not systematically discussed.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: This is a descriptive practitioner report with no formal research design, no validated measures, no systematic data collection or analysis, and no control conditions. Claims about effectiveness are not supported by empirical evidence. The study provides useful pedagogical descriptions but carries high risk of bias for drawing conclusions about game effectiveness.

pdf_filename: Sustaining mobile learning with pervasive game An example of cultural history exploration.pdf

bibliographic.title: Sustaining mobile learning with pervasive game: An example of cultural history exploration
bibliographic.venue: Mobile Learning: A Handbook for Developers, Educators, and Learners

study_characteristics.sample_description: Thirty college students divided into five groups of six, exploring the historic site Provintia in Tainan, Taiwan
study_characteristics.study_design: pre-experimental (one-group pretest-posttest)
study_characteristics.game_name: Cultural History Exploration Pervasive Game (Provintia exploration game)
study_characteristics.aim: To establish a pervasive game framework to design an exploratory game that allows participants to explore historical locations to learn about interrelated cultural history knowledge, and to investigate the effectiveness and sustainability of this approach

eligibility.concerns: The study uses a one-group pretest-posttest design without a control group, which limits causal inference. The chapter is part of an edited book rather than a peer-reviewed journal article.

rq1.explicit_definition: A pervasive game (PG) is a mobile game that seamlessly integrates the physical environment with virtual scenarios. According to Walther (2005), a PG implies a mixed-reality gaming space; that is, the gameplay connects the virtual world with the tangible world.
rq1.conceptualization: Pervasive gaming is conceptualized as an extension of mobile learning (mlearning) that blurs the boundary between games and real life. The Instructional Pervasive Game (IPG) approach combines mobile technology, augmented reality, location-based exploration, social networking, and cooperative game mechanics to create a seamless learning environment where students explore authentic historical sites. The framework includes six factors: user, environment, information, context, mobility, and gamist.
theoretical_frameworks: Technology integration model for game-based pervasive learning (Laine et al., 2010)
Walther's four axes of pervasive games (distribution, mobility, persistence, transmediality)

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Pre-test and post-test scores on Provintia history and culture understanding (14 riddle-based questions); pervasive game effectiveness evaluation questionnaire covering four aspects: game rules, game mechanism, game interaction, and game content (using Likert-scale items)
rq2.statistical_results: Learning effectiveness: pre-test mean=31.33 (SD=12.65), post-test mean=88.50 (SD=7.44), t=22.46, p<.001 -- significant improvement. Game rules: pre-test m=25.36, post-test m=25.86, t=-0.803, p=.429 (not significant). Game mechanism: pre-test m=23.73, post-test m=23.56, t=0.22, p=.821 (not significant). Game interaction: pre-test m=29.30, post-test m=29.23, t=0.100, p=.921 (not significant). Game content: pre-test m=12.90, post-test m=20.96, t=-9.950, p<.001 (significant).
rq2.comparative_methodology: One-group pretest-posttest design with paired t-tests to compare pre- and post-test scores on both learning effectiveness and game effectiveness evaluation
rq2.key_outcomes: Participants showed highly significant improvement in understanding of Provintia history and culture after the pervasive game activity (pre-test 31.33 to post-test 88.50). Participants performed better on geographical (93.3%) and architectural (92.3%) aspects than on historical (89.4%) and cultural (82.7%) aspects. Game content evaluation showed significant improvement, indicating participants gained more understanding of the site. Game rules, mechanism, and interaction aspects showed no significant differences, meaning the game met participants' expectations in these areas.
rq2.engagement_results: Participants reported feeling excited and happy when able to solve riddles, which enhanced their sense of achievement. AR storytelling was noted as making site exploration more interesting. Participants said they would cooperate and share with group members and preferred AR content over textual tourist sign descriptions. The bingo Q&A competition at the end was effective for refreshing memories. Facebook was used for group cooperation, information management, and sharing, though participants preferred shorthand note-taking over smartphone typing.

game_design_elements: Riddle-solving (14 riddles based on historical content)
Location-based exploration of authentic historical site (Provintia)
Augmented reality content (AR presentations showing historical clips and talking figures)
Group competition and cooperation (5 groups of 6)
Bingo Q&A competition (49 questions on history, artefacts, observations, environments)
Social networking integration (Facebook for group communication and sharing)
Mission completion structure
Tourist brochure distribution as game scaffolding
technological_platforms: Facebook (social networking service for group spaces)
Mobile cameras for AR content recognition
instructional_strategies: Inquiry-based learning through riddle-solving at historical site
Cooperative learning in small groups (6 members per group)
Augmented reality for multimedia cognitive support
Social networking for collaborative documentation and sharing
Pre-test and post-test assessment
Group bingo Q&A for knowledge consolidation
Guided exploration with research observers providing task guidance
Four-aspect content design: historical, geographical, architectural, and cultural
rq3.content_integration: Learning content was collected from historical literature, books, textbooks, web information, Tainan government tourist bureau information, field study, tour guides, and oral history interviews. Content covered four aspects of Provintia: (1) historical - stories about the fort, ordnance depot, hospitals, and schools across various historical periods; (2) geographical - importance of location and position during wartime; (3) architectural - objects and features such as stone lions and sculptures; (4) cultural - historical monuments such as tombstones and wells. The content was embedded in 14 riddles that participants solved by physically exploring the site and using AR on their smartphones to access multimedia historical narratives.

implementation_barriers: Hardware factors influenced participant motivation (e.g., AR image recognition failures due to sunlight, shadows, or photo-taking angles)
Need for a rich image database to increase interaction fluency
Participants preferred shorthand note-taking over typing on smartphones, reducing Facebook engagement
Technical challenges with AR content recognition in outdoor environments
Sustainability concerns regarding making mobile learning widespread without requiring high-level technical knowledge
Need for budget support and knowledge of applicable instructional strategies for teachers to adopt mobile technologies
methodology_limitations: One-group pretest-posttest design without a control group limits causal inference
Small sample size (n=30)
Single site and single session study limits generalizability
No long-term follow-up to assess retention of learning
Game effectiveness evaluation post-test scores were sometimes lower than pre-test (game interaction, game mechanism), suggesting expectation mismatch
Qualitative data from interviews not systematically analyzed with established qualitative methods
negative_effects: Game mechanism aspect (use of smartphone, AR, and Facebook) did not significantly influence gaming behaviours and attitudes beyond expectations
Game interaction post-test was slightly lower than pre-test, suggesting technology may have reduced rather than enhanced some interactions
Facebook content was mostly photos or short notes rather than substantive documentation due to inconvenience of smartphone typing
Some participants found historical and cultural content more difficult to grasp because it was more conceptual and abstract
mitigation_strategies: Use of markless AR to create seamless learning environments combining virtual and real settings
Design a quick upload mechanism with keywords or icons to enhance Facebook usage motivation
Provide AR cognitive support (short clips as clues) for more abstract conceptual content
Include research observers in each group for task guidance and hardware/software problem-solving
Distribute tourist brochures as supplementary scaffolding material
Use bingo Q&A activity to consolidate learning and refresh memories after exploration

domain1.q1_evidence: The study clearly describes participants as 30 college students who were invited to participate, divided into 5 groups of 6. However, no explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria or recruitment process details are provided.
domain1.q2_evidence: The sample consists of only 30 college students from a single institution in Taiwan. No information about how students were selected or whether they are representative of a broader population. The convenience sample limits generalizability.

domain2.q3_evidence: Pre-test and post-test were based on the same 14 riddle questions used in the game, and a pervasive game effectiveness evaluation questionnaire was used. However, no information about validity or reliability of the instruments is provided. The riddle-based test may conflate game-specific knowledge with broader historical understanding.
domain2.q4_evidence: Paired t-tests were appropriately used for pre-post comparisons. Means, SDs, t-values, and p-values are reported. However, no effect sizes are reported. The one-group design without a control group limits the ability to attribute changes to the intervention. Qualitative data from interviews and Facebook observations are discussed but not systematically analyzed.

domain3.q5_evidence: The authors generally interpret findings consistently with data. They acknowledge non-significant results (game rules, mechanism, interaction) and discuss possible explanations. However, they frame non-significant differences positively (as meeting expectations) rather than as potential limitations. The conclusion somewhat overstates the evidence given the weak research design.
domain3.q6_evidence: The authors discuss some practical limitations such as AR recognition difficulties and smartphone typing inconvenience. However, they do not explicitly discuss the major methodological limitations of the one-group pretest-posttest design, the small sample size, or the absence of a control group. The sustainability discussion is mostly aspirational rather than evidence-based.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study has high risk of bias due to: (1) weak research design (one-group pretest-posttest without control group), making it impossible to rule out maturation, testing effects, or other threats to internal validity; (2) small convenience sample (n=30) from a single institution; (3) lack of validated instruments with no reported reliability or validity; (4) no effect sizes reported; (5) insufficient discussion of methodological limitations; and (6) potential conflation of game-specific knowledge with genuine historical learning outcomes.

pdf_filename: Teaching History in an Age of Pervasive Computing The Case for Games in the High School and Undergraduate Classroom.pdf

bibliographic.title: Teaching History in an Age of Pervasive Computing: The Case for Games in the High School and Undergraduate Classroom
bibliographic.venue: Pastplay: Teaching and Learning History with Technology

study_characteristics.sample_description: Undergraduate history and computing science students at Brock University (St. Catharines, Ontario) in a 2007/08 upper-level course project, plus first-year course students, and online Civfanatics community members; no formal sample size reported
study_characteristics.study_design: Qualitative descriptive / practitioner reflection with case examples
study_characteristics.game_type: Commercial strategy games (Civilization IV, Caesar IV), game mods/scenarios, student-built games (ex novo), augmented reality games, web-based games (The Nethernet/PMOG)
study_characteristics.game_name: Civilization IV, Caesar IV, Brigade: A War of 1812 Saga, Tavern Keeper, Niagara 1812: Return of the Fenian Shadow, Queenston 1812: The Bomber's Plot, The Nethernet (PMOG)
study_characteristics.aim: To argue that collaborative learning with computer games (analyzing, modding, and building games) is the best way to teach history in an age of pervasive computing, and to propose a typology of time and space for selecting appropriate history games for classroom use

eligibility.concerns: This is a theoretical/practitioner chapter rather than an empirical study with controlled outcomes. It presents pedagogical arguments, a game typology, case examples from courses and online communities, and assessment rubrics, but does not report formal quantitative or systematic qualitative research data.

rq1.conceptualization: Games are conceptualized as synthetic worlds analogous to historical narratives (books and articles), where rules encoded in computer code constitute procedural rhetoric that embodies particular epistemologies of history. The authors distinguish between games as 'tools' (the prevailing view they reject) and games as 'artifacts' to be deconstructed in the tradition of historiography. History games are further conceptualized through a typology of movement based on Aarseth et al.'s framework (space and time dimensions), which helps historians select games that align with particular historical epistemologies. The 'meta-game' concept refers to engagement beyond playing -- analyzing, modding, and building games as forms of historical expression analogous to writing historiographical essays.
theoretical_frameworks: Aarseth et al.'s multi-dimensional typology of games (space and time)
James Paul Gee's learning principles in games
Goal-oriented vs. goalless game typology (Jesper Juul)

rq2.key_outcomes: The chapter presents qualitative case evidence rather than measured outcomes. Key reported observations include: (1) Civfanatics community members engaged in sustained peer review of historical mods for Civilization IV, debating historical accuracy (e.g., Crusades scenario with detailed discussions about religious denominations, territorial boundaries, and historical figures); (2) Undergraduate students in a 2007/08 course successfully designed and built original history games about the War of 1812 using C++ and OpenGL, including Brigade: A War of 1812 Saga and Tavern Keeper; (3) Student reflections noted that game development allowed them to combine political and social history perspectives and express nuanced micro-histories; (4) Students initially resisted game-based assessment (preferring traditional essays) due to unfamiliarity with grading criteria; (5) Augmented reality games (Niagara 1812) demonstrated potential for blending virtual and real-world historical spaces.
rq2.engagement_results: Students showed enthusiasm for game development but also experienced anxiety about unfamiliar assessment formats. The Civfanatics community demonstrated high voluntary engagement with historical content through modding, with peer review processes emerging organically. Students were reluctant to replace traditional essays with game diaries in first-year courses.

game_design_elements: Procedural rhetoric (rules as historical arguments)
Typology of space (perspective, topography, environment)
Typology of time (pace, representation, teleology)
Game modding and scenario creation
Ex novo game building
Peer review through online forums/wikis
Assessment rubrics for game-based projects
Augmented reality with GPS-enabled smartphones
Web-based mission/tour game mechanics (The Nethernet)
technological_platforms: CivFanatics forums and Apolyton University (modding communities)
instructional_strategies: Analyzing games as historical artifacts (deconstructing procedural rhetoric)
Game modding as analogous to writing historiographical essays
Collaborative ex novo game development in interdisciplinary teams (history + computing science students)
Staged assessment with rubrics (Draft Proposal, Design Document, testing reports, final product)
Game diaries for reflection at particular gameplay points
Peer assessment for group project contributions
Using Aarseth et al.'s typology to select appropriate games for specific historical topics
Augmented reality games linking virtual events with real historical sites
rq3.content_integration: History content is integrated through multiple approaches: (1) selecting commercial games whose procedural rhetoric aligns with desired historical epistemologies (e.g., Caesar IV for microeconomics of ancient cities, Civilization IV for large-scale cultural evolution); (2) students creating mods that embed historically accurate content into game rule systems (e.g., Crusades scenario in Civilization IV); (3) students building original games from primary and secondary sources about specific historical events (War of 1812); (4) augmented reality games overlaying fictional historical events onto real historical locations (Niagara-on-the-Lake). The key principle is that games express historical arguments through code rather than language.

implementation_barriers: Genre confusion in the marketplace makes it difficult to select appropriate history games for teaching
Commercial history games are built by gamers, not educators, and prioritize mechanics over historical learning
Games like Civilization embed problematic assumptions (technological progress as prime mover of history) that may mislead students
Deep playing of simulation games teaches manipulation of algorithms rather than historical content
Programming skills required for game building (C++, OpenGL) are beyond most humanities undergraduates
Augmented reality games require students to be physically present at historical sites, limiting accessibility
The Nethernet and similar web-based platforms may become unavailable (The Nethernet was no longer online at time of publication)
Students are reluctant to engage with unfamiliar assessment formats ('play for marks')
Managing and marking the large volume of material produced in game development projects is challenging
Free-rider problems in group-based game development projects
methodology_limitations: No formal empirical study design; relies on practitioner reflection and anecdotal case examples
No control group or systematic comparison with traditional teaching methods
No formal measurement of learning outcomes or historical understanding
Sample descriptions are informal (e.g., CivFanatics poll of 111 participants is mentioned but not systematically analyzed)
Student experiences reported through selective quotation rather than systematic data collection
Generalizability limited to specific institutional context (Brock University, Canada)
negative_effects: Students in first-year course all opted for traditional essays over game diaries, suggesting resistance to game-based assessment
Anxiety among students about unfamiliar assessment formats and group project dynamics
Risk that simulation games teach players to manipulate code rather than engage with historical content
Content in games like Civilization can be 'window dressing' that erases its own historical content
mitigation_strategies: Use Aarseth et al.'s typology of time and space to systematically select appropriate games rather than relying on marketplace genre labels
Develop detailed rubrics with clear criteria for game-based assessments (Table 13.3)
Stage game development with incremental graded milestones (proposal, design document, testing, final product)
Pair history students with computing science students in interdisciplinary teams to address technical skill gaps
Implement peer assessment where students divide marks among team members to address free-rider problem
Provide regular feedback opportunities through professors and teaching assistants at each development stage
Focus on meta-game (analyzing procedural rhetoric) rather than treating games as simple teaching tools

domain1.q1_evidence: No formal selection criteria for case examples or participants. The Civfanatics community discussion and student projects are presented as illustrative examples without systematic selection methodology.
domain1.q2_evidence: Cases drawn from a single institution (Brock University) and one online community (CivFanatics). No attempt to establish representativeness. The CivFanatics poll (111 participants) was informal and not designed for research purposes.

domain2.q3_evidence: No formal data collection instruments used. Evidence comes from anecdotal observations, selected forum posts, student reflections (quoted selectively), and the authors' teaching experience. No validated measures of learning outcomes.
domain2.q4_evidence: No systematic analysis methods employed. The chapter is structured as a theoretical argument with illustrative examples. No coding scheme, thematic analysis, or other qualitative research methodology is described.

domain3.q5_evidence: The authors present a coherent argument supported by their examples and theoretical framework. However, interpretations are shaped by their advocacy position -- they are arguing for games in history education rather than objectively evaluating evidence. Potential counter-evidence (e.g., student resistance to game diaries) is acknowledged but not deeply explored.
domain3.q6_evidence: Some limitations are acknowledged implicitly (e.g., students' reluctance, technical barriers, games erasing their own content), but there is no formal limitations section. The chapter does not discuss the limitations of its own methodology or evidence base.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: This is a practitioner-oriented theoretical chapter rather than a formal empirical study. It presents valuable pedagogical arguments and a useful game typology, but lacks systematic research methodology, formal data collection, validated outcome measures, and transparent analytical procedures. The evidence base consists of selectively presented case examples from the authors' own courses and one online community. Risk of bias is high across all domains due to the absence of empirical research design.

pdf_filename: Acquiring the History of the City with Collaborative Game Based Learning.pdf

bibliographic.title: Acquiring the History of the City with Collaborative Game Based Learning
bibliographic.venue: Teaching and Learning in a Digital World, Advances in Intelligent Systems and Computing

study_characteristics.sample_description: 30 postgraduate computer science students (21 male, 9 female, aged 21-23) from Lublin University of Technology who had completed secondary-level history education. 17 considered themselves game players; the rest preferred other types of amusement.
study_characteristics.study_design: descriptive
study_characteristics.game_name: 3D Maze Collaborative Game (custom-built web-based 3D maze game for learning the history of Lublin)
study_characteristics.aim: To study the influence of collaborative gameplay in a 3D maze game on acquiring historical facts about the home city (Lublin), including examining student gaming preferences, motivations, and attitudes toward collaborative game-based learning.

eligibility.concerns: The study uses a descriptive design with no control group and relies on self-reported survey data and interviews rather than pre/post knowledge tests. The sample consists of computer science students rather than history students, which may limit generalizability to typical history education contexts.

rq1.conceptualization: The paper conceptualizes game-based learning as learning through fun, where games motivate, accelerate user response time, and simulate real situations. Cooperative/collaborative games are described as focusing on promoting collaboration, learning work in a team, and making common decisions, combining elements of teaching, training, communication and information with entertainment elements. The hidden educational objective is embedded within the game mechanics (solving history riddles/quests to progress through the maze).

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Knowledge retention measured by quest type: Set colours - 70% memorised proper order; Set date - 27% memorised; Set order (historical facts) - 17% remembered proper order; Set order (other subtypes) - average over 51%; Answer select - 40% acquired new knowledge. Motivation: 73% positively motivated, 17% not motivated, 10% negatively motivated. Gaming habits: 40% played collaborative games often, 53% regularly, 7% never. Prior game-based learning experience: only 34%.
rq2.key_outcomes: Students can acquire home town historical facts through collaborative gameplay, though retention varies significantly by quest type (visual/colour tasks best retained at 70%, date-based tasks worst at 27%). Over 73% of students were positively motivated by the collaborative game-based learning experience. 23 out of 30 students found acquiring historical knowledge through the 3D maze game interesting. Students showed greater willingness to cooperate in groups during gameplay compared to their general learning preferences (54% prefer independent learning normally, but collaborative gaming shifted preference).
rq2.engagement_results: Over 73% were positively motivated by the collaborative game-based learning; almost 17% were not motivated; 10% were negatively motivated. 23 out of 30 students said acquiring historical knowledge with the 3D maze game could be interesting. Primary motivations among game players were mental challenge and social experience.

game_design_elements: 3D maze environment with first-person navigation
Riddles/quests embedded on maze walls (four types: set order, set date, set colours, answer select)
Collaborative roles (Lost player navigates, Helpmates advise)
Time-limited gameplay (5, 10, or 15 minutes)
Trophy cup as win condition (appears after all quests solved)
Random maze generation per game session
Difficulty levels for quests
Communication system via text messages (limited to max 50 messages per game)
Reward for correct answers; quest reappears for incorrect answers
Player statistics and leaderboard
technological_platforms: Web-based application (browser: Chrome 30+, Firefox 30+, IE 11, Opera 12.10+)
instructional_strategies: Collaborative/cooperative learning through designated player roles (Lost and Helpmates)
Problem-based learning through historical riddles/quests
Learning by doing (embedded knowledge acquisition during gameplay)
Peer consultation and group problem-solving via chat communication
Randomized quest selection from database to provide varied content
rq3.content_integration: Historical content about the city of Lublin is integrated as riddles/quests placed on the walls of the 3D maze. Four quest types cover different historical knowledge: ordering events (universities, districts, historical facts, annexations), entering dates (city history, WWII), identifying colours (city coat, voivodeship), and selecting correct answers (monuments, local authorities). The game was developed in context of Lublin's 700th anniversary. Quests are stored in a database and randomly drawn per game session with assigned difficulty levels.

implementation_barriers: Only 34% of students had prior experience with game-based learning, suggesting low awareness/adoption
10% of students were negatively motivated by the game-based learning approach
54% of students prefer to learn independently, which may conflict with the mandatory collaborative nature of the game
Technical requirements (specific browser versions, server infrastructure) may limit deployment
methodology_limitations: Small sample size (n=30) limits generalizability
No control group or pre/post test design to measure actual knowledge gain
Participants were computer science postgraduate students known to researchers, introducing potential selection and social desirability bias
Self-reported data on knowledge retention rather than objective assessment
No validated measurement instruments; simple three-point motivation scale acknowledged as limited
Homogeneous sample (computer science students aged 21-23) may not represent typical history learners
negative_effects: 10% of participants were negatively motivated by the experience
Low retention for date-based quests (only 27%) and historical facts ordering (only 17%)
Some quest types showed poor knowledge retention suggesting the game design may not be equally effective for all types of historical content
mitigation_strategies: Use of multiple quest types to address different learning modalities
Adjustable difficulty levels for quests
Flexible game duration options (5, 10, 15 minutes)
Quest reappearance mechanism when wrong answers are given, reinforcing learning

domain1.q1_evidence: No formal inclusion/exclusion criteria for participant selection. Participants were 'students who were known to the researchers' - a convenience sample from a single university department (computer science). No justification for sample size or selection method provided.
domain1.q2_evidence: Sample consists entirely of postgraduate computer science students aged 21-23 from Lublin University of Technology (21 male, 9 female). This is a highly homogeneous group not representative of typical history education learners. The gender imbalance (70% male) and the fact they were known to the researchers further limits representativeness.

domain2.q3_evidence: The study used an unvalidated 10-question survey and informal interviews. The motivation measurement used only a three-point scale (positively motivated, not motivated, negatively motivated), which the authors themselves acknowledged as limited: 'At this stage of the research this three-point scale was sufficient to differentiate between positive and negative perceptions.' Knowledge retention was assessed by self-report on quest recall, not validated knowledge tests.
domain2.q4_evidence: Analysis is purely descriptive with simple percentages. No statistical tests were applied. No pre-test/post-test comparison. No control group. No inferential statistics to support claims about knowledge acquisition effectiveness.
