The conclusion that 'students can acquire the home town historical facts much faster when they are playing collaborative game' is not supported by the study design.

domain3.q5_evidence: The conclusion states 'the results of the research clearly showed that the students can acquire the home town historical facts much faster when they are playing collaborative game' but the study had no comparison condition or baseline measurement to support 'much faster' claims. The study only measured recall of game content after playing, not comparative speed or effectiveness vs. any alternative.
domain3.q6_evidence: The authors acknowledge that the three-point motivation scale was limited ('At this stage of the research this three-point scale was sufficient'). They also note that some participants were negatively motivated. However, they do not discuss the lack of a control group, the convenience sampling, the absence of validated instruments, or the small sample size as limitations.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study has high risk of bias across all three domains. The sample is a small (n=30) convenience sample of computer science students known to the researchers, with no formal selection criteria. Data collection used unvalidated instruments (simple survey and informal interviews) with no pre/post design or control group. The analysis is purely descriptive with no statistical tests. Most critically, the conclusions overstate what the data can support - claiming collaborative gaming leads to faster knowledge acquisition when no comparative condition existed. The study functions primarily as a design description and preliminary user feedback report rather than a rigorous evaluation of learning outcomes.

pdf_filename: Teaching History With Custom-Built Board Games.pdf

bibliographic.title: Teaching History With Custom-Built Board Games
bibliographic.venue: Simulation & Gaming

study_characteristics.sample_description: 88 participants from History and Indigenous Studies: 61 undergraduate students (from two second-year American History survey courses and one fourth-year Aboriginal History seminar) and 18 M.A. students (from Indigenous Studies and History programs across two iterations of a Methods in Historical Research course) plus 9 undergraduate students from a fourth-year seminar, at the University of Saskatchewan
study_characteristics.study_design: qualitative pilot study with mixed-methods data collection (anonymous feedback forms with Likert-scale ratings, facilitator observation, and external observation)
study_characteristics.aim: To investigate the potential of a custom-built board game as a means to teach historical empathy, improve class participation, and improve student understanding of the limitations of archival collections

eligibility.concerns: The study is a pilot with primarily qualitative and descriptive survey data; no control group or formal experimental design is used.

rq1.conceptualization: The study conceptualizes gamification through custom-built board games as controlled, immersive, and interactive environments that allow players to make decisions within a constrained historical setting. Games are distinguished from simulations by being non-obligatory, pleasure-providing activities bound by rules with meaningful choices. The author frames custom-built games as distinct from commercial off-the-shelf games because they can model disciplinary approaches, theoretical concepts, and structural limitations in evidence directly from archival research.

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Anonymous feedback forms (n=88) using 1-5 Likert scales on three questions: enjoyability (mean 4.7/5), whether the game made clear historical arguments (mean 4.5/5), and effectiveness compared to traditional means (lecture). The vast majority rated the game at least 4 out of 5 on both enjoyment and historical argument clarity.
rq2.statistical_results: Descriptive statistics only. Mean enjoyability rating: 4.7 out of 5. Mean historical argument clarity rating: 4.5 out of 5. No inferential statistics or significance testing was conducted.
rq2.comparative_methodology: Comparison between graduate (n=7 from one observed session, n=18 total) and undergraduate (n=28 from one observed session, n=70 total) student responses. Also a survey question comparing game effectiveness to traditional lecture. No formal control group.
rq2.key_outcomes: Student participation and understanding of historical context improved during the game. Custom-built board games increase student participation and teach not only historical content (facts, names, dates) but also complex ideas such as research methodologies and historical empathy. Groups resolved confusion more efficiently than individuals. Time-constrained decision-making helped maintain engagement. Inability to win did not cause disengagement in short games. Structured debriefing was essential for achieving educational goals.
rq2.engagement_results: External observers noted that by the second round, every student appeared engaged; only one student did not engage during the first round. High levels of engagement in the debrief after the game exceeded other activities attempted in the course (primary source readings, short movie clips). Increased participation during the game did not last beyond the game session itself. Graduate and undergraduate students showed similar enjoyment and belief in historical argument quality, but curricular differences influenced how each group approached the game.

game_design_elements: Asymmetric gameplay (eight community teams vs. one customs inspector team)
Bluffing/risk assessment mechanic (adapted from Sheriff of Nottingham)
Custom-made cards and components based on archival records
Time-constrained decision-making (3-4 minutes per round for team discussion)
Five rounds progressing from 1879 to 1892 in three-year intervals
Wealth accumulation as victory condition
Card-based resource management (community-specific product decks)
Uneven resource distribution across communities to reflect historical inequalities
Semi-structured debriefing questions (7 questions in Appendix A)
Facilitator-led map introduction and backstory
technological_platforms: Non-digital tabletop board game (cardstock and illustration board, later printed cards from Printer Studio, CowCow, ArtsCow)
instructional_strategies: Game-based learning with custom-built board game
Structured post-game debriefing session (approximately 40 minutes)
Small group collaborative decision-making (teams of varying sizes)
Whole-class discussion during debriefing
Informal surveys interspersed with debriefing discussion (show of hands)
Asymmetric roles to foster multiple historical perspectives
Archival research integration into game mechanics
Facilitator observation and anonymous written feedback
rq3.content_integration: The game POLICING THE SOUND is built directly from archival records from the Customs and Immigration records at the National Archive in Seattle (U.S. Customs Service, 1886-1912) and U.S. District Courts Western District Washington. The game models smuggling along the BC-Washington border in the nineteenth century, with cargo values changing over time to reflect historical progression. Communities represent real West Coast locations (New Westminster, Point Roberts, Port Townsend, Neah Bay, Bellingham Bay/Lummi Island, Victoria, Colville, and Metlahatla/Haida Gwaii). The game models both the historical content and the limitations and biases of archival sources, prompting students to interpret how accurately the archival collection represents the past.

implementation_barriers: The term 'instructional game' is considered an oxymoron since game play is voluntary while instruction is nonvoluntary
Good game design (meaningful decisions) conflicts with the historical profession's emphasis on studying what actually happened rather than counterfactuals
Commercial off-the-shelf games often use ahistorical timelines, counterfactual narratives, or supernatural overtones
Variable class duration, changing numbers of students, and limited access to equipment
In-game bookkeeping and rule enforcement must be handled manually in board games (no computer automation)
Detailed rule explanations require additional setup time
Board games do not allow saving game state, requiring reserved physical space or single-session completion
High learning curve and time investment required to develop custom interactive activities
Participation increased during the game but returned to pre-game levels by the next class session
Commercial off-the-shelf games focus on military conquest and civilization building, with few games covering social and cultural history topics taught at university level
methodology_limitations: Pilot study with no control group or formal experimental design
Primarily qualitative and descriptive survey data without inferential statistics
Small graduate student sample (n=7 in some analyses, n=18 total)
Feedback forms were anonymous, limiting ability to track individual student changes
External observation was conducted for only one session (a forty-person undergraduate class)
No pre-test/post-test design to measure learning gains
Self-reported enjoyment and perceived learning may not reflect actual knowledge acquisition
Engagement effects did not persist beyond the game session
negative_effects: Occasional student confusion about rules, especially when playing individually rather than in groups
Disengagement during first round as some students finished turns before others
Uneven distribution of resources made winning difficult or impossible for some communities, recognized by mid-game
Students skipped over in-game text and content to reach gameplay goals faster
Increased participation during the game did not last beyond the session
mitigation_strategies: Grouping players into small teams to resolve rule confusion more efficiently than individual play
Time-constrained decision-making to maintain engagement and reduce waiting
Structured debriefing session to ensure learning objectives were met even when game mechanics were simplified
Debriefing questions designed in tandem with game design to address omissions from streamlined gameplay
Using the inability-to-win situation as a debriefing discussion opportunity about aggregate vs. per capita wealth and misleading depictions of historic communities
Cutting complex mechanics (e.g., bribery) during playtesting and replacing them with debriefing questions to maintain educational goals

domain1.q1_evidence: The study clearly describes the target population: 88 participants across five undergraduate and graduate classes at the University of Saskatchewan. The inclusion of both undergraduate and graduate students is explicitly stated and justified.
domain1.q2_evidence: The sample is drawn entirely from one university (University of Saskatchewan, Canada) and from specific history and indigenous studies courses. The convenience sample of classes taught or associated with the author limits generalizability. No randomization or systematic sampling was employed.

domain2.q3_evidence: Data were collected via anonymous feedback forms with three Likert-scale questions (1-5), facilitator observation by the author, and external observation by two colleagues for one session. The feedback instrument was not validated, and the Likert items were custom-designed without reported psychometric properties.
domain2.q4_evidence: Analysis is primarily descriptive (means reported) and qualitative (observation narratives, student comments). No inferential statistics, no pre-/post-test design, and no systematic qualitative analysis method (e.g., thematic coding) is described. The author served as both game designer, facilitator, and primary data analyst, introducing potential bias.

domain3.q5_evidence: The findings are presented as seven practical lessons supported by participant feedback and observation data. The interpretations are generally consistent with the data presented, and the author acknowledges limitations and alternative explanations (e.g., engagement not persisting beyond the session).
domain3.q6_evidence: The author openly discusses limitations including the pilot nature of the study, the lack of persistent engagement effects, the challenge of the 'instructional game' oxymoron, and the high learning curve for developing custom games. The conclusion appropriately frames findings as suggestive rather than definitive.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: While the study provides valuable qualitative insights into the use of custom-built board games in history education, the overall risk of bias is high due to: (1) a convenience sample from a single institution with the researcher as facilitator, (2) unvalidated measurement instruments, (3) absence of inferential statistics or a control group, (4) the author serving in multiple roles (designer, facilitator, analyst) without independent verification, and (5) reliance on self-reported data. The transparent discussion of limitations partially mitigates these concerns but does not eliminate the fundamental methodological weaknesses.

pdf_filename: Teaching history with the video game Assassin’s Creed effective teaching practices and reported learning.pdf

bibliographic.title: Teaching history with the video game Assassin’s Creed: effective teaching practices and reported learning
bibliographic.venue: Review of Science, Mathematics and ICT Education

study_characteristics.sample_description: 329 high school students (mostly 13 years old, 60% boys) and 4 teachers at two Quebec schools. 81% of students (n=269) in four classes responded to the questionnaire.
study_characteristics.study_design: exploratory mixed-methods case study (questionnaires, individual and group interviews, videotaped classroom observations; quantitative descriptive/inferential statistics via SPSS 22 and qualitative content analysis)
study_characteristics.game_type: commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) video game used as educational resource (not directly played by students in class)
study_characteristics.game_name: Assassin's Creed (Assassin's Creed II, Assassin's Creed: Brotherhood, Assassin's Creed: Revelations)
study_characteristics.aim: To gain a deeper understanding of the pedagogical use of Assassin's Creed in Quebec high school history classrooms, including: (1) how the game is used at school, (2) the benefits for teaching and learning, and (3) the challenges of this learning approach.

eligibility.concerns: Students did not directly play the game in class; rather, teachers extracted and presented game content (clips, cinematics, screenshots) as instructional materials. This is a use of commercial game content for educational purposes rather than direct gameplay-based gamification.

rq1.conceptualization: The study conceptualizes the use of video game content (from Assassin's Creed) as a form of 'profane rhetoric' or secondary historical source that can be used alongside traditional sources in history teaching. The authors distinguish this from games-based learning (GBL) and serious games, noting that Assassin's Creed is a commercial game that 'falls into the category of a commercial game, parts of which can be used for classroom learning.' The approach involves teachers extracting historical characters, buildings, events, and scenarios from the game to contextualize and vivify history lessons, aligning with the Quebec Education Program (QEP) competencies. The theoretical framing draws on games-based learning theory, historiographical thinking, and the concept of 'teachable moments.'

rq2.quantitative_metrics: ANOVA tests for gender differences in game enjoyment: F(1,152)=65.69, p=.000 (boys played more); F(1,138)=29.70, p=.000 (boys enjoyed more). ANOVA for teacher quality differences: F(3,205)=6.30, p=.000 (T1 lower than T2/T3); F(3,148)=9.23, p=.000 (students wanted more AC use with T2/T3/T4 than T1); F(3,183)=4.26, p=.006 (recommendations more positive for T2/T3 vs T1). 55% of students had played at least one AC game. 96% of those who played enjoyed it. 78% liked it 'a lot' or 'really loved' it. 59% found the classroom use very interesting or loved it. 66% recommended other teachers use AC. 52% wished it were used more in class.
rq2.statistical_results: Significant gender differences in playing and liking Assassin's Creed (boys > girls). Significant differences in student appreciation across teachers: T1 (illustration-only approach) rated significantly lower than T2, T3, T4 (historical thinking approach). ANOVA results all at p<.01 level.
rq2.comparative_methodology: Cross-teacher comparison of four teachers' different pedagogical approaches to using Assassin's Creed: T1 used lecture-style illustration (screenshots, clips as visual support without critical comparison); T2, T3, T4 used dialectic/investigative inquiry approach (comparing game content with other historical sources, fostering historical thinking). Students rated T2-T4 approaches significantly higher.
rq2.key_outcomes: Five categories of student-reported learning: events (n=205), characters (n=63), places (n=33), monuments and buildings (n=33), cultures (n=13). Almost all learning was declarative knowledge. Students reported increased motivation, engagement, and interest in history. The multimedia aspects of video games (images, music, cinematics) served as effective learning vectors. Students reported feeling immersed and that the game helped them make connections between school content and outside knowledge. Teaching practices that fostered historical/critical thinking (T2-T4) were significantly more appreciated and effective than illustration-only approaches (T1).
rq2.engagement_results: 59% of students found classroom use of AC very interesting or loved it. 52% wished it were used more. Students reported increased curiosity and motivation: 'It makes me feel like learning more about the subject,' 'It's more fun to learn history.' Students described feeling 'almost there' and immersed. The game had direct repercussions on classroom behavior: 'I tend to listen more when it's more interesting.' 54% had already played the game and felt a home-school connection.

game_design_elements: Historical characters and their actions
Cinematic sequences and video clips
Screenshots and in-game images
Historical settings (buildings, places, monuments)
Historical events depicted in gameplay
Immersive visual fidelity and realistic reconstruction
Narrative storylines set in historical periods
technological_platforms: Classroom screen/projector for displaying game content
instructional_strategies: Teacher-mediated extraction and presentation of game content (not direct student gameplay)
Using game clips, cinematics, and screenshots as visual support alongside lectures (T1 approach)
Dialectic and investigative inquiry: comparing game content with documentary sources to foster historical thinking (T2-T4 approach)
Applying the 5W+H questions (who, what, when, where, why, how) to game scenarios
Triangulation exercises: comparing game depictions with other secondary sources to corroborate or refute information
Using game elements in assessment exams
Splitting class screen into two parts to compare course content with game extracts
Group work combined with lectures and game-based content
rq3.content_integration: Teachers selected specific game content (characters, events, buildings, scenes) from Assassin's Creed that aligned with the Quebec Education Program (QEP) history curriculum. The game was used as a form of profane rhetoric / secondary historical source. Content was organized and presented in various forms (clips, screenshots, cinematics) rather than having students play the game directly. Teachers contextualized historical scenarios from the game (e.g., the Storming of the Bastille, the American Revolution, Benjamin Franklin, Samuel Adams) and used them to teach historiographical thinking competencies such as comparing sources, identifying anachronisms, and distinguishing fact from fiction.

implementation_barriers: Game is rated 'mature' (17+) so students younger than 17 were not allowed to play it on school premises
Social acceptability concerns: the game's stated goal involves assassination
Students sometimes confused between actual history and the game's virtual version
Polychrony and historical inaccuracies/anachronisms in the game
T1's illustration-only approach was significantly less effective, showing that teacher skill/approach matters greatly
Controversy around video games in education; public debate about merits of Assassin's Creed series
Risk of the game taking up too much class time (60% of recommending students suggested only occasional use)
9% of students did not appreciate the game being used in class at all
methodology_limitations: Exploratory study - not in a position to formulate specific recommendations
Students did not directly play the game in class, so games-based learning theories cannot be applied in the traditional sense
Self-reported learning outcomes (no pre-post achievement tests)
Sample limited to two Quebec schools and four teachers
Almost all reported learning was declarative knowledge; deeper learning not measured
Gender imbalance in game appreciation (boys significantly more positive)
Cultural specificity: study conducted in Quebec with Quebec-specific curriculum (QEP)
negative_effects: Students sometimes confused between actual history and the game's virtual version
Gender disparity: girls significantly less engaged with and appreciative of the game content
When teacher used only illustration approach (T1), educational impact was significantly lower and less appreciated
Game content contains historical inaccuracies and polychrony that could mislead students without proper teacher guidance
mitigation_strategies: Teacher acts as essential guide to point students in the right direction and help them assess quality of secondary sources
Using dialectic/investigative inquiry approach rather than mere illustration (T2-T4 model)
Comparing game content with other historical sources (triangulation) to develop critical thinking
Having students apply historiographical thinking to identify inaccuracies and anachronisms
Using game content selectively rather than having students play directly (addresses age-rating barrier)
Recommending occasional rather than excessive use to avoid taking too much class time

domain1.q1_evidence: The study clearly describes participants: 329 high school students and 4 teachers at two Quebec schools. Inclusion criteria are implicit (students in classes where teachers used Assassin's Creed content). 81% response rate (n=269) on questionnaires is well documented. Demographics reported (age, gender distribution).
domain1.q2_evidence: Convenience sample of only two schools and four teachers in Quebec who already used Assassin's Creed. Not representative of broader population. The study acknowledges this is exploratory. Gender imbalance in game appreciation noted but not controlled for in main analyses.

domain2.q3_evidence: Data collected via anonymous online questionnaires (Likert and open responses), individual and group interviews (transcribed and anonymized), and videotaped classroom observations. SPSS 22 used for quantitative analysis. Qualitative content analysis used semi-open coding system (L'Ecuyer 1990; Miles & Huberman 2003). However, no validated instrument is described; the questionnaire appears to be researcher-developed without reported reliability/validity testing.
domain2.q4_evidence: Mixed methods combining descriptive/inferential statistics (ANOVA) with thematic content analysis. Statistical results are reported with F-values and p-values. However, learning outcomes are entirely self-reported by students (no objective achievement measures). The five learning categories emerged from content analysis of open responses but the coding process reliability (e.g., inter-rater agreement) is not reported.

domain3.q5_evidence: Findings are interpreted consistently with the data presented. The cross-teacher comparison is well-grounded in observed differences. The authors appropriately note that GBL theories cannot be fully applied since students did not play the game. Conclusions about the importance of teaching practices are well-supported by the ANOVA results comparing teacher approaches.
domain3.q6_evidence: The authors acknowledge the exploratory nature of the study and state they are 'not in a position to formulate specific recommendations.' They note the key limitation that students did not play the game directly. However, several limitations are not explicitly discussed: lack of validated instruments, absence of objective learning measures, limited generalizability of a two-school Quebec sample, and potential self-selection bias among teachers who already chose to use the game.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: This is a well-designed exploratory mixed-methods study that provides rich qualitative and quantitative data on the use of Assassin's Creed content in history teaching. Strengths include multi-source data collection (questionnaires, interviews, observations), a useful cross-teacher comparison, and transparent reporting of statistical results. However, moderate concerns arise from: (1) convenience sampling limited to two schools; (2) researcher-developed instruments without reported validity/reliability; (3) entirely self-reported learning outcomes with no objective achievement measures; (4) limited discussion of several methodological limitations. The study is appropriate for its stated exploratory aims but should be interpreted with caution regarding generalizability and the strength of learning outcome claims.

pdf_filename: The Architectural Jewels of Lublin Game as a Tool for Collaborative Interactive Learning of History.pdf

bibliographic.title: The "Architectural Jewels of Lublin" Game as a Tool for Collaborative Interactive Learning of History
bibliographic.venue: Teaching and Learning in a Digital World, Advances in Intelligent Systems and Computing

study_characteristics.sample_description: Two groups of 12 K14 pupils each from the Lublin province in Poland: one group of permanent residents of Lublin and one group living outside Lublin. Each participant was randomly selected from a different school in Lublin and the region.
study_characteristics.study_design: Survey-based descriptive study with game design presentation
study_characteristics.game_type: Technology-enhanced board game with 3D printed models, RFID sensing, and palmtop software
study_characteristics.aim: To assess the level of knowledge of K14 pupils about architectural monuments of Lublin, and to present a gamified board game designed to improve collaborative interactive learning of local history through 3D models of architectural monuments

eligibility.concerns: The study primarily presents a knowledge survey and a game design/description rather than an empirical evaluation of the game's educational effectiveness. No pre-post testing of the game itself was conducted; the survey establishes baseline knowledge levels, and the game is presented as a proposed solution. The effectiveness study is listed as future work.

rq1.conceptualization: Gamification is implicitly conceptualized as the use of competition, point scoring, prizes, and structured game rules (turn-based cycles) within an educational board game context to transmit strictly defined historical content. The authors state the game 'realises the idea of gamification, which assumes that in addition to the competition phase, winning points and prizes by participants, it also allows the transmission of strictly defined content.'
theoretical_frameworks: Gamification as competition and point-scoring mechanism

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Relative knowledge level (k) measured as ratio of absolute knowledge index (K) to maximum possible (Kmax=42). Average relative knowledge for all pupils: 23.1% (median 26.2%, SD 13.2%, range 0-50%). For pupils from outside Lublin: average 20.2% (median 20.2%, SD 13.7%, range 0-40.5%). Self-esteem of knowledge on 1-4 scale: overall mean 1.96, outside Lublin 1.41, Lublin residents 2.50.
rq2.statistical_results: Hypothesis H1 confirmed: average knowledge level of K14 pupils about Lublin architectural monuments is very low (around 20-23%). Hypothesis H2 confirmed: knowledge levels do not substantially differ between Lublin residents and non-residents. No student exceeded the 50% threshold.
rq2.comparative_methodology: Comparison between two groups (Lublin residents vs. non-residents, 12 pupils each) on the same knowledge test using weighted scores across 7 monuments and 3 question types (name, time period, architectural style). Descriptive statistics (mean, median, min, max, standard deviation) and histograms were used.
rq2.key_outcomes: K14 pupils have very low knowledge of Lublin's architectural monuments and their history, confirming the need for the educational game. The game itself was not empirically tested for learning effectiveness in this study; this is listed as future work.

game_design_elements: Points for correct model placement on the board
Points for correct answers to questions
Competition between two players (turn-based)
Escalating point values for incorrectly placed models returned to the bank
Time limits for actions (placement and answers)
Question takeover mechanic (opponent can answer Question 2)
LED feedback (green for correct placement, red for incorrect)
Sound messages via loudspeakers
Visual feedback on palmtop display (questions, scores, historical info)
Win condition based on accumulated points
technological_platforms: Physical board game (125x142 cm city plan)
RFID readers for automatic model identification and placement verification
Arduino boards for controlling RFID readers and RGB LEDs
Palmtop computer with game control software
instructional_strategies: Collaborative interactive learning through physical manipulation of 3D models
Knowledge assessment through quiz questions about monument names, time periods, and architectural styles
Competitive turn-based gameplay to motivate engagement
Historical content delivery integrated into game flow (historical information displayed after each monument)
Tangible learning with physical 3D models of real architectural monuments
Spatial learning through placing models on a city map
rq3.content_integration: Historical content about Lublin's architectural monuments is integrated directly into game mechanics: players must identify monuments by name, know their historical time period, answer questions about the city's history, and correctly locate them on a city map. The game covers 7 key monuments selected by experts, each associated with questions about name (P1), time period (P2), and architectural style (P3). After each turn, historical information about the monument is displayed on the palmtop screen.

implementation_barriers: Low baseline historical knowledge among target audience (K14 youth) as demonstrated by the survey
Complex technical infrastructure required (RFID, Arduino, 3D printing, real-time software, over 130m of wiring)
Game currently limited to 2 players at a time
Physical size and complexity of the board (125x142 cm) limits portability
3D models lack realistic colors (monochrome prints)
methodology_limitations: Small sample size (24 pupils total, 12 per group) for the knowledge survey
No empirical evaluation of the game's actual educational effectiveness was conducted
Effectiveness study described only as future work (survey-gameplay-survey experiment planned)
Convenience sampling (pupils visiting the university)
No control group for game-based learning comparison
Survey only covers pupils from Lublin province, limiting generalizability
mitigation_strategies: Future work planned: study of learning effectiveness via pre-post survey design (survey-gameplay-survey)
Future work planned: increasing number of players from 2 to 4 for enhanced collaboration
Future work planned: improving 3D model realism with realistic colors
Future work planned: adaptive algorithms for point calculation based on game progress
Future work planned: ergonomics study of the game control interface

domain1.q1_evidence: The study clearly defines the target population (K14 pupils from Lublin province), divided into two explicit groups (Lublin residents and non-residents). The knowledge assessment criteria are well-defined with a formal mathematical framework (weighted knowledge index K and relative knowledge k).
domain1.q2_evidence: The sample is very small (24 pupils total, 12 per group) and was drawn from pupils visiting the Lublin University of Technology, which is a convenience sample. Each pupil was from a different school, but selection method beyond 'randomly selected' is not described. This limits representativeness and generalizability.

domain2.q3_evidence: The knowledge assessment questionnaire is clearly structured with 7 monuments x 3 questions each, with defined weighted scoring. Questions were designed by experts who selected the monuments and assigned difficulty weights. The use of 3D models as visual aids for identification is a reasonable approach.
domain2.q4_evidence: Basic descriptive statistics (mean, median, min, max, standard deviation) and histograms are presented. However, no inferential statistics or formal hypothesis testing was conducted to support the hypotheses. The verification of H1 and H2 relies only on descriptive comparison of means and visual inspection of distributions.

domain3.q5_evidence: The interpretation that K14 pupils have low knowledge of Lublin's architectural monuments is consistent with the data (averages around 20-23%, no student exceeding 50%). The authors appropriately distinguish between the survey findings and the game presentation, and correctly identify the game effectiveness study as future work.
domain3.q6_evidence: The authors acknowledge that the game effectiveness study is future work and outline planned improvements. However, they do not explicitly discuss the limitations of the knowledge survey (small sample size, convenience sampling, lack of inferential statistics). The limitations of the game design (2-player limit, lack of realistic colors, etc.) are acknowledged as areas for future development.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study has high risk of bias primarily due to: (1) very small convenience sample of 24 pupils for the knowledge survey, (2) lack of inferential statistical analysis to support hypothesis verification, (3) no empirical evaluation of the game's educational effectiveness (only the game design is presented; effectiveness testing is listed as future work), and (4) limited discussion of methodological limitations. The study is primarily a design paper with a preliminary needs assessment rather than an empirical evaluation of gamification effectiveness.

pdf_filename: The Development and Evaluation of an Online Educational Game Integrated with Real Person-NPC mechanism for History Learning.pdf

bibliographic.title: The Development and Evaluation of an Online Educational Game Integrated with Real Person-NPC mechanism for History Learning
bibliographic.venue: Proceedings of the 29th International Conference on Computers in Education (ICCE 2021), Asia-Pacific Society for Computers in Education
bibliographic.publisher: Asia-Pacific Society for Computers in Education

study_characteristics.sample_description: 12 adults in Taiwan (9 males, 3 females), grouped with three members in each group (4 groups total)
study_characteristics.study_design: pre_post
study_characteristics.aim: To develop an online educational game integrating real person-NPC mechanism and simulated environment for military monument history learning, and to evaluate learners' learning performance and flow state through preliminary empirical research

eligibility.concerns: Very small sample size (n=12); described as 'preliminary empirical research'; short 3-page conference paper with limited methodological detail; participants described as 'adults' without specifying education level; no control group

rq1.conceptualization: The study conceptualizes game-based learning through an online educational game integrating real person-NPC (Non-Player Character) mechanisms within situated learning. A real person-NPC is defined as 'a real person as NPC and participating in online in-game role-playing' that 'can provide players with more realistic verbal dialogues and behavioral interactions.' This mechanism is conceived as a 'dynamic scaffold, providing players with real-time realistic feedback and guidance to facilitate their reflective and planning thinking, as well as to diagnose and monitor learners' progress at any time.' The approach draws on situated learning theory, emphasizing context, authenticity, and learning transfer through role-play based interactions.
theoretical_frameworks: Flow theory (as operationalized via Hou & Chou, 2012 flow scale)

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Learning performance measured via pre-test and post-test (18 questions across 4 major tasks covering knowledge of military base history, base structure, geography, and strategic planning). Flow state measured via Kiili's flow scale (2006, translated/revised by Hou & Chou, 2012) with two dimensions (flow antecedent and flow experience) on a five-point Likert scale (Cronbach's alpha = 0.931).
rq2.statistical_results: Wilcoxon signed rank test for learning performance: pre-test M=5.50, SD=3.63; post-test M=9.00, SD=3.54; Z=-2.77, p=.006 (p<.01). Overall flow score M=4.23, SD=0.49. Flow antecedents M=4.18, SD=0.58 (Challenge M=4.17, SD=0.91; Goal M=4.25, SD=0.54; Feedback M=3.88, SD=0.88; Control M=4.42, SD=0.51; Playability M=4.17, SD=0.89). Flow experience M=4.28, SD=0.46 (Concentration M=4.50, SD=0.55; Time distortion M=4.33, SD=0.49; Autotelic experience M=4.54, SD=0.53; Loss of self-consciousness M=3.29, SD=1.05).
rq2.comparative_methodology: Single-group pre-test/post-test design using Wilcoxon signed rank test (non-parametric) to compare learning performance before and after game-based intervention. No control group.
rq2.key_outcomes: Significant improvement in learners' knowledge of history and capabilities of strategic planning after playing the game (pre-test M=5.50 to post-test M=9.00, Z=-2.77, p=.006). The authors state: 'learners' knowledge of history and the capabilities of strategic planning improved through this game.'
rq2.engagement_results: High flow state reported: overall flow M=4.23 (above median of 3 on 5-point scale). Highest sub-dimension scores: Autotelic experience M=4.54, Concentration M=4.50, Control M=4.42. Lowest: Loss of self-consciousness M=3.29, Feedback M=3.88. The authors conclude: 'learners were deeply involved in the game.'

game_design_elements: Real person-NPC mechanism (real persons role-playing as NPCs: a 'commander' and a 'soldier')
Role-playing (learners play the role of military officers)
Task-based missions (three tasks related to military base investigation)
Simulated environment (virtual military base in northern Taiwan)
Scaffolding (real person-NPCs provide clues and guidance based on learner needs)
Limited help opportunities (limited chances to call real person-NPCs for assistance)
Exploration and discovery (visiting military sites, observing appearance, topography, clues)
Strategic planning tasks (planning facility use, attack positions, patrol routes)
Collaborative gameplay (groups of three)
technological_platforms: Gather Town (gather.com) - online virtual world platform
Personal computers with microphones for voice communication
instructional_strategies: Situated learning with context and authenticity
Role-play based situated learning (learners as military officers)
Real person-NPC as dynamic scaffolding with real-time feedback
Task-based learning (three investigation tasks)
Collaborative group learning (groups of three)
Exploration-based learning (investigating virtual military sites)
Strategic planning exercises (facility planning, attack positions, patrol routes)
rq3.content_integration: Historical content about a real military base in northern Taiwan was integrated into the game environment. Learners investigated an abandoned virtual military base, visiting various military sites to learn about the base's establishment background, structure, and geography. Historical knowledge was embedded in the environment through visual clues (appearance, topography, artifacts left behind) that learners needed to observe and interpret. The three tasks required learners to synthesize historical knowledge with strategic planning, including planning further use of facilities, attack positions, and patrol routes.

implementation_barriers: Requires trained researchers to play real person-NPC roles (a 'commander' and a 'soldier'), limiting scalability
Beta version of the game, indicating incomplete development
Reliance on Gather Town platform for game development (platform dependency)
Need for personal computers and microphones for each group
methodology_limitations: Very small sample size (n=12) limiting statistical power and generalizability
No control group for comparison
Single-group pre-post design without randomization
Preliminary/pilot study nature acknowledged by authors
Short conference paper format (3 pages) with limited methodological detail
Participants described only as 'adults' without specifying education level or recruitment criteria
No effect size reported
No information about test validity or reliability for the learning performance test
Self-reported flow measure (potential social desirability bias)
negative_effects: Loss of self-consciousness sub-dimension scored lowest among flow dimensions (M=3.29, SD=1.05), suggesting learners maintained self-awareness rather than becoming fully immersed
Feedback sub-dimension scored relatively low (M=3.88, SD=0.88), suggesting room for improvement in how feedback was delivered
mitigation_strategies: Future study proposed to employ quasi-experimental design with control group (e.g., teaching approach, role-playing method)
Plans to continue exploring learners' geographic awareness, historical empathy, and learning motivation in future research

domain1.q1_evidence: No selection criteria are described for the 12 participants. The paper states only: 'Participants in this study were 12 adults in Taiwan (9 males, 3 females).' No information is provided about how they were recruited, whether they were students, or any inclusion/exclusion criteria. Convenience sampling is implied.
domain1.q2_evidence: Very small sample of 12 adults from Taiwan with no description of the target population. Only basic demographic information given (9 males, 3 females). No information about age, education level, prior gaming experience, or history knowledge. The sample cannot be assessed for representativeness.

domain2.q3_evidence: The flow questionnaire is based on Kiili's flow scale (2006), translated and revised by Hou and Chou (2012), with reported Cronbach's alpha of 0.931 indicating high internal consistency. However, the learning performance test (18 questions across 4 tasks) has no reported validity or reliability information. The paper states: 'The test was designed referring to the case of investigating the virtual military base' but provides no psychometric properties.
domain2.q4_evidence: The Wilcoxon signed rank test is an appropriate non-parametric test for the small sample size and paired design. However, no effect size is reported, no confidence intervals are provided, and descriptive statistics for the flow scale are limited to means and standard deviations without inferential testing against the median. The analysis is basic but not inappropriate for a preliminary study.

domain3.q5_evidence: The authors' interpretations are generally consistent with the statistical results presented. The significant Wilcoxon test result supports the claim of improved learning performance, and the flow scores above the median support the claim of high engagement. The authors appropriately describe the study as 'preliminary empirical research' and 'preliminary findings.'
domain3.q6_evidence: There is no explicit limitations section. The conclusion briefly mentions plans for future quasi-experimental designs with control groups, implicitly acknowledging the current design's weakness, but does not explicitly discuss limitations such as the very small sample size, lack of control group, or generalizability concerns.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study has high overall risk of bias primarily due to the very small sample size (n=12) with no selection criteria described, no control group, and no reported validity/reliability for the learning performance instrument. It is a preliminary pilot study presented as a short conference paper (3 pages), which inherently limits methodological detail. The flow instrument has good reliability (alpha=0.931), and the non-parametric statistical test is appropriate for the design, but the absence of effect sizes, the lack of an explicit limitations discussion, and the inability to establish causality without a control group all contribute to high overall risk of bias.

pdf_filename: The Development of a Role-Playing Game for History Instruction and the Evaluation of Flow State and Learning Performance.pdf

bibliographic.title: The Development of a Role-Playing Game for History Instruction and the Evaluation of Flow State and Learning Performance
bibliographic.venue: Work-in-Progress Poster Proceedings of the 21st International Conference on Computers in Education (ICCE 2013), Asia-Pacific Society for Computers in Education
bibliographic.publisher: Asia-Pacific Society for Computers in Education

study_characteristics.sample_description: 40 university students (20 males and 20 females) from a university in northern Taiwan
study_characteristics.study_design: pre_post
study_characteristics.aim: To develop a historical educational role-playing game (Romance at Dadaocheng) combining a love story with problem-solving, and to evaluate learners' flow state and learning effectiveness through pre-and post-tests

eligibility.concerns: Short 3-page conference poster paper with limited methodological detail; no control group; single-group pre-post design only; no explicit selection criteria for participants

rq1.conceptualization: The study conceptualizes game-based learning through a custom-developed role-playing game (RPG) for history instruction. The approach combines situated learning with role-playing instructional methods. The game is framed as providing 'opportunities for repeated practices and trials under a challenging situation' in contrast to traditional history instruction where 'instructional content of history is mostly memorized declarative knowledge.' The instructional game 'plans strategies, builds up hypotheses about the questions, and allows learners to try and solve problems continuously' to achieve 'higher-level thinking.' The study integrates authentic geographical and historical content into the game narrative as problem-solving hints, emphasizing situated cognition where learners interact with the historical environment through gameplay.
theoretical_frameworks: Situated learning / Situated cognition (Brown, Collins, & Duguid, 1989)
Flow scale (Hou & Chou, 2012 Chinese adaptation of Kiili's scale)

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Learning performance measured via pre-test and post-test with 20 items covering history knowledge and geographical location knowledge related to Dadaocheng. Questions designed by a geographical expert. Flow state measured via Kiili's (2006) flow scale (Chinese edition translated and revised by Hou & Chou, 2012) with 23 items on a five-point Likert scale across two dimensions: flow antecedents and flow experience (Cronbach's alpha = 0.92).
rq2.statistical_results: Paired-samples t test results: History score: post-test M=12.58, SD=1.32; pre-test M=6.55, SD=2.28; t=15.52, p=.000 (p<0.001). Geography score: post-test M=2.58, SD=1.11; pre-test M=1.75, SD=1.03; t=4.62, p=.000 (p<0.001). Flow questionnaire results: Overall flow antecedents M=4.06, SD=0.62; challenge-skills balance M=3.96, SD=0.87; goals of an activity M=4.11, SD=0.75; unambiguous feedback M=3.91, SD=0.74; control M=4.18, SD=0.78; action-awareness merging M=4.13, SD=0.76. Overall flow experience M=3.82, SD=0.64; concentration M=3.85, SD=0.75; transformation of time M=3.68, SD=0.79; autotelic experience M=3.66, SD=0.77; loss of self-consciousness M=4.24, SD=0.80.
rq2.comparative_methodology: Single-group pre-test/post-test design using paired-samples t test to compare learning performance before and after the game-based intervention. No control group.
rq2.key_outcomes: Significant improvement in both history knowledge (pre-test M=6.55 to post-test M=12.58, t=15.52, p<.001) and geographical location knowledge (pre-test M=1.75 to post-test M=2.58, t=4.62, p<.001) after game-based learning. The authors state: 'after game-based learning, students' knowledge of history (t=15.52, p=.000) and knowledge related to geographical location (t=4.62, p=.000) were significantly improved.'
rq2.engagement_results: All flow dimensions scored above the median of 3.00 on the 5-point Likert scale. Flow antecedents (M=4.06) and flow experience (M=3.82) both above median. Four dimensions scored above 4.00: flow antecedents overall, goals of an activity, control, action-awareness merging, and loss of self-consciousness. The highest scoring dimension was loss of self-consciousness (M=4.24, SD=0.80). The authors conclude: 'this game has the elements to arouse learner's flow experience as a whole' and 'the content of this game can arouse learners' engagement to a certain degree.'

game_design_elements: Role-playing (learners become the leading character in the game)
Narrative/storyline (romantic love story combined with mystery plot - resolving the mystery of the heroine's birth)
Problem-solving tasks (historical knowledge used as problem-solving hints)
Exploration mechanics (survey of hints and adventure in authentic geographical space)
Character interaction and dialogue (NPC interactions provide historical information and plot hints)
Feedback system (choosing right answers to get right feedback and advance the plot)
Fighting/combat tasks
Authentic scene design (buildings painted from photos of real locations with real proportions and positions)
technological_platforms: Custom-developed digital RPG (Romance at Dadaocheng, developed by NTUST MEG research team)
instructional_strategies: Situated learning / Situated cognition (game story and space based on authentic photos, historical backgrounds, and real geographical environment)
Role-playing instructional method (learners become the leading character to arouse empathy)
Problem-based learning (learners solve mysteries using historical knowledge as clues)
Authentic context (real geographical space of Dadaocheng used as game scene with real proportions and positions)
Integration of historical content into game narrative (historical backgrounds embedded in character interaction and plot hints)
rq3.content_integration: Historical content about Taiwan's Dadaocheng monument was deeply integrated into the game mechanics. All building scenes were painted from authentic photos of real locations with real geographical proportions and positions. Historical backgrounds and corresponding geographical scenes were embedded in character interactions and plot hints, requiring learners to judge the accuracy of history and geography knowledge during the searching process. The game used authentic geographical space as the scene and adopted historical knowledge as problem-solving hints in the game mechanism. Learners had to choose the right answer about historical/geographical facts to receive correct feedback and advance the plot, thereby strengthening their cognitive processes.

implementation_barriers: Development of custom RPG with authentic scene design requires significant resources (painting all building scenes from real photos with correct proportions)
Game content specific to one historical location (Dadaocheng), limiting transferability to other topics
methodology_limitations: No control group for comparison (single-group pre-post design)
Short conference poster paper format (3 pages) with limited methodological detail
Small sample size acknowledged by authors: 'a larger sample size in the experiment is suggested'
No effect sizes reported
No information about test validity or reliability for the learning performance test (20 items)
Self-reported flow measure (potential response bias)
Same questions used for pre-test and post-test (potential testing/practice effect)
No randomization or blinding
No analysis of potential confounding variables (e.g., prior knowledge, gaming experience)
negative_effects: Transformation of time scored lowest among flow experience dimensions (M=3.68, SD=0.79), suggesting players may have been somewhat aware of time passing rather than fully immersed
Autotelic experience also scored relatively low (M=3.66, SD=0.77), suggesting the intrinsically rewarding nature of the game experience could be improved

The authors note that high loss of self-consciousness may result from cognitive resource depletion: 'while playing the game, learners need to understand the hints provided by the stories which will deplete their cognitive resources (Killi, 2006)'
mitigation_strategies: Authors suggest future studies 'analyze learners' behavioral patterns in a game'
Authors suggest future studies 'explore learner's technology acceptance'
Authors recommend 'a larger sample size in the experiment is suggested to explore the effect of this game on learning completely'

domain1.q1_evidence: No selection criteria are described for participants. The paper states only: 'There were 40 participants (including 20 males and 20 females), coming from a university in northern Taiwan, in this study.' No information on recruitment method, inclusion/exclusion criteria, or how participants were selected. Convenience sampling is implied.
domain1.q2_evidence: The sample of 40 university students from northern Taiwan is described with only gender information (20 males, 20 females). No information about age, year of study, major, prior gaming experience, or prior history knowledge. The target population is not explicitly defined, making representativeness assessment difficult. The balanced gender ratio (50/50) is a positive aspect but insufficient alone.

domain2.q3_evidence: The flow questionnaire is based on Kiili's (2006) flow scale, translated and revised by Hou and Chou (2012), with reported Cronbach's alpha of 0.92 indicating good internal consistency. However, the learning performance test (20 items about history and geography of Dadaocheng) was described only as being 'set by a geographical expert' with no reported validity or reliability information. No psychometric properties are provided for the knowledge test.
domain2.q4_evidence: Paired-samples t tests are an appropriate parametric test for pre-post comparisons with n=40. However, no effect sizes are reported, no confidence intervals are provided, no assumption checks (e.g., normality) are described, and the same test was used for both pre and post (potential practice effect not addressed). Descriptive statistics for flow are reported but without inferential comparison to the median. The analysis is basic but not inappropriate for a preliminary conference paper.

domain3.q5_evidence: The authors' interpretations are consistent with the reported results. The significant t-test results support the claim of improved learning, and the flow scores above the median support the engagement claims. The authors appropriately characterize their evaluation as 'preliminary': 'Through a preliminarily empirical evaluation, the results indicated that this game is beneficial to students' history and geography learning.' The interpretation of loss of self-consciousness as possibly related to cognitive resource depletion is a reasonable theoretical interpretation.
domain3.q6_evidence: There is no explicit limitations section. The conclusion briefly acknowledges the need for a larger sample size ('a larger sample size in the experiment is suggested to explore the effect of this game on learning completely') and suggests future directions (behavioral pattern analysis, technology acceptance), implicitly acknowledging some weaknesses. However, key limitations such as the lack of a control group, potential practice effects from same-test pre-post design, and absence of test validation are not discussed.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study has high overall risk of bias primarily due to: (1) no participant selection criteria described, (2) single-group pre-post design with no control group, making it impossible to attribute learning gains solely to the game intervention, (3) the same test used for pre-test and post-test creating potential practice/testing effects, (4) no reported validity or reliability for the learning performance instrument, (5) no effect sizes reported, and (6) very limited discussion of limitations. The flow instrument has acceptable reliability (alpha=0.92) and the statistical tests are appropriate, but the overall design weaknesses and the short conference paper format (3 pages) with minimal methodological detail contribute to high overall risk of bias.

pdf_filename: The Development of History Educational Game as a Revision Tool for Malaysia School Education.pdf

bibliographic.title: The Development of History Educational Game as a Revision Tool for Malaysia School Education
bibliographic.venue: International Visual Informatics Conference (IVIC 2011), Part II, LNCS 7067

study_characteristics.sample_description: A sample of twenty students from various gender selected to participate in the PUEU survey after playing the game prototype; the game targets Form 3 students in Malaysia Secondary School
study_characteristics.study_design: descriptive
study_characteristics.game_name: History of Japanese Occupation in Malaya (educational game prototype)
study_characteristics.aim: To develop an educational computer game prototype as a revision tool for history subject in Malaysia secondary school, dedicated to the topic of Japanese invasion on Malaya (Form 3 history syllabus of SMA), and to test its functionality and perceived usefulness/ease of use

eligibility.concerns: This is primarily a design/development paper with only a descriptive usability evaluation (PUEU survey with 20 students). There is no experimental or quasi-experimental design, no pre-post test, and no control group. The evaluation focuses on perceived usefulness and ease of use rather than learning outcomes. The study is more of a prototype development report than an effectiveness study.

rq1.explicit_definition: An educational game, one designed for learning, is a subset of both play and fun. It is a melding of educational content, learning principles, and computer games [13]. An educational game is combining the element of joy and learns in a playable situation.
rq1.conceptualization: The study conceptualizes educational games as a revision tool for history learning. The game is framed as a medium to overcome the 'boring phenomenon' in history education and to integrate fun into learning. The authors describe their game as a first-person perspective educational game where students walk in the game room, encounter enemies (Japanese army characters), and must answer multiple-choice history questions to shoot the enemies. The game merges entertainment (first-person shooter mechanics) with educational content (history quiz questions about Japanese invasion of Malaya). The conceptual approach positions the game as a supplementary revision tool for home use rather than a replacement for classroom instruction, noting 'The prototype can be used as teaching aid in class or as a revision tool at home.'
theoretical_frameworks: Multimedia Design and Planning Pyramid (MUDPY) model (Sharda, 2004)

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Perceived Usefulness and Ease of Use (PUEU) test consisting of 12 questions on a 7-point Likert scale (unlikely to likely). Questions 1-6 measured perceived usefulness; questions 7-12 measured ease of use. Descriptive statistics (mean, standard error, median, mode) computed using Microsoft Excel.
rq2.statistical_results: Perceived Usefulness (7-point scale): Question 1 Mean=6.25, SE=0.25, Median=7, Mode=7; Question 2 Mean=5.9, SE=0.26, Median=6, Mode=7; Question 3 Mean=5.31, SE=0.41, Median=6, Mode=6; Question 4 Mean=5.75, SE=0.28, Median=6, Mode=7; Question 5 Mean=5.8, SE=0.32, Median=6.5, Mode=7; Question 6 Mean=6.31, SE=0.26, Median=7, Mode=7. Ease of Use: Question 7 Mean=5.15, SE=0.43, Median=5, Mode=7; Question 8 Mean=4.57, SE=0.53, Median=6, Mode=7; Question 9 Mean=5.85, SE=0.34, Median=6, Mode=7; Question 10 Mean=5.63, SE=0.32, Median=6, Mode=7; Question 11 Mean=5.2, SE=0.40, Median=6, Mode=6; Question 12 Mean=5.89, SE=0.43, Median=7, Mode=7.
rq2.comparative_methodology: No comparative methodology; single-group descriptive survey design with no control group or pre-post comparison. Only a post-use PUEU questionnaire was administered.
rq2.key_outcomes: The average score from the prototype is around 4.5 to 6.3 on a 7-point scale. The authors state: 'From the result we can concluded that the average score from the prototype is around 4.5 to 6.3. This is because the users are unfamiliar with the game environment and new to the system. The median of every question is around five to seven.' The highest rated item was Question 6 (perceived usefulness, M=6.31) and the lowest was Question 8 (ease of use, M=4.57). From user feedback, 'the most positive aspect is about the effectiveness of the game to help the users to revise the history subject. They can revise the subject quickly and much more fun compare to the conventional methods.'
rq2.engagement_results: From qualitative feedback: 'the most positive aspect is about the effectiveness of the game to help the users to revise the history subject. They can revise the subject quickly and much more fun compare to the conventional methods.' However, 'the most negative aspect is the violent and the use of gun in the game and it's not really appreciated by the users.' The perceived usefulness scores (M range 5.31-6.31) were generally higher than ease of use scores (M range 4.57-5.89), suggesting the game was seen as useful but somewhat difficult to use.

game_design_elements: First-person perspective gameplay
Shooting/combat mechanics (player shoots enemies by answering quiz questions)
Multiple-choice quiz questions (pop-up questions when encountering enemies)
Scoring system (bonus mark for correct first answer, normal score for correct second try, health deduction for wrong answers)
Health system (health value decreases with wrong answers; game over at zero)
Progressive levels (10 enemies/questions to complete the game)
Two-chance retry mechanic (player gets two attempts per question)
Final score display at end of game
Character design (antagonist: Japanese army; protagonist: Malay army)
Narrative/storyline (Japanese invasion of Malaya theme)
Linear navigation structure
instructional_strategies: Game-based revision/review of history content
Multiple-choice question-answer assessment embedded in gameplay
Immediate feedback through scoring (bonus marks for correct answers, health deduction for wrong answers)
Content derived from Form 3 history syllabus (KBSM) on Japanese invasion of Malaya
Multimedia Design and Planning Pyramid (MUDPY) model for development process
Three-phase development cycle: Plan, Design, Produce
Requirements gathering through e-brainstorming, teacher interviews, and classroom observation
Integration of educational content with entertainment (first-person shooter genre)
rq3.content_integration: Historical content about the Japanese invasion of Malaya was integrated into the game as multiple-choice quiz questions. The educational objectives were: (1) State the reasons for Japan's expanding power, (2) Describe the arrival of the Japanese to Malaya, and (3) List the success factors of Japan dominates Malaya. Players navigate through a jungle-themed environment (reflecting the wartime setting) and encounter enemy characters (Japanese army). To shoot enemies, players must correctly answer history questions via pop-up quiz interfaces. The antagonist character was pictured as Japanese army who invaded Malaya while the protagonist character was pictured as Malay army that secured the Malaya. Content was gathered through Internet sources and history textbooks, then integrated using Game Maker 8.0.

implementation_barriers: Students were unfamiliar with the game environment and new to the system, leading to moderate scores
Teachers reported lack of teaching aids and difficulty finding good multimedia resources for history class
Violence in the game (use of guns) was the most negative aspect reported by users
Platform-specific requirements (Windows only, requires Intel Pentium 4, 1MB RAM, 500KB disk, CD-ROM)
methodology_limitations: Very small sample size (n=20) for the PUEU evaluation
No experimental or quasi-experimental design; only descriptive statistics
No learning outcome measurement (no pre-test/post-test for knowledge gains)
No control group or comparison condition
No inferential statistics performed (only means, standard errors, medians, modes)
No reliability or validity data reported for the PUEU instrument
No demographic details of participants beyond 'various gender'
Self-reported perceptions only; no objective learning metrics
Black box testing used for functionality but details not reported
Selection method for the 20 student participants not described
negative_effects: Violence and use of guns in the game were the most negative aspect identified by users: 'the most negative aspect is the violent and the use of gun in the game and it's not really appreciated by the users'
Ease of use scores were lower than usefulness scores, with Question 8 scoring lowest (M=4.57), suggesting usability issues
mitigation_strategies: Authors express confidence the game can contribute to history revision: 'With this feedback, we are confident that this game can make a contribution to help the student to do revision for history subject in school'
Requirements gathering phase included teacher interviews and classroom observations to align game with actual classroom needs
Two-chance retry mechanism provides scaffolding for incorrect answers rather than immediate punishment

domain1.q1_evidence: No selection criteria are described for the 20 participants in the PUEU evaluation. The paper states only: 'A sample of twenty students was selected from various gender to participate in this survey.' No information on how students were recruited, from which school, what age/form they were, or any inclusion/exclusion criteria. The game is designed for Form 3 students but there is no confirmation that participants were Form 3 students.
domain1.q2_evidence: The sample of 20 students is described with almost no demographic detail beyond 'various gender.' The target population is Form 3 secondary school students in Malaysia, but it is unclear whether the 20 participants belonged to this target group. The sample size of 20 is very small. No information about age, school, academic level, or prior gaming experience is provided, making representativeness impossible to assess.

domain2.q3_evidence: The PUEU (Perceived Usefulness and Ease of Use) questionnaire consists of 12 questions with a 7-point Likert scale. However, no source, validation, or reliability information is provided for this instrument. It is unclear whether this is based on the well-known Davis (1989) Technology Acceptance Model PUEU instrument or a custom tool. No Cronbach's alpha or other psychometric properties are reported. The black box testing for functionality is mentioned but no details are provided about test cases or results.
domain2.q4_evidence: Only descriptive statistics (mean, standard error, median, mode) were computed using Microsoft Excel. No inferential statistical analysis was conducted. No justification is given for the choice of descriptive-only analysis. The analysis is limited to reporting central tendency measures for each of the 12 questions individually, with no aggregate scores, no statistical tests, and no effect sizes. The authors' conclusion that scores of 4.5-6.3 on a 7-point scale indicate the game 'will help paced the history revision' is not statistically supported.

domain3.q5_evidence: The authors interpret the PUEU results as positive: 'From the result we can conclude that this game will help paced the history revision and the system was easy to use in the process.' However, some scores were moderate (e.g., Question 8 M=4.57 on a 7-point scale), and the authors themselves acknowledge 'the users are unfamiliar with the game environment and new to the system' as an explanation for lower scores. The claim that the game is effective for history revision is based only on perceived usefulness ratings, not on any actual learning outcome measurement, which represents an overreach in interpretation.
domain3.q6_evidence: The paper does not include a limitations section or explicitly discuss any methodological limitations. There is no acknowledgment of the small sample size, lack of experimental design, absence of learning outcome measures, or limitations of using only descriptive statistics. The conclusion makes broad claims without qualifying them: 'Using PUEU test, the result shows that this educational game has fulfilled the user requirement, easy to be use by the user and it is usefull to the student in learning.'

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study has high overall risk of bias due to multiple critical weaknesses: (1) no participant selection criteria described and minimal sample demographics, (2) very small sample size (n=20) with no justification, (3) no experimental design -- only a post-use descriptive survey with no pre-test, post-test, or control group, (4) no actual learning outcome measurement (only perceived usefulness/ease of use), (5) no validity or reliability data for the PUEU instrument, (6) only descriptive statistics with no inferential analysis, (7) overreaching conclusions about learning effectiveness based solely on usability perceptions, and (8) no discussion of limitations whatsoever. The paper is primarily a prototype development report with a minimal, methodologically weak evaluation component.

pdf_filename: The Effect of the Game-Based Learning Model on Student Engagement in History Learning.pdf

bibliographic.title: The Effect of the Game-Based Learning Model on Student Engagement in History Learning
bibliographic.venue: Paramita: Historical Studies Journal

study_characteristics.sample_description: 66 students in classes XI IPS 4 (control, 33 students) and XI IPS 1 (experimental, 33 students) at SMA Negeri 1 Gambiran, Banyuwangi Regency, East Java Province, Indonesia, during the even semester of the 2021-2022 Academic Year. Classes were selected through a homogeneity test based on average daily test scores of the Indonesian History subject.
study_characteristics.study_design: quasi_experimental
study_characteristics.aim: To examine the effect of the game-based learning model on student engagement in history learning

eligibility.concerns: The study uses Quizizz as a game-based learning platform for history education. While Quizizz is a gamified quiz platform rather than a full game, the authors frame it explicitly within the game-based learning (GBL) model, satisfying the gamification criterion. The dependent variable is student engagement (measured via questionnaire) rather than learning outcomes, but this is still relevant to gamification effectiveness research.

rq1.conceptualization: The study conceptualizes game-based learning (GBL) as a model that 'focuses on student engagement by fostering creativity and independence and increasing student interest and motivation' (citing Cheng & Su, 2011). The GBL model is described as having three stages: (1) Input stage - the teacher maps teaching content into game content and directs students to enter the game; (2) Process stage - the teacher describes game characteristics, attractiveness, and attention, links learning objectives to new skills, directs students to the game; (3) Output stage - the teacher provides feedback, conducts evaluations to assess results, monitors student performance and makes improvements. The model is seen as encouraging 'active learning by involving teachers and students in a game' and aims 'to improve teaching, learning, assessment, and evaluation.' Student engagement is conceptualized through three components: (1) behavioral engagement (effort, persistence, concentration, following norms), (2) emotional engagement (positive reactions to teachers, friends, academics), and (3) cognitive engagement (desire to be involved in learning, acquire knowledge, seek information, strategies for schoolwork).
theoretical_frameworks: Student engagement framework (Fredricks, Blumenfeld & Paris, 2004) - three components: cognitive, emotional, behavioral engagement
Student engagement components (Appleton et al., 2006) - academics, behavior, cognitive, psychological/emotional
Ching-Hsue & Chung-Ho (2012) - three stages of GBL: input, process, output
Newmann (1992) - engagement as participation and 'being there'
Vlachopulos & Makri (2017) - game-based learning model effectiveness

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Student engagement measured via a post-test-only questionnaire using a 4-point Likert scale (Strongly Agree=4, Agree=3, Disagree=2, Strongly Disagree=1) adopted from Sinulingga (2018). The instrument had 3 aspects: behavioral engagement, emotional engagement, and cognitive engagement. Instrument validity tested via Product Moment correlation (rhit > rtab at significance level 0.000); reliability tested via Cronbach's Alpha = 0.911 (very high reliability). One-way ANOVA and LSD follow-up test used for hypothesis testing.
rq2.statistical_results: One-way ANOVA: F(1,64) = 4.408, p = .040 < .05, Mean Square Between Groups = 87.515, Mean Square Within Groups = 19.853. LSD follow-up test results: Control Pre-test vs Control Post-test: Mean Difference (I-J) = -9.57576*, Std. Error = 1.18233, Sig. = .013; Control Pre-test vs Experimental Pre-test: Mean Difference = .12121, Std. Error = 1.18233, Sig. = .893; Control Pre-test vs Experimental Post-test: Mean Difference = -12.03030*, Std. Error = 1.18233, Sig. = .000; Experimental Pre-test vs Control Post-test: Mean Difference = -9.69697*, Std. Error = 1.18233, Sig. = .000; Experimental Pre-test vs Experimental Post-test: Mean Difference = -12.15152*, Std. Error = 1.18233, Sig. = .020. Normality test (Kolmogorov-Smirnov): control class post-questionnaire significance = 0.066 > 0.05 (normal); experimental class post-questionnaire significance = 0.200 > 0.05 (normal). Homogeneity test (Levene's Statistic): significance = 0.069; Levene's significance = 0.793 > 0.05. Ftable at df=65, alpha=0.05 is 3.989; Fcount (4.408) > Ftable (3.989).
rq2.comparative_methodology: Quasi-experimental design with a post-test-only non-equivalent control-group design. Experimental group (XI IPS 1, n=33) received game-based learning model assisted by Quizizz application; control group (XI IPS 4, n=33) received discovery learning model. Groups were selected based on homogeneity test of average daily test scores. Comparison via one-way ANOVA with LSD follow-up test at 5% significance level.
rq2.key_outcomes: The one-way ANOVA test showed a significant influence on student engagement when students were taught using the game-based learning model (F=4.408, p=0.040<0.05). The LSD follow-up test showed a mean difference (I-J) of 2.45455 between the experimental post-test and control post-test with a significance value of 0.069 > 0.05. The experimental group taught using the game-based learning model had better student engagement effect than the control group taught using the discovery learning model.
rq2.engagement_results: The experimental group (GBL with Quizizz) showed significantly higher student engagement than the control group (discovery learning). Several engagement indicators had highest averages: Statement 7 'I will arrive at school before the bell rings' (avg 121.5); Statement 17 'I respect all teachers in this school' and Statement 18 'all teachers must be respected' (avg 121.5); Statement 29 'I will record all the lessons delivered by the teacher' (avg 121); Statement 20 'even though we students are different, we should respect each other' (avg 119); Statement 4 'when the teacher explains the lesson, I fully concentrate on understanding the material' (avg 117.5); Statement 2 'I look for information in other media if I struggle with schoolwork' (avg 117); Statement 8 'all the attributes on my school uniform' (avg 116.5). The GBL model increased student engagement across all three indicators: behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement.

game_design_elements: Quiz-based gameplay (Quizizz platform)
Competition/competitive elements (students play against competitors)
Scoring system (highest score determined based on student's efforts)
Group-based play (students log into Quizizz in groups)
Interactivity
Feedback mechanisms (game score levels, teacher feedback at output stage)
Time-based challenges
Fun/entertainment elements
instructional_strategies: Game-based learning (GBL) model with three stages: Input (teacher maps teaching content into game content), Process (teacher describes game characteristics and links learning objectives), Output (teacher provides feedback and evaluates)
Post-test-only non-equivalent control-group quasi-experimental design
Group-based collaborative gameplay in Quizizz
Active learning through game participation
Student-centered learning approach
History content on Basic Competency (KD) 3.5: nature of Japanese occupation and Indonesian response
Three meetings of intervention in the even semester
Discovery learning model used as comparison/control condition
rq3.content_integration: The game-based learning model was applied to teach Basic Competence (KD) 3.5 in Indonesian History, which covers the nature of the Japanese occupation and the response of the Indonesian people. The teacher mapped teaching content into game content on the Quizizz platform and directed students to enter the game. During gameplay, students used creativity, communication skills, analysis, and problem-solving in the game, and developed strategies to solve the game. The Quizizz application served as the technological medium to deliver history quiz content within a competitive, gamified format. The implementation followed the three-stage GBL model: input (content mapping), process (gameplay with teacher facilitation describing characteristics, attractiveness, linking to learning objectives), and output (feedback and evaluation).

implementation_barriers: The study was carried out in the short term (only three meetings), limiting longitudinal assessment
Impossibility of randomizing research subjects necessitated quasi-experimental design
Threats to internal and external validity including differences in cognitive abilities, classroom environmental conditions, test results, and interaction of treatments in the sample
One questionnaire item ('positive reactions to academics' from emotional engagement) was removed because it would take too long to obtain data
Online learning implementation reduces students' opportunities to engage in an active learning environment
