methodology_limitations: Post-test-only design: no pre-test measurement of student engagement, so baseline equivalence on the dependent variable is unverified
Non-equivalent control-group design: classes were not randomly assigned; selection was based on homogeneity of average daily test scores in history, not on prior engagement levels
Small sample size (66 total, 33 per group) from a single school
Self-report questionnaire only: no observational or behavioral measures of engagement
Removal of one questionnaire indicator (positive reactions to academics) may affect construct validity
Short intervention period (three meetings only)

The LSD follow-up test between experimental post-test and control post-test showed p=0.069 > 0.05, which is not statistically significant at the conventional alpha level, contradicting the abstract's claim
Single school in a specific region (Banyuwangi, East Java) limits generalizability
No effect size reported
negative_effects: Online learning reduces students' opportunities to engage in an active learning environment that creates opportunities for students (citing Martin & Bolliger, 2018)
Using technology may reduce critical thinking, academic skills, motivation, and student engagement if skills are not appropriately honed (citing Yu & Canton, 2020)
mitigation_strategies: Homogeneity test was used to address threats to internal and external validity by confirming samples are from the same population variance
Validity testing of instrument items (Product Moment correlation, rhit > rtab) and reliability testing (Cronbach's Alpha = 0.911) to ensure measurement quality
Normality test (Kolmogorov-Smirnov) and homogeneity of variance test (Levene's Statistic) performed before hypothesis testing
Authors recommend the game-based learning model as a reference for increasing student engagement, active learning, and student-centered learning

domain1.q1_evidence: Selection criteria are described: 'The population in this study were students of class XI IPS at SMA Negeri 1 Gambiran during the even semester of the 2021-2022 Academic Year, consisting of 4 classes, namely IPS 1, IPS 2, IPS 3, and IPS 4, with a total number of 131 students. The experimental class was not determined randomly but through a homogeneity test by calculating the average score of the Indonesian History test.' The research sample was selected from 2 classes with the first highest average (XI IPS 1, mean=80.54, experimental) and second highest average (XI IPS 4, mean=80.48, control), with 33 students each.
domain1.q2_evidence: The sample comes from a single school (SMA Negeri 1 Gambiran) in Banyuwangi Regency, East Java, Indonesia. Classes were not randomly assigned but selected based on highest average daily test scores. This purposive selection of the two highest-performing classes may not represent the broader population of secondary history students. Additionally, only 66 of 131 available students (50%) were included. The two classes selected had very similar means (80.54 and 80.48) and were the top performers, potentially limiting generalizability to average or lower-performing students.

domain2.q3_evidence: The student engagement questionnaire was adopted from Sinulingga (2018), 'whose validity has been tested from the results of the product moment formula with a significance level of 0.000 and the reliability from the results of the Cronbach's Alpha formula of 0.955 (very high).' The researchers also independently tested validity: 'all question items on the student engagement variable had a rcount > rtable with a sig (significance) of less than 5% (0.05). This shows that the question items were valid.' Reliability was confirmed: 'Cronbach's Alpha of 0.911 in the category 0.80 < r11 ≤ 0.911 (very high reliability).'
domain2.q4_evidence: The analysis methods are described and justified: 'Hypothesis testing used a one-way ANOVA test, assisted by the SPSS 22.0 software for Windows.' Prerequisites were checked: normality via Kolmogorov-Smirnov (control sig.=0.066>0.05; experimental sig.=0.200>0.05) and homogeneity via Levene's Statistic (sig.=0.793>0.05). The LSD follow-up test was used to determine mean differences. Decision-making criteria are stated: 'significance level of 5%, with H0 being accepted if the sig. > 0.05, and vice versa.'

domain3.q5_evidence: There is an inconsistency in the interpretation of results. The abstract states 'the probability value (sig.) in the experimental group was 0.040 > 0.05, with the LSD follow-up test LSD of 2.45455. Therefore, it is concluded that there was an effect of student engagement on the experimental group.' However, 0.040 < 0.05 (not > 0.05 as stated). More importantly, the LSD follow-up test comparing experimental post-test vs control post-test shows a significance value of 0.069 > 0.05, which means the direct comparison between the two groups' post-test scores is NOT statistically significant at the 0.05 level. Despite this, the authors conclude the experimental group had 'better student engagement effect than the control group.' The overall ANOVA is significant (p=.040), but the specific pairwise comparison most relevant to the research question (experimental post-test vs control post-test) is not significant (p=.069).
domain3.q6_evidence: The paper does not include a dedicated limitations section. The authors do not explicitly discuss the limitations of the post-test-only design, the non-random assignment, the small sample size, the single-school setting, the short intervention period, or the removal of a questionnaire indicator. The conclusion makes broad claims without qualifying limitations: 'There is a significant influence on student engagement when using the game-based learning model.' No mention is made of the non-significant LSD result (p=.069) between the two groups' post-tests in the conclusion.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study has high overall risk of bias primarily due to: (1) inconsistent interpretation of statistical results -- the ANOVA is significant (p=.040) but the direct LSD comparison between experimental and control post-tests is not significant (p=.069), yet the authors conclude a significant effect; (2) the abstract contains an error stating '0.040 > 0.05' when it should be '0.040 < 0.05'; (3) no limitations are discussed anywhere in the paper; (4) post-test-only design without baseline engagement measurement makes it impossible to confirm groups were equivalent on the dependent variable before intervention; (5) purposive selection of the two highest-performing classes from a single school limits generalizability; (6) no effect size is reported. While the data collection instruments show adequate validity and reliability, and analysis methods are properly described with prerequisite tests, the interpretation domain has serious concerns that elevate the overall risk.

pdf_filename: The Effects of Online Interactive Games on High School Students' Achievement and Motivation in History Learning.pdf

bibliographic.title: The Effects of Online Interactive Games on High School Students' Achievement and Motivation in History Learning
bibliographic.venue: International Journal of Distance Education Technologies

study_characteristics.sample_description: Thirty students from a certain Taichung Municipal Junior High School. Based on pretest average score 90, nineteen students who got higher scores were assigned to the control group (high achievers), and eleven students who got lower scores were assigned to the experimental group (low achievers). The experimental group used IGLS to learn Taiwan history for a month.
study_characteristics.study_design: quasi_experimental
study_characteristics.aim: To survey whether the online game in junior high school students can encourage learning effect in Taiwan's History, by applying Interactive Game-based Learning System (IGLS) to junior high history teaching as an ancillary tool to enhance users' learning motivation and academic performance.

eligibility.concerns: The study uses a custom-built web-based interactive game-based learning system (IGLS) for teaching Taiwan history to junior high school students. The game involves quiz-based competition, hit points, team-based gameplay, and online community features. The assignment to groups was based on pretest scores (high vs. low achievers) rather than random or class-level assignment, and sample size is very small (N=30, with only 11 in the experimental group). The design is quasi-experimental with unequal group sizes.

rq1.explicit_definition: DGBL was first proposed by Marc Prensky in 2001. Through digital games, learners obtain sense of achievement in solving problems and dealing with challenges. Digital game based learning takes both entertainment and education into consideration.
rq1.conceptualization: The study conceptualizes digital game-based learning (DGBL) as an integration of entertainment and education through online interactive games. The authors frame IGLS within Prensky's (2001, 2003) vision of changing from 'learning is depressing' to 'learning by playing, learning through playing.' The study draws on Keller's (1983) ARCS motivation theory (attention, relevance, confidence, satisfaction) combined with Csikszentmihalyi's (1991) Flow theory, arguing that 'a good digital game design immerses learners in games, and then brings about effective learning process.' The system is positioned as an ancillary tool for history teaching that uses online community mechanisms (group competition, chat rooms, knowledge sharing) to enhance learning motivation and academic performance. Vygotsky's (1966) Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) and Bruner's (1960, 1989) spiral curriculum are also referenced to support the idea that games can adjust teaching for both fast and slow learners.
theoretical_frameworks: ARCS motivation theory (Keller, 1983) - attention, relevance, confidence, satisfaction

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Taiwan History (Vol. 1) Achievement Test: Four hundred multiple-choice questions drawn from IGLS's contents and Taiwan history textbook 1. Pre-test and post-test administered to both groups. IGLS Questionnaire: Likert Five-Point scale measuring interface satisfaction, function satisfaction, and motivation satisfaction. Paired sample t-test for pre-post comparison within groups. One-way ANCOVA for analyzing effects of gender, weekly time of surfing the Net, affection network leisure type, and login IGLS per week on post-test scores.
rq2.statistical_results: Paired sample t test (Table 2): Control group pretest-posttest: Mean difference = -1.68421, SD = 3.66746, SEM = .84137, 95% CI [-3.45187, .08345], t = -2.002, df = 18, Significance (Two-Tailed) = .061. Experimental group pretest-posttest: Mean difference = -7.27273, SD = 7.55104, SEM = 2.27672, 95% CI [-12.34558, -2.19987], t = -3.194, df = 10, Significance (Two-Tailed) = .010. Descriptive statistics (Table 1): Control group Pretest1 Mean = 94.5263, N = 19, SD = 3.04354, SEM = .69824; Control group Posttest1 Mean = 96.2105, N = 19, SD = 2.57291, SEM = .59027; Experimental group Pretest2 Mean = 84.1818, N = 11, SD = 3.51620, SEM = 1.06017; Experimental group Posttest2 Mean = 91.4545, N = 11, SD = 10.04354, SEM = 3.02824. ANCOVA Table 3 (Gender): F = .163, p = not significant; gender F = .098; R Squared = .405 (Adjusted R Squared = .235), p < .05. ANCOVA Table 4 (Weekly time surfing the Net): F = .786; weekly time surfing the Net F = .821; R Squared = .152 (Adjusted R Squared = -.272), p < .05. ANCOVA Table 5 (Affection network leisure type): F = .171; affection network leisure type F = .130; R Squared = .541 (Adjusted R Squared = .312), p < .05. ANCOVA Table 6 (Login IGLS per week): F = .059; Login IGLS per week F(2,6) = 5.687, p = .041; R Squared = .687 (Adjusted R Squared = .531), p < .05.
rq2.comparative_methodology: Quasi-experimental design with non-equivalent groups. Control group (n=19, high achievers with pretest scores above average of 90) and experimental group (n=11, low achievers with pretest scores below average of 90). Four-week experiment. Pre-test of Taiwan history (Vol. 1) used as covariate in ANCOVA analyses. Post-test scores used as dependent variable. Paired sample t-test used to compare pretest-posttest improvement within each group.
rq2.key_outcomes: The experimental group (low achievers using IGLS) showed statistically significant improvement from pretest to posttest (mean improvement of 7.27 points, t = -3.194, p = .010), while the control group (high achievers without IGLS) did not reach significance (mean improvement of 1.68 points, t = -2.002, p = .061). ANCOVA showed that only the number of days logging into IGLS per week had a significant effect on post-test scores (F = 5.687, p = .041), with R Squared = .687. Gender, weekly time surfing the Net, and affection network leisure type did not significantly affect post-test scores.
rq2.engagement_results: IGLS Questionnaire results (Likert 5-point scale): Interface satisfaction (Table 7): 'The interface is easy to handle' Mean = 4.64, SD = 0.505; 'The content is clearly expressed' Mean = 4.73, SD = 0.467; 'The buttons are easy to click on' Mean = 4.82, SD = 0.405; 'Convenience of the design' Mean = 4.55, SD = 0.688. Function satisfaction (Table 8): 'The records do help me with learning' Mean = 4.55, SD = 0.688; 'The group competition help me with learning' Mean = 4.55, SD = 0.688; 'The online version help me with learning' Mean = 4.55, SD = 0.522; 'The message board makes communication easier for me' Mean = 4.09, SD = 0.831; 'I can handle the situation in group competition' Mean = 4.45, SD = 0.820. Motivation satisfaction (Table 9): 'The game arouses my participation' Mean = 4.55, SD = 0.688; 'The game improves my performance' Mean = 4.64, SD = 0.505; 'The game eases my pressure in learning' Mean = 4.64, SD = 0.674; 'The game attracts my interest in history' Mean = 4.36, SD = 0.809; 'I think the system is suitable for learning history' Mean = 4.36, SD = 0.809. Grand mean = 4.51. Over ninety percent students approve of the system's attraction to their participation and intension. Result distribution: strongly agree (61.82%), agree (27.27%), neutral (10.91%), disagree (0%), strongly disagree (0%).

game_design_elements: Quiz-based gameplay (multiple choice, match items, random argument computational problems)
Hit points system (each team has 100 hit points; correct answers reduce opponent's points)
Team-based competition (2 vs. 2, 3 vs. 3, etc.)
Score tracking and performance records (chart showing each unit's score)
Compound attack option (players attack any opponent or choose compound attack)
Randomized question generation (three types of item generation algorithms)
Learning management module (teachers/managers monitor learning process)
Online chat rooms for knowledge sharing
Stand-alone and online version options
Self-evaluation through performance records
Unit selection system (players select units and start game with equal team members)
technological_platforms: Interactive Game-based Learning System (IGLS) - custom web-based platform
Online/Internet-based system accessible wherever Internet is available
instructional_strategies: Game-based learning as ancillary tool to regular history teaching
Online community learning mechanism (group competition, chat rooms, knowledge sharing)
Cooperative learning through free grouping and collaborative knowledge exploration
Competition-based motivation through team-based quiz battles
Student-centered game design based on interaction and healthy competition
Formative assessment through game performance monitoring
After-school supplementary use (students reminded to use IGLS after school every week)
Four-week experiment duration with pre-test and post-test
Content aligned with Taiwan history textbook (Vol. 1) covering prehistory, international competition, Cheng's governance, and earlier stage of Ching dynasty's occupation
rq3.content_integration: IGLS includes content from seven graders' sociology textbook 'Taiwan history (Vol. 1)', covering prehistory, international competition, Cheng's governance, and earlier stage of Ching dynasty's occupation. The quiz game module generates questions directly from the Taiwan history curriculum using three types of item generation algorithms: multiple choice with random options, match items, and random argument computational problems. The learning management module allows teachers to monitor student progress. Students form free groups and explore history knowledge through competitive quiz battles, sharing information in chat rooms. The game mechanics (hit points, team battles, score tracking) are directly tied to correctly answering history content questions, creating a direct link between game success and content mastery.

implementation_barriers: Non-random group assignment based on pretest scores created unequal groups (19 high achievers vs. 11 low achievers)
Very small sample size (N=30 total, only 11 in experimental group)
Four-week experiment duration may be insufficient for long-term effects assessment
System requires Internet access, which may not be equally available to all students
The message board functionality received the lowest satisfaction rating (Mean = 4.09) among all items
methodology_limitations: Non-equivalent groups: experimental group consisted of low achievers (pretest below 90) while control group consisted of high achievers (pretest above 90), making direct comparison problematic
Very small sample size (N=30; experimental n=11, control n=19) severely limits statistical power and generalizability
Single school in Taichung, Taiwan limits external validity
No random assignment; groups defined by pretest performance threshold
ANCOVA analyses conducted on experimental group only (n=11), with extremely small cell sizes for multi-level factors
The control group did not use any alternative digital tool, making it unclear whether effects are due to IGLS specifically or digital learning generally
No reliability or validity information reported for the achievement test (400 multiple-choice questions)
Survey administered only to the experimental group in the fourth week, with no control group comparison for motivation/satisfaction
No effect size reported for any statistical test
The post-test standard deviation for the experimental group (SD=10.04) is much larger than their pretest SD (SD=3.52), suggesting high variability in outcomes
negative_effects: Risk of game addiction noted: 'if digital learning turns into games addiction, game type learning will brings down learners' motivation' (citing Mitchell and Savill-Smith, 2004)
Potential for students to focus too much on playing games instead of learning itself (citing Mitchell and Savill-Smith, 2004)
mitigation_strategies: Paired sample t-test used to assess within-group improvement to partially address non-equivalence of groups
ANCOVA used with pretest scores as covariate to control for pre-existing differences
Content validity of IGLS questionnaire maintained through discussion with professors and program designers
Likert Five-Point scale used for systematic measurement of student opinion and motivation
Teachers serve as managers who can check learners' performance records and make adjustments

Prensky's six key elements for digital game-based learning patterns used as design reference: (1) rules, (2) goals or objectives, (3) outcomes and feedback, (4) conflict/competition/challenge/opposition, (5) interaction, (6) representation and story

domain1.q1_evidence: Selection criteria are described: 'The study took sample of thirty students from a certain Taichung Municipal Junior High School. Based on the pretest average score 90, nineteen students who got higher scores are in the control group (high achievers), whereas another eleven students who got lower scores are in the experimental group (low achievers).' However, the basis for the cutoff score of 90 and the specific school selection are not fully justified.
domain1.q2_evidence: The sample is highly unrepresentative. Only 30 students from a single unnamed junior high school in Taichung, Taiwan were included. The groups were divided by academic performance (high vs. low achievers), creating fundamentally non-equivalent groups with different baseline characteristics. The experimental group (n=11) is extremely small. The sample cannot represent the broader population of junior high school history students.

domain2.q3_evidence: The achievement test consisted of 'four hundred multiple-choice questions about Taiwan history (Vol. 1) which came from both IGLS's contents and Taiwan history textbook 1,' but no reliability or validity information is reported for this instrument. For the IGLS questionnaire, the authors state it was 'discussed and analyzed with professor and program designers, to keep content validity' using a Likert Five-Point scale, but no psychometric properties (Cronbach's alpha, factor analysis) are reported. The questionnaire was only administered to the experimental group.
domain2.q4_evidence: Analysis methods are described: paired sample t-test was used for pretest-posttest comparison within each group, and one-way ANCOVA was used to examine effects of gender, weekly surfing time, affection network leisure type, and login IGLS per week on post-test scores, with pretest scores as covariate. Statistical results are reported with means, SDs, SEMs, 95% CIs, t-values, df, p-values, and ANCOVA tables with Type III Sum of Squares, F-values, and R-squared values.

domain3.q5_evidence: The interpretation has several issues: (1) The study compares low achievers (experimental) to high achievers (control) but interprets the greater improvement of the experimental group as evidence of IGLS effectiveness, without adequately acknowledging the regression to the mean effect -- low achievers naturally have more room to improve; (2) The abstract claims 'the paired sample t test analysis considerably impact on experimental group to significance .05(P=.010)' and that 'one-way ANCOVA showed login IGLS the number of days every week more learning effect to be better,' but the ANCOVA analyses were conducted only on the experimental group (n=11) with extremely small cell sizes, making statistical inferences unreliable; (3) The conclusion states 'IGLS benefits academic performance in junior high history learning' and 'IGLS especially provides low achievers with confidence and positive attitude' but these claims are not supported by the study design which did not provide IGLS to high achievers for comparison.
domain3.q6_evidence: The paper contains no dedicated limitations section. The fundamental design limitation of comparing low achievers (experimental) to high achievers (control) is never acknowledged. The extremely small sample sizes, non-random assignment, single-school setting, and lack of psychometric validation of instruments are not discussed. The conclusion makes broad claims such as 'IGLS has positive effects on history learning, thus, it can be of assistance in history teaching' without any qualification of limitations.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study has high overall risk of bias due to multiple serious methodological concerns: (1) The fundamental design flaw of assigning low achievers to the experimental group and high achievers to the control group makes it impossible to attribute improvements to IGLS rather than regression to the mean; (2) Extremely small sample size (N=30, experimental n=11) severely limits statistical power and generalizability; (3) No reliability or validity data reported for the 400-item achievement test; (4) ANCOVA analyses on the experimental group alone (n=11) with multiple categorical predictors result in cell sizes too small for meaningful inference; (5) The questionnaire was only administered to the experimental group, precluding comparison; (6) No limitations are discussed anywhere in the paper; (7) Interpretations overreach the data -- concluding IGLS benefits history learning when the design cannot isolate the IGLS effect from baseline group differences. While the study does employ appropriate statistical procedures (paired t-tests, ANCOVA) and reports results with adequate detail, the design and interpretation issues are severe enough to warrant a high risk of bias rating.

pdf_filename: The End Game in Kuhlthau’s ISP Model Knowledge Construction for Grade 8 Students Researching an Inquiry-Based History Project.pdf

bibliographic.title: The End Game in Kuhlthau's ISP Model: Knowledge Construction for Grade 8 Students Researching an Inquiry-Based History Project
bibliographic.venue: Journal of the Association for Information Science and Technology

study_characteristics.sample_description: 10 volunteer Grade 8 students (5 boys and 5 girls, approximately 14 years old) from a private Canadian school, a subset of a larger study group of 44 Grade 8 students (41% girls, 59% boys). The students were researching self-selected history topics for an inquiry-based class history assignment over a 12-week period (February-May 2011).
study_characteristics.study_design: qualitative
study_characteristics.aim: To define an end game for the ISP model by investigating how Grade 8 students' feelings, thoughts, and information behavior combine to enable knowledge construction on their school history assignment topic, answering three research questions: (1) Do the data support Kuhlthau's ISP model stages? (2) Do the data support the evolution of the ISP model's feelings, thoughts, and actions? (3) How can we chart the study participants' implicit-to-explicit knowledge construction as it evolves over ISP stages?

eligibility.concerns: CRITICAL: This study does NOT involve gamification or game-based learning in any form. The term 'End Game' in the title is a metaphorical/theoretical concept referring to the final outcome or culmination of knowledge construction within Kuhlthau's Information Search Process (ISP) model. The 'end game' is defined by the authors as 'the addition to or modification of the students' belief system as a result of completing the class assignment' and 'the students' actualization of their belief system through the new topic information they seek, find, and use over the course of completing the assignment.' The study is a qualitative field study of information-seeking behavior using grounded theory analysis of student interviews -- there are no games, no game elements, no gamification mechanics, no digital games, and no game-based learning interventions whatsoever. This is an information science study about how students construct knowledge while doing a history research assignment. It was likely included in the review's candidate set due to the word 'Game' appearing in the title, which is a false positive.

rq1.conceptualization: Not applicable. This study does not address gamification. The study conceptualizes Kuhlthau's Information Search Process (ISP) model and knowledge construction theory. The 'end game' concept refers to the culmination of the knowledge construction process: 'we define the end game of the student's knowledge construction process as the actualization of self-knowledge of their belief system about the world, but particularly their assignment topic (i.e., rendering it explicit so that is consciously available to the student) by adding to and/or modifying their belief system.' The theoretical framework draws on constructivist learning theory (Piaget, Vygotsky, Bruner, Dewey, Kelly), Polanyi's theory of implicit-to-explicit knowledge conversion, and Kuhlthau's 7-stage ISP model.
theoretical_frameworks: Constructivist learning theory (Piaget, Vygotsky, Bruner, Dewey, Kelly)
Polanyi's theory of tacit/implicit knowledge and explicit knowledge conversion
Ausubel's subsumption theory and progressive differentiation
Glaser and Strauss's grounded theory methodology

rq2.key_outcomes: Not applicable -- this study does not evaluate gamification effectiveness. The study's qualitative findings indicate: (1) Data generally support Kuhlthau's ISP model stages, with exceptions for stage 1 (initiation) and stage 5 (collection); (2) Students front-loaded their knowledge construction and information seeking activities in the first 4 weeks rather than in the middle stages as predicted by the ISP model; (3) A three-phase model of knowledge construction was proposed: Phase 1 'making questions' from previous knowledge, Phase 2 'asking questions' as topic information raises new questions, Phase 3 'answering questions' using newly found topic information; (4) In the assessment stage (interview 6), students became more introspective and able to articulate their thoughts and actions.

instructional_strategies: Inquiry-based history project with self-selected topics
Topic-to-thesis structure for constructivist perspective teaching
Multiple presentation formats (documentary video, newscast, skit, art exhibit, historical re-enactment, PowerPoint)
Research process emphasized over final product (60% of grade for research/proposal, 40% for presentation)
Students encouraged to develop personal perspective/thesis on self-selected history topic
rq3.content_integration: Not applicable -- no game mechanics were used. The history content was integrated through an inquiry-based assignment where Grade 8 students selected their own history topics (examples mentioned include the Mafia, the Titanic, chess and warfare, terrorist attacks, child labor), researched them over 12 weeks using diverse sources, developed a thesis statement, and presented their findings in various formats.

methodology_limitations: Qualitative exploratory study with small sample (n=10) -- purpose was to create a coding scheme for future studies
Self-selected convenience sample from a private school where tuition fees may limit access, reducing external validity
The optimal nature of the study participants' school and parental learning environments compared to larger population of North American 14 year olds limits generalizability
Intercoder reliability not established -- noted as important for future studies
Only 23% of 14 year olds may have reached Piaget's formal operational stage (Eylon & Linn, 1988), questioning whether participants could engage in the abstract thinking required
Coding scheme limitations concerning validity and reliability acknowledged
Atlas.ti software facilitates but does not ensure objective counting of coding categories
mitigation_strategies: Use of Atlas.ti (v.7) qualitative data analysis software for systematic coding
Three-step grounded theory coding process (open, axial, selective) for rigor
Six interview points over 12-week period to capture temporal evolution
Semi-structured interview schedule with multiple dimensions (feelings, thoughts, actions)
Building on prior published work from same research project (Beheshti et al., 2015; Cole et al., 2013)

domain1.q1_evidence: Selection is described: 'In 2010, from a total of five Grade 8 history classes at the school, two classes were chosen by the teachers to participate in the assignment.' From the larger study group of 44 students, '10 volunteer study participants for the study we report on in this article were a subset of the larger total study group of 44 Grade 8 students.' Consent procedures are described in detail, including parental consent forms and voluntary participation with option to withdraw.
domain1.q2_evidence: The 10 study participants were volunteers (self-selected) from a private Canadian school. The authors themselves acknowledge the limitation: 'the 10 study participants in the present study were a self-selected sample of Grade 8 students in a private school where tuition fees may limit access. The optimal nature of the study participants' school and parental learning environments compared to the larger population of North American 14 year olds increases the percentage of study participants who have achieved the Piaget formal operational stage of cognitive development. The results of this study therefore cannot be considered statistically representative of any larger population.'

domain2.q3_evidence: Data was collected through semi-structured interviews lasting approximately 10 minutes each, conducted at six time points over 12 weeks. The interview schedule included broad questions about feelings ('How do you feel about your history assignment at this point?'), thoughts ('How did you come up with your topic?'), and actions ('How did you search for information on your topic?'). However, no formal validity or reliability information is reported for the interview instrument. The authors acknowledge: 'For limitations of the coding scheme, particularly concerning validity and reliability, the reader is directed to the Limitations section of this article.'
domain2.q4_evidence: Analysis methods are clearly described and justified: Glaser and Strauss's (1967) grounded theory approach was used, with Atlas.ti (v.7) for coding and analysis. The three-step coding process is well documented: Step 1 open coding (first-, second-, third-order coding based on ISP stages, feelings/thoughts/actions, and descriptive terms), Step 2 axial coding around the core category of knowledge construction with fourth-order coding, and Step 3 selective coding. The rationale for grounded theory ('designed to lead to middle-range model/theory making in an exploratory or new area of study') is clearly justified.

domain3.q5_evidence: Interpretations are generally consistent with the qualitative data presented. The authors use language like 'tentatively indicate,' 'speculatively,' and 'we conjecture' when making interpretive claims that go beyond the direct data. For example: 'Study findings tentatively indicate that knowledge construction results from an iterative process between the student and information.' The proposed three-phase model of knowledge construction (making questions, asking questions, answering questions) is supported with illustrative student quotes from the interviews. Results that contradict the ISP model (e.g., front-loading of activities in first 4 weeks rather than middle stages) are also honestly reported.
domain3.q6_evidence: A dedicated Limitations section acknowledges key weaknesses: 'This was a qualitative, exploratory study. Its purpose was to create a coding scheme for future studies utilizing the same data collection instrument. Reliability, particularly intercoder agreement, is of utmost importance in these future studies. Concerning external validity, the 10 study participants in the present study were a self-selected sample of Grade 8 students in a private school where tuition fees may limit access.' The authors also note that the results 'cannot be considered statistically representative of any larger population.'

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study has mixed risk of bias characteristics. Domain 1 (selection) is rated High due to the small, self-selected convenience sample from a single private school, which the authors themselves acknowledge limits generalizability. Domain 2 (data collection/analysis) is rated Unclear because while the grounded theory methodology is well-described and systematic, the interview instrument lacks formal validity/reliability testing and intercoder reliability was not established. Domain 3 (interpretation) is rated Low because the authors are appropriately cautious in their interpretations, use hedging language for speculative claims, honestly report contradictory findings, and include a dedicated limitations section. However, it must be noted that this study is INELIGIBLE for the systematic review as it does not involve gamification or game-based learning -- the 'End Game' in the title refers to the culmination of the knowledge construction process in Kuhlthau's ISP model, not to any actual game or gamification intervention.

pdf_filename: The Evaluation Study of Gamification Approach in Malaysian History Learning via Mobile Game Application.pdf

bibliographic.title: The Evaluation Study of Gamification Approach in Malaysian History Learning via Mobile Game Application
bibliographic.venue: 2017 IEEE 17th International Conference on Advanced Learning Technologies (ICALT)

study_characteristics.sample_description: Five students who have playing games experience participated in the focus group evaluation to determine the effectiveness and impact of HLMG on history learning.
study_characteristics.study_design: qualitative
study_characteristics.aim: To evaluate and analyze gamification approach in Malaysian History Learning via a mobile game application (HLMG), including verification of game components, validation of game functions, and evaluation of effectiveness via a focus group study on user experience (UX), story, gameplay complexity, estimated average play session, engagement, and historical content delivered.

eligibility.concerns: Very small sample size (n=5) with only qualitative focus group evaluation. No quantitative learning outcome measures or statistical analysis. The study is essentially a prototype evaluation rather than a rigorous empirical study of gamification effectiveness. The evaluation criteria are descriptive (qualitative judgments like 'excellent', 'sufficient', 'needs improvement') rather than measured with validated instruments. The 9-item questionnaire used is not described in detail, and no reliability or validity information is provided.

rq1.conceptualization: The study conceptualizes gamification broadly in terms of game-based learning (GBL) applied to history education via mobile game applications. Gamification is framed as the use of gamified elements in educational settings to achieve learning outcomes, with emphasis on careful design: 'the gamified solutions need to be designed carefully so that it can be successfully sustain longer and help to achieve the learning outcomes in education field.' The study treats gamification and GBL somewhat interchangeably, discussing how 'GBL is efficient to use in history learning, which use action despite of narration, develop personal satisfaction and motivation, suite for divergent learning styles and skills, reinforce mastery skills and cater an interactive context.' The approach centers on creating a custom mobile game application (HLMG) that delivers Malaysian history syllabus content through narrative-driven gameplay with chapters, challenges, quizzes, and an arena mode.

rq2.comparative_methodology: Focus group evaluation with 5 students using a 9-item questionnaire assessing six criteria: user experience (UX), story, gameplay complexity, estimated average play session, engagement, and historical content delivered. Results were qualitative descriptive judgments rather than quantitative measures. The game's final prototype was also compared to similar games (though details of comparison games are not provided).
rq2.key_outcomes: Qualitative evaluation results from focus group: User Experience (UX) -- 'The UX is rather lackluster, due to lack of animations and disjointed graphics and themes' (needs improvement); Story -- 'The story is consistent with the syllabus, and follows a narrative flow. Each chapter has its own unique narrative' (excellent); Gameplay Complexity -- 'Simple, using only touch inputs. Challenges are easy to comprehend and overcome' (sufficient); Estimated Average Play Session -- '8-20 minutes, depending on familiarity of the chapter' (excellent); Engagement -- 'High engagement. Supported by natural flow of story and challenges' (sufficient); Historical Content Delivered -- 'Very high. Due to the game designed around delivering the content of history syllabus to the student' (excellent). Game validation confirmed all five research objectives were met (all passed).
rq2.engagement_results: Engagement was rated as 'High engagement. Supported by natural flow of story and challenges' and deemed 'sufficient for the effectiveness level of HLMG.' However, the authors note that 'HLMG has obvious flaws and short comings in graphics which in turns it influences the level of engagement.' The implicit engagement and motivation triggered by learning contents and gamification features were identified as vital for maximising thinking skills during the history learning process.

game_design_elements: Narrative/storyline (chapter-based historical narrative consistent with syllabus)
Challenges (arena-based challenges within each chapter)
Quizzes (post-chapter quiz for assessing comprehension)
Player progress tracking
Menu navigation system
Game manager (overarching game logic)
Touch-based input controls
Chapter-based content structure
Introductory scene with objectives display
instructional_strategies: Game-based learning (GBL) for history education
Narrative-driven learning with chapter-based historical storylines
Interactive learning as alternative to traditional textbook method
Portable and ubiquitous learning via mobile devices
Quiz-based assessment after chapter completion for comprehension review
Repetitive chapter play for revision and fact refreshment
Story-driven content delivery aligned with Malaysian history syllabus (SPM)
Collaborative or individual play modes (can be played by oneself or with a group)
rq3.content_integration: Historical content was tightly integrated with game mechanics by designing the game around the Malaysian secondary school history syllabus (SPM). Each chapter corresponds to a historical period with its own unique narrative that follows the syllabus content. The game restricts content to one historical period per chapter due to time constraints. Historical facts are delivered through the narrative flow, with challenges and quizzes embedded within chapters to reinforce learning. The introductory scene presents objectives, and the player progress scene tracks actions and behaviors during gameplay. The game was validated as meeting the objective to 'Increase a student's comprehension on their syllabus' through repetitive chapter play and quiz-based evaluation.

implementation_barriers: Lackluster user experience (UX) due to lack of animations and disjointed graphics and themes
Content restricted to one historical period due to time constraints in development
Graphics shortcomings that influence the level of engagement
Limited visual and audio assets reducing immersion
methodology_limitations: Very small sample size (n=5) for focus group evaluation
No quantitative learning outcome measures or statistical analysis
9-item questionnaire not described in detail; no reliability or validity information provided
No control group or comparison condition
Qualitative descriptive evaluations rather than systematic measurement
No pre-test/post-test design to measure actual learning gains
Criteria for determining 'excellent', 'sufficient', and 'needs improvement' not explicitly defined
Selection criteria for the 5 focus group participants not clearly specified beyond 'students who have playing games experience'
negative_effects: User experience rated as needing improvement due to poor visual design
Graphics shortcomings may negatively influence engagement levels
mitigation_strategies: Redesign mini-games and chapter storylines to provide a more effective learning tool
Improve UX design with better animations, graphics, and thematic consistency
Add visual and audio elements to increase level of immersion
Future versions should address UX to enhance player's experience and effectiveness for SPM history exam preparation

domain1.q1_evidence: The selection criteria for participants are minimally described. The only information provided is: 'Five students who have playing games experience have participated this evaluation to determine its effectiveness and impact on history learning among students.' No details are given about age, grade level, recruitment process, inclusion/exclusion criteria, school, or how 'playing games experience' was defined or verified. The education level (secondary) is inferred from the context that the game targets Malaysian SPM history curriculum, but participant demographics are not explicitly reported.
domain1.q2_evidence: With only 5 participants selected based on the vague criterion of 'playing games experience,' the sample cannot be considered representative of the target population (Malaysian secondary school students studying history). The sample size is extremely small for any generalization. No demographic information is provided (gender, age, academic performance, history subject attitudes). The institutional affiliation of authors is Taylor's University (a private university), but it is unclear whether participants were secondary school students or university students, further undermining representativeness.

domain2.q3_evidence: The study mentions 'They need to fill up the questionnaire which contains 9 items to evaluate the effectiveness level of the HLMG,' but the questionnaire itself is not presented, described in detail, or referenced. No information about the source, development, validation, or reliability of the 9-item instrument is provided. The evaluation criteria (UX, story, gameplay complexity, estimated average play session, engagement, historical content delivered) are presented in Table 2 with descriptive qualitative judgments, but how these were derived from the 9-item questionnaire responses is not explained. No scoring rubric or rating scale is described.
domain2.q4_evidence: No data analysis methods are described or justified. The results in Table 2 are presented as qualitative summative judgments (e.g., 'excellent', 'sufficient', 'needs improvement') without any explanation of how raw questionnaire data was analyzed or aggregated to arrive at these conclusions. There is no description of coding procedures, thematic analysis, or any systematic approach to synthesizing the focus group feedback. The verification and validation process (Table 1) uses simple Passed/Failed judgments with justifications but no systematic evaluation methodology.

domain3.q5_evidence: The interpretations in the abstract and conclusion are broadly consistent with the results presented in Table 2 -- the authors correctly report that UX needs improvement while story, historical content delivered, and estimated play session are excellent, and gameplay complexity and engagement are sufficient. However, the basis for these judgments is unclear since the underlying data (questionnaire responses) are not presented. The conclusion that 'the implicit engagement and motivation which triggered by the learning contents and gamification features were vital for maximising thinking skills while in the history learning process' goes beyond what the reported evaluation data can support, as no thinking skills were measured.
domain3.q6_evidence: No formal limitations section is included. While the conclusion acknowledges that 'HLMG has obvious flaws and short comings in graphics' and suggests improvements, there is no discussion of methodological limitations such as the very small sample size, lack of quantitative measures, absence of a control group, or limitations of the focus group approach. The authors present recommendations for future improvement of the game (redesign mini-games, improve UX, add visual and audio) but do not acknowledge limitations of the research design itself.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: All three domains are rated High risk of bias. Domain 1 (selection) is High because participant selection criteria are vaguely described and the sample of 5 participants with no demographic information is not representative. Domain 2 (data collection/analysis) is High because the 9-item questionnaire is neither described nor validated, and no data analysis methods are reported -- results are presented as qualitative summary judgments without transparent methodology. Domain 3 (interpretation) is High because while surface-level interpretations match the reported results, the absence of a limitations discussion and claims that go beyond the evidence (e.g., about thinking skills) are concerning. The study essentially constitutes a brief prototype evaluation with minimal methodological rigor rather than a systematic empirical evaluation of gamification effectiveness.

pdf_filename: Age of Computers An Innovative Combination of History and Computer Game Elements for Teaching Computer Fundamentals.pdf

bibliographic.title: Age of Computers: An Innovative Combination of History and Computer Game Elements for Teaching Computer Fundamentals
bibliographic.venue: 34th ASEE/IEEE Frontiers in Education Conference (FIE 2004)

study_characteristics.education_level: Higher education (2nd year M.Sc. program in computer science/telecommunications)
study_characteristics.sample_description: 246 enrolled students in a Computer Fundamentals course at NTNU; approximately 55% (134 students: 101 male, 33 female) completed the questionnaire. Students were a large, inhomogeneous class ranging from computer hobbyists with 6-8 years experience to novices with very little knowledge of computer fundamentals.
study_characteristics.study_design: Descriptive/evaluative case study with post-implementation survey (Likert-scale questionnaire) and analysis of player log data; no control group
study_characteristics.game_type: Online multiplayer educational game (web-based exercise environment with game elements)
study_characteristics.aim: To develop and evaluate an online multiplayer game-based exercise environment for teaching computer fundamentals, using computer history as a narrative framework, as a motivating alternative to traditional paper-based exercises for a large and inhomogeneous class

eligibility.concerns: This study is NOT about history education. It is about computer science education (computer fundamentals: computer architecture, digital logic, ALU operations, addressing modes, assembler coding). Computer history is used merely as a narrative framing device and organizational structure for the game levels (Mechanical Age, Vacuum Tube Age, Transistor Age, etc.), not as the subject matter being taught or assessed. The learning outcomes measured relate to computer science knowledge, not historical understanding. The authors explicitly state the goal is 'to teach computer fundamentals using history as a governing idea' -- history is the thematic wrapper, not the educational target.

rq1.conceptualization: The authors do not define gamification as a concept. They describe AoC as an 'educational computer game' and use the term 'edutainment' (combination of education and entertainment). The game incorporates elements inspired by real-time strategy games like Age of Empires II, including point scoring, levels/epochs, high-score lists, map exploration, collaborative chat, and narrative progression through computer history. The concept is closer to game-based learning than gamification per se.

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Likert-scale survey responses (5-point: Strongly Agree to Strongly Disagree); weekly question answering rates; percentage of correct answers by gender; relative effort per week tracked through points
rq2.statistical_results: Close to 95% of students strongly or somewhat agreed that 'AoC is more motivating than traditional exercises'. On learning effect compared to traditional exercises, the majority responded positively (Strongly Agree or Somewhat Agree), with female students slightly more positive than males despite less gaming experience. Female students answered an average of 45 questions/week vs. 35 for males; males had 70.1% correct answers vs. 65.5% for females. In a follow-up questionnaire months after the exam, 67% rated AoC on top for 'total learning', 16% rated auditorium lectures, and 14% rated textbook reading. AoC was clearly rated best for 'relative learning effect' (perceived learning per time spent).
rq2.comparative_methodology: No formal control group; comparisons were self-reported perceptions of AoC vs. traditional exercises, auditorium lectures, and textbook reading. Male vs. female student responses were compared.
rq2.key_outcomes: Very high motivation (95% agreed AoC more motivating than traditional exercises); majority perceived good learning effect; students spent slightly less time on AoC than exercises in other courses while perceiving greater learning; 67% rated AoC highest for total learning in follow-up survey; collaborative peer-to-peer learning via chat was heavily used; students preferred online assistant availability over physical lab presence
rq2.engagement_results: Students were highly engaged; high-score list motivated extra efforts; many students preferred working outside scheduled lab hours; chat functionality was extensively used for peer help; 'instant gratification' from immediate feedback was cited as key motivator; work patterns were strongly influenced by obligatory milestones (peaks at weeks 9, 13, 15)

game_design_elements: Points and scoring system
Levels/epochs (progression through historical periods)
High-score list / leaderboard
Map exploration with rooms/places
Narrative storyline (time travel through computer history)
Collaborative chat (one channel per epoch)
Immediate feedback on answers
Penalty delay for wrong answers (enforced waiting period)
Happy Hour mechanism (timed bonus questions in chat)
Obligatory milestones (progression checkpoints at weeks 9, 13, 15)
Progressive room unlocking based on player progress
Historical characters (e.g., meeting Charles Babbage)
More than 500 problems across four problem types
technological_platforms: Java chat applet and chat server
DARK assembler simulator (by Ola Ågren, Umeå University)
instructional_strategies: Collaborative learning via peer-to-peer chat support
Learning by doing (problem-solving in context)
Progressive difficulty and topic unlocking synchronized with lecture pace
Multiple problem types (multiple choice, number problems, ALU control signals, assembler coding)
Flexible learning environment (can be used as game or as online exercise database)
Teaching assistant support both in-game via chat and in physical labs
Exercise lectures complementing AoC content
Optional challenge problems for advanced students
rq3.content_integration: Computer history serves as the organizational framework: the game is divided into six historical epochs (Mechanical Age 1642-1945, Vacuum Tube Age 1945-1953, Transistor Age 1954-1965, Integrated Circuit Age 1965-1980, Present Time 1980-today, Future). Course content on computer fundamentals is distributed across these epochs with links to history where applicable, but presented in pace with lectures rather than strictly chronologically. Historical information is mixed with technical problems from the computer science syllabus.

implementation_barriers: Strong limitations of time and budget forced simple GUI for first version
Large and very inhomogeneous class (200-300 students with widely varying backgrounds)
Some students do not like computer games and resist non-traditional exercises
Need for sufficient teaching assistant support for large classes
Software written in Norwegian, requiring translation effort for broader adoption
Students tended to procrastinate without early milestones, requiring enforcement mechanisms
methodology_limitations: No control group for formal comparison of learning outcomes
Self-reported perceptions of learning effect rather than objective measures
Only 55% survey response rate
Too early to claim increased learning; only perceptual data available
First version prototype with limited time for refinement before deployment
Gender imbalance in survey respondents (101 male vs. 33 female)
negative_effects: Some students disliked the penalty delay mechanism for wrong answers (initially)
DARK assembler problems were polarizing: most popular for some, most disliked for others
Some students viewed the game elements as unnecessary overhead unrelated to course content
mitigation_strategies: Designed AoC so game elements can be ignored; students can use it as an online textbook with interactive problems
Provided links to guide students through content without engaging with game aspects
Made difficult DARK problems optional to avoid frustrating less advanced students
Students accepted penalty delay after recognizing it promotes 'read, think and try' over 'trial and failure'
Plans for AoC-2 with improved maps, redesigned levels, more content, and stronger history-course links based on student feedback
Added early milestones in AoC-2 to prevent procrastination

domain1.q1_evidence: The study clearly describes the population: 246 students enrolled in a 2nd year Computer Fundamentals course at NTNU during fall 2003. Inclusion is straightforward (all enrolled students). The course context, student background variability, and division into groups are well described.
domain1.q2_evidence: Only 55% of enrolled students completed the questionnaire (134 out of 246). The non-response rate of 45% introduces potential selection bias, as students who enjoyed AoC may have been more likely to respond. Gender breakdown was heavily skewed (101 male vs. 33 female). The single-institution, single-course context limits generalizability.

domain2.q3_evidence: The questionnaire used Likert scales, which is a standard approach. However, the instrument is not described as validated. All outcome data relies on self-reported perceptions of learning and motivation rather than objective learning measures. Player log data (questions answered, correctness rates) provides some objective behavioral data but does not directly measure learning outcomes.
domain2.q4_evidence: Analysis is primarily descriptive (percentages, averages). No statistical tests are reported. No control group exists for comparison. The claim of learning effect is based on student self-report rather than pre-post testing or comparison with a control condition. Log data analysis is basic (averages, weekly distributions).

domain3.q5_evidence: The authors present findings cautiously, noting it is 'too early to claim that it increases learning' while highlighting that survey data is 'very promising'. They distinguish between motivation (strongly supported) and learning outcomes (tentatively supported). Negative aspects (e.g., polarizing DARK problems, students who dislike games) are also reported.
domain3.q6_evidence: Some limitations are acknowledged implicitly (e.g., first version prototype, need for improvements). However, the paper does not contain a formal limitations section. The lack of a control group and reliance on self-report are not explicitly discussed as methodological limitations. The potential for response bias in the 55% survey completion rate is not addressed.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study is primarily a descriptive case study of a first implementation without a control group. While it provides useful descriptive data on student perceptions and engagement patterns, the reliance on self-reported data, absence of statistical testing, lack of objective learning outcome measures, and 55% survey response rate all introduce concerns. The authors are appropriately cautious in their claims but do not formally discuss methodological limitations. Additionally, this study is about computer science education (not history education), which fundamentally affects its relevance to a systematic review on gamification of history education.

pdf_filename: The Game-based Learning Activity Integrating Board Game and Mobile Online Searching Tasks for History Learning.pdf

bibliographic.title: The Game-based Learning Activity Integrating Board Game and Mobile Online Searching Tasks for History Learning
bibliographic.venue: Proceedings of the 23rd International Conference on Computers in Education (ICCE 2015)
bibliographic.publisher: Asia-Pacific Society for Computers in Education

study_characteristics.sample_description: 74 students (41 males and 33 females) from 9th grade classes in one high school in Taoyuan city. All participants had not played this board game before.
study_characteristics.study_design: pre_post
study_characteristics.game_name: Historical Battleship (using the board game 'Voyage with Taiwan')
study_characteristics.aim: To explore students' flow experience in a game-based learning activity integrating a board game and mobile devices with online searching tasks for history learning, and to compare students' perceived learning processes at two stages (board game only vs. board game with mobile devices) to understand the influence of mobile devices on students' perceived learning process.

eligibility.concerns: This is a short conference paper (3 pages) with limited methodological detail. The study uses a within-subjects comparison of two stages rather than a traditional pre-post or experimental-control design. No actual learning achievement test was administered -- only self-reported perceived learning process indicators were measured. The statistical tests used (paired t-tests implied) are not explicitly named. No effect sizes are reported. The study is preliminary in nature, as acknowledged by the authors ('preliminary findings').

rq1.conceptualization: The study conceptualizes game-based learning (GBL) rather than gamification per se. GBL is framed as an approach that integrates board games and mobile devices to support history learning. The study draws on the 'mini-flipped GBL' model proposed by Hou, Chou, & Chen (2014), which designs GBL activities for 5-20 minutes that integrate learner autonomy and cognitive evaluation to promote learning motivation. The board game 'Voyage with Taiwan' was designed according to 'Taiwan historical education curriculum guideline, cognitive theories, scaffolding strategies, and social interaction theories.' The activity combined physical board game play with mobile-device-supported online information searching to enhance discussion, engagement, and history knowledge construction.
theoretical_frameworks: Flow theory (Csikszentmihalyi, via Kiili's Flow Scale for Games, 2006)

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Four perceived learning process indicators (self-reported, 1-5 scale): attention, cognitive engagement, discussion within group, and usefulness of history learning. Nine sub-dimensions of flow state measured via the Flow Scale for Games (Kiili, 2006) on a 5-point Likert scale (Cronbach's alpha = 0.93): challenge, goal, feedback, control, playability, concentration, time distortion, autotelic experience, and loss of self-consciousness.
rq2.statistical_results: Perceived learning process (Initiate Game Playing Stage vs. Mobile Devices Intervention Stage): Attention: M=3.41 (SD=1.281) vs. M=3.80 (SD=1.135), t=-2.776, p<0.05; Cognitive Engagement: M=2.88 (SD=1.170) vs. M=3.43 (SD=1.304), t=-2.907, p<0.05; Discussion within Groups: M=3.68 (SD=1.336) vs. M=4.08 (SD=1.070), t=-2.722, p<0.05; Usefulness of History Learning: M=3.45 (SD=1.240) vs. M=3.74 (SD=1.159), t=-2.191, p<0.05. Flow state scores (all above 3.0 median): Challenge M=3.85 (SD=0.81); Goal M=4.06 (SD=0.74); Feedback M=3.73 (SD=0.80); Control M=3.77 (SD=0.92); Playability M=3.47 (SD=0.76); Concentration M=3.84 (SD=0.77); Time distortion M=3.87 (SD=1.06); Autotelic experience M=3.85 (SD=0.84); Loss of self-consciousness M=3.09 (SD=0.99).
rq2.comparative_methodology: Within-subjects comparison of two stages of the same game activity: Stage 1 (initial game playing stage, 9 minutes, board game only) vs. Stage 2 (mobile devices intervention stage, 1 minute, board game with mobile device online searching). Paired t-tests were used to compare perceived learning process scores between the two stages. Flow experience was assessed descriptively by comparing all dimension means against the scale median (3.0).
rq2.key_outcomes: Students at the mobile devices intervention stage had significantly higher perceived attention, cognitive engagement, discussion within group, and usefulness of history learning compared with the initial game playing stage (all p<0.05). Students demonstrated flow scores higher than 3.0 (the median of the five-point Likert-type scale) across all nine flow dimensions, indicating high overall flow experience during the combined board game and mobile device activity.
rq2.engagement_results: Students demonstrated high flow experience when playing the board game combined with mobile devices, with all nine flow dimensions scoring above the scale median (3.0). The highest flow dimension was Goal (M=4.06), followed by Time distortion (M=3.87), Challenge and Autotelic experience (both M=3.85), Concentration (M=3.84), Control (M=3.77), Feedback (M=3.73), Playability (M=3.47), and Loss of self-consciousness (M=3.09). Discussion within group also increased significantly from M=3.68 to M=4.08 when mobile devices were introduced.

game_design_elements: Board game (physical card-based game 'Voyage with Taiwan')
Historical event cards (front: event name; back: date and story)
Chronological ordering task (arranging cards in correct historical sequence)
Group competition (teams compete for highest scores)
Time constraint (10-minute total game period)
Two-stage game structure (9 minutes board game only, 1 minute with mobile devices)
Score-based assessment (scores calculated based on card arrangement accuracy)
Mobile device integration for online information searching
Collaborative group discussion mechanics
technological_platforms: Physical board game ('Voyage with Taiwan' by TwoPlus Studio)
instructional_strategies: Game-based learning (GBL)
Mini-flipped GBL model (short 5-20 minute GBL activities integrating learner autonomy and cognitive evaluation)
Collaborative learning through group discussion and card arrangement
Scaffolded information access (restricting mobile search to the final minute to promote prior knowledge activation first)
Competition-based motivation (inter-group competition)
Active learning through physical manipulation of cards and discussion
Integration of self-directed online searching with board game play
Social knowledge construction through interpersonal interaction
rq3.content_integration: Historical content was integrated into the board game through event cards based on the Taiwan historical education curriculum. Each card featured the name of a historical event on the front and the date and story on the back. Players had to use their existing knowledge and group discussion to arrange events chronologically without initially seeing the answers (back of cards). In the final minute, mobile devices allowed students to search online for information to verify or correct their arrangements, blending physical game-based collaboration with technology-supported information seeking. The game design was based on Taiwan's historical education curriculum guidelines, ensuring alignment between game content and educational objectives.

implementation_barriers: Empirical research focusing on GBL that integrates board games, mobile learning, and online searching tasks is scarce, limiting available design guidance
Flipped-classroom implementation faces challenges in promoting students' self-learning motivation
The mobile device intervention stage was limited to only 1 minute, constraining the depth of online searching
methodology_limitations: Short conference paper (3 pages) with very limited methodological detail
No actual learning achievement test administered -- only self-reported perceived learning process indicators
Within-subjects comparison of two stages with unequal durations (9 minutes vs. 1 minute), potentially confounding time and novelty effects
No control group for comparison
Statistical test type not explicitly named (paired t-tests implied but not stated)
No effect sizes reported
Self-reported measures may not reflect actual cognitive engagement or learning
No reliability or validity information reported for the perceived learning process indicators (only flow scale Cronbach's alpha reported)
Sample drawn from a single high school in one city (Taoyuan), limiting generalizability
Authors acknowledge findings are 'preliminary'
No description of how groups were composed or whether group-level effects were accounted for in the analysis
The perceived learning process indicators were developed by the current study without reference to validation procedures
mitigation_strategies: Future research recommended to record and analyze students' learning process to investigate behavioral patterns using sequential analysis (e.g., Hou, 2015)
The mini-flipped GBL model was proposed as a strategy to address the challenge of promoting self-learning motivation in flipped classrooms

domain1.q1_evidence: The paper states 'The participants for this study were 74 students (including 41 males and 33 females) from 9th grade classes in one high school in Taoyuan city. All participants had not played this board game before.' While grade level, gender composition, location, and prior game experience are mentioned, no formal inclusion/exclusion criteria are articulated. It is unclear how or why this particular high school or these particular classes were selected. The phrase 'The students of one class were first divided into six groups randomly' suggests only one class was used, but the total of 74 students seems too large for a single class, creating ambiguity about whether one or multiple classes were involved.
domain1.q2_evidence: The sample of 74 ninth-grade students from a single high school in Taoyuan city, Taiwan, provides some demographic information but representativeness is unclear. The sample is a convenience sample from one school. No information about the school type (public/private), academic level, socioeconomic context, or how typical these students are of the broader population of Taiwanese 9th graders is provided. The sample size (n=74) is reasonable for a single-school study but limited for generalization.

domain2.q3_evidence: Two instruments were used: (1) perceived learning process indicators developed by the current study with four dimensions (attention, cognitive engagement, discussion within group, usefulness of history learning) scored 1-5, for which no reliability or validity data are reported; and (2) the Flow Scale for Games developed by Kiili (2006) with nine sub-dimensions on a five-point Likert scale, for which a Cronbach's alpha of 0.93 is reported. The flow scale is a published instrument with reported reliability, but the perceived learning process indicators appear to be ad hoc measures without established psychometric properties.
domain2.q4_evidence: The results present means, standard deviations, and t-values with significance levels (p<0.05) for the comparison of two stages, implying paired-samples t-tests were used, but the statistical test is never explicitly named. For the flow scale, only descriptive statistics (means and SDs) are reported. No effect sizes, confidence intervals, or assumption checks are reported. The unit of analysis is individual students, but students worked in groups, potentially violating the independence assumption of t-tests -- this is not discussed.

domain3.q5_evidence: The interpretations in the abstract and conclusion are consistent with the statistical results presented. The authors correctly report that 'students at the stage using board game with mobile device for online searching had more perceived attention, cognitive engagement, discussion within group, and usefulness of history learning, compared with the stage using the board game only' and that 'students also had high flow experience when playing this board game combined with mobile devices.' The conclusion appropriately characterizes the findings as 'preliminary' and does not overstate the results.
domain3.q6_evidence: No formal limitations section is included in this short conference paper. The authors briefly acknowledge the findings are 'preliminary' and suggest future research directions ('Future research can record and analyze students' learning process to investigate their behavioral patterns using sequential analysis'), but no explicit discussion of methodological limitations is provided. Key limitations such as the lack of a control group, the use of self-reported rather than objective learning measures, the unequal stage durations, the lack of validation of the perceived learning process indicators, and the single-school convenience sample are not acknowledged.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The overall risk of bias is rated High primarily due to concerns in Domains 2 and 3. Domain 1 (selection) is Unclear because the sample is described with basic demographics but lacks formal selection criteria and representativeness information. Domain 2 (data collection/analysis) is High because one of the two instruments (perceived learning process indicators) lacks any reported validity or reliability, the statistical methods are not explicitly named, no effect sizes are reported, and the nested data structure (students within groups) is not accounted for. Domain 3 (interpretation) is High because, although interpretations are consistent with results, no limitations are discussed despite significant methodological weaknesses (no control group, self-reported measures only, no actual learning achievement test, unequal stage durations, single school, ad hoc instruments). The brevity of this 3-page conference paper inherently limits the methodological detail that can be provided, but critical information about instrument validity and analytical choices is absent.

pdf_filename: The Pedagogical Application of Alternate Reality Games using Game-Based Learning to revisit history.pdf

bibliographic.title: The Pedagogical Application of Alternate Reality Games: Using Game-Based Learning to Revisit History
bibliographic.venue: International Journal of Game-Based Learning

study_characteristics.sample_description: Twenty-five players (approximately 14-15 years old) who were minors (under the age of eighteen). The DkIT Ethics Research Committee approved the research, while the parents or guardians provided their consent. On Day 1, nine players played; on Day 2, twelve players played; and on Day 3, four players played. Players were initially split into groups of three, while the Day 3 group comprised four players.
study_characteristics.study_design: mixed_methods
study_characteristics.aim: To outline how the creation of a Serious ARG, titled Plunkett's Pages, correlated the game play with the desired learning outcomes, motivated players to learn, and enriched player learning. The study also aimed to extract evaluation criteria from player reflections to enable novice ARG designers or educators to formatively evaluate an emerging ARG design.

eligibility.concerns: The study uses an Alternate Reality Game (ARG), which is a form of game-based learning rather than gamification in the strict sense (adding game elements to non-game contexts). However, ARGs are widely considered within the broader gamification/GBL domain. The study focuses on the 1916 Easter Rising in Irish history, making it clearly about history education. The quantitative results are limited to pre-post knowledge percentage comparisons without statistical significance testing.

rq1.explicit_definition: Alternate Reality Games (ARGs) are cross media narrative-based games that use the Internet as a central communications platform. The interactions of participants drive the progression and direction of the story and play experience. Boundaries between reality and fiction are disguised, as game designers ensure that the characters and scenarios react dynamically to player input. Working collaboratively, players collate a fragmented narrative by deciphering codes and clues.
rq1.conceptualization: The study conceptualizes game-based learning through the lens of Serious ARGs (Alternate Reality Games). A Serious ARG is distinguished from entertainment ARGs by having 'a primary objective to impart knowledge.' The study uses TINAG ('This Is Not A Game') as a core design philosophy where 'ARGs blur the lines of reality and fiction, asking players to suspend their disbelief and deem what they are experiencing as real.' The ARG is framed as a novel form of GBL that 'encourages critical thinking, develops problem-solving skills and fosters collaborative learning.' Game-based learning is operationalized through a cross-media narrative game that integrates multiple platforms (YouTube, Facebook, website with encrypted pages, audio recordings) to create an immersive historical learning experience. The study develops four evaluation criteria for educational ARG quality: Assessment, Feedback, Collaborative Learning, and Debriefing.
theoretical_frameworks: Design-based research (Offermann et al., 2009; Brown, 1992; Hevner, 2004; Sandoval and Bell, 2004; Wang and Hannafin, 2005)
TINAG (This Is Not A Game) philosophy

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Pre- and post-ARG knowledge questionnaire percentage scores (Questionnaire A). A benchmarking system was devised between the researcher and the teachers to maintain consistency and reliability when dealing with the players' pre- and post-game quantitative data.
rq2.statistical_results: The results of the comparative analysis indicated that all twenty-five players improved their knowledge. Indeed, all players showed a noteworthy increase in their post-ARG percentage scores with improvements of knowledge in Players 7, 30, 18 and 21 increasing significantly by 600%, 814%, 1020% and 1800% respectively.
rq2.comparative_methodology: Pre-post comparison of knowledge questionnaire scores administered before and after the ARG game play. No control group. Questionnaire A gathered quantitative data (pre- and post-game test results). A benchmarking system was devised between the researcher and the teachers to maintain consistency and reliability. Qualitative data was collected through participant-observation, Questionnaire C (enjoyment/learning factors), Questionnaire E (follow-up validation of evaluation criteria), and eight focus groups involving 3-4 participants per session, ranging from 40-75 minutes.
rq2.key_outcomes: All 25 players improved their knowledge of the 1916 Easter Rising after playing the ARG. Some players showed dramatic improvements (600%-1800% increases in knowledge percentage scores). The qualitative thematic analysis identified four key evaluation criteria that contributed to successful learning: Assessment, Feedback, Collaborative Learning, and Debriefing. Each of the 23 players who completed the follow-up Questionnaire E agreed with the interim evaluation criterion on Assessment.
rq2.engagement_results: Players were highly engaged with the collaborative, narrative-driven ARG. Key engagement factors identified through thematic analysis include: (1) The rewarding aspect of completing challenges 'sufficiently motivated and engaged players to continue playing, whilst also aiding the retention of information'; (2) Diversity of challenges retained player interest, bringing 'freshness' to the game; (3) Collaborative play enhanced focus and attentiveness -- players reported it was 'a lot better than classroom learning' and that they were 'more alert' than 'sitting down with a textbook'; (4) The TINAG philosophy successfully blurred fact/fiction boundaries, with players stating 'I thought Lucy Reilly was real. I couldn't really distinguish between what was fact and what was fiction'; (5) Feedback system motivated continued play and learning.

game_design_elements: Narrative-driven cross-media storytelling (fragmented narrative across multiple platforms)
TINAG (This Is Not A Game) philosophy -- blurring reality and fiction
Rabbit holes / trailheads (YouTube video blog as entry point)
Player-character interaction through multiple media (Facebook, email, website, audio)
