Narrative with white space (gaps in narrative developed by players through gameplay)
Agency (player control and influence over game progression)
Collaboration and community (hive mind, no single player can complete the game alone)
In-game assessments (crosswords, grids, encrypted codes, diverse challenge types)
Feedback system (immediate notification of performance after each assessment)
Debriefing session (post-game reflection to distinguish fact from fiction)
Code deciphering and puzzle solving
Encrypted webpages requiring clue-based progression
Time pressure (race against time to retrieve diary pages)
Progressive unlocking of content (page-by-page diary discovery)
technological_platforms: Custom website (www.plunkettspages.com) with encrypted pages and historical content
YouTube (video blog / rabbit hole featuring fictional character Lucy Reilly)
Facebook (character interaction platform for Lucy Reilly)
Audio recordings (dictaphone recording by fictional character Tom)
instructional_strategies: Game-based learning (GBL) via Serious ARG
Design-based research methodology (Offermann et al., 2009)
Collaborative learning through group play (groups of 3-4 players)
Problem-based learning (deciphering codes and clues to progress)
Experiential learning in high-fidelity and meaningful contexts
Cross-media narrative immersion (blending historical facts with fiction)
Formative assessment through diverse in-game challenges
Immediate constructive feedback on player performance
Post-game debriefing to distinguish factual and fictional elements
Peer-to-peer learning and knowledge sharing
Alignment of learning outcomes with game challenges (co-designed with educators)
Multi-day structured play sessions (3 days)
rq3.content_integration: Historical content about the 1916 Easter Rising was integrated into the ARG through a fictional narrative layered over real historical events. The website PlunkettsPages.com served as an online repository containing information about the Easter Rising, housing the hidden writings and diary entries of Joseph Plunkett (a real historical figure who was one of the seven members of the Irish Republican Brotherhood's Military Council). Players encountered the historical content through encrypted webpages that required deciphering codes and clues. The narrative framework involved a fictional 14-year-old girl (Lucy Reilly) whose grandfather (Tom) had a box of artefacts connected to the Easter Rising. This fictional wrapper motivated players to engage with genuine historical facts about the Easter Rising, including its aims, key figures, and events. The game challenges (crosswords, grids, code-breaking) were directly aligned with the historical learning outcomes, developed through open dialogue between the researcher and educators during the planning phase.

implementation_barriers: The Serious ARG field is relatively young and there exists little literature on instructional design models, on their use in schools or universities, or on how best to implement them
Linking a game and its challenges with learning outcomes, assessment, or formal education is a complex matter
The TINAG philosophy creates potential confusion for players between factual and fictional elements, requiring careful debriefing
Debriefing defies the ethos of TINAG (allowing post-game discussions breaks the 'this is not a game' illusion), yet is necessary for learning
Balancing collaboration with competition is an important design consideration -- some players wanted more competition while others feared it would reduce learning quality
Initial bouts of competitiveness between groups had to be overcome before effective collaboration emerged
methodology_limitations: No control group -- all 25 players received the ARG intervention with no comparison to traditional instruction
Small sample size (n=25) from a single school context
Pre-post knowledge percentage improvements reported without formal statistical significance testing (no p-values, t-tests, or effect sizes)
Unequal group sizes across the three days (9, 12, and 4 players) with no discussion of potential day effects
Sample limited to minors (14-15 year olds) at a single institution (DkIT campus), limiting generalizability
No validated pre/post knowledge assessment instrument described -- only 'a benchmarking system devised between the researcher and the teachers'
Questionnaire E for validation of evaluation criteria was completed by only 23 of the 25 players
The percentage improvement figures (600%-1800%) may reflect very low baseline scores rather than meaningful absolute gains
Observer as participant role may have influenced player behavior (Hawthorne effect)
No inter-rater reliability reported for the thematic analysis
The study does not report actual pre and post scores, only percentage improvements for selected players
negative_effects: Some players expressed concern that competition could reduce learning: 'if competition was brought into the game, we would have really rushed through the game...you'd just find things here and there and skip other things' (EP20L115)
Players had difficulty distinguishing fact from fiction: 'I thought Lucy Reilly was real. I couldn't really distinguish between what was fact and what was fiction and who was real' (P13L153)
Without debriefing, players' knowledge of factual vs. fictional elements would have been 'mixed up' (EP29L134)
mitigation_strategies: Post-game debriefing sessions to explicitly distinguish factual and fictional elements of the ARG
Open dialogue between researcher and educators during planning to align learning outcomes with game challenges
Benchmarking system between researcher and teachers for consistency in assessment
Collaborative play as dominant mechanism (rather than competition) to support learning
Constructive and positive feedback at all times to motivate continued play
Ethics committee approval and parental consent for research with minors
Follow-up Questionnaire E to validate interim evaluation criteria with players

domain1.q1_evidence: The paper states that 'Plunkett's Pages is a Serious ARG, created from November 2012 to March 2013, which provided twenty-five players (approximately 14-15 years old) with the means to learn about the events surrounding the 1916 Easter Rising through the medium of play.' A footnote notes 'Minors (those under the age of eighteen) were the research population for the study. The DkIT Ethics Research Committee approved the research, while the parents or guardians provided their consent.' However, no formal inclusion/exclusion criteria are described, and it is unclear how these 25 players were recruited or selected from the broader school population.
domain1.q2_evidence: The sample consists of 25 players aged approximately 14-15 at the DkIT campus in Ireland, playing in a computer laboratory. No information is provided about the school type, demographic composition, academic ability levels, or how representative these students are of the broader Irish secondary school population. The sample is a convenience sample from a single site. Unequal group sizes across three days (9, 12, and 4 players) further complicate representativeness.

domain2.q3_evidence: Multiple data collection methods were used: (1) Pre- and post-game questionnaires (Questionnaire A) for knowledge testing, with 'a benchmarking system devised between the researcher and the teachers' for consistency and reliability, but no formal validity/reliability metrics are reported; (2) Participant-observation following the 'observer as participant' role (Saunders et al., 2009); (3) Questionnaire C on enjoyment/learning factors; (4) Questionnaire E for follow-up evaluation criteria validation; (5) Eight focus groups of 3-4 participants, 40-75 minutes each. While the mixed-method approach provides triangulation, none of the questionnaire instruments report psychometric properties (Cronbach's alpha, test-retest reliability, content validity).
domain2.q4_evidence: The qualitative analysis used Braun and Clarke's (2006) six phases of thematic analysis, which is a well-established method. However, the quantitative analysis is poorly described: only percentage improvements are reported for selected players (600%, 814%, 1020%, 1800%) without reporting actual scores, means, standard deviations, or any inferential statistics. No formal statistical tests were applied to the pre-post comparison. The qualitative findings are well-structured with extensive participant quotes, but no inter-rater reliability is reported for the thematic coding process.

domain3.q5_evidence: The interpretations are broadly consistent with the data presented. The quantitative claim that 'all twenty-five players improved their knowledge' is supported by reporting that all players showed post-ARG increases. The four evaluation criteria (Assessment, Feedback, Collaborative Learning, Debriefing) are well-supported by extensive player quotes and follow-up validation through Questionnaire E. The conclusion appropriately frames the findings as 'lessons' from a case study rather than making strong causal claims. The discussion section correctly ties findings back to existing literature on GBL and ARGs.
domain3.q6_evidence: The paper does not include a formal limitations section. No explicit acknowledgment is made of the lack of a control group, the small sample size, the absence of statistical testing for the pre-post comparison, the single-site convenience sample, or the potential Hawthorne effect from the researcher-observer presence. The gap in the market for 'a comprehensive study of what makes a Serious ARG a pedagogically sound, teaching tool' is acknowledged, but the study's own methodological limitations are not discussed.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The overall risk of bias is rated High. Domain 1 (selection) is Unclear because while the sample is described (25 players, aged 14-15, at DkIT campus), no formal selection criteria or representativeness information is provided. Domain 2 (data collection/analysis) is High because the knowledge assessment instrument lacks any reported psychometric properties, the quantitative results are limited to percentage improvements without statistical significance testing or reporting of actual scores, and no inter-rater reliability is reported for the thematic analysis. Domain 3 (interpretation) is High because, although the interpretations are consistent with the presented data, no limitations are discussed despite significant methodological concerns including the absence of a control group, small convenience sample, no formal statistical analysis, and potential observer effects. The study provides rich qualitative insights and useful evaluation criteria for ARG design, but the quantitative evidence for learning effectiveness is weak.

pdf_filename: The Utilization of History Module in the Development of Multiculturalism-Based Team Games Tournament Model.pdf

bibliographic.title: The Utilization of History Module in the Development of Multiculturalism-Based Team Games Tournament Model to Improve the Bhineka Attitudes on 10th Grade Students in SMA Erlangga Pematangsiantar
bibliographic.venue: Budapest International Research and Critics Institute-Journal (BIRCI-Journal)
bibliographic.publisher: Budapest International Research and Critics Institute

study_characteristics.sample_description: 10th grade students at SMA Erlangga Pematangsiantar High School, divided into an experimental group (24 students) and a control group (24 students, Class X IPA). The study focused on history education within the 2013 Curriculum framework in Indonesia.
study_characteristics.study_design: quasi_experimental
study_characteristics.aim: To produce alternative teaching materials in the form of a multiculturalism-based TGT model history module for increasing the diversity attitudes of students at Erlangga Pematangsiantar High School, and to increase learning resources in the classroom and innovate learning media.

eligibility.concerns: The study uses Team Games Tournament (TGT), which is a cooperative learning model with game/tournament elements rather than digital gamification. TGT incorporates competitive tournament-style game mechanics (team competition, scoring, tournament rounds) applied to history education. While the gamification elements are non-digital and embedded in a cooperative learning structure, TGT is a recognized form of game-based learning. The study is primarily a development research (R&D) study that also includes an effectiveness test. The focus is on multiculturalism/diversity attitudes in history education rather than purely on historical knowledge acquisition.

rq1.conceptualization: The study conceptualizes gamification through the Team Games Tournament (TGT) cooperative learning model, which incorporates tournament-based competition among student teams in history class. TGT is used as a pedagogical framework where students compete in teams through structured academic tournaments. The TGT model is combined with a multiculturalism-based history module covering local culture (Siantar City Multiculturalism) to develop students' diversity attitudes. The approach merges cooperative/competitive learning with contextual, rational, and scientific approaches, elaborated through a Learning Implementation Plan. The competitive nature of TGT is positioned as an alternative to developing a competitive attitude within a multicultural framework.
theoretical_frameworks: Borg and Gall's theory of development (R&D)
Team Games Tournament (TGT) cooperative learning model (Slavin, 2010)

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Cognitive domain pre-test/post-test scores, affective domain attitude scale questionnaire scores (pre-post), material expert validation scores (content and language components), independent sample t-test for between-group comparison, paired sample t-test for within-group comparison.
rq2.statistical_results: Independent sample t test (cognitive): t_count > t_table (3.101 > 1.711) so H0 is rejected and H1 is accepted, indicating a difference in the mean cognitive scores of the experimental and control group students. Independent sample t test (attitude scale): t_count > t_table (2.527 > 1.711) so H0 is rejected and H1 is accepted, indicating diversity attitudes of students who use the history module are higher than students who use conventional models. Paired sample t test (cognitive domain, experimental group): t_count (-6.271) < -t_table (-1.711), H0 rejected. Paired sample t test (affective domain, experimental group): t_count (-3.698) < -t_table (-1.711), H0 rejected. Paired Samples Test (attitude scale, experimental group): Mean difference = -1.542, SD = 2.043, t = -3.698, df = 23, Sig. (2-tailed) = .001. Paired Samples Test (attitude scale, control group): Mean difference = -2.208, SD = 2.187, t = -4.948, df = 23, Sig. (2-tailed) = .000. Kolmogorov-Smirnov normality test: Pre-questionnaire significance = 0.230, Post-questionnaire significance = 0.885. Expert validation: content component average score = 8.8, language component average score = 8.6, total average = 8.7 ('Highly Valid'). Normality test significance values: X1 (post-test A) = 0.305, Y1 (post-questionnaire A) = 0.885, X2 (post-test B) = 0.367, Y2 (post-questionnaire B) = 0.327. Homogeneity test for post-test (cognitive) = 0.5.
rq2.comparative_methodology: Quasi-experimental design with experimental group (n=24, using multiculturalism-based TGT history module) and control group (n=24, Class X IPA, using conventional models). Independent sample t-tests compared between-group differences on cognitive scores and attitude scale scores. Paired sample t-tests compared within-group pre-post differences for both the experimental and control groups. Normality verified via Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Shapiro-Wilk tests; homogeneity verified via Levene's Variance Homogeneity Test. Statistical analysis performed using SPSS Version 19.
rq2.key_outcomes: Students using the multiculturalism-based TGT history module showed significantly higher cognitive scores and diversity attitudes compared to students using conventional models. The experimental group showed significant pre-to-post improvement in both cognitive domain (paired t = -6.271) and affective domain (paired t = -3.698, p = .001). The control group also showed significant pre-to-post improvement in attitude scores (paired t = -4.948, p = .000). The expert-validated module achieved 'Highly Valid' status with an average score of 8.7 out of 10.

game_design_elements: Team-based competition (Team Games Tournament structure)
Tournament rounds with academic content
Team scoring and performance comparison
Group discussion and collaboration within teams
Competitive academic games between groups
technological_platforms: Learning videos integrated into classroom instruction
instructional_strategies: Team Games Tournament (TGT) cooperative learning model
Multiculturalism-based content integration (local culture of Siantar City)
Contextual, rational, and scientific approaches combined with TGT learning steps
Dick & Carey instructional design model adapted with Borg and Gall development procedures
Expert validation process (content and language components)
Readability/legibility testing (one-to-one, small group, large group)
Pre-test and post-test assessment
Attitude scale questionnaire (pre-post)
Learning Implementation Plan (RPP)
Needs analysis based on teacher and student learning needs
Integration of local issues and regional cultural potential into history curriculum
rq3.content_integration: Historical content about local multiculturalism in Pematangsiantar/Siantar City was integrated into a specially developed history module aligned with the Indonesian 2013 Curriculum (K13). The module addressed the concept of diversity through topics including human interaction in relation to religious symbolism, the concept of diversity, diversity of ethnic groups, cultures and religious systems, tolerance of worship as part of societal multiculturalism, government policies, and tradition (local wisdom). The content was designed to connect national curriculum Core Competencies and Basic Competencies with local cultural themes, allowing students to learn about their regional socio-cultural heritage through the competitive TGT model structure. The module went through a multi-stage development process: problem identification, design, deployment, expert validation (Draft A through D), one-to-one legibility test, small group legibility test, large group legibility test, and final revision.

implementation_barriers: Lack of teaching materials for running the TGT learning model in history classes
Teacher-centered characteristics in history learning at Erlangga High School, with dominant lecture-based instruction
Lack of reading culture among students leading to limited insight
Limited and not yet optimal learning innovation from teachers
School policy prohibiting students from bringing mobile phones and Android devices, limiting access to digital learning media
Limited history of learning media use including minimal multimedia-based resources
No History laboratory available at the school
Discussion activities rarely implemented optimally in class despite 2013 Curriculum demands
Students not understanding the learning model concept; reluctance to engage in group discussions
Teacher difficulty dividing time across activity stages during initial trial
methodology_limitations: Small sample size (n=24 per group) from a single school
Only formative evaluation conducted (up to step 9 of Dick & Carey model); no summative evaluation
Single school site (SMA Erlangga Pematangsiantar) limits generalizability
Control group descriptive statistics (Table 6) show different baseline means from experimental group, suggesting potential selection bias
No random assignment described; groups appear to be intact classes
No effect size reported
Attitude scale questionnaire psychometric properties not reported (no Cronbach's alpha or validity evidence beyond expert validation)
The control group also showed significant improvement (t = -4.948, p = .000), which complicates interpretation of the intervention's unique effect
No description of what 'conventional model' entailed for the control group
negative_effects: Student participation was minimal during initial trial; enthusiasm dominated by a few students
Discussion process was not going well initially
Students reluctant to group with those who were not close friends
Male students joked around too much during discussions and presentations
Students did not understand what was meant by the learning model
mitigation_strategies: Development of dedicated multiculturalism-based history module as alternative teaching material
Multi-stage module validation process (expert validation, one-to-one, small group, large group legibility tests)
Integration of learning videos to maintain student attention and engagement
Discussion and recommendations with teachers to activate students and develop strategies for material understanding
Needs analysis conducted to align module with actual teacher and student requirements
Combining TGT learning steps with contextual, rational, and scientific approaches

domain1.q1_evidence: The study describes participants as '10th Grade Students in SMA Erlangga Pematangsiantar' with experimental and control groups of 24 students each, but no formal inclusion/exclusion criteria are described. The control group is identified as 'Class X IPA' but no equivalent specification is given for the experimental class. No information is provided about how students were assigned to experimental vs. control conditions or whether intact classes were used.
domain1.q2_evidence: The sample comes from a single private high school (SMA Erlangga) in Pematangsiantar, Indonesia, with only 24 students per group. The control group descriptive statistics (Table 6: Pre-questionnaire Mean = 67.25, SD = 6.102) differ notably from the experimental group statistics (Table 3: Pre-questionnaire Mean = 71.00, SD = 4.845), suggesting non-equivalent groups at baseline. No demographic information beyond grade level is provided, and results from a single school in a specific Indonesian city cannot be generalized to broader populations.

domain2.q3_evidence: The study used pre-test/post-test instruments for cognitive assessment and an attitude scale questionnaire for the affective domain. The module itself was validated by material experts who scored content (8.8/10) and language (8.6/10) components, achieving 'Highly Valid' status based on Akbar (2015) criteria. However, no psychometric properties (Cronbach's alpha, test-retest reliability, construct validity) are reported for the cognitive test or the attitude scale questionnaire. The normality of data was tested using Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Shapiro-Wilk tests, and homogeneity was tested via Levene's test, but instrument validity/reliability is not established.
domain2.q4_evidence: Statistical analysis methods are clearly described and justified: 'The model's effectiveness test used a parametric type statistical test, including the independent sample t test and paired sample t test.' Prerequisite tests were conducted including 'the Normality Test and Lavene's Variance Homogeneity Test.' The Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Shapiro-Wilk normality tests confirmed normal distribution (all sig. > 0.05), and homogeneity was confirmed (sig. = 0.5 > 0.05). Analysis was performed using SPSS Version 19. Descriptive statistics, paired samples correlations, and paired samples tests are presented in full tabular form with means, standard deviations, confidence intervals, t-values, df, and significance levels.

domain3.q5_evidence: The interpretations are consistent with the statistical results presented. The conclusion that 'the history module is able to develop students' diversity attitudes' is supported by significant independent sample t-test results (t_count 2.527 > t_table 1.711) and paired sample t-test results (t = -3.698, p = .001). The conclusion that there is 'a difference in the mean cognitive scores of the experimental and control group students' is supported by the independent sample t-test (t_count 3.101 > t_table 1.711). The expert validation conclusion of 'Highly Valid' is supported by documented scores of 8.8 and 8.6 averaging to 8.7.
domain3.q6_evidence: The paper does not contain any explicit limitations section or discussion of methodological limitations. There is no acknowledgment of the small sample size, single-site design, lack of random assignment, absence of instrument reliability/reliability reporting, the fact that only formative (not summative) evaluation was conducted, or the complication that the control group also showed significant pre-post improvement. The challenges encountered during implementation (e.g., minimal student participation, discussion difficulties) are described as observational findings rather than framed as methodological limitations.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The overall risk of bias is rated High. Domain 1 (selection) is High because participant selection criteria are not described, groups appear non-equivalent at baseline (experimental group mean 71.00 vs. control group mean 67.25 on pre-questionnaire), and there is no evidence of randomization. Domain 2 (data collection/analysis) is Unclear because while statistical analysis methods are well-described and appropriate (independent and paired t-tests with prerequisite normality and homogeneity testing via SPSS), the cognitive test and attitude scale instruments lack any reported psychometric properties. Domain 3 (interpretation) is High because although interpretations are consistent with the presented statistical results, no limitations whatsoever are acknowledged despite significant methodological concerns including non-equivalent groups, small convenience sample from a single school, no random assignment, no instrument reliability evidence, and the complication that the control group also showed significant improvement. The study is primarily a development research (R&D) study focused on module creation, with the effectiveness testing being secondary and methodologically limited.

pdf_filename: Towards an Online Multiplayer Serious Game Providing a Joyful Experience in Learning Art History.pdf

bibliographic.title: Towards an Online Multiplayer Serious Game Providing a Joyful Experience in Learning Art History
bibliographic.venue: 2011 Third International Conference on Games and Virtual Worlds for Serious Applications (VS-GAMES)

study_characteristics.sample_description: A usability test session with two adults and two juveniles; no further demographic details provided
study_characteristics.study_design: descriptive
study_characteristics.aim: To introduce the design and prototype of the online multiplayer Serious Game ThIATRO that helps students learn art history by combining aspects of learning and fun in an immersive 3D environment, fostering collaborative learning, and raising interest in art history, contemporary culture and cultural heritage

eligibility.concerns: The paper is primarily a design/prototype description paper rather than a full empirical evaluation. The only empirical component is a minimal usability test with 4 participants (2 adults, 2 juveniles). The focus is on art history specifically, not general history education. No formal learning outcomes or quantitative evaluation data are reported. The paper describes a planned future evaluation but has not yet conducted it. The study is borderline as a primary study since it is largely a system description with only informal usability feedback.

rq1.explicit_definition: The term Serious Game describes a game designed for a primary purpose other than pure entertainment.
rq1.conceptualization: The study does not provide an explicit definition of gamification per se, but conceptualizes their approach through the lens of Serious Games. The game-based learning approach is conceptualized as combining entertainment with educational objectives, where learning occurs as 'collateral learning' (citing Zyda) or 'stealth learning' -- i.e., learning that happens incidentally as a consequence of game activity rather than formal teaching. The paper frames ThIATRO as a tool that 'not only increases the motivation to learn but also compels the player to think about, organize and use information in ways that encourage active construction of knowledge.'
theoretical_frameworks: Constructivism (knowledge is constructed, not transmitted; learners play an active role)
Collateral learning (Zyda 2005) - learning that happens by mechanisms other than formal teaching
Stealth learning (Johnson et al. 2007) - learning occurs as an incidental consequence of game activity
Motivation guidelines (Greitzer et al. 2007) - leveling-up, clear goals, interaction with other players, shared experience

rq2.comparative_methodology: The paper describes a planned future evaluation: 'We will split up the test group into an experimental group that plays the game, and a control group that is taught using prevalent methods such as classroom teaching. In the end, both results will be compared to get an insight in the learning success of ThIATRO.' However, this evaluation had not yet been conducted at the time of publication.
rq2.key_outcomes: Only informal usability feedback from a test session with 4 participants is reported. The test 'showed first positive results concerning the style of the game level and the presentation of the learning content.' No formal learning outcomes were measured.
rq2.engagement_results: The usability test showed 'first positive results concerning the style of the game level and the presentation of the learning content.' Players provided qualitative feedback about navigation difficulties due to limited house textures and HUD obstructing the view of paintings.

game_design_elements: Capture the Flag game mechanic (two teams compete to find and capture artwork)
Team-based multiplayer competition
Power-ups (upgrade player abilities such as 'increase speed', provide location hints, or complicate opponent's search)
Leveling-up through power-up collection
Scoring system (team scores compared after every round; winner team receives an award)
Mission/quest system (assignments displayed in HUD at all times)
Three assignment types of increasing difficulty (find any painting by artist; find specific artwork; identify painting from thumbnail only)
Time-limited rounds
First-person 3D exploration
Head-Up Display (HUD) with current mission tasks
Role-playing element (player assumes role of art thief)
Avatar with first-person view control (mouse and WASD keys)
technological_platforms: Unity Game Engine (3D multiplayer game engine, web-based deployment)
Google 3D Warehouse (source of existing 3D building models)
Web browser (game runs in browser window)
Web Gallery of Art (data source for ~18,000 artworks by ~2,200 European artists, 1100-1850)
Getty Union List of Artist Names (ULAN) (contextual information on artists and their relations)
instructional_strategies: Constructivist learning through active exploration and manipulation of virtual environment
Stealth/collateral learning - learning occurs incidentally through game activity
Collaborative learning through team-based gameplay and multiplayer interaction
Contextual embedding of learning content (art movements linked to architectural building styles)
Scaffolded difficulty through three types of assignments (artist recognition, specific artwork identification, visual memory)
Chunking of information - material organized into small comprehensible units (one artifact/era per game turn)
Competitive motivation through team-vs-team gameplay
rq3.content_integration: Art historical content is deeply integrated with the game mechanics. The game world is a fictitious town resembling inner districts of Vienna, containing different buildings that act as virtual museums. Each museum building architecturally represents a specific era in art history (e.g., a virtual replica of a baroque church holds paintings by baroque artists like Caravaggio or Rubens), with banners indicating the era. Players must apply knowledge of art movements, artists, and their works to locate and 'capture' the correct paintings. The Web Gallery of Art provides ~18,000 artworks covering 1100-1850, and the Getty ULAN provides relational context between artists (e.g., 'Caravaggio was influenced by Angelo Caroselli'). Three assignment types progressively test different aspects: painting style recognition, artist-artwork association, and visual memory.

implementation_barriers: Limited number of house textures causing players to get lost in the 3D world
HUD blocking players' view of paintings in the galleries
Need to keep polygon count low for browser-based performance without lags
Need to scale down from 18,000 paintings to a manageable subset for evaluation
Game logic implementation was incomplete at time of publication
methodology_limitations: Only an informal usability test with 4 participants (2 adults, 2 juveniles) was conducted
No formal evaluation of learning outcomes
No control group comparison
No pre-test/post-test design
No quantitative data collected or reported
Game logic and data integration were not yet complete at time of publication
The paper is primarily a design description, not a completed empirical study
negative_effects: Risk of players getting lost in the 3D world due to limited environmental variety
HUD obstructing view of paintings during gallery exploration
mitigation_strategies: Planned integration of a mini-map into the HUD to help navigation
Planned placement of guideposts in the game level
Planned functionality to hide/unhide the HUD at the push of a button
Planned future evaluation with experimental and control groups to assess learning effectiveness

domain1.q1_evidence: No selection criteria are described for the test session participants. The paper states only: 'A usability test session with two adults and two juveniles showed first positive results.' No recruitment method, inclusion/exclusion criteria, or demographic details are provided.
domain1.q2_evidence: The sample consists of only 4 participants (2 adults and 2 juveniles) with no description of their background, prior gaming experience, or art history knowledge. This is not representative of the target population (grammar school students in Austria). The paper targets students until 6th grade in grammar schools (about 16 years), but the test group composition and representativeness are unknown.

domain2.q3_evidence: No validated data collection instruments were used. The usability test is described in a single paragraph with no mention of questionnaires, observation protocols, or any structured data collection method. Only informal qualitative feedback is reported.
domain2.q4_evidence: No data analysis methods are described. The results of the usability test are reported as brief qualitative observations ('showed first positive results concerning the style of the game level and the presentation of the learning content') without any systematic analysis, coding, or quantitative measures.

domain3.q5_evidence: The paper does not overstate its findings -- it appropriately frames the usability test as showing 'first positive results' and acknowledges the need for future formal evaluation. The authors state: 'As soon as ThIATRO is finished, it will be crucial to evaluate the game with respect to playability, level of fun and the learning effect.' However, the evidence base is so thin that any interpretation is essentially unsupported.
domain3.q6_evidence: The paper implicitly acknowledges limitations by framing the work as a prototype and describing planned future evaluation: 'As soon as ThIATRO is finished, it will be crucial to evaluate the game with respect to playability, level of fun and the learning effect. We plan to conduct the evaluation together with a group of students.' The paper also acknowledges specific design limitations identified in the test session (navigation difficulties, HUD issues).

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study has high overall risk of bias because it is fundamentally a prototype design description, not an empirical evaluation. The only empirical component is an informal usability test with 4 participants, with no structured data collection instruments, no formal analysis methods, and no learning outcome measures. There is no control group, no pre-test/post-test design, and no quantitative results. The participant selection is entirely undocumented. While the authors appropriately acknowledge the preliminary nature of their work and plan for future formal evaluation, the current evidence base is insufficient for drawing any conclusions about the effectiveness of the game for learning art history.

pdf_filename: Using Learning Games to Teach Texas Civil War History to Public Middle School Students.pdf

bibliographic.title: Using Learning Games to Teach Texas Civil War History to Public Middle School Students
bibliographic.venue: IEEE Conference on Games (CoG)

study_characteristics.sample_description: 8th grade public middle school students in a local Texas history class. 56 students took the pretest but only 33 completed the full experiment (17 in the game group, 16 in the text packet group). Students were minors requiring parental consent and student assent forms.
study_characteristics.study_design: experimental
study_characteristics.aim: To compare an educational video game (The War of the Rebellion) designed to teach about the Battles of Galveston with a textual information packet in their ability to increase learning gain and interest in 8th grade public middle school students studying Texas Civil War history

eligibility.concerns: The study has a relatively small sample size (33 completers) and lacks some methodological rigor (e.g., unequal time-on-task between conditions, no delayed posttest). However, it is a genuine primary empirical study of a game-based learning intervention for history education with quantitative outcome measures.

rq1.conceptualization: The study conceptualizes the intervention as a 'learning game' or 'educational video game' rather than using the term 'gamification' explicitly. The approach is game-based learning where a purpose-built video game is used as an instructional tool to supplement a traditional Texas history lesson. The game is framed as an alternative to textbook-style learning, with the core idea that gameplay mechanics should closely mirror the desired learning outcomes. The authors emphasize that games should be 'created in close collaboration with the instructor with gameplay emphasis on the most important concepts.'

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Pre-post test scores on a 10-question knowledge survey about the Battles of Galveston (each question worth one point). Three additional posttest Likert-scale items measuring interest in learning about history, interest in learning about the Civil War, and likelihood of recommending the tool to a friend (5-point scale: much less interested, less interested, no change, more interested, much more interested).
rq2.statistical_results: Overall learning gain: text packet group showed 3.7 point improvement; game group showed 2.6 point improvement. One-tailed t-test: p = 0.91, t = 1.76 (no significant difference favoring game). Fischer's exact test on individual questions: Question 5 ('What strategy did the Confederate forces use to attack Galveston during the second battle of Galveston?') showed statistically significant difference favoring game, p = .0007. Mann Whitney U test on Likert data: 'share this learning tool with a friend' -- p = 0.002, U = 58.5, Cohen's d = 1.112 (between large and very large effect); 'interested in learning about the Civil War' -- p = 0.065, U = 93.5, effect size = 0.553 (medium); 'interested in learning about history' -- p = 0.075, U = 95.5, effect size = 0.525 (medium).
rq2.comparative_methodology: Randomized experimental design comparing game group (n=17) vs. text packet control group (n=16). Students were randomly assigned based on seating. Both groups took the same pretest and posttest. One-tailed t-test was used for overall learning gain comparison; Fischer's exact test was used for question-by-question analysis; one-tailed Mann Whitney U test was used for ordinal Likert scale interest data.
rq2.key_outcomes: The game did not produce significantly greater overall learning gains compared to the text packet. However, the question most closely tied to the gameplay (Question 5, about Confederate attack strategy in the second Battle of Galveston) showed a statistically significant learning gain for game players (p = .0007). Game players also reported significantly higher likelihood of sharing the learning tool with a friend (p = 0.002, Cohen's d = 1.112) and marginally higher interest in learning about the Civil War (p = 0.065) and history generally (p = 0.075).
rq2.engagement_results: Game participants reported statistically significantly higher likelihood of wanting to share the learning tool with a friend (p = 0.002, U = 58.5, Cohen's d = 1.112). Game participants reported marginally significantly higher interest in learning about the Civil War (p = 0.065, U = 93.5, effect size = 0.553) and in learning about history (p = 0.075, U = 95.5, effect size = 0.525). The authors note: 'The sole experience of getting to play in class greatly excited the students, whose enthusiasm seems to extend to a greater interest in the subject material.'

game_design_elements: Two-stage strategic gameplay (defense placement then scouting/attack)
Historical role-playing (player takes role of Confederate army in both stages)
Strategic decision-making (placing defenses at key locations, allocating scouts and troops)
Fog of war mechanic (concealment of enemy positions requiring scouting)
Win/lose conditions based on historical accuracy of tactical decisions
Narrative feedback after each stage (description of the actual battle and aftermath)
Historical maps and period artwork (game board from Baylor Texas Civil War map archive; unit pictures from era drawings)
Limited resource allocation (limited number of scouting units; artillery of different calibers and firing arcs)
Success/failure feedback tied to historical events (Union attack unfolded both by land and sea)
technological_platforms: Desktop PC (game installed on machines set up in the classroom)
Baylor Texas Civil War map archive (source for historical map imagery)
instructional_strategies: Close collaboration between game developers and classroom teacher on game design and survey design
Gameplay mechanics aligned with key learning outcomes (gameplay emphasis on most important concepts)
Experiential learning through simulated historical decision-making
Pre-test/post-test assessment design with 10-question knowledge survey
Comparison with traditional textbook-style information packet (two-page text with pictures)
Integration into regular class period as supplementary learning activity
Active learning through strategic placement and tactical decision-making rather than passive reading
rq3.content_integration: Historical content was deeply integrated with game mechanics across two stages. In Stage 1, players learned about the first Battle of Galveston by taking the role of the Confederate army and placing defenses (artillery of different calibers and firing arcs) at predefined locations based on actual historical defenses around the Port of Galveston. Success or failure was determined by how the Union attack actually unfolded, both by land and sea. In Stage 2, players learned about the second Battle of Galveston by controlling the attacking Confederate army, using limited scouting units to reveal port defenses hidden by fog of war, then allocating troops to attack locations. After each stage, players received a textual description of the actual battle and its aftermath. The game board used authentic historical maps from the Baylor Texas Civil War map archive, and unit images were drawings from the Civil War era. The information packet created by the teacher collaborator contained the same instructional content as the game.

implementation_barriers: Time constraints of a single class period limited the number of students who could complete the full experiment (only 33 of 56 finished)
Limited number of computer stations required students to go in waves to play the game
The game took 10-15 minutes to complete while the text packet took only a few minutes to read, creating unequal time-on-task between conditions
Parental consent and student assent forms required for minor participants
Game required two undergraduate students (one computer science, one museum studies) for development
methodology_limitations: Small sample size (33 completers: 17 game, 16 text packet) with significant attrition from original 56 participants

Unequal time-on-task between conditions: game took 10-15 minutes while text packet took only a few minutes, creating a confound where text packet participants had information fresh in short-term memory during posttest
No delayed posttest to measure long-term retention
Random assignment based on seating rather than true randomization
Only measured short-term recall, not deep understanding or long-term learning
No control for time delay between treatment and posttest across conditions
Single class in a single school limits generalizability
negative_effects: Overall learning gain was lower for game participants (2.6 points) than text packet participants (3.7 points), though the difference was not statistically significant and may be due to the time-on-task confound
mitigation_strategies: Authors recommend ensuring participants in both groups have an equal amount of time before posttest evaluation in future studies
Authors recommend that learning games should be created in close collaboration with the instructor with gameplay emphasis on the most important concepts
Designing game mechanics to closely mirror the most important learning outcomes (as evidenced by Question 5 results)

domain1.q1_evidence: The paper states the experiment was conducted in 'a local public middle school 8th grade history class' but does not describe inclusion/exclusion criteria beyond being students in that class. It is noted that 'Since the students were minors, their parents had to sign a form providing consent and the students had to sign an assent form.' 56 students took the pretest but only 33 completed the experiment, and 'Due to the time constraints of the class period, not every student was able to finish the experiment, so their data were removed.' The reasons for attrition (23 students, ~41%) are attributed only to time constraints, not further specified.
domain1.q2_evidence: The sample is drawn from a single 8th grade history class at one local public middle school in Texas. While this represents a convenience sample of the target population (8th grade Texas history students), the single-class single-school design limits representativeness. No demographic information (gender, race, socioeconomic status, prior gaming experience) is reported. The high attrition rate (23 of 56 students) further threatens representativeness, as it is unknown whether completers differed systematically from non-completers.

domain2.q3_evidence: The 10-question pre/post knowledge survey 'was designed in collaboration with the local middle school history teacher who paired with us on the project,' which provides some content validity. However, no information about instrument validation, reliability testing, or psychometric properties is provided. The three posttest interest items use a 5-point Likert scale but no validated instrument is referenced. An excerpt of the survey is shown in Figure 3, revealing multiple-choice questions about the Battles of Galveston.
domain2.q4_evidence: The authors clearly describe their statistical methods: 'a one-tailed t test was used to measure the difference between the posttest and pretest questions answered correctly. The individual questions were also analyzed using Fischer's exact test to see if students performed differently on a question by question basis due to the treatments.' For Likert data: 'a one-tailed Mann Whitney U test was run on the ordinal Likert scale data.' Effect sizes (Cohen's d) are reported for the Mann Whitney U results. The choice of non-parametric tests for ordinal data is appropriate.

domain3.q5_evidence: The authors appropriately acknowledge that Hypothesis 1 was not supported: 'the students who played the game did not show a greater improvement than the students who read the packet, p = 0.91, t = 1.76.' They do not overstate their findings and offer a plausible methodological explanation for the result (unequal time-on-task). They correctly identify that only the question most closely aligned with gameplay showed significant improvement. They accurately report both significant and non-significant results for Hypothesis 2, noting that interest in Civil War and history were only 'marginally significantly higher.'
domain3.q6_evidence: The authors explicitly discuss a key limitation: 'It is hypothesized that a weakness in the experimental design could partially account for this result. Since the text packet was short and the participants could take the posttest survey as soon as they were finished with the treatment, the participants might have had the knowledge fresh in short term memory when taking the posttest.' They also note: 'If we reran this study, we would make sure the participants in both groups had an equal amount of time before the evaluation of the posttest.' The conclusion acknowledges 'this experiment only tested the short-term recall of the students.'

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study has high overall risk of bias primarily due to Domain 1 concerns. The sample is drawn from a single classroom with high attrition (41% of initial participants), no demographic reporting, and convenience-based random assignment (by seating). A critical methodological confound exists in the unequal time-on-task between conditions (game 10-15 minutes vs. text packet a few minutes), meaning text readers took the posttest with information fresh in short-term memory while game players had a substantial delay. The assessment instrument, while teacher-designed, lacks documented validity or reliability. On the positive side, the statistical analyses are appropriate and clearly described, effect sizes are reported, the authors honestly acknowledge their null main finding (Hypothesis 1), and limitations are discussed transparently. The small sample size (n=33) limits statistical power and generalizability.

pdf_filename: Using the Rutgers Oral History Archives and Historical Games to Teach Undergraduates Concepts in American Immigration History.pdf

bibliographic.title: Using the Rutgers Oral History Archives and Historical Games to Teach Undergraduates Concepts in American Immigration History
bibliographic.venue: Journal of American Ethnic History

study_characteristics.sample_description: Undergraduate students in a writing-intensive history course covering American immigration history. Teams of up to six students per side participated. No specific sample size, demographic breakdown, or number of course sections reported.
study_characteristics.study_design: descriptive
study_characteristics.aim: To describe a classroom activity using the Rutgers Oral History Archives (ROHA) and a custom turn-based board game ('European Immigration Game') to teach undergraduate students rudimentary concepts in American immigration history, including ethnic enclave formation and immigration restriction policies

eligibility.concerns: This is a descriptive practitioner report rather than a rigorous empirical study. It contains no quantitative or qualitative data collection, no formal assessment of learning outcomes, no student feedback data, and no systematic evaluation methodology. The paper is essentially a teaching practice description with no empirical evidence of effectiveness. It is a borderline case for inclusion as a 'primary study' since it describes an implemented classroom activity but provides no collected data or formal research findings.

rq1.conceptualization: The study does not use the term 'gamification' explicitly. Instead, it describes a 'historical game' approach — a custom-designed turn-based board game integrated into a writing-intensive undergraduate history course. The game is conceptualized as a tactile, team-based classroom activity that uses physical game components (gridded historical map, figurines, dice) combined with primary source oral history documents to create an engaging pedagogical experience. The approach is game-based learning where the game mechanics (movement, enclave establishment, scoring) are designed to simulate and teach historical processes (immigration, ethnic enclave formation, and immigration restriction). The author describes it as an activity that 'pique[s] student interest in immigration history in a tactile way' while allowing 'a real assessment of student research and writing skills in the process.'

rq2.key_outcomes: No formal assessment of learning outcomes is reported. The author makes anecdotal claims about the activity's value, stating: 'Not only does the "European Immigration Game" pique student interest in immigration history in a tactile way, but it allows a real assessment of student research and writing skills in the process.' The author also claims: 'core concepts and events in American immigration history can be conveyed, and more importantly, assessed in a tangible way.' However, no empirical evidence (test scores, survey data, student work analysis) is provided to substantiate these claims.
rq2.engagement_results: No formal engagement data collected. The author makes qualitative claims that the activity is engaging: 'Of the greatest value, of course, is that undergraduate students are actively engaged with a rich archive of primary source material in an enjoyable way.' No student survey, interview, or observational data is reported.

game_design_elements: Turn-based gameplay with three rounds representing different historical periods
Team competition (two teams of up to six students each)
Gridded historical map of the Atlantic Seaboard as a game board (two-foot-by-three-foot with one inch squares)
Physical figurines (1:72 scale, 24 total) representing immigrants
Dice-based movement mechanic (roll determines number of spaces moved)
Enclave establishment mechanic (must roll four or above to establish an enclave on a grid square)
Point scoring system (one point per enclave in round one; two points for enclaves adjacent to existing enclaves in round two)
Rule changes across rounds to simulate historical policy changes (open immigration in round one; enclave bonuses in round two; immigration restriction with no new figurines in round three)
Extra credit reward for winning team on the research essay
Individual worksheets for recording actions in each round
Moderator role for instructor
technological_platforms: Rutgers Oral History Archives (ROHA) online digital archive (oralhistory.rutgers.edu)
Physical board game components (historical map, grid overlay, figurines, dice)
ROHA website with full-text oral history interviews in HTML and PDF formats with keyword search
instructional_strategies: Integration of primary source documents (oral history transcripts) with game-based activity
Writing-intensive group exercise with individual accountability (individual worksheets and individual research essays)
Three-round game structure that progressively introduces historical concepts (open immigration, ethnic enclave advantages, immigration restriction)
Scaffolded learning: game activity followed by guided questions followed by independent research essay
Open-ended reflection questions after each round (e.g., 'What movements did you make in this round, and why?')
Compare-and-contrast writing assignment requiring students to use game worksheet as evidence
Independent archival research assignment using ROHA's searchable online collection
Role-playing as immigrant groups (Polish vs. Italian) to build empathy and historical understanding
Team-based collaborative learning with competitive element
rq3.content_integration: Historical content and game mechanics were tightly integrated across three rounds. Round 1 simulated pre-restriction era open immigration: students moved freely across the map, establishing 'ethnic enclaves' anywhere on the Atlantic Seaboard, with each enclave worth one point. Round 2 incorporated oral history excerpts from ROHA interviews with Polish and Italian immigrants (e.g., Matthew Drag's account of Polish community in Putnam, Connecticut; Peter Sarraiocco's account of Italian enclave in Port Richmond, Philadelphia). After reading these primary sources, students moved new figurines with the added rule that enclaves adjacent to existing ones were worth two points, representing the historical advantages of ethnic networks for new immigrants. Round 3 implemented immigration restriction rules (no new figurines introduced), simulating the Immigration Restriction Act of 1921 and the Immigration Act of 1924. Open-ended questions prompted reflection on the causes and consequences of restriction. The culminating research essay required students to compare Polish/Italian game experiences with a Hungarian immigration narrative (Julius Fabos, post-1956 revolution) and a self-selected ROHA immigration narrative.

implementation_barriers: Requires physical materials: two-foot-by-three-foot historical map, grid overlay, 24 figurines (1:72 scale), dice
Activity can only be conducted in-person in the classroom, limiting applicability in online learning environments
Requires instructor to serve as moderator during game play
Limited to specific historical topics where oral history materials are available (relies heavily on ROHA collection)
Group activity drawbacks acknowledged: 'one student shouldering the academic burden, or random absences'
methodology_limitations: No empirical data collected — entirely descriptive practitioner report
No sample size, demographics, or participant characteristics reported
No formal assessment of learning outcomes or student performance data
No control group or comparison condition
No student feedback, surveys, or interview data reported
No measure of engagement, motivation, or satisfaction beyond anecdotal claims
No discussion of how many times the activity has been implemented or in how many course sections
Effectiveness claims are entirely based on the author's subjective impressions
mitigation_strategies: Individual research essays ensure individual accountability despite group game activity, eliminating drawbacks of group grading
Worksheet design incentivizes note-taking during game for use in later essay
Open-access nature of ROHA materials eliminates physical and economic barriers to student research

domain1.q1_evidence: No participant selection criteria are described. The paper does not report who the participants were beyond 'undergraduates' and 'students.' No sample size, number of course sections, semesters of implementation, inclusion/exclusion criteria, or any demographic information is provided. The paper describes the activity design but not its implementation with specific participants.
domain1.q2_evidence: No information is provided about the sample. The author describes the activity in general terms ('When I play the game with my students') without specifying any particular implementation instance, sample characteristics, or participant demographics. It is impossible to assess representativeness when no sample is described.

domain2.q3_evidence: No data collection tools are described. The paper mentions individual worksheets and research essays as classroom assignments, but these are not used as research instruments. No surveys, tests, rubrics, observation protocols, interview guides, or any other data collection instruments are reported. There is no systematic data collection of any kind.
domain2.q4_evidence: No data analysis methods are described because no data was collected. The paper contains no quantitative analysis, no qualitative coding, no thematic analysis, and no systematic evaluation. All claims about the activity's effectiveness are based solely on the author's impressionistic account (e.g., 'it allows a real assessment of student research and writing skills').

domain3.q5_evidence: Since no empirical data is presented, there are no 'results' to interpret. The author makes broad positive claims about the activity (e.g., 'Of the greatest value, of course, is that undergraduate students are actively engaged with a rich archive of primary source material in an enjoyable way') without any supporting evidence. These claims cannot be verified as consistent or inconsistent with findings because no findings exist.
domain3.q6_evidence: No limitations of the activity or the paper itself are discussed. The author briefly acknowledges drawbacks of group activities in general ('one student shouldering the academic burden, or random absences') and notes that the individual essay component addresses this, but does not discuss any limitations of the game-based approach, the lack of empirical evaluation, potential biases, or constraints on generalizability.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: This paper has a high overall risk of bias across all three domains. It is a descriptive practitioner report that presents no empirical data whatsoever — no sample description, no data collection instruments, no outcome measurements, no statistical or qualitative analysis, and no formal evaluation of the intervention's effectiveness. All claims about the educational value of the 'European Immigration Game' are based entirely on the author's subjective impressions without supporting evidence. No limitations are acknowledged. The paper is essentially a teaching activity description rather than a research study, which fundamentally limits its ability to provide reliable evidence about the effectiveness of game-based learning in history education. Its inclusion in a systematic review should be noted with the caveat that it provides design ideas but no empirical evidence.

pdf_filename: Validity of a Simulation Game as a Method for History Teaching.pdf

bibliographic.title: Validity of a Simulation Game as a Method for History Teaching
bibliographic.venue: Simulation & Gaming

study_characteristics.sample_description: Three CEGEP-level history classes (College of General and Vocational Education), Quebec, Canada; students aged 17 to 25. A class in Trois-Rivieres served as the control group, while two classes in Drummondville were the experimental groups using the simulation game. 44 of the 65 students were in the experimental group and were observed continuously over a 4-month term. 330 variables were identified involving personality, intellectual capacity, scholastic results, attitudes, and opinions.
study_characteristics.study_design: quasi_experimental
study_characteristics.game_name: International Relations Simulation Game (loosely based on DIPLOMACY)
study_characteristics.aim: First, to determine the validity of a simulation game as a method of teaching and an instrument for the development of reasoning and, second, to study the relationship between learning and students' behavior toward games in a History of International Relations course

eligibility.concerns: Originally published in French in 1986 in Revue des sciences de l'education, republished in English in Simulation & Gaming in 2011. The study is from the 1980s, making it quite dated in terms of educational research methodology. Uses a quasi-experimental design with intact classes (not randomized), with control and experimental groups in different cities (Trois-Rivieres vs. Drummondville), introducing potential confounds.

rq1.explicit_definition: The simulation game, as opposed to the role-playing game, does not try to provoke certain feelings in the participant, but rather places him in a context, with certain givens, where he must attempt to increase his chances of winning and decrease his chances of losing. Givens and results are more explicit in a simulation game than in a role-playing game.
rq1.conceptualization: The study conceptualizes the simulation game as a pedagogical tool grounded in Piaget's theory of cognitive development, specifically the development of formal operational thought. The simulation game is understood as a method that bridges concrete and formal operational stages of reasoning. A key theoretical contribution is Table 1 which maps game assimilation stages (using rules, coordination of rules, coordination of strategies, coordination of outcomes) to Piaget's accommodation stages (learning context, learning strategies, learning outcomes, learning from the game, learning about the game/meta-game). The game is seen not just as a teaching method but as a tool for developing reasoning capacities in adolescents. The authors also connect the simulation game to historicism -- putting oneself in historical characters' shoes -- and view it as creating simplified problems that make the past 'come alive' through student interaction.
theoretical_frameworks: Piaget's theory of cognitive development (formal operational thought)
Hallam's application of Piaget to history education (1969a, 1969b)
Verstehen (subjective understanding) as per Foster et al. (1980)
Torkia-Lagace (1980) on development of formal operations in humanities students
Laveault & Corbeil (1983) model of student operational levels in simulation games

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Six dependent variables measured: (1) LAM-30P questionnaire for learning styles, (2) tests of operational development, (3) questionnaire on attitudes toward the game, (4) questionnaire on opinions regarding knowledge and history, (5) objective test of historical knowledge at end of term, (6) five-series test of comprehension in historical analysis. Also measured: correlation between involvement and comprehension (r), correlation between formal level and historical knowledge (r), ANOVA on knowledge and comprehension scores between groups.
rq2.statistical_results: Table 2.1 - Test of Historical Knowledge: No significant difference between experimental groups (Group 1, M = 17.42; Group 2, M = 15.65) and control group (Group 0, M = 16.86), F = 0.912, p = .410 (n = 31 experimental vs control). Table 2.2 - Historical Comprehension Test 1: Experimental groups had significantly better results (max = 5.00; Group 1, M = 2.67; Group 2, M = 3.24) than control group (Group 0, M = 1.73), F = 5.578, p = .007 (n = 44). Second comprehension test favored experimental groups but not significantly (Group 1, M = 2.42; Group 2, M = 2.29; Group 0, M = 1.87). Table 2.3 - Historical Knowledge: Formal vs Preformal Students (experimental groups only): Intergroup F = 8.84, p = .006 (Preformal n = 19, M = 15.47, SD = 3.37; Formal n = 14, M = 19.41, SD = 3.80). Formal level as predictor of historical knowledge: r = .53, p = .049, n = 21. No significant difference between formal and preformal for comprehension tests: r = .23, p = .614, n = 21. Involvement and historical comprehension: r = .50, p = .011. Sensorimotor learning style and motivation: Spearman rho = .4297, p = .009. Table 3 correlations: Proprioceptive cinematic and second chance rho = .5011, p = .003; Proprioceptive temporal rho = .4519, p = .007; Sensorimotor rho = .5686, p = .001; Kinesthetic rho = .4674, p = .005; Transactional rho = .4485, p = .007; Auditive and absenteeism rho = .4560, p = .006. Table 4.1: Proportion chi-squared = 0, significance level = 1; Combination chi-squared = 0.13, significance level = .91. Table 5 - Opinions by attitude: Opinion A chi-squared = 9.20, p < .01; Opinion B chi-squared = 15.13, p < .01; Opinion C chi-squared = 10.89, p < .01.
rq2.comparative_methodology: Quasi-experimental design with two experimental groups (simulation game) and one control group (regular lectures) in a History of International Relations course. Three CEGEP-level classes were used: two experimental classes in Drummondville and one control class in Trois-Rivieres. All groups received developmental and learning tests at different times during the term. Control group attended ordinary lectures while experimental groups participated in the simulation game with four scenarios of increasing difficulty. Both groups completed the objective knowledge test and comprehension tests at end of term.
rq2.key_outcomes: Experimental groups had significantly higher scores on the first comprehension test (p = .007) compared to the control group. No significant difference on historical knowledge test (p = .410), meaning the game was as efficient as lectures for knowledge acquisition. Within experimental groups, formal students scored significantly higher on knowledge (M = 19.41 vs M = 15.47, p = .006). The game benefited preformal students most in terms of comprehension (no significant difference between formal and preformal on comprehension). The game motivated certain learning styles (sensory-motor, kinesthetic). 64.7% of students found the game more motivating and diversified than a lecture course.
rq2.engagement_results: 64.7% found the game more motivating and more diversified than a lecture course; 20.6% found it equally motivating and 23.4% found it equally diversified; 97.1% thought it required an equal or less amount of work than other courses (less work: 55.9%; equal work: 41.2%). The only significant relationship between attitude variables and historical comprehension test results was involvement (r = .50, p = .011). Active involvement was the only affective factor significantly linked to learning. Students preferring sensory-motor learning found the course more motivating (Spearman rho = .4297, p = .009). Proprioceptive, sensorimotor, kinesthetic, and transactional learners enjoyed being able to study abstract matter with tools appropriate to their styles. A great majority would take the course again and thought more than 51% of their peers enjoyed the simulation game.

game_design_elements: World map with Antarctic polar projection as game board
Movement of pieces on the map representing teams and resources
Four scenarios of increasing difficulty
Team-based gameplay with each team pursuing objectives
Rules and conditions that change across scenarios
Concrete material supports (maps and pieces) materializing abstract concepts
Strategy coordination and meta-game elements
Collection of historical documents including a chronology for experimental groups
Loosely based on DIPLOMACY board game (originally by Waddington/Avalon Hill/Hasbro)
technological_platforms: Physical board game (world map with Antarctic polar projection)
Five-series comprehension test in historical analysis
instructional_strategies: Simulation game as alternative to traditional lectures for history teaching
Progressive scenario difficulty (four scenarios of increasing complexity)
Integration of concrete materials to represent abstract historical concepts
Historical document analysis alongside game play
Two-phase comprehension test: first phase with no context, second phase with new information to assess capacity to use context and group information to solve historical problems
Control of three variables: participant (operational level, learning style), activity (scenarios with changing rules/conditions), material (concrete supports for abstract concepts)
Debriefing and attitude assessment at end of term
Alignment with Piaget's developmental theory to scaffold from concrete to formal operational thought
rq3.content_integration: The simulation game was set in the context of a History of International Relations course. The game involved movement of pieces on a world map (Antarctic polar projection) where each team managed resources within scenarios pursuing objectives. Historical content was integrated through: (1) a collection of historical documents and chronology given to experimental groups, (2) four scenarios of increasing difficulty that simulated international relations situations, (3) rules and conditions modifying across scenarios to reflect different historical dynamics. The game was loosely based on the DIPLOMACY board game. Learning from the game involved grouping causal factors (alliances, geographic proximities, role of colonies), which mapped onto actual historical causal relationships. At the highest level of assimilation, students could link game events with historical factors that had similar effects, creating new rules and constraints, and considering the game as one form of history and history as one form of game (meta-game level).

implementation_barriers: Requires game-experienced teachers; the authors note a true multivariate study would require 500 students and 20 game-experienced teachers
Students do not assimilate the game in identical fashions, affecting how they learn through the game
For many students, the game is only a game until they understand the symbolic import of the material -- they pay more attention to rules than to meaning of ongoing events
Set effect: presentation of the game and students' expectations affect learning
Experience: teacher's personality, variations in procedure, and type of debriefing introduce variability
Personal variables: group dynamics, personality differences, and cognitive styles are underexplored
Game-playing skills differ from academic skills, depending mostly on verbal ability and abstract thinking
Different cities for control vs. experimental groups introduces potential confounds
methodology_limitations: Non-randomized quasi-experimental design with intact classes from different cities (Trois-Rivieres vs. Drummondville)
Small sample size (n = 65 total, n = 44 experimental, control group size approximately 21)
330 variables identified but intensive rather than extensive analysis was used due to limited sample
A true statistical multivariate study would require 500 students and 20 game-experienced teachers, which was impossible
Originally conducted in the early 1980s and published in French in 1986; republished in English in 2011
Comprehension test significant in only one of five tests
Cannot determine impact of scenario difficulty variations on formal vs. preformal students due to varying test difficulty
Research took for granted that once students played correctly they were ready to learn, but the authors found students assimilate games differently
negative_effects: Auditive students tended to be absent most often from the simulation game course (rho = .4560, p = .006), suggesting the method may disadvantage certain learning styles
No significant advantage on knowledge acquisition (p = .410) -- the game was not superior to lectures for factual knowledge retention
Comprehension advantage was significant in only 1 of 5 tests
mitigation_strategies: Control three variables (participant, activity, material) to isolate factors and generalize beyond this particular simulation game
Progressive scenario difficulty to scaffold learning
Provide concrete material supports (maps, pieces) to help students understand abstract concepts
Use multiple assessment methods (knowledge tests, comprehension tests, attitude questionnaires, learning style inventories, operational development tests) to triangulate findings
Combine intensive clinical approach with standard statistical methods
Give students mobile and tactile instruments they can manipulate as tools to study and understand abstract concepts
Allow participants to discuss hypotheses, methods, and approaches among themselves

domain1.q1_evidence: The paper states 'Three CEGEP-level history classes were involved in the research (i.e., College d'Enseignement General et Professionel [College of General and Vocational Education], Quebec, Canada; students aged 17 to 25). A class in Trois-Rivieres was used a control group, whereas two classes in Drummondville were the experimental groups using the simulation game.' However, no explicit criteria for selecting these particular classes are given, no information on how or why these specific classes were chosen, and no discussion of potential selection bias from using classes in two different cities.
domain1.q2_evidence: The sample consists of 65 CEGEP-level students from two cities in Quebec, Canada. While the age range (17-25) and educational level are specified, no demographic information, prior history knowledge, or baseline equivalence data between control and experimental groups is provided. The use of intact classes from different institutions (Trois-Rivieres vs. Drummondville) raises representativeness concerns. The authors acknowledge that 'A true statistical multivariate study would require 500 students and 20 game-experienced teachers, which was impossible in the present circumstances.'

domain2.q3_evidence: Six instruments were used to measure dependent variables: (1) the LAM-30P questionnaire for learning styles (Lamontagne, Lamontagne, & Lamy, 1982), (2) tests of operational development (Laveault, 1981; Noelting, 1982), (3) a custom questionnaire on attitudes, (4) a questionnaire on students' opinions, (5) an objective knowledge test, and (6) a five-series test of comprehension in historical analysis (Corbeil et al., 1984). Several instruments are established, published tools with citations. The comprehension test used a two-phase approach designed to measure capacity to use context and group new information to solve a historical problem.
domain2.q4_evidence: ANOVA was used to compare experimental and control groups on knowledge and comprehension tests (Tables 2.1, 2.2, 2.3 with df, MS, F, and p values reported). Correlation analyses (Pearson r and Spearman rho) were used to examine relationships between involvement and comprehension (r = .50, p = .011), formal level and knowledge (r = .53, p = .049), and learning styles and attitudes (Table 3). Chi-square tests were used for frequency comparisons (Tables 4.1, 4.2, 5). Methods are described and results reported with standard statistical values, though effect sizes are not reported.

domain3.q5_evidence: The authors' interpretations are generally consistent with the statistical results. They correctly note that the game showed no significant advantage for knowledge acquisition (F = 0.912, p = .410) while showing significant advantages for comprehension on one test (F = 5.578, p = .007). They accurately state that 'In terms of knowledge, the game is, on average, as efficient as a lecture course' and that the comprehension difference was 'significant in only a single case.' They correctly identify that formal students scored higher on knowledge but that no significant difference existed between formal and preformal on comprehension. The discussion of learning styles and motivation is grounded in the correlation data presented.
domain3.q6_evidence: The authors acknowledge several limitations: 'A true statistical multivariate study would require 500 students and 20 game-experienced teachers, which was impossible in the present circumstances.' They note that 'With so many variables, an intensive analysis was preferred to an extensive superficial one.' They acknowledge that 'it is impossible at the present time to make a statement about the impact of variations in scenario difficulty, concerning either formal or preformal students, owing to the varying difficulty of the five tests.' However, the limitation of using non-randomized intact classes from different cities is not explicitly acknowledged.
