risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study presents a mixed risk of bias profile. Domain 1 (selection) is high risk due to the use of non-randomized intact classes from two different cities with no baseline equivalence data and limited sample description. Domain 2 (data collection/analysis) is low risk: the study employed multiple established instruments (LAM-30P, operational development tests) and reported appropriate statistical analyses (ANOVA, correlation, chi-square) with full statistical values. Domain 3 (interpretation) is low risk: interpretations are generally consistent with the data, and key limitations are acknowledged. The overall assessment is 'Unclear' because the high-risk selection domain (non-equivalent groups, different institutions, small sample of 65) is partially offset by methodologically sound data collection and honest interpretation of mixed results (acknowledging that the game was not superior for knowledge, only for one comprehension test). The study's age (originally 1980s research) also limits its generalizability to modern educational contexts.

pdf_filename: Virtual Reality and Educational Game to Learn Madurese History and Alphabet for Elementary School Students.pdf

bibliographic.title: Virtual Reality and Educational Game to Learn Madurese History and Alphabet For Elementary School Students
bibliographic.venue: Journal of Physics: Conference Series (International Conference on Science Education and Technology (ICOSETH) 2020)

study_characteristics.sample_description: 3rd grade students of Pangarangan III Elementary School of Sumenep, Madura, Indonesia. Testing involved multiple stages: individual trial (3 students), small group trial (6 students), and large group trial (20 students). Additionally, one media design expert and one material/content expert served as validators.
study_characteristics.study_design: design_based
study_characteristics.game_name: Madurese History Virtual Reality ('Heritage Objects' / Sumenep Palace Museum VR) and 'Halo Madura' Educational Game
study_characteristics.aim: To develop a learning media that collaborates virtual reality and educational game to learn Madurese history and alphabet for 3rd grade students of Pangarangan III Elementary School of Sumenep, facilitating distance learning during the Covid-19 pandemic

eligibility.concerns: The study is primarily a development research (R&D) study using the ADDIE model rather than an experimental study measuring learning outcomes. It evaluates product feasibility through expert validation and user satisfaction questionnaires, not through pre-post testing or controlled comparisons. The historical content is specifically about Madurese cultural heritage (historical objects in the Sumenep Palace Museum), combined with Madurese alphabet (ghajang script) learning. The gamification element is present through the 'Halo Madura' educational game component, but the VR component is more of a virtual museum tour than a game. No statistical learning outcome data (pre-test/post-test) is reported.

rq1.conceptualization: The study does not provide an explicit definition of gamification. It conceptualizes the intervention as a combination of two learning media: (1) a Virtual Reality experience for exploring Madurese historical heritage objects in a virtual museum (Sumenep Palace Museum), and (2) an educational game ('Halo Madura') for learning the Madurese alphabet (ghajang script). The educational game component is described as combining play elements with educational content: 'The element of play in this media, apart from being entertainment, also functions as a strengthening of the Madura alphabet material for students.' The authors cite a definition of Educational Games as 'games that are packaged with the aim of stimulating the thinking power of students and also useful for training in increasing the concentration of students as educational game users.' The VR component is framed as enabling immersive historical exploration: 'VR makes it possible to visit any location, time, or person in a relatively inexpensive way via virtual field trips.'
theoretical_frameworks: ADDIE instructional design model (Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, Evaluation)
Educational Digital Games as defined by AlShaiji (2017) - games that provide the opportunity to reinforce previous knowledge in a comfortable and ludic environment

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Product feasibility percentage scores based on a 5-point Likert scale questionnaire assessing effectiveness, efficiency, and attractiveness of the learning media. No pre-test/post-test learning outcome measures were used.
rq2.statistical_results: Media design expert validation: 91% (Very High). Material/content expert validation: 84% (High). Individual trial (three 3rd grade students): 85% (High). Small group trial (six 3rd grade students): 87% (High). Large group trial (twenty 3rd grade students): 86% (High). Percentage formula used: Percentage of answers = F/N x 100%, where F = The total value of the respondents, N = Total the maximum value.
rq2.comparative_methodology: No comparative methodology was used. The study employed a development research (R&D) approach using the ADDIE model. Evaluation consisted of expert validation (media design expert and material/content expert) and user testing at three scales (individual, small group, large group) using feasibility questionnaires with a 5-point scale: (1) Very low, (2) Less High, (3) High Enough, (4) High, (5) Very High.
rq2.key_outcomes: All feasibility scores were in the 'High' or 'Very High' category (84-91%), indicating the product was deemed well worth it with no need to revise. The media design expert gave the highest rating at 91% (Very High). The authors concluded that 'the virtual reality and educational games are well worth it and no need to revise' and that 'The application of this media in learning will have an impact on increasing the effectiveness, efficiency and attractiveness of learning Madura history and alphabet.'
rq2.engagement_results: The authors report that 'The students showed high enthusiasm for learning when they learned to use this Halo Madura educational game.' User trial scores (85-87%) suggest positive reception among students. The study notes the media can 'divert students to not only play other games that are entertainment in nature which has become a trend among children, especially elementary school students.'

game_design_elements: Virtual museum walkthrough with 3D historical objects (Sumenep Palace Museum)
Interactive information display on historical heritage objects when approached
Educational game with multiple difficulty levels for Madurese alphabet (ghajang script)
Word games using Madurese script (Latin to Madurese script conversion and vice versa)
Video tutorials for writing ghajang alphabet
Read-aloud functionality for ghajang alphabet pronunciation
Menu-based navigation (Hint, Learn, Information, Exit buttons)
Sound/audio integration
Basic competency (KI KD) reference integration
Progressive learning structure (reading alphabet, writing alphabet, word games)
technological_platforms: Android-based mobile platform (implied by VR Box usage)
instructional_strategies: ADDIE instructional design model (Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, Evaluation)
Virtual field trip to historical museum via VR for immersive historical learning
Combination of VR (for history) and educational game (for alphabet) in single integrated media
Support for multiple learning styles (visual, auditory, kinesthetic)
Distance learning support during Covid-19 pandemic
Progressive skill-building: from reading Madurese alphabet to writing to word games
Expert validation prior to student deployment (media design expert and content expert)
Multi-stage user testing (individual, small group, large group)
Cultural preservation through technology-mediated learning
rq3.content_integration: The learning media integrates two distinct components: (1) 'Madurese History' Virtual Reality, which recreates the Sumenep Palace Museum room where users can walk around and view Madurese historical relics in 3D using a VR Box and controller, with informational text appearing when users approach each historical object; and (2) 'Halo Madura' educational game for Madurese alphabet learning, where students progress from learning ghajang script letter forms, to watching video tutorials on writing, to playing word games converting between Latin and Madurese scripts at several difficulty levels. The homepage provides buttons to enter either the VR museum experience or the educational game. Historical content focuses on Madurese cultural heritage objects in the Sumenep Palace Museum, while the alphabet component teaches the traditional ghajang writing system of the Madura region.

implementation_barriers: Students in remote areas of Madura have minimal internet access, necessitating offline-capable media
Existing textbooks for Madurese history and alphabet were deemed 'not representative'
Only 55% of students could score above the minimum passing criteria in Madurese history and alphabet lessons before the intervention
Students cannot easily visit Madurese museums or cultural sites due to long distances
Covid-19 pandemic restrictions prevented face-to-face learning
Museum visitor numbers decreased drastically during the pandemic
Requires hardware (VR Box, controller, computer/smartphone) which may not be available at all schools
The habits of students regarding Madurese history and alphabet are being eroded by modern globalization
methodology_limitations: No pre-test/post-test design to measure actual learning outcomes or knowledge gains
Feasibility evaluation based solely on questionnaire percentages, not on standardized assessments
Very small sample sizes for validation stages (1 media expert, 1 content expert, 3 individual trial, 6 small group)
No control group or comparative condition
No reliability or validity information provided for the feasibility questionnaire instrument
Simple percentage formula (F/N x 100%) used for data analysis without inferential statistics
All participants from a single school (Pangarangan III Elementary School of Sumenep), limiting generalizability
No long-term follow-up on learning outcomes or sustained usage
mitigation_strategies: Designed media to support offline/distance learning to accommodate pandemic restrictions and areas with limited internet
Used ADDIE model for systematic development and iterative evaluation
Multi-stage validation process (expert validation before user testing; individual, small, then large group trials)
Addressed multiple learning styles (visual, auditory, kinesthetic) in media design
Suggested distribution of learning media products to all elementary schools in Madura Island, including those in remote areas

domain1.q1_evidence: The paper states the media was 'created to facilitate the difficulties of 3rd grade students of Pangarangan III Elementary School of Sumenep in learning Madurese history and alphabet.' The school and grade level are specified, but no explicit selection criteria for which students participated in each trial stage are provided. The abstract notes 'trials on individual users (three students),' 'testing trials in small group users (six students),' and 'trials in large group users (twenty students),' but no information is given about how these specific students were selected from the class.
domain1.q2_evidence: All participants are from a single school (Pangarangan III Elementary School of Sumenep) on Madura Island. Only 29 students total across all trial stages, with 20 in the large group trial. No demographic details beyond grade level (3rd grade) are provided. The authors acknowledge the context is specific by recommending 'the distribution of learning media products be carried out to all elementary schools in Madura Island,' implying the study sample is not representative of the broader target population. Only one expert was used for each type of validation.

domain2.q3_evidence: The evaluation used a questionnaire 'using a scale of five ratings of products, namely: (1) Very low, (2) Less High, (3) High Enough, (4) High, (5) Very High.' No information is provided about the validity or reliability of this questionnaire instrument. The percentage formula used (F/N x 100%) is a basic descriptive calculation. No standardized learning assessment tools, validated instruments, or established measurement scales are referenced. The conversion table (Table 4) mapping percentages to qualifications (e.g., 90-100% = Very High) is cited from Sudarma (2006) but no psychometric properties are discussed.
domain2.q4_evidence: Data analysis consisted solely of calculating percentage scores using the formula 'Percentage of answers = F/N x 100%' where 'F = The total value of the respondents' and 'N = Total the maximum value.' No inferential statistics, measures of central tendency, standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported. The analysis consists of comparing percentage scores to a qualification table. No interrater reliability for expert evaluations is reported. The methods lack rigor for making claims about effectiveness, efficiency, and attractiveness.

domain3.q5_evidence: The authors claim 'The application of this media in learning will have an impact on increasing the effectiveness, efficiency and attractiveness of learning Madura history and alphabet' based solely on feasibility questionnaire percentages (84-91%). This overinterprets the data: feasibility ratings from expert validators and student satisfaction do not demonstrate actual learning effectiveness or efficiency. No learning outcomes were measured. Similarly, the conclusion states the media 'can improve the learning process so that students' grades are expected to increase,' which is an unsupported claim since no grades or test scores were collected or analyzed.
domain3.q6_evidence: The paper does not include an explicit limitations section. The conclusion and discussion sections make no mention of methodological limitations, sample size concerns, lack of learning outcome measures, or threats to validity. The discussion focuses entirely on positive aspects of the developed media. The only future direction mentioned is distributing the media to more schools, with no acknowledgment of the need for further empirical validation of learning effectiveness.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: All three domains present high risk of bias. Domain 1 (selection): participants were drawn from a single school with no clear selection criteria and very small sample sizes (1 expert per validation type, 3-20 students per trial stage). Domain 2 (data collection/analysis): the study used an unvalidated questionnaire with only basic percentage calculations and no inferential statistics; no actual learning outcome measures were employed. Domain 3 (interpretation): the authors make claims about learning effectiveness and improved grades that are not supported by the data collected, and no limitations are acknowledged. This is a development-focused study (R&D using ADDIE model) that reports product feasibility rather than empirical evidence of learning effectiveness, yet draws conclusions about effectiveness without the requisite evidence.

pdf_filename: When Everyone Wins Dialogue, Play, and Black History for Critical Games Education.pdf

bibliographic.title: When Everyone Wins: Dialogue, Play, and Black History for Critical Games Education
bibliographic.venue: Media and Communication

study_characteristics.sample_description: Nineteen students, mostly first-semester freshmen in a game design program at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute (RPI), in the game simulation arts and sciences program. The course was 'History and Culture of Games' co-facilitated by two instructors over three years, with the detailed 2019 fall iteration involving two sections of students across twenty-nine course meetings in the semester. Two students also provided longitudinal reflections two years after the course.
study_characteristics.study_design: qualitative
study_characteristics.game_name: Multiple games used: Learning Edges (physical activity), Sim City (simulation), Barnga (card game), Memoir Games (student-designed); analyzed games include Brenda Romero's The New World (2008), Playing History: Slave Trade (2013), Mission US: Flight to Freedom (2012), National Geographic's Underground Railroad: Journey to Freedom (2014), Scholastic's The Underground Railroad: Escape From Slavery (2013), Brian Meyer's Freedom: The Underground Railroad (2012). Student-designed games for exhibition: Guided, Combahee, Safehouse, Family or Foe?
study_characteristics.aim: To reflect on the process and outcomes of using dialogue, play, and a focus on Black women's history to support critical media literacy in game design education, specifically through a dialogue-based introductory undergraduate course intended to deepen engagement by students in game design practice

eligibility.concerns: The study is primarily about game design education rather than history education per se, but it centrally involves learning about Black history (specifically Harriet Tubman's life and legacy, the history of slavery, the Underground Railroad, and the Combahee River Raid) through game design and play. The gamification component involves students both playing existing games about historical topics and designing their own board games focused on Harriet Tubman's history for a public exhibition. The study is qualitative with no control group or quantitative learning outcome measures. It is a reflective pedagogical article rather than a traditional experimental study, but it reports primary empirical data (dialogue transcripts, student work, survey responses, instructor observations, and longitudinal student reflections).

rq1.conceptualization: The study does not use the term 'gamification' explicitly. Instead, it conceptualizes the intersection of games and education through the lens of dialogic pedagogy and critical media literacy. Games and play are positioned as experiential learning activities that serve as catalysts for intergroup dialogue about social identity, privilege, oppression, and historical narratives. The authors describe their approach as combining 'both dialogic pedagogy and more traditional design pedagogy methods to work across personal experience, theory, and practice, to build an integrative critical literacy for students, inclusive of their own social identities.' Play and game design are framed as vehicles for critical engagement with history, not merely as motivational tools. The paper cites David Bohm's characterization of dialogue: 'In a dialogue, however, nobody is trying to win. Everybody wins if anybody wins.' Game-based learning is thus conceptualized within a framework of dialogue, social justice education, and anti-racist pedagogy rather than through typical gamification frameworks (points, badges, leaderboards).
theoretical_frameworks: Intergroup dialogue (Zuniga, 2003) - four stages of dialogue: group beginnings, identity/social relations/conflict, issues of social justice, empowerment/allies/action
Multipartial facilitation and power balancing (Fisher & Petryk, 2017)
Dialogic pedagogy - transformational as opposed to informational learning
Critical media literacy - ability to critically 'read' and 'write' in the medium of games
Procedural rhetoric (referenced in analysis of games about slavery)
Digital literacy pedagogies (Lund et al., 2019; Bali, 2019)

rq2.comparative_methodology: No comparative methodology was used. The study employs qualitative reflective analysis drawing on student dialogue transcripts, instructor observations, student game design artifacts, survey responses, and two longitudinal student reflections collected two years after the course. The authors explicitly note: 'As opposed to more instrumentalized forms of pedagogy, our assessment and outcomes are not focused on the evaluation of something our students produce as an end in itself (a research paper, a project, etc.). Instead, we are observing for evidence of deep connections within the group, between the students, and between students and the complexity of the subject.'
rq2.key_outcomes: Four of eight student-designed Harriet Tubman board games were selected for inclusion in a public exhibition at a local art gallery (The Albany Barn), representing a 50% 'success rate.' The authors note this reflects the pedagogical challenges of the course where some students struggled with connecting to the historical material. The four selected games (Guided, Combahee, Safehouse, Family or Foe?) demonstrated 'genuine engagement and curiosity to the story of Tubman' and teams 'were open to receiving constructive feedback on improving their designs.' Students who created successful games demonstrated critical media literacies including the ability to 'articulate the self as politically situated in mediatized culture' and 'communicate across differences.' The course produced powerful shifts: 'shifting focus from new to old, from white to black identity, from male to female identity, from simplification to complexity' in game design.
rq2.engagement_results: Mixed engagement results were observed. In successful dialogues, students demonstrated ability to listen and share 'across difference,' acknowledged 'their intersectional entanglement with games, society, and each other,' and displayed willingness to ask difficult questions. One student (Sarah, a Black female, two years later) reported: 'That intersection of history, social issues, and thought-provoking conversation, in my opinion, is greatly overlooked and underrepresented in the game industry at large.' Another student (Matthew, a white male, two years later) reported: 'it encouraged student engagement, resulting in us having to reflect and think more about the material taught instead of us just listening to the professor.' However, the study also documented significant resistance: some students dismissed dialogues, lacked engagement, and resisted learning through discomfort. In one dialogue, a white male student left the classroom for a quarter of an hour. Some students maintained that games are 'just for fun' and that culture is 'outside the purview of games.' The authors note that 'not all students were able to deeply engage the critical concepts we were asking them to reflect on.'

game_design_elements: Board game design (student-designed games for Harriet Tubman exhibition)
Card game mechanics (Barnga - tournament-style rotation with hidden rule variations)
Role-playing elements (Sim City simulation with assigned administrative roles)
Turn-based strategy (Combahee, Safehouse)
Cooperative gameplay (Family or Foe? - collaborative storytelling RPG for 4-10 players)
Blindfolded sensory play (Guided - simulating escape on Underground Railroad)
Physical movement/embodied play (Learning Edges - spectrum activity)
Memoir/narrative game design (personal story-based game creation)
Historical resource management (Freedom board game analysis)
Puzzle mechanics (critique of Playing History: Slave Trade 'slave Tetris')
Map-based movement (Family or Foe? - historically accurate 1850s US map)
Chance/card-drawing mechanics (slave catcher cards in Family or Foe?)
Asymmetric gameplay (Safehouse - one player hides, other hunts; Combahee - Union vs. Confederacy)
Hidden information (Safehouse - masked board space)
Time pressure (Combahee - strict time limit; Safehouse - 10 turn limit)
technological_platforms: Physical board games (primary medium for student designs)
Physical/embodied activities (Learning Edges, Sim City simulation)
Digital games analyzed in class (Playing History: Slave Trade, Mission US: Flight to Freedom, National Geographic's Underground Railroad, Scholastic's Underground Railroad, Brian Meyer's Freedom)
Some student memoir games were digital
instructional_strategies: Intergroup dialogue with four sequential stages across the semester
Multipartial facilitation and power-balancing techniques
Experiential learning activities rooted in games
Community agreements co-created by students
Critical game analysis through dialogue (analyzing representations of slavery in games)
Semester-long small group design project (Harriet Tubman board games for public exhibition)
Co-facilitation by two instructors (game designer and dialogue facilitator)
Collaboration with external historian expert (Professor Janell Hobson, Tubman expert)
Integration of historical reading materials (Kate Clifford Larson's Tubman biography, Sarah Bradford's 1869 book, Sarah Juliet Lauro's 2020 research on slavery in games)
Reflective dialogue processing after each game/activity
Small group reflection followed by large group sharing
Memoir game design assignment for personal storytelling
Public exhibition as authentic assessment and audience
Longitudinal follow-up with former students (two years later)
Active listening and affirming inquiry techniques (LARA)
Social identity exploration activities (Social Identity Terminology, Identity Profiles, Cycle of Socialization, Social Identity Timelines)
rq3.content_integration: Historical content was deeply integrated with game mechanics through a multi-layered approach. First, students played and critically analyzed existing commercial and educational games about slavery and the Underground Railroad through dialogic facilitation, examining how game mechanics create meaning (procedural rhetoric) and whether they honor or exploit enslaved people's experiences. Second, students researched Harriet Tubman's history, the Combahee River Raid, the Underground Railroad, and the broader context of slavery, then designed original board games that translated this historical knowledge into playable mechanics. For example, the student game 'Combahee' recreated the Combahee River Raid as a 1v1 turn-based strategy game with historically accurate geography; 'Guided' simulated the Underground Railroad escape experience using blindfolds and musical codes to represent oral tradition; 'Family or Foe?' used a historically accurate 1850s US map with chance-based slave catcher cards to represent the brutality and uncertainty of escape. The course produced four 'powerful shifts' in game design: shifting focus from new to old (historical material), from white to Black identity, from male to female identity, and from simplification to complexity. The figure of Harriet Tubman served as a 'generative and critical catalyst' that pushed 'the buttons of the field in meaningful ways.'

implementation_barriers: Student resistance to engaging with uncomfortable topics about race, privilege, and oppression in games
Some students maintained that games are 'just for fun' and serious historical topics should not be part of game design
Student disengagement: one white male student left the classroom for a quarter of an hour during a dialogue
Sexist resistance from male class members to accept female co-facilitators' experiences
Predominantly male and predominantly white student demographics created consistent power imbalance challenges
Structural whiteness in the games classroom (Wu, 2022) creating barriers to critical engagement
Difficulty for some students in finding a connection to the Harriet Tubman topic, reflecting dominant views that many areas of culture are 'outside the purview of games'
Institutional and structural power dynamics present in the class affecting dialogue
Some students unable to successfully create original and meaningful games on the topic of Tubman (4 of 8 teams failed to meet exhibition quality)
The 'viscerally aggressive' reactions toward critical perspectives (Wu, 2022) and resistance to 'announcing the illegitimacy of anything illegible'
methodology_limitations: No quantitative learning outcome measures or pre-test/post-test design
No control group or comparative condition
Small sample size (19 students in the detailed 2019 iteration)
Single institution (Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute) limiting generalizability
Reflective/narrative methodology based primarily on instructor observations and selected dialogue excerpts
Only two former students responded to the longitudinal follow-up two years later
Selection bias in presented dialogue excerpts - authors chose which dialogues to include
Self-reported student reflections may be influenced by social desirability
No systematic coding framework or formal qualitative analysis methodology described
Authors acknowledge their own positionality as white female co-facilitators may have affected the Harriet Tubman project experience
negative_effects: Some students experienced pain and discomfort in recognizing privilege during Sim City activity: 'It hurts me to think society is like this because I am privileged'
Student resistance and lack of engagement when confronted with critical perspectives on race in games
Potential for students to reinforce harmful perspectives: one white male student suggested women harassed in multiplayer games 'should just use the mute button' instead of being 'harsh'
Risk of students experiencing alienation, as Black students in white-dominated field found the industry 'already alienating'
Facilitators acknowledged 'our limitations and our inability to fully prevent harm to any students within our class'
Some dialogue experiences were 'challenging' with 'resistance' - failed or stunted dialogues that were 'charged' for facilitators
Students who created unsuccessful games had 'struggled with finding a connection to the Tubman topic' suggesting possible disengagement or alienation from the material
mitigation_strategies: Using multipartial facilitation techniques to balance power dynamics and make space for counter-narratives
Building classroom community through four sequential stages of dialogue before tackling difficult topics
Creating community agreements at start of course
Collaboration with external Black feminist scholar and Tubman expert (Professor Janell Hobson) as guest lecturer
Bringing in readings and materials from Black perspectives to center marginalized voices
Framing failed or stunted dialogues as valuable learning experiences through the lens of dialogic pedagogy
Power-balancing facilitation to ensure marginalized students were heard
Conscious self-reflection by facilitators about their own white racial identity and potential biases
The practice of 'stepping back from dialogue to reflect, as a group, on the process of the dialogue'
Making the facilitator/teacher 'included, learning alongside the students' rather than positioned as authority

domain1.q1_evidence: The paper describes participants as 'nineteen students, mostly first-semester freshmen in a game design program' who were 'gathered around a large square configuration of tables, facing each other' for an in-class dialogue. These were students enrolled in the 'History and Culture of Games' course at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute. No explicit selection criteria are provided beyond enrollment in the course. It is unclear whether this was a required or elective course, or how students came to be enrolled. The 2019 iteration 'included two sections of students' but the relationship between sections is not clarified.
domain1.q2_evidence: The sample consists of students from a single elite private institution (Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute) in a game design program. The authors note 'our course was predominantly male' and acknowledge their institution 'is predominantly white, despite the racial and ethnic diversity we had in our course.' The 19 students represent a very specific population (first-semester freshmen game design students at a US technical university) and are not representative of broader student populations. Only two former students responded to the longitudinal follow-up, further limiting representativeness of reported outcomes.

domain2.q3_evidence: Data collection involved multiple qualitative sources: 'student work, survey responses, and instructor observations' as well as dialogue transcripts and longitudinal student reflections collected two years later. However, no details are provided about the survey instrument (questions, validity, reliability), the systematic nature of observations, or how dialogue excerpts were recorded and selected. The authors state they 'recorded observations in notebooks' during dialogues. No established qualitative data collection protocols or validated instruments are described. The longitudinal follow-up appears to have been informal ('we also reached out to former students and asked for their longer-term reflections').
domain2.q4_evidence: No formal data analysis methods are described. The paper presents selected dialogue excerpts, instructor reflections, and two student testimonials without describing any systematic coding, thematic analysis, or qualitative analysis framework. The authors explicitly state their assessment approach is not focused on traditional evaluation: 'our assessment and outcomes are not focused on the evaluation of something our students produce as an end in itself (a research paper, a project, etc.). Instead, we are observing for evidence of deep connections within the group.' While this is consistent with dialogic pedagogy, it means there is no described or justified analytical method for drawing the conclusions presented.

domain3.q5_evidence: The authors' interpretations are generally consistent with the evidence presented. They honestly report both successes and failures: four of eight student games met exhibition quality (50%), some dialogues were clearly successful while others involved resistance and disengagement. They do not overstate their findings, acknowledging that 'not all students were able to deeply engage the critical concepts we were asking them to reflect on' and that 'despite our dialogic pedagogy approach, not all students were able to successfully create original and meaningful games on the topic of Tubman.' Their conclusion that 'through dialogue we ultimately increased the capacity of everyone in the course, students and co-facilitators, to engage in an uncomfortable design process' is qualified and hedged appropriately.
domain3.q6_evidence: The authors acknowledge several limitations, particularly their own positionality: 'Our own identities as white female co-facilitators affected the experience of the course for both ourselves and our students,' 'we hold privilege within that identity as the institution is predominantly white,' and 'we acknowledge our limitations and our inability to fully prevent harm to any students within our class as well as the role of institutional and structural power dynamics present in the class which we have reflected on (Corron & Rouse, 2022).' They also cite Wu (2022) to contextualize the resistance they encountered. However, methodological limitations (small sample, no systematic analysis) are not explicitly discussed as such.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The overall risk of bias is high primarily due to methodological concerns in Domains 1 and 2. Domain 1 (selection): participants are from a single elite institution with no clear selection criteria and a very small, non-representative sample (19 students, only 2 longitudinal respondents). Domain 2 (data collection/analysis): while multiple qualitative data sources are mentioned, no validated instruments, systematic data collection protocols, or formal qualitative analysis methods are described; the authors explicitly frame their assessment as non-instrumentalized observation. Domain 3 (interpretation) is more favorable as the authors honestly acknowledge both successes and failures and discuss their own positionality and limitations, but the lack of systematic analysis means interpretations rest on selectively presented evidence. The study is best understood as a reflective pedagogical article sharing practitioner insights rather than a rigorous empirical study, which is consistent with its venue and stated aims but limits the strength of its evidence claims.

pdf_filename: Work, Trade, Learn Developing an Immersive Serious Game for History Education.pdf

bibliographic.title: Work, Trade, Learn: Developing an Immersive Serious Game for History Education
bibliographic.venue: Communications in Computer and Information Science (CCIS), iLRN 2023

study_characteristics.sample_description: 38 university students (19 per condition: VR and Desktop) recruited for course credit. Mean age 22.61 (SD = 2.57). 29 identified as female, 8 as male, 1 as neither. 36 spoke German as native language, 2 business fluent. Only 4 used VR weekly or daily; 30 had only experienced VR in studies or never at all. 12 played computer games weekly or daily; 11 had only experienced computer games in studies or never. All participants used computers daily or weekly. The game was designed for 7th grade secondary school students in Germany but the evaluation was conducted with university students due to COVID-19 pandemic restrictions.
study_characteristics.study_design: experimental
study_characteristics.game_name: Work, Trade, Learn (immersive serious game about medieval miller's apprentice life)
study_characteristics.aim: To investigate the benefits of using VR for serious games targeting the learning of history by developing a serious game for desktop-3D and VR, and comparing the two versions to determine whether the degree of immersion influences learning outcomes and topic interest

eligibility.concerns: The game was designed for 7th grade secondary school history education but the evaluation was conducted with university students due to COVID-19 pandemic constraints. The authors acknowledge this limits generalizability to the target audience. The study is a between-subjects experimental design comparing VR and Desktop conditions of the same serious game about medieval life (Middle Ages history curriculum). It is clearly about history education and involves a custom-developed serious game.

rq1.conceptualization: The study does not use the term 'gamification' explicitly. Instead, it is framed around 'serious games' and 'immersive learning.' Serious games are conceptualized as games that 'utilize the entertaining aspects of video games for educational purposes by turning learning content into the central game element.' The study draws on the concept that 'the mechanics of video games can be used to encode the knowledge of history lessons to create what is commonly known as a serious game.' The approach follows situated learning theory: by placing learners in a historically authentic virtual environment where they take on the role of a medieval miller's apprentice, they can 'directly experience situations of the past as well as interact and communicate with agents representing people of the respective era.' The paper also distinguishes between immersive VR and desktop-3D as different delivery modalities for serious games, with immersion defined following Slater and Wilbur as 'the extent to which the computer displays are capable of delivering an inclusive, extensive, surrounding and vivid illusion of reality to the senses of a human participant.' The game encodes learning content through game mechanics (knowledge encoding in game mechanics), where historical facts are embedded in interactive tasks and NPC dialogues rather than presented didactically.
theoretical_frameworks: Situated learning theory (Lave & Wenger, 1991) - knowledge is best learned in its natural context through authentic experiences
Constructivism (Bodner, 1986) - 'Knowledge is constructed in the mind of the learner'; learner's knowledge is constructed through their own experiences
Interest theory - differentiating individual interest, situational interest, and topic interest (Ainley et al., 2002; Hidi, 1990)
Immersion framework (Slater & Wilbur, 1997; Steuer, 1992) - immersion broken into vividness and interactivity components
Presence theory (Skarbez et al., 2017; Slater & Wilbur, 1997) - feeling of 'being there' in a virtual environment
Knowledge encoding in game mechanics (Oberdorfer & Latoschik, 2019) - learning content packaged in gameplay elements

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Knowledge test scores (10-item test, 2 questions per topic, administered pre-test/post-test and at 2-week follow-up); Topic interest questionnaire (adapted from Ferdinand, 2013, via Baumgartner, 2014); Situational interest questionnaire (post-game only, from same source). Pre-test had 5 questions (1 per topic), post-test had the remaining 5. Questions randomized per participant. Additional 2-week follow-up knowledge test administered online with 10 questions.
rq2.statistical_results: Knowledge test (pre vs. post): Shapiro-Wilk W = 0.96, p = 0.16 (normal); paired samples t-test: post-test M = 3.39, SD = 1.27 significantly higher than pre-test M = 1.66, SD = 1.08; t(37) = 6.113, p < 0.001. Knowledge gain comparison between conditions: Desktop M = 1.95, SD = 1.28 vs. VR M = 1.53, SD = 1.76; independent samples t-test t(36) = 0.82, p = 0.42 (not significant). Levene test F = 2.95, p = 0.09. Knowledge after 2 weeks vs. pre-test: Shapiro-Wilk W = 0.91, p < 0.01 (non-normal); Wilcoxon signed rank test: 2-week M = 3.00, SD = 1.11 significantly higher than pre-test M = 1.74, SD = 1.09; Z = 6.5, p < 0.001. Knowledge after 2 weeks vs. post-test: Shapiro-Wilk W = 0.93, p < 0.05 (non-normal); Wilcoxon signed rank test: 2-week M = 3.00, SD = 1.11 not significantly different from post-test M = 3.32, SD = 1.30; Z = 217, p = 0.13. 2-week knowledge gain between conditions: Desktop M = 1.32, SD = 0.98 vs. VR M = 1.2, SD = 0.98; Mann-Whitney U = 149.5, p = 0.81 (not significant). Topic interest (pre vs. post): Shapiro-Wilk W = 0.96, p = 0.23 (normal); paired t-test: post-test M = 20.8, SD = 5.54 significantly higher than pre-test M = 19.58, SD = 6.03; t(37) = 2.58, p < 0.05. Topic interest gain between conditions: Desktop M = 1.47, SD = 2.66 vs. VR M = 1.05, SD = 3.25; independent samples t-test t(36) = 0.43, p = 0.67 (not significant). Situational interest comparison: Desktop M = 31.58, SD = 5.30 vs. VR M = 29.11, SD = 5.60; independent samples t-test t(36) = -0.88, p = 0.38 (not significant).
rq2.comparative_methodology: Between-subjects experimental design with two conditions: VR (immersive VR with HTC Vive HMD) and Desktop-3D (standard PC with keyboard/mouse). 19 participants per condition, randomly assigned. Pre-test and post-test knowledge assessments, with additional 2-week follow-up (34 of 38 completed). Knowledge gains compared between conditions using independent samples t-tests, Mann-Whitney U tests, or Wilcoxon signed rank tests depending on normality. Statistical analysis performed using R in R-Studio.
rq2.key_outcomes: The serious game significantly increased participants' knowledge of history from pre-test to post-test (p < 0.001), with scores roughly doubling from M = 1.66 to M = 3.39 out of 5. Knowledge gains persisted at the 2-week follow-up (M = 3.00, significantly higher than pre-test, p < 0.001) and were not significantly different from immediate post-test scores (p = 0.13), suggesting lasting retention. Topic interest in history also significantly increased after playing (p < 0.05). However, there was no significant difference between VR and Desktop conditions on any measure: knowledge gain, 2-week retention, topic interest change, or situational interest. Hypotheses H1, H3, and H6 were supported (knowledge increase, topic interest increase, 2-week retention). Hypotheses H2, H4, H5, and H7 were rejected (no VR advantage over Desktop on any measure).
rq2.engagement_results: Situational interest did not differ significantly between conditions (Desktop M = 31.58, SD = 5.30 vs. VR M = 29.11, SD = 5.60; t(36) = -0.88, p = 0.38). Qualitative positive feedback: 10 participants liked the controls, 8 each liked the tasks, virtual environment, and character dialogues, and 4 liked the object highlighting system. Qualitative negative feedback: 11 participants wanted better graphics, 5 wanted more interactive elements, 4 wanted more content, and 3 criticized the controls.

game_design_elements: Role-playing (player takes the role of a medieval miller's apprentice)
Narrative-driven gameplay (short narrative of a day in the apprentice's life)
Object interaction (pick up, carry, and use objects like flour bags, bread loaves)
Task-based mechanics (operating the mill machinery, grinding grain into flour)
NPC dialogue system with branching choices (player approaches characters and selects dialogue options via speech bubbles)
Trading mechanics (trading flour for bread at the market)
Exploration of historically reconstructed environments (mill, market square, church area)
Knowledge encoding in game mechanics (historical facts embedded in tasks and dialogues)
Object highlighting (interactive objects highlighted in green to guide player)
Tutorial scene for learning interactions
Inventory system (bag at avatar's waist for carrying small objects)
Scene transitions (four scenes: mill morning, market, mill evening, tutorial)
technological_platforms: HTC Vive Head Mounted Display (VR condition)
Desktop PC with keyboard, mouse, and headphones (Desktop condition)
Unity Asset Store (free asset packs for 3D models and modular character agents)
instructional_strategies: Situated learning - placing the learner in the historical context of a medieval mill to experience daily life firsthand
Knowledge encoding in game mechanics - learning content (5 history topics) embedded in gameplay tasks and NPC dialogues rather than presented didactically
Social interaction with virtual agents - conversations with miller, baker, and priest characters who discuss historical topics
Authentic historical environment reconstruction - mill modeled after real Franconian Open-Air Museum in Bad Windsheim
Curriculum alignment - game content modeled after official German school curriculum for 7th grade history
Pre-service history teacher collaboration - questions designed with help from a pre-service history teacher
Voice-acted dialogue in end modern German - authentic but understandable language for historical immersion
Progressive narrative structure - player follows a structured day sequence (morning mill work, market visit, return to mill)

Multi-topic coverage within single narrative - five curriculum topics (life in medieval towns, work of a miller, religion and Protestantism, printing press, plague cures) woven into game through different mechanics (Table 1)
rq3.content_integration: Historical content was integrated into game mechanics through a systematic encoding approach where each of five curriculum topics was assigned to a specific gameplay mechanic. 'Life in medieval towns' was encoded through a dialogue with the baker at the market; 'Work of a miller' was encoded through the interactive task of operating the mill (grinding grain into flour using levers and machinery); 'Religion and Protestantism,' 'Printing press,' and 'Cures for the plague' were all encoded through dialogues with the priest character. The game follows a narrative arc: the player as a miller's apprentice learns to operate the mill (hands-on task), trades flour for bread at the market (trading mechanic with baker dialogue), and encounters a priest who discusses religion, the printing press, and plague cures (dialogue mechanic). The virtual mill was modeled after a real historical mill from the Franconian Open-Air Museum in Bad Windsheim, Germany. The 10 knowledge test questions (2 per topic) were co-designed with a pre-service history teacher to align with the learning goals embedded in the gameplay.

implementation_barriers: COVID-19 pandemic prevented evaluation with the target audience (7th grade secondary school students), requiring evaluation with university students instead
Low graphics quality was the most commonly criticized aspect (11 of 38 participants mentioned it)
Limited content scope - only 3.39 out of 5 questions answered correctly on average, partly because answers not clearly stated in dialogues were harder to learn
Hardware requirements for VR condition (HTC Vive HMD, controllers, tracking space) limit accessibility
Rare availability of HMDs at most schools limits practical classroom deployment of VR version
The developer was a computer science student, requiring collaboration with a pre-service history teacher for content accuracy
Room disinfection required between participants due to COVID-19 (15-minute airing out period)
methodology_limitations: Sample not representative of target population: university students (mean age 22.61) instead of 7th grade secondary school students; 'university students might have more previous knowledge about history'
Most students came from technology-centered courses, so 'the general attitude towards using technology for learning may also be different' from the target audience
Small sample size (N = 38, 19 per condition) limiting statistical power to detect between-group differences
Knowledge test had only 5 items per test occasion (pre-test 5, post-test 5), potentially limiting measurement sensitivity
Some questions were easier than others, and randomization across test forms may not fully control for item difficulty
No control group without any game intervention - cannot attribute knowledge gains solely to the game versus other factors
Only 34 of 38 participants completed the 2-week follow-up knowledge test
The study does not measure other potential benefits of VR such as 'general motivation or the players' emotions'

Questions whose answers were only implied in dialogues (rather than clearly stated) had the lowest correct answer rates, suggesting measurement may underestimate learning from dialogue-implied content
negative_effects: No significant advantage of immersive VR over desktop-3D on any learning outcome, suggesting VR hardware costs may not be justified for this specific application
Only 3.39 out of 5 post-test questions answered correctly on average, indicating incomplete learning of the targeted content

Questions where answers were only implied (rather than clearly stated) in NPC dialogue had lowest correct answer rates, suggesting dialogue-based knowledge encoding may not effectively convey implicit information
3 participants criticized the application controls regardless of condition
mitigation_strategies: Authors recommend replicating the study with actual 7th grade students in the future to validate findings for the target population
Important information in dialogues should be presented 'as clearly as possible' rather than only implied
Players should have the option to repeat important dialogues to reinforce learning
More interactivity should be added to dialogue mechanics, such as allowing players to choose conversation topics rather than having a predefined order
The Desktop-3D version can be safely deployed in schools without loss of learning effectiveness, avoiding VR hardware costs
Future versions should improve graphics quality based on participant feedback
Future versions should add more interactive elements and content based on participant feedback
The game could be used as an exhibit in a museum as well as in school lessons

domain1.q1_evidence: The paper describes selection criteria clearly: 'Participants were recruited from students who received course credit for participation. 38 people took part in the evaluation, with 19 participants per condition.' Demographic details are provided including age (M = 22.61, SD = 2.57), gender distribution (29 female, 8 male, 1 neither), language background (36 native German, 2 business fluent), VR experience, and computer game experience. Random assignment to conditions is stated: 'We randomly assigned the participants to one of the conditions.'
domain1.q2_evidence: The sample is explicitly not representative of the intended target population. The authors acknowledge: 'The main target audience for this game are 7th grade students in a German secondary school. Since an evaluation with school students was difficult to organize during the covid pandemic the study was instead conducted with university students. The results may therefore not be fully generalizable for the target audience, because university students might have more previous knowledge about history. Since most students came from technology centered courses of study the general attitude towards using technology for learning may also be different.' Additionally, 29 of 38 participants were female, and the sample was recruited from a single university (Goethe University Frankfurt / University of Wurzburg).

domain2.q3_evidence: The study used multiple established measurement instruments. Knowledge was assessed with a custom 10-item test 'designed with the learning goals of the application in mind' with questions co-designed by a pre-service history teacher (2 questions per covered topic). Topic interest was measured 'with a questionnaire from Ferdinand [11] in the version adapted by Baumgartner [5] for the topic of history.' Situational interest used a questionnaire 'from the same source.' All questionnaires were digitally administered via Limesurvey. Normality was checked with Shapiro-Wilk tests before selecting appropriate parametric or non-parametric tests. While the knowledge test was custom-designed (not externally validated), the interest measures are adapted from established instruments.
domain2.q4_evidence: Statistical analysis methods are clearly described and justified throughout. 'The results of this study were evaluated with R in R-Studio.' For each analysis: normality was first checked with Shapiro-Wilk tests; variance equality was checked with Levene tests; appropriate tests were selected based on these diagnostics (paired t-tests for within-subjects comparisons when normal, Wilcoxon signed rank tests when non-normal, independent samples t-tests or Mann-Whitney U tests for between-subjects comparisons). All test statistics, degrees of freedom, means, standard deviations, and exact p-values are reported. For example: 't(37) = 6.113, p < 0.001' for knowledge gain; 'Z = 6.5, p < 0.001' for 2-week retention.

domain3.q5_evidence: Interpretations are well-aligned with the statistical results. The authors correctly accept H1 (knowledge increase, p < 0.001), H3 (topic interest increase, p < 0.05), and H6 (2-week retention, p < 0.001), while honestly rejecting H2, H4, H5, and H7 (no VR advantage on any measure). They state: 'The remaining hypotheses (H2, H4, H5, H7) therefore have to be rejected. It can therefore be assumed that the level of immersion does not have any influence on these learning factors, at least in the context of this specific game.' They appropriately note this finding 'is not very surprising since learning is very challenging to measure with many factors influencing it and often did not show any significant differences in other studies comparing different kinds of media.' They do not overclaim and note potential unmeasured benefits: 'it cannot be guaranteed that there are no other learning benefits of the VR version that were not covered by this evaluation, like general motivation or the players' emotions.'
domain3.q6_evidence: Limitations are discussed in a dedicated section (7.3 Limitations). The authors acknowledge: the mismatch between target audience and actual participants ('The main target audience for this game are 7th grade students in a German secondary school. Since an evaluation with school students was difficult to organize during the covid pandemic the study was instead conducted with university students'); potential differences in prior knowledge ('university students might have more previous knowledge about history'); attitude differences ('the general attitude towards using technology for learning may also be different'); and the need for future replication ('the study should be replicated with 7th grade students in the future'). They also discuss design limitations such as dialogue clarity affecting learning outcomes.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The overall risk of bias is unclear, reflecting a mix of strengths and weaknesses. Domain 1 (selection) is rated High because the sample (university students) is explicitly acknowledged as non-representative of the target population (7th grade secondary school students), creating a fundamental validity concern. Domain 2 (data collection/analysis) is rated Low because the study uses established interest questionnaires, a curriculum-aligned knowledge test co-designed with a pre-service history teacher, appropriate statistical tests with normality diagnostics, and reports all results with full statistical detail. Domain 3 (interpretation) is rated Low because the authors interpret results conservatively, honestly reject unsupported hypotheses, discuss limitations thoroughly, and avoid overclaiming. The study design is methodologically sound (randomized between-subjects, pre/post with follow-up, appropriate statistics) but the participant mismatch is a substantial limitation that prevents confident generalization to the intended educational context.

pdf_filename: An Exploration of Computer Game-Based Instruction in the World History Class in Secondary Education: A Comparative Study in China.pdf

bibliographic.title: An Exploration of Computer Game-Based Instruction in the "World History" Class in Secondary Education: A Comparative Study in China
bibliographic.venue: PLOS ONE

study_characteristics.sample_description: 103 second-grade senior high school students (52 boys and 51 girls, aged 17-18, mean age 17.54, SD = 0.50) from two randomly selected classes (out of 13 classes) in a senior high school in Nanjing, capital of Jiangsu Province, China. Class A (CGBI) and Class B (NCGBI).
study_characteristics.study_design: quasi-experimental pretest/posttest comparative study with mixed methods (quantitative and qualitative)
study_characteristics.game_type: commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) real-time strategy computer game
study_characteristics.game_name: The Age of Empires: The Conquerors Expansion
study_characteristics.aim: To identify the effectiveness of computer game-based instruction (CGBI) by answering two research questions: (1) Will CGBI significantly stimulate motivation and improve learning achievement compared with non-computer game-based instruction (NCGBI)? (2) Will boys obtain significantly more learning achievement and be more motivated than girls in the CGBI class?

eligibility.concerns: The study uses a commercial strategy game (Age of Empires) rather than a purpose-built educational game, but the game was explicitly used for history education instruction with aligned learning materials and assessment. The game content is mapped to world history curriculum.

rq1.conceptualization: The study conceptualizes computer game-based instruction (CGBI) as using commercial computer games as the primary instructional medium in a classroom setting. CGBI is presented as a blended learning approach where students access history learning through game playing, with the game integrated into the formal curriculum. The authors reference Prensky's concept of 'Digital Game-Based Learning' (DGBL). Six design elements are adopted to govern learning with computer games: (a) rules, (b) definite goals, (c) catalysts activating participation, (d) levels of achieving goals, (e) control over participation, (f) unknown results, and (g) feedback in time.
theoretical_frameworks: Blended learning framework combining game play with traditional instruction
Motivational dimensions framework: overall appeal, availability of learning materials, educational value

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Pretest/posttest world history knowledge test (30 multiple-choice questions); posttest feedback questionnaire with 9 items on 5-point Likert scale measuring three motivational dimensions (overall appeal, availability of learning materials, educational value); open-ended qualitative questions on CGBI perceptions.
rq2.statistical_results: Hypothesis 1 (Learning achievement): Pretest means not significantly different (CGBI M=13.53 vs NCGBI M=13.21, t=0.51, p=.61). Posttest CGBI (M=18.22) significantly higher than NCGBI (M=16.92, t=2.01, p=.05). Hypothesis 2 (Motivation): Overall motivation CGBI (M=22.34) significantly higher than NCGBI (M=21.37, t=2.05, p=.04). Availability of learning materials dimension significantly higher in CGBI (M=7.71 vs M=6.83, p=.00). Overall appeal and educational value not significantly different. Hypothesis 3 (Gender achievement): No significant gender differences in learning achievement in either class (CGBI: female M=17.53, male M=18.98, t=-1.48, p=.14; NCGBI: female M=17.45, male M=16.68, t=1.01, p=.31). Hypothesis 4 (Gender motivation): Boys significantly more motivated by CGBI than girls in both Class A (male M=24.15, female M=20.79, t=5.32, p=.04) and Class B (male M=22.85, female M=19.98, t=3.48, p=.002).
rq2.comparative_methodology: Paired samples t-tests for comparing CGBI vs NCGBI on biographic data, pretest/posttest scores, and motivational dimensions. Independent samples t-tests for comparing gender differences in learning achievement and motivation within each class. SPSS used for quantitative analysis. Qualitative data from open-ended questions analyzed through summarizing and reasoning.
rq2.key_outcomes: CGBI produced significantly greater learning achievement than NCGBI. Participants were significantly more motivated by CGBI compared with NCGBI, particularly in the availability of learning materials dimension. No significant gender differences in learning achievement were found. Boys were significantly more motivated by CGBI than girls in both classes.
rq2.engagement_results: Qualitative data showed strong engagement: male students were familiar with the game, felt excited about using it for education, and valued its role in memorizing historical events. Female students, though less familiar with the game, expressed curiosity and interest when games were applied to education, and nearly universally agreed that games could make education less tedious and improve learning. Both genders eagerly longed for future learning via gaming.

game_design_elements: Six levels of difficulty (easiest, easy, moderate, difficult, more difficult, most difficult)
Multiple civilizations with unique economic and military technologies (Aztecs, Huns, Koreans, Mayans, Spanish, etc.)
Combat rules and military/economic units (Conquistadors, Eagle Warriors, Halberdiers, etc.)
Unique unit or team bonus for each civilization
Medieval fights and empire construction
Rules governing learning with computer games
Definite goals
Catalysts activating participation
Levels of achieving goals
Control over participation
Unknown results
Feedback in time
technological_platforms: PC/Computer (The Age of Empires: The Conquerors Expansion by Ensemble Studios Corp. for Microsoft Corporation)
instructional_strategies: Blended learning combining game play with history content
Formal training session (6 hours over 2 days) on how to play the game before the intervention
Same instructor taught both CGBI and NCGBI classes
Same teaching outline, learning objectives, materials, and contents for both groups
Preview before gaming and review after gaming
Assignments completed mainly during game play in class
Participants encouraged to play before and after classes for familiarization
Peer tutoring: good players helped unfamiliar participants
Game oriented to neutral rather than gender-specific content to minimize gender bias
Violence, indulgence, and pornography-oriented content minimized
Intervention duration: 2 hours per week for 16 weeks (one semester)
rq3.content_integration: The game content was directly aligned with the World History curriculum designed by the Ministry of Education of China. The 30-question knowledge test was based on learning materials contained in the game (e.g., unique military technology, historic events). Students needed to learn about military, agriculture, industry, economy, religion, and technologies of different nations through gameplay. The goal-reaching process in the game was described as 'no less than a world knowledge acquisition class.' All informational content in the test was contained in the game's learning materials.

implementation_barriers: Game initially set at 'difficult' level exceeded the restricted 2-hour weekly teaching period; had to be adjusted to 1-hour sessions
Some participants were unfamiliar with the game after training, leading to time-consuming operation
Same teacher taught both classes using different teaching styles, which may have caused confusion or mixing of approaches
Very few studies conducted on CGBI in China, making it a relatively unexplored context
Few female students had experience playing the game; they preferred small-scale games over large-scale ones with violence
Commercial game not specifically designed for educational purposes
methodology_limitations: Same teacher taught both CGBI and NCGBI classes, potentially mixing teaching styles and approaches
Questionnaires should have undergone further validation and reliability testing despite being designed by experienced instructors
Many other variables may influence results besides the game (previous gaming experience, student attitudes, actual enjoyment, motivation for participation, instructional quality)
Small sample from a single school limits generalizability
Only two classes compared, selected from 13 available
No long-term follow-up to assess retention of learning gains
negative_effects: Violence, attack, and thrillingness in the game were characteristics that female students found unappealing
Gender differences in motivation: boys significantly more motivated than girls by CGBI, suggesting potential inequity
Despite higher motivation, boys did not achieve significantly higher learning outcomes than girls, suggesting motivation from gaming may not directly translate to academic achievement
mitigation_strategies: Game difficulty was adjusted from 'difficult' to a lower level to fit the teaching period
Game content oriented to neutral rather than gender-specific to minimize gender bias
Violence, indulgence, and pornography-oriented content were minimized
Good players were encouraged to help unfamiliar participants as peer tutors
Participants were encouraged to practice the game before and after classes
Formal 6-hour training session provided before the intervention began

domain1.q1_evidence: The study clearly describes the selection criteria: two randomly selected classes from 13 classes in a senior high school in Nanjing, China. Participants were second-grade senior high school students learning world history. Inclusion was based on enrollment in these classes. The biographic data comparison (Table 2) confirmed no significant differences between groups on gaming frequency, liking, and experience.
domain1.q2_evidence: The sample is from a single senior high school in Nanjing, Jiangsu Province, China. Only 103 students from 2 classes out of 13 were included. The sample is limited to one geographic location and one school, which severely limits generalizability to other Chinese schools or other cultural contexts. No information on socioeconomic diversity or school characteristics provided.

domain2.q3_evidence: The world history knowledge test (30 multiple-choice questions) was designed by researchers and reviewed by experienced high school teachers. The posttest feedback questionnaire used 9 Likert-scale items measuring three motivational dimensions (overall appeal, availability of learning materials, educational value). However, the authors acknowledge that the questionnaires should have undergone further validation and reliability testing. No Cronbach's alpha or other reliability/validity measures are reported for any instrument.
domain2.q4_evidence: Paired samples t-tests and independent samples t-tests were used appropriately for the comparisons made. SPSS was used for analysis. Biographic data were compared to establish baseline equivalence. Both quantitative and qualitative methods were employed. Statistical significance level was set at .05. However, effect sizes were not reported.

domain3.q5_evidence: The findings are generally interpreted consistently with the data. However, the borderline significance of the posttest achievement comparison (p = .05 exactly) is presented as clearly significant without discussion of the marginal nature. The authors interpret the lack of gender differences in achievement alongside gender differences in motivation thoughtfully, proposing a 'dynamic balance' explanation. Some interpretations of qualitative data are somewhat subjective.
domain3.q6_evidence: The authors explicitly discuss several limitations: the same teacher teaching both classes with potentially mixed approaches, the need for further validation of questionnaires, and the influence of confounding variables (previous experience, attitudes, motivation, instructional quality). They also note the broader limitation of few CGBI studies in China.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study has notable risk of bias concerns. The sample is drawn from a single school with only two classes, limiting representativeness and generalizability. The measurement instruments (knowledge test and motivational questionnaire) lack reported validity and reliability data. The same teacher instructing both groups introduces potential contamination. The borderline statistical significance (p = .05 exactly) for the primary outcome is not discussed. No effect sizes are reported. While limitations are openly discussed and baseline equivalence was established, the combination of unvalidated instruments and limited sampling leads to an overall high risk of bias assessment.

pdf_filename: Your iPhone Cannot Escape History, and Neither Can You Self-Reflexive Design for a Mobile History Learning Game.pdf

bibliographic.title: Your iPhone Cannot Escape History, and Neither Can You: Self-Reflexive Design for a Mobile History Learning Game
bibliographic.venue: Mobile Learning: Perspectives on Practice and Policy

study_characteristics.sample_description: Forty-three fifth- to seventh-grade learners (24 girls, 21 boys) from Jewish supplementary schools (after-school programs) who participated in gameplay over the course of six game events and three design iterations.
study_characteristics.study_design: design_based
study_characteristics.aim: To explore the use of self-reflexivity in mobile history games through the case study of Jewish Time Jump: New York, specifically examining how self-reflexive design techniques can be deployed in a mobile augmented reality game to tie history to contemporary concerns and implicate the learner in enduring historical themes of labor disputes

eligibility.concerns: This is a design-based research study that focuses primarily on the design rationale and iterative development of a self-reflexive game design element rather than reporting formal quantitative learning outcomes. The chapter presents qualitative observations and design iterations rather than controlled experimental results. It is a primary empirical study (part of the author's doctoral dissertation design-based research), it is clearly about history education (Jewish history, labor history, women's history related to the Uprising of 20,000 and Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire), and it involves a mobile augmented reality game (game-based learning).

rq1.conceptualization: The study does not use the term 'gamification' explicitly. Instead, it frames the intervention as a 'mobile augmented reality game (ARG)' and 'mobile history learning game' built on the ARIS platform. The approach is conceptualized through the lens of self-reflexive design, drawing from Brechtian Verfremdungseffekt (alienation effect) traditions in theater, cinema, and video games. The core design concept is self-reflexivity: using the mobile device itself (the iOS device) as a means of implicating the learner in the historical themes being studied. The game is conceived as both a learning intervention and a design-based research project. The author describes game design as a vehicle for civic and democratic education, where the game serves as a situated documentary that connects historical enduring themes (labor disputes, women's suffrage) to the present through the materiality of the mobile device itself.
theoretical_frameworks: Design-based research (Barab & Squire, 2004; The Design-Based Research Collective, 2003; Hoadley, 2004)
History education theory - enduring themes and democratic citizenship (Barton & Levstik, 2004/2012)
Civic and democratic education theory - three models of citizenship: personally responsible, participatory, justice-oriented (Westheimer & Kahne, 2004)
Brechtian Verfremdungseffekt / alienation effect - self-reflexive design drawing from theater traditions (Brecht via Polan, 1974)
Mobile affordances for place-based learning (Klopfer & Squire, 2004, 2008)
Levstik and Barton's 'start locally, connect globally' and 'start globally, connect locally' strategies (2005/2010)

rq2.comparative_methodology: Design-based research with iterative design cycles. Data collection included pre- and post-survey data, interviews, video and audio observation of players, and ARIS back-end server logs tracking each player's moves. Three design iterations were conducted across six game events, with analysis between iterations informing design modifications. No formal statistical comparisons are reported in this chapter; the author notes that full data sets and detailed description of the full study are published elsewhere (Gottlieb, 2015).
rq2.key_outcomes: The study reports qualitative outcomes across three design iterations of the self-reflexive element: (1) In the pilot iteration, only a few students completed the game and did not receive the Foxconn news story (the self-reflexive reveal). (2) In the first iteration, after adding an Afikoman (hidden bonus containing the contemporary articles), some students picked up the tip but did not read the article about Foxconn, jumping ahead to complete the game. One girl's short answer revealed lack of connection to enduring historical themes despite exposure. (3) In the final iteration, using a 'suprareveal' strategy (presenting a Bangladesh factory collapse article at the start of the game rather than only at the end), discussions of the factory collapse began immediately. There was 'no evidence in either postgame interviews or open-ended answers on postgame surveys of lack of awareness of the contemporary global issues of worker safety.' The suprareveal approach was found to offset 'issues of lack of attention to contemporary cases as well as provide a conscious frame for the game to come.'
rq2.engagement_results: Qualitative engagement observations: In the final iteration with the suprareveal, learners read the Bangladesh article out loud prior to the game and asked questions about the article, demonstrating evidence of awareness of the historic theme. Players asked questions like 'What does this article have to do with Jewish history?' and 'What is the date on the article?' indicating active engagement with the contemporary content. There was a shift from evidence of lack of awareness regarding contemporary labor struggles to an iteration 'devoid of disconfirming cases of awareness.' The Foxconn and Bangladesh articles, when used together, generated discussion of contemporary labor disputes in the context of historic labor disputes and eliminated confusion and erroneous conclusions about contemporary labor disputes.

game_design_elements: Role-playing (players take on the role of time-traveling reporters for the fictional Jewish Time Jump Gazette)
Narrative / storytelling (players retrieve a story 'lost to time' involving the Uprising of 20,000 and Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire)
Time travel mechanic (players travel from 1909 to 1911 and then return to the present day)
GPS-based location triggers (photographs and content delivered based on player GPS location)
Digital inventory system (players pick up newspapers, pamphlets, ephemera, and primary source documents)
Character interaction (players interact with dozens of digital characters: striking workers, factory owners, labor organizers, journalists, Tammany Hall police, thugs for hire)
Self-reflexive reveal / fourth wall break (the iOS device itself is revealed as nexus of contemporary labor disputes via Foxconn article)
Afikoman / Easter egg mechanic (hidden bonus containing contemporary videos and news article, designed to ensure all players encounter the self-reflexive reveal)
Suprareveal (presenting a global framing article about Bangladesh factory collapse at the beginning of the game)
Place-based / on-site gameplay (played on-site in Washington Square Park, Greenwich Village, New York)
Primary source documents integration (translated Yiddish newspapers, historical photographs, ephemera)
Multiple narrative perspectives (characters represent different viewpoints in labor disputes)
technological_platforms: ARIS platform (open-source mobile game authoring platform for iOS)
Video content delivery (contemporary videos of investment banker and rabbi embedded in game)
instructional_strategies: Design-based research methodology with iterative cycles of prototyping, field trial, data gathering, analysis, and redesign
Self-reflexive design - implicating the learner in the historical theme through the materiality of the mobile device itself
Place-based learning - on-site gameplay at historical locations in Greenwich Village, New York
Enduring themes approach - connecting historical labor disputes (1909-1911) to contemporary labor issues (Foxconn, Bangladesh factory collapse)
Civic and democratic education goals - designing for participatory and justice-oriented citizenship
Suprareveal strategy - 'start globally, connect locally' approach to frame the game with a contemporary article before gameplay begins
Post-game debriefing and interview/discussion sessions
Modular curriculum development (four modules developed with Jewish Women's Archive for deployment in various educational settings)
Pre- and post-survey assessment
Multiple entry points for self-reflexive content (end-game reveal, Afikoman bonus, suprareveal at start)
rq3.content_integration: Historical content about the 1909 Uprising of 20,000 (the largest women-led strike in U.S. history) and the 1911 Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire (in which 146 people died) was integrated through a time-travel narrative where players assume the role of reporters investigating 'lost' stories. Players physically travel to Washington Square Park in Greenwich Village, New York, where these events took place. They interact with dozens of digital characters representing historical figures (striking workers, factory owners, labor organizers, journalists, Tammany Hall police). Historical primary sources (Yiddish newspapers, pamphlets, photographs) are delivered to players' digital inventories based on GPS location. The self-reflexive design element ties the historical content directly to the present by revealing that the iOS device players are using is itself the nexus of contemporary labor disputes (Foxconn factory conditions in China). The design evolved through three iterations: (1) placing the reveal at the game's end, (2) adding an Afikoman hidden bonus to ensure encounter, and (3) adding a suprareveal with a Bangladesh factory collapse article at the game's start to frame the enduring theme of labor disputes before gameplay.
